title: The moment I knew: I admitted I had a crush on her. She replied, ‘Well, that’s good. Isn’t it?’ | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: Actors Peter Houghton and Anne Browning played lovers onstage, but a shared sense of humour and a magazine horoscope flipped the script on their real-life relationship
Author: James Norman
Headline: Actors Peter Houghton and Anne Browning played lovers onstage, but a shared sense of humour and a magazine horoscope flipped the script on their real-life relationship
Content: ‘I liked that when she’d come to my place, living in such a bohemian setting made me look a bit more impressive and artistic than I was’: Peter Houghton and Anne Browning in 1998View image in fullscreen‘I liked that when she’d come to my place, living in such a bohemian setting made me look a bit more impressive and artistic than I was’: Peter Houghton and Anne Browning in 1998The moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: I admitted I had a crush on her. She replied, ‘Well, that’s good. Isn’t it?’ActorsPeter Houghtonand Anne Browning played lovers onstage, but a shared sense of humour and a magazine horoscope flipped the script on their real-life relationshipFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesPeter Houghton, as told toJames NormanSat 24 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 17.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnne and I met in Melbourne in 1997 when we were cast in a production of Hamlet. We were both single and playing onstage lovers. The first time I saw her in the Melbourne Theatre Company cafeteria, she had a sleepy, grumpy face. I still recall those intense, slightly scary green eyes looking at me. I thought to myself: she is very attractive, but also quite formidable.At first it was a little awkward, but humour was the key. We’d sit on the dusty rehearsal room floor in our tracksuits while the director was working with another actor. Instead of practising our lines, we’d flip through the faded 70s magazines left in the corner and make jokes about what the models in flares or with chopped beards might be saying as they shot the images.The moment I knew: I burst into the living room with his letter held high and screeched, ‘I’m getting married!’Read moreOne day by chance I flipped to the horoscopes. I asked Anne what the stars could have in store for us in 1972. She told me her sign was Scorpio – the same as mine. My aim was just to laugh at the bullshit of horoscopes but when I read it out, it stopped me cold: “You have met someone now through work who will be one of the most important people in your life, perhaps a partner and soulmate.”It was weird and uncanny but we just laughed it off. I felt embarrassed because it sounded like some kind of calculated romantic ploy. I quickly flicked to the next page but somewhere in my brain I knew it was the truth.Later, when the show was well under way, we were walking along St Kilda Road after a performance. We stopped at the lights and I summoned the courage to say: “I think I’ve got one of those crushes on you.” She looked at me and said: “Well, that’s good. Isn’t it?”I took her cryptic and understated response as confirmation she felt the same way. It is very much her style – and I liked that it had a question mark on the end of it.View image in fullscreen‘There’s a levity and lightness Anne brings’: Peter and Anne with their childrenAfter the show closed our connection grew and we officially became a couple, filling our days and nights with dinner and theatre dates. She was living with her sister and I was living in this big groovy warehouse in Richmond with other actors. I liked that when she’d come to my place, the bohemian setting made me look a bit more impressive and artistic than I was.The moment I knew: I’d lost his number and was about to switch off my old phone for good – then a text pingedRead moreEarly on, we went on a hiking trip toWilsons Prom. We were massively overpacked and it quickly emerged that neither of us was good at camping. As soon as we got back to the car we made a beeline to KFC and gorged ourselves on fried chicken after days of miserable camping stodge, secretly thankful we weren’t in nature any more.Anne was violently ill all the way back – all that rich food after rehydrated dust!We both exposed ourselves as kind of daggy on that trip, and that was OK.Anne and I share a clown-like heart that over the decades has helped us through hard times. Big life events like losing a parent have been somewhat easier because there’s a levity and lightness Anne brings – never letting me go into the dark places or stay there for too long.View image in fullscreen‘Romantic love has its seasons, but really loving someone also has to do with trust’: Peter and Anne with their children in 2020.Photograph: Krystyna HessovaSince meeting in that rehearsal room we’ve spent almost 30 years together, had two children and performed all over the world. Romantic love has its seasons, but really loving someone also has to do with trust. I trust her implicitly, she trusts me, and we don’t let each other down. We always show up for each other when it matters. We help each other realise our own dreams. That’s the thing about having a teammate you can rely on – it’s priceless.We met working with each other as theatre artists, which we’re still doing now after all these years. A magazine from the 70s with an out-of-date horoscope written by a charlatan brought us together. I don’t believe in horoscopes … but I do believe in that one.Peter Houghton, Anne Browning and Tom Gutteridge perform in the world premiere ofCrapbox, showing from 27 October to 7 November at the Explosives Factory in St Kilda, Melbourne.Tell us the moment you knewShare your experienceShare your love storyDo you have a romantic realisation you'd like to share? title: ‘Our third date was at Buckingham Palace’: Marlon James and Nicholas Boggs on life as a literary power couple | Books | The Guardian
description: Shortlisted for the Booker and Baillie Gifford prizes respectively, the novelist and biographer talk about working and living together – and giving a voice to Black queer history
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Shortlisted for the Booker and Baillie Gifford prizes respectively, the novelist and biographer talk about working and living together – and giving a voice to Black queer history
Content: Marlon James, left, and Nicholas Boggs.Photograph: Maria Spann/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMarlon James, left, and Nicholas Boggs.Photograph: Maria Spann/The GuardianBooksInterview‘Our third date was at Buckingham Palace’: Marlon James and Nicholas Boggs on life as a literary power coupleEmma LoffhagenShortlisted for the Booker and Baillie Gifford prizes respectively, the novelist and biographer talk about working and living together – and giving a voice to Black queer historySat 24 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 14.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe literary power couple is a historically seductive concept. Two writers sharing a life, their private and creative worlds entwined, each becoming witness to and critic of the other’s work. Think Simone de Beauvoir and Jean-Paul Sartre, Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne. Or, less auspiciously, Sylvia Plath and Ted Hughes.Now, into this illustrious company steps a new pair: the novelist Marlon James and the biographer Nicholas Boggs, whose books have each been shortlisted for one of Britain’s most prestigious literary awards – James for the Booker prize and Boggs for theBaillie Gifford prize for nonfiction. Between them, they have produced two formidable books, each the culmination of years of work, and each concerned with the lives of Black queer men whose stories have often been overlooked.“I’m not sure what to do with it,” James says, when I ask how they feel about the inevitable impending “literary power couple” label. “I have all these romantic notions that we were like Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne or something – I don’t know. What do you think?” He turns to Boggs, who laughs. “It’s all very new,” he says. “We’re still getting used to it.”It is a warm October morning in Williamsburg, the fashionable writerly enclave in Brooklyn, and I am sitting across from the pair at their apartment. They are relaxing on a chaise longue, looking comfortable enough to have been there all morning. Their exchanges have the easy rhythm of a long relationship, full of small corrections and private jokes.James, the 55-year-old Jamaican-born novelist whose 2015 bookA Brief History of Seven Killingswon the Booker prize, is back on the shortlist this year withThe Disappearers, a sprawling, dark reckoning with the brutality of Aids-era gay life and homophobia in Jamaica. Boggs, his 53-year-old partner of nearly nine years, has been shortlisted for the Baillie Gifford prize for his first book,Baldwin: A Love Story, a biography of James Baldwin that draws on two decades of research into the writer’s intimate life and creative relationships.“The Baillie Gifford’s a prize I know well,” James says. “So when Nick was on the shortlist, I knew what a big deal it was.” Boggs remembers James’s reaction when the nonfiction shortlist was announced on 1 October. “His eyes got very wide. I don’t think I’ve seen his eyes get quite that wide before.”James had the first taste of the excitement, when the Booker shortlist was announced in September. “You got shortlisted first, so the pressure was on!” Boggs jokes. “No matter how many times you do this, it’s always a great surprise,” James adds.View image in fullscreenBoggs and James at home in Brooklyn, New York.Photograph: Maria Spann/The GuardianThe pair have been together since 2018 and have lived in this apartment for a little under a year. Its walls form something of a shrine to their work and interests, crowded with art by African American and queer artists, from intimate, often erotic photography to paintings. At one point they rummage beneath the bed to retrieve an original 1938 painting by Beauford Delaney, the Harlem renaissance artist who became one of Baldwin’s mentors, and features heavily in Boggs’s book. A monumental horse sculpture dominates the room – or, as Boggs points out with a laugh, “it’s really just the horse’s ass, isn’t it!” Bought by James after his 2015 Booker win and christened “Booker” by Boggs, it stands alongside a similarly imposing gorilla.Their romance began not in a rarefied literary salon, but through the very ordinary business of a dating app. “I was on the apps and was like, well, I’m only dating in my neighbourhood,” Boggs says. “He was three blocks away, so it was perfect.”double quotation markMarlon has an incredible work ethic – we’re not screaming from the other room or complaining at dinnerBy then, they were both in their 40s. Boggs, who had never been out with a writer before – “it was mostly bartenders”, he jokes – knew of James’s work, but hadn’t read any of his books. James, for his part, didn’t know Boggs was a writer prior to their first meeting.“It was a very chaste first date,” James says, with a twinkle in his eye. “We were gentlemen.” The relationship developed “healthily slowly” over a summer spent apart while Boggs was teaching in London, until they reunited when James invited Boggs to a Booker anniversary event in the capital. He was keen to set the bar high.“Our third date was at Buckingham Palace,” James says, with a faux shrug. “I try to keep it classy, you know, gotta impress him. We actually made out in the queen’s bathroom.”Their relationship may have brought them into the same orbit, but the worlds they each came from – and the experiences that inform their writing – are markedly different.Growing up in Washington DC, where his father was a civil rights attorney, Boggs read Baldwin from a young age. While studying the writer at college, he came across a reference in a 1994 biography to an out-of-print children’s book by Baldwin, illustrated by a French artist, Yoran Cazac. Boggs had suspicions that there was a love affair behind the collaboration, tried to track down Cazac, but was told he was most likely dead. A few weeks later, the phone rang.“It was Yoran saying, ‘I’m alive, I’m in Paris, come on over, I have many stories to tell you about Jimmy,’” Boggs recalls. “That was 23 years ago, and it began a realisation that there were these untold stories in Baldwin’s life that needed to be unearthed.”For James, rampant homophobia shaped his upbringing and his storytelling. Growing up gay and closeted in 1980s Kingston, in the classroom he was “the school homo”; at church, he tried to become straight. He only began to build a more comfortable queer identity after moving to Minneapolis to teach in 2007, away from the scrutiny of family and friends in Jamaica. Unlike Boggs, his queer literary education came late. He picked up Baldwin’s Giovanni’s Room for the first time when he was 50. “The first thing I thought was I could never have read this at 20,” he says. “I was so in the closet.”Across his fiction, James has repeatedly excavated Jamaica’s histories of violence and political upheaval, from his debut 2005 novel John Crow’s Devil (famously rejected 78 times by publishers), to the gang warfare and state corruption of A Brief History of Seven Killings, which made him the first Jamaican to win theBooker prize. The Disappearers, his sixth novel, grew out of a rumoured homophobic attack in a middle-class area of Kingston in the late 1980s.“I first heard about it when I was 21,” he says. “I knew it happened, I just couldn’t prove it. It haunted me: the idea that that could happen – and in a posh neighbourhood – was one of the things that certainly pushed me firmly into the closet.”He was unable to establish exactly what had happened until he began researching the novel, interviewing almost 20 people in Jamaica who helped him piece together the incident over several years. “I wanted to fill in the blanks,” he says. “I wanted to give those guys back some sort of agency and power.”In different ways, both men are trying to recover Black queer histories that have been marginalised or lost. “We both respond to gaps,” Boggs says.For James, one such gap became the starting point for The Disappearers. He wanted to build his novel around the production of a play, but couldn’t find one that would fit. The solution came, serendipitously, from Boggs: while researching his biography, he discovered Baldwin directed a 1969 production of John Herbert’s Fortune and Men’s Eyes in Turkey. He suggested James consider it for his novel.“At first you were like, ‘no’,” Boggs recalls. “And I was like, ‘just read these 60 pages’. And I was right.”It is no exaggeration to say that the play serves as the novel’s structural and emotional scaffolding, and is central to Boggs’s chapters on Baldwin’s life in Turkey, too. “I like to say I plundered his book with his permission,” James says, smiling. “It’s one way in which our books wouldn’t be possible or wouldn’t have ended up the way they did were we not together.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenOn a table in the couple’s living room there sits a 25 September edition of the New York Times. It contains a review now infamous in the literary world, in which the notoriously harsh critic Dwight Garner devoted an almostnovella-length appraisalto The Disappearers, hailing it as “a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century”, placing it alongside the work of Salman Rushdie, Toni Morrison and William Faulkner.“I still don’t quite believe it,” James says. The morning the piece came out, an author friend had emailed to alert him to what he described as a “stonking review” from Garner. “I didn’t know what stonking meant, I thought it was something bad!” he laughs. “So I’m like, ‘God, no. I’m not going to read this.’” But he clicked the link anyway, and saw the word “masterpiece”.“I went to the newsstand to go find it, because I still didn’t believe it,” he says. “I was like, ‘if I leave this bed, I’m going to wake up.’”He is wary of the idea that acclaim should ever become an expectation, or success a fait accompli. “There’s a part of me that still thinks I’m this underground, scrapping writer who got lucky,” he says. “For me, it’s still a genuine surprise. It still catches me off guard. I don’t know if I want to get to that point where I start to expect good reviews. I don’t know if I want that level of entitlement.” He laughs. “I know some writers who are like that – I’m not going to name any names,” he adds, with a mischievous look.Joan Didion once described her collaboration with John Gregory Dunne as a process of creative osmosis: “One of us writes the first draft, and the other functions as really kind of a super-editor and writes the second draft. In the end, you can’t really tell who has done what.”View image in fullscreenJames receives the Man Booker prize for fiction in 2015.Photograph: Neil Hall/ReutersThere is no such blurring of authorship in the James-Boggs household. The pair keep their manuscripts to themselves until the work is finished, even as they discuss the ideas and research behind it.“People are always surprised to hear that,” Boggs says. “Marlon didn’t read my book until after it was finished, I finished his on the publication date.”Their working habits are almost opposite, too. Boggs describes himself as a binge writer, while James writes every day and keeps regular hours. James needs music – “lots of free jazz” – while Boggs requires “perfect peace and quiet”. They work on opposite sides of the house, and Boggs also has a separate office a few blocks away. But living with James has helped Boggs reconsider his idea of what writing should feel like.“Marlon has an incredible work ethic, and it was really a reminder that this is a job,” he says. “That was really helpful. It’s not screaming from the other room in frustration, or complaining about it at dinner every night.”They insist there is no competition between them. “I think I really worried about that when we first met,” Boggs says. “But we write so differently, even stylistically. And because of the time that we’re living in, getting these stories told is so much more important than any individual anyway.”Just this month, new research from PEN America found that the US saw almost 12,000 book bans in public schools during the 2025-2026 school year, the highest number in a single year. For James and Boggs, whose work is concerned with recovering the lives and histories that have been overlooked or suppressed, the stakes are difficult to ignore.James refuses to censor himself in anticipation of a backlash, but he is not oblivious to the risks. “I do sometimes get this fear that the oppressors are coming, because they always burn the books first,” he says. “The forces stacked against me are immense. But then, when have the forces against us not been immense?”I ask if they have thought about leaving the US altogether. “Yes, 100%,” James says, without skipping a beat. He is uncompromising in his diagnosis of the country’s downward slide. “For me, it’s weird seeing America become the type of country America has spent the past 60 years creating everywhere else. I think we’re becoming a banana republic, which, coming from the Caribbean, I know a lot about.”He is not, however, a pessimist. “I have to have a pretty big sense of optimism to think that my big-ass books are going to sell,” he says. “Throughout all of this, I’ve never lost faith in the reader. Writing has always been an art form that had to struggle against oppression, that speaks truth to power. If you decide to be a writer, part of it is to say that you’re going to take this on.”For all their independence on the page, Boggs and James are now embarking on a creative collaboration. Baldwin: A Love Story has been optioned for film by Anonymous Content. Higher Ground (Barack and Michelle Obama’s production company) will be co-producing. Boggs knew immediately with whom he wanted to write the screenplay: James, who has experience writing for the screen, including the television series Get Millie Black. Anonymous Content hired them to write the screenplay together.So far, the process has been seamless. “I think even we are surprised how smooth it’s going,” Boggs says, laughing. “But we’re just so interested in each other’s work and interested in how one another thinks.”I ask how it feels to be adding to the queer literary canon, in their shared and solo endeavours. They look at each other for a moment before Boggs responds. “Just to be alive is wonderful,” he says. “Something that Marlon and I both share is that when you grow up in the shadow of Aids, you don’t necessarily think that you have a future.”“We lost so many great artists, gay artists,” Boggs adds. “So there’s a certain kind of responsibility to telling those stories. There are so many that still need to be told.”Explore more on these topicsBooksMarlon JamesFictionBooker prizeBaillie Gifford prize for nonfictionBiography booksAwards and prizesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: The AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting back
Author: Tom Wall
Headline: The AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting back
Content: A house in the shadow of a datacentre in Newport, south Wales. All photographs: Joel Redman/The GuardianThe AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting backByTom Wall. Photographs: Joel RedmanSat 24 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDale Johnston opens the gate to his neat suburban garden on the western fringes of Newport in SouthWales. There’s a trampoline and a slide on the lawn for his grandchildren, and chairs for him and his wife. He should be enjoying the light draining from the perfect autumnal sky – but almost his entire view is blotted out by a vast expanse of prefabricated panels.The 23 metre-high grey hulk looming over him and his neighbours is a hyperscale datacentre. It is heralded by the area’s Labourpoliticiansas a job creator, yet all Johnston can think about is what he has lost: “Before, the sun used to come around here and it was lovely.” The way residents have been treated is “disgusting”.Johnston, who used to work for a chemical company in the city, worries what their lives will be like when the centre is switched on: the 36 sets of air blast coolers, needed to stop the chips inside overheating, most likely generate a constant drone, while regular testing of 60 back-up diesel generators, to prevent costly interruption to the flow of data, could produce harmful fumes. He already has to keep his bathroom window closed to stop the low hum from another facility on the rapidly expanding 46-acre datacentre campus that borders the small enclave of 27 houses. His wife, a nurse who works night shifts, can barely sleep already. He shakes his head in despair: “We just don’t know what’s going to happen.”View image in fullscreen‘The MPs backing the development won’t come round here to see what they’ve done’: Dale Johnston in his gardenJohnston can talk about little else, but he feels no one in authority is listening. He’s invited councillors and MPs backing the development to visit his garden. But “they won’t come around here to see what they’ve done”.This is the frontline of Britain’s datacentre boom, which is pitting residents against giant US tech firms seeking to build a network of facilities capable of providing the immense computing muscle for powerful AI models. There are315 hyperscale datacentreswaiting to connect to the national grid, which carries electricity from power plants to homes and businesses (hyperscale typically means facilities with at least 5,000 servers and 10,000 sq ft in size). Combined, these new centres will require 73GW of power, 28GW higher than the typical peak energy demand of 45GW on a cold winter’s day.Wales is one of the main development hotspots outside London. It already has the largest datacentre capacity beyond the capital, with new hyperscale facilities planned for former industrial and urban sites. The Keir Starmer-led Labour government viewed this as aninevitable revolution, which the country must embrace or be left behind. It establishedfive AI growth zonesto push more datacentres through the planning system and speed up connections to the national grid. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has signalled little will change,turning down calls for a moratoriumand insisting datacentres bring economic benefits. But anti-datacentre groups springing up in villages, towns and cities across the country see it rather differently: as the imposition of a resource-hungry, polluting industry that increases profits for often US big tech, with little tangible benefit to local people or the country as a whole.Digital storage is nothing new. The first home PC users saved files on floppy discs and hard drives; businesses used their own server rooms in the 80s and 90s, then moved to off-site facilities as their needs grew. But the development of cloud computing services in the 2010s, such as Google Drive, and AI chatbots in the 2020s, like ChatGPT, led to even greater information and processing demands, which the tech industry insists can only be met by larger and larger datacentres. This has driven huge speculative bets on hyperscale hubs, which investors and tech firms hope will one day reap the rewards of an AI-led transformation of the economy. Globally, it isestimatedspending on new facilities could reach $7tn by 2030 –morethan double the cost of the New Deal, the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe after the second world war and the Apollo space programme combined, even allowing for inflation.The US is at the forefront of the boom, already hosting roughlyhalfof the world’s hyperscale capacity. But the industry is facing afuriousbacklash, with three- quarters of Americans now opposed to datacentre development and blaming it forincreasingenergy bills,threateningwater supplies in drought-hit areas andspewingout toxic fumes. More than 500 counties and municipalities have passed permanent or temporarydatacentre bans.‘This is not an anti-tech town’: backlash to datacenter in city once home to IBMRead moreLoudoun County in northern Virginia sits in what is known as Data Center Alley because it ishometo more facilities than anywhere else in the world. Greg Pirio’s life was turned upside down when a gas-powered datacentre opened 150 metres from his home last year. “This neighbourhood was calm and peaceful, and it’s turned into this nightmare,” he says on a video call. “Our quality of life has been degraded so much.”The noise from the centre’s eight gas turbines is “like being at an airport with all these engines roaring,” Pirio says. “It has given many of my neighbours headaches. It has kept children up at night.” Pirio, who used to work for the Voice of America radio station, has also developed health problems since it opened, including dry eyes and chest tightness. Once he had to leave his house because he was struggling to breathe: “I know whenever the diesel generators are on, because I feel it in my lungs.”View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the datacentre in Newport …View image in fullscreen… and the outside of the buildingThe UK has not yet seen the same level of opposition as the US. But anti-datacentre groups are gathering momentum. Residents in east London are waging a high-profile campaign against a new datacentre on Brick Lane, including protesting outside the offices of Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, whooverturned a council decisionblocking the scheme.Seasoned campaigner Owen Espley, who works for environmental charity Global Action Plan, is helping scores of residents’ groups organise against planned datacentres. “This summer has been wild. Every other week a new group has popped up. Petitions are getting thousands of signatures in days,” he says. “Communities are in uproar, and most politicians are playing catch-up.”Espley has been taken aback by the gulf between the government’s conviction that there is no alternative and ordinary people’s deepening understanding of the complex issues at stake. “There has been a real grassroots questioning of datacentres that connects British Bangladeshis in Brick Lane with Hertfordshire villagers and communities in Northumberland, who want good jobs to come back,” he says. “It is astounding.”In fact, there are many alternative pathways to market-­led expansion – from tougher regulation to prioritising publicly-owned data infrastructure – which serve communal goals, such as theheart diseaseanddementiaresearch powered by Bristol University’s new Isambard-AIfacility. “First, we need strong standards for private datacentres,” Espley says. “Second, we need industrial strategy to deliver our own public computer, rather than an assumption that US big tech building and owning everything is the only way forward.”On the deprived eastern edges of Cardiff, the early morning sunshine is warming a car park dotted with scraggly weeds. The perimeter fence is overgrown with brambles, with patches of singed, blackened grass from a recent wildfire visible just beyond. It looks abandoned but soon cars carrying doctors, nurses and other NHS staff start arriving. They are here to catch free buses to Cardiff’s Heath hospital, the largest in Wales.Hundreds are said to use the park and ride every day, but it is under threat because Labour-controlled Cardiff council wants to sell the land to a property developer, Curtis Hall, to build a hyperscale data facility. The centre will use up to 150 megawatts (MW) of electricity a year, more than triple the demand of a city the size of Cardiff.The development is one of the most controversial in Wales. Council meetings have been disrupted and more than 1,200 planning objections lodged. Last month, the new Plaid Cymru-led government ordered the council to put the application on hold while it considered whether to take the decision out of councillors’ hands.Campaigners are determined to keep up the pressure on the Welsh government. Sue Elias, a retired librarian with seemingly endless reserves of energy, dashes back and forth reattaching her “Ditch the datacentre” banner to the car park fence and taping leaflets to the bus stop glass. “What is going to happen to all the people who use the park and ride? It’s bonkers,” she says.View image in fullscreenSue Elias rallying opposition to the building of a datacentre on the local park and ride …View image in fullscreen… which Abi George, a midwife, uses it every day to get to workElias has leafleted the park and ride every Wednesday morning for six weeks. Today she is collecting signatures for an open letter to prove it is well used – so far she has added the names of 1,300 staff and patients. “I’ve not done anything like this before but I’m told I’m a natural,” she says with a mischievous smile, before breaking off to speak to staff arriving for the next bus.She belongs to community-based union Acorn, which has campaigned against the scheme, and has taken part inprotests, including bursting into a council planning meeting in July. “We’d sent emails, done petitions, but we’d had nothing back – tumbleweed. They’re our elected representatives … They should be talking with us.”It is hard to find anyone in support of the plan in the queue for the bus, which runs three times an hour. “I use it every day. Without it, I probably wouldn’t continue working at the hospital,” says Ami George, a midwife. “Parking there causes that much stress.”Across Cardiff’s Rhymney River, which curves around the proposed datacentre development, the area’s newest residents have only recently moved into 100 homesbuiltunder the city council’s flagship house-building programme. Nick Richards, a freelance filmmaker and skateboarder, and his wife arrived in November. “It felt like the stars had aligned because there is a brand new skate park up the road … the best in Cardiff. It’s amazing,” he says. “I never pictured myself living in suburbia but when we came we saw kids playing outside and thought, this is a really nice area.”double quotation markI feel trapped. I couldn’t look prospective buyers in the eye and not tell themView image in fullscreenNick Richards, who moved to a new estate two months before a datacentre planning application was submittedLike many other residents on the estate, Richards had no idea the council was planning to sell the park and ride to a datacentre developer. They moved in two months before the planning application was submitted. Instead of enjoying their new life, they now fear they will never be able to sell. Their home is 300 metres from what the plans describe as the temporary energy centre, which includes seven giant gas turbines. They are expected to power the facility around the clock for five years, according to documents filed by the developer. “I feel trapped,” Richards says, pacing his kitchen. “I couldn’t look prospective buyers in the eye and not say there’s going to be seven gas turbines right next to them.”Richards has pored over the planning documents and leafleted every house on the new estate, including a care home, which will be just 150 metres from the turbines. “This datacentre will be powered by gas turbines,” he says. “They will pump nitrogen dioxide into our atmosphere. There will also be fine particulate matter and formaldehyde. All these toxins cause health conditions, such as asthma, COPD and heart disease.”Air quality assessments commissioned by the developer estimate the emissions will be within safe levels. Curtis Hall says the scheme cannot proceed without 100% compliance with all environmental and public health regulatory requirements.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are more than100 other planned UK datacentresaiming to use gas turbines due to the long wait to be connected to the grid. Richards doesn’t want his estate to be a test case. “Within a mile of this datacentre are 30,000 people. But the people building this centre don’t live here ... They don’t give two shits about Welsh people.”Astone’s throw away is Llanrumney Hall, once the home of privateer and slave trader Sir Henry Morgan, who gave his name to Captain Morgan rum. It is now a thriving community centre, with a cafe, recording studio and creche. Labour councillor Lee Bridgeman is vaping on an outdoor table, dressed in a hoodie and baseball cap. He ran the local youth centre until it was lost to austerity-era cuts, and though he’s a high-ranking councillor, jointly responsible for housing and communities, he does regular youth work shifts in the area, one of the poorest in Cardiff.“Llanrumney runs through my veins,” he says. “I’m not your usual politician. I don’t go to conferences. I got into politics to help the community.”Bridgeman is charming and friendly – but he is not afraid of a fight. He is one of the few public figures in the area who has spoken out in support of the development, sometimes clashing with anti-datacentre campaigners on local Facebook groups. “Some of the information being spread is scaremongering,” he says. “They are telling residents their electricity bills will go up … the river and reservoir will be drained … It’s false information.”View image in fullscreenLabour councillor Lee Bridgeman, who supported plans for a datacentre in Cardiff …View image in fullscreen… until local residents, like those at this public meeting in a boxing club, changed his mindMany of these fears stem from the US, where the rapid expansion of hyperscale facilities has been linked to rising electricity bills, water shortages and toxic air pollution. Bridgeman argues that “planning processes are totally different in the UK. So whereas [US authorities] turn a blind eye to some of the environmental impacts of those monstrosities, that would never happen in the UK.” He “wouldn’t be comfortable” if the gas turbines were running for five years but thinks they might not be needed if the datacentre can connect to the grid sooner.The backlash has caught him by surprise, but he blames outside activists. “I didn’t see it coming. I didn’t think there would be this much interference,” he says.Emotions are running high in the city. Some residents say they have been blocked by councillors when trying to question them on Facebook. Planning committee members have received threatening emails, Bridgeman says. “Threats like ‘I will come after you ... we will make your life hell.’ That shouldn’t happen.”Although the datacentre will employ only up to125people when it is built, Bridgeman believes it could encourage other big companies to east Cardiff: “I’m told the knock-on effect could lead to thousands of jobs.”Later that day, residents squeeze into the local boxing club for a public meeting about the datacentre plan. It is standing room only, with people lining the walls. Bridgeman repeats his claim that few locals have complained: “I have hundreds of emails from residents ... So far I’ve had two emails with regards to the datacentre.”Some in the audience react angrily. There are shouts of, “We don’t know you, that’s why” and, “Have you heard of social media?” One woman stands up and says, “Don’t tell me you haven’t been privy to the meetings … or things online.” In a show of hands, roughly three-quarters of the 80 to 100 people in the room indicate they are from Llanrumney, almost all opposed. There are cries of, “There you are … you don’t need emails!” and, “That’s every person!” Almost three weeks later, Bridgeman performs a sudden about-turn, submitting a formal letter of objection to the scheme, noting that he has heard from a large number of residents.The UK hyperscale buildout has been focused on London, but datacentre developers are increasingly targeting areas outside the south-east, to escape severe electrical grid capacity limits. Wales already has the largest datacentre capacity of anywhere outside the capital. Many more could be coming: five of Wales’s largest new and proposed datacentres will consume more electricity than all Welsh homes put together. While the previous Welsh Labour administrationwelcomedthe building spree, claiming giant tech firms’ investment would generate thousands of jobs, the Plaid Cymru-led government has been more circumspect, with ministers emphasising it must benefit Wales.In the light and airy Welsh parliament building, which overlooks Cardiff Bay, opposition is growing. Plaid Cymru’s Nick Carter, who is the Senedd member for Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, which includes Cardiff East, worries that the surging market will benefit developers and US tech firms rather than the public. “As a party, we’re not going to want to see a proliferation of datacentres, haphazardly being built across the country, on what may be an opportunistic basis,” he says.double quotation markThey could be a front for someone else: Google, Microsoft, whoeverView image in fullscreenPlaid Cymru’s Nick Carter, who fears datacentres benefit only developers and US tech firmsCarter, who has a background in commercial property, has examined the Cardiff plans in detail. He says the developer, Curtis Hall, has no track record in datacentres; “They could be a front for someone else: Google, Microsoft, whoever. I can understand why these operators need datacentres, but I’m not sure members of the public share the need.” In response, Curtis Hall says it never claimed it would operate the facility itself, adding it had been working on datacentre projects for five years.Carter is glad the Welsh government has intervened in Cardiff. But he doesn’t believe Wales needs to follow Scotland by imposing amoratoriumon new datacentres: “The Welsh government is developing a strategy for datacentres nationally. We’ll see what comes out of that.”However, it is not clear how the Welsh government can meet its goal to reach net zero by 2040 without limiting datacentre expansion. Carter admits, “It’s massively problematic.” In Westminster, similar questions have been asked. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology tells me the government will enable the development of datacentres by generating unprecedented amounts of clean power.Asoft autumnal dusk descends on the residents living beside the new datacentre in Newport. Its sleek industrial-grey walls cast shadows across the closest gardens and homes. Much of the anger and frustration that met the original proposals has given way to weariness and resignation. Some residents talk of moving away, while others are mollified by meetings with the US-based data campus operator, Vantage.Yet their troubles may only just be beginning – right now, only one of the three Vantage datacentres is operational. Microsoft will be opening its own nearby soon. When all are running, there could be upwards of 500 air handling units working at the same time, with back-up diesel generators needing regular testing, so they can immediately fire up if there is a power cut.Newport council’s chief scientific officer warned during the planning process that the fumes from all the generators had the “potential to cause unacceptable air pollution levels under use, and testing needs to be understood and mitigation proposed, if needed”.The council tells me it doesn’t have a duty to monitor emissions from generators, but says its officers check air quality management plans, and ask managers to minimise the impact of generator tests. Vantage says all its facilities operate in accordance with noise and air quality controls. It says it will monitor impacts and investigate concerns when the new centre opens.Some residents have already given up on democratic process. Johnston fought the proposals through the planning process but felt he was ignored. “We’ve been let down by all of them. I’ve had electoral roll cards come through my door. But I’m voting for none of them … I can’t trust them. They don’t care about any of us.”Over the road are older homes, where staff working on a nearby wealthy estate once lived. Sonia Thomas, a retired teacher, has lived in the same housekeeper’s cottage since 1969. She can remember when orchards and fields fanned out in front of their gardens but now she doesn’t even know if the sun is shining. “From inside you see grey, not blue,” she says, glancing at the datacentre filling the sky. “It’s horrible.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Big dataWalesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Older, calmer, but still playing the hits: Mourinho and Madrid primed for clásico | La Liga | The Guardian
description: Once Bobby Robson’s translator at the Camp Nou, José Mourinho is tasked with bringing down Barcelona on Sunday
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Once Bobby Robson’s translator at the Camp Nou, José Mourinho is tasked with bringing down Barcelona on Sunday
Content: José Mourinho avoided media duties after Real Madrid’s 1-0 win against Villarreal because he did not want to risk being banned for Sunday’s clásico against Barcelona.Photograph: Sergio Pérez/EPAView image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho avoided media duties after Real Madrid’s 1-0 win against Villarreal because he did not want to risk being banned for Sunday’s clásico against Barcelona.Photograph: Sergio Pérez/EPALa LigaOlder, calmer, but still playing the hits: Mourinho and Madrid primed for clásicoOnce Bobby Robson’s translator at the Camp Nou, José Mourinho is tasked with bringing down Barcelona on SundaySid LoweSat 24 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 07.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJosé Mourinho has done thepor que?,the printoutand the press conference no-show, and he’s been here only three months. The Real Madrid manager has played the classics without even playing aclásico.Not yet anyway, but it’s time: on Sunday night he returns to the stadium he first arrived at 30 transformative years ago as Bobby Robson’s talented young translator, andlast visited in 2013as the most famous manager in football.The coach who once declared “today, tomorrow and always, Barcelona in my heart,” and claimed he would only ever go toReal Madridto destroy them, has been entrusted with attempting to bring about the destruction of Barcelona. It is not the first time: if his return is about nostalgia, which it is, that’s wrapped up in their rivals too.Is el clásico still the world’s biggest match? Three questions before Barcelona v Real MadridRead more“Theclásicois just another game in the championship but to say it’s a game like any other would be to lie, totally unreal,” Mourinho said on Wednesday, and he knows. As for Barcelona’s latest star, he’s looking forward to seeing Mourinho again. “I love the needle,” Lamine Yamal says. “The Mourinho-Guardiola era, I loved all that. That’s football. Sport is serious but I want a show and we have more fun.”There are bigger things, sure; life beyond Barcelona. Madrid’s astonishing Champions League record since Mourinho was last here – following up the elusivedecima, the 10th title which had evaded them for 12 years, with the 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th and 15th in 10 years – played out without Barcelona. There has not been a Europeanclásicosince the 2011 Champions League semi-final when the man Pep Guardiola had just called theputo amo, the fucking master, produced hispor quespeech,asking why Barcelona were favouredby the continent’s referees and accusing Uefa of fixing it for them.Yet right now it doesn’t feel as if anything is bigger, this week’s Champions League matches framed around what they meant for the game thatreallymatters, evenwith Barcelona going to Paris. The rivalry is always there; in Mourinho’s case it is at the heart of it. The day he got the Madrid job in 2010 was the day he won the Champions League with Inter but its genesis lay in the semi-final, when he hadsprinted across the Camp Nou pitch, finger raised, celebrating. Madrid were relieved and grateful, spared the sight of Barcelona lifting the European Cup in their stadium and shown how to stop a team that appeared unbeatable. Mourinho, leaving the Santiago Bernabéu in Florentino Pérez’s car while his joyful players returned to Milan, was asked to repeat that with Madrid.Pérez, who had presided over thegalácticos’failureand walked away,had returnedin 2009 but won nothing. Instead, Barcelona dominated. They had the core of Spain’s World Cup 2010 winners: six starters in the final. Madrid needed a culture shift, to go to war, a manager to rule over the dressing room. “This year’sgalácticois José Mourinho,”the president said.View image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho (left) with Bobby Robson and Ronaldo after Barcelona defeated Paris Saint-Germain in the Cup Winners’ Cup final in 1997.Photograph: Colorsport/ShutterstockBy thetime Mourinho left, it had turned nasty, his enemies internal too. They had been, Mourinho later said, “three intense, almost violent years”. Yet Pérez had always felt drawn towards the only manager he has truly liked. Including when Mourinho was belligerent;especiallywhen he was belligerent. Mourinho had, Pérez said, returned Madrid to their rightful place. After every subsequent success the president called to tell him he started this. And if Mourinho’s firstclásicobroughta 5-0 defeat, Barcelona going on to win the league and Champions League; if his final season had ended trophyless; and if Guardiola had won twice as many trophies, it was also true that of the four competitions Guardiola failed to win at Barcelona, three were taken from him by Mourinho.Time has passed, things have changed, but the parallels are clear. Madrid have gone two years without a trophy. In the first of those, Barcelona won the league with two weeks to spare, completing a domestic treble. They had defeated Madrid four times, scoring 16 goals. Last season they wrapped it up with three weeks to sparevia aclásicovictoryas incontestable as their superiority throughout a season whenMadrid’s splitsplayed out in public. Then Spain won the World Cup with eight Barcelona players in the squad. Madrid’s only representative, Marc Cucurella, joined the club after the tournament started.If this was a crisis, it was time for Mourinho. A man whose flaws had been forgotten over time, nostalgia eclipsing all else. A man with the authority – a manaffordedthe authority – to impose on the dressing room. One with the personality to fight, go to war again. With just about everyone, and Barcelona especially. When you listened toPérez’s extraordinary rantin May, the quiet part said out loud, all campaigning and conspiracy, politics and paranoia, it made sense.When it comes to the still unresolvedNegreira case, in which Barcelona paid the vice-president of the referees’ committee, José María Enríquez Negreira, more than €7m between 2001 and 2018, there is substance to Madrid’s complaints. Barcelona have denied corruption, saying Negreira worked as an adviser, but that case has become the centrepiece of Madrid’s discourse, unlike when the two clubs were still holding out in the Super League. It doesn’t help when the league presidentlikens your TV channel to Joseph Goebbels’ propaganda.Whether those complaints have validitynowis a different question; whether the discourse of conspiracy does is another step again, even when decisions go against you. Every mistake – and decisions that are not even mistakes – is framed as a machiavellian plan, the insinuations constant – when they are not said outright.When Mourinho arrived he said he was older, calmer, but here he is. In defeat, perhaps he was always likely to be. After losing to Betis, he askedpor que?(Why? Because that’s the rule, the decision correct.) After losing to Atlético, he turned up with a printout. And then he didn’t turn up to the press conference after he had run on to the pitch to embrace Vinícius Júnior after the Brazilian scored against Villarreal only for the goal to be ruled out and Vinícius sent off for pulling Nathan Saliba’s hair. That led to a four-game suspension, the forward ruled out of theclásico.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe reason for the no-show was that Mourinho didn’t want to risk saying something that would earn him a suspension for theclásico, thegame.And he is happier now, if only for a little while, something shifting. When last Saturday Barcelona made it 11 wins from 11, averaging more than four goals a game, most agreed they would win theclásicoand the title would be done: they were flying,led by Lamine Yamal, while Madrid, beaten twice, hadn’t taken off. Mourinho’s team had not been very good, familiar problems still there. In short, there was not much football.The previous Wednesday Madrid had delivered another of their seemingly inexplicable comebacks, from 3-1 down at Roma, to win 4-3 in the final seven minutes, but was there really anything to build on? It turned out therewassomething of an explanation. In those minutes Arda Güler played, Yan Diomande played, Fede Valverde played at right-back, and Viníciusdidn’tplay.It seemed so obvious to everyone, including the manager. So he did it again, and Madrid scored four against Sevilla – three of them glorious – last Sunday and four more against Leipzig on Wednesday, Diomande belting in a wonderful volley once Vinícius had gone off. The night before, Barcelonaconcededfour at the Parc des Princes.PosTeamPGDPts1Barcelona930272Atletico Madrid911223Real Madrid914214Real Betis92195Real Sociedad9016Hansi Flick admitted he prioritised theclásicoover PSG, leaving out Rodri and withdrawing Pedri and Raphinha early to keep them fresh for a game that could be decisive and tends to shape a season. But he has injury concerns at the back and warned his players that 15 goals conceded is too many. Mourinho couldn’t resist complaining that Madrid have a day less rest for theclásico– something perhaps mitigated, much like any analysis, by playing at home against Leipzig rather than away at Paris Saint-Germain – which got the excuse in early, moreevidenceof how “they” have it in for his side.“We need to cut the gap and we can only do that by winning,” said the Real Madrid goalkeeper, Thibaut Courtois, of the six-point deficit. “We’re going with confidence.” Yet things do feel a little better now, defeat for Madrid not inevitable, a title still there to played for and something like a team taking shape. “I had to get to know them,” Mourinho said on Wednesday night. “I’ve only been here 105 days; it’s not long.”Explore more on these topicsLa LigaReal MadridBarcelonaJosé MourinhoEuropean club footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: At Aberfan, I saw fathers digging for their missing children. And the lessons society should have learned, it hasn’t | John Humphrys | The Guardian
description: Each of those 144 deaths was entirely avoidable, but nobody was held to account. We still don’t know how to get justice for ordinary people, says journalist John Humphrys
Author: John Humphrys
Headline: Each of those 144 deaths was entirely avoidable, but nobody was held to account. We still don’t know how to get justice for ordinary people, says journalist John Humphrys
Content: Rescue workers digging in the wreckage of the school in Aberfan, 21 October 1966.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenRescue workers digging in the wreckage of the school in Aberfan, 21 October 1966.Photograph: PAOpinionAberfan disasterAt Aberfan, I saw fathers digging for their missing children. And the lessons society should have learned, it hasn’tJohn HumphrysEach of those 144 deaths was entirely avoidable, but nobody was held to account. We still don’t know how to get justice for ordinary peopleSat 24 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 12.41 EDTShareAberfan taught us a lot. Mostly, of course, that those in power cannot be trusted. Correction: must not be trusted.Too sweeping?I might have thought so until 60 years ago this week when I stood alongside mothers weeping and praying as they watched their husbands digging for the bodies of their children who lay crushed beneath the ruins oftheir little school.The parents’ faces were black, save for the streaks of white from their tears. Two hours earlier those men had been digging coal from deep beneath the ground. With the coal, of course, came the waste that would have to be separated to become the great mounds that disfigured every mining valley.My best friend’s father was a miner. I had been a reporter on the local paper and I once went down the mine to watch him at work. I begged to return to the surface after no more than an hour of breathing in the deadly coal dust. I tried to imagine every working hour trapped in that living hell and failed.This, surely, was the most dangerous and demanding job in the land. Few miners escaped serious lung damage. I never once spoke to a Valleys mother who wanted her son to follow his father down the pit. But what I witnessed that day was something even the toughest miners, let alone their wives, could not have dreamed of in their darkest nightmares.Every so often, one of the diggers would shout for silence. He thought he had heard a child cry out. We stood and prayed, hardly daring to breathe. Sometimes our prayers were answered. I watched a little girl handed to a policeman. She was unconscious but, thank God, she was breathing. She would live. Most did not.I did my best to tell the outside world what was happening from a phone in the local pub overlooking the school. But what I failed to report until many hours later was the terrible truth that this was a disaster that need never have happened.Correction: a disaster thatshouldnever have happened.In Wales, we’re one more flood away from another disaster like Aberfan | Aaron ThierryRead moreWhat every miner in that village and every miner’s wife had always known was that the massive waste tip that was to destroy their lives should never have been built. Or at least, should never have been built on that spot. This was not one of those disasters that might eventually be written off as part of the price society was reconciled to paying if we were to enjoy the benefits of what we once called “black gold”.Every miner knew he faced danger from the moment he stepped into the cage that would drop him a couple of thousand feet below ground. Until the nightmare of Aberfan, the most painful job I was ordered to do as a teenage reporter on the Merthyr Express was knocking on the door of a miner’s cottage a few hours after his wife had been told she was now a widow.The first time I was scared. Surely I would be ordered by the newly bereaved widow to clear off? But I learned quickly that they almost always wanted to talk about their dead husbands. And there was seldom any anger. They had always known – even if it was never talked about – that he might never come home. Accidents were inevitable.But what happened in Aberfan was no accident.View image in fullscreenA young John Humphrys reporting from Aberfan in October 1966.Photograph: Archif Ddarlledu Cymru/Wales Broadcast Archive/ITV WalesIt was the result of grotesque indifference on the part ofthe men who ran the National Coal Board(NCB) and were responsible for the location of every waste tip of every nationalised colliery in the land. Above all, of the man who chaired that board: Alfred Robens.Such was his unbelievable disregard for the hell that had been visited on that little Welsh village that he couldn’t even spare a few hours to share their grief. While they were still digging through the filth that had choked the lives from so many children, His lordship was being chauffeured to a new university for a ceremony where he was to be made chancellor. And the year of the disaster, he also accepted an honorary degree for his services to the mining industry.His “services”? Has ever the English language been more abused?What Lord Robens had always known – if only because he would have been briefed by his team of senior officials – was that to build a massive tip on that particular spot on the hillside was the equivalent of lighting a bonfire in a dynamite factory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI can state that as an absolute fact after all these years, because even as those brave miners and their wives were trying so desperately to deal with their grief, they were showing me copies of the letters they had written over and over again warning the NCB that it was criminally reckless to site the tip on that spot.There was a simple reason that even an ignoramus such as me could understand. It rains a lot in the Welsh valleys and there are many springs beneath the surface of the hills. The spot the officials chose for the tip was notorious for its springs. But it was directly above the village. And Pantglas junior school.Local journalism made me what I am today. Without it, we’ll all be the poorer | John HumphrysRead moreEvery morning two miners would trudge up the hillside of their own volition to examine the state of the tip. When they saw what was happening on 21 October 1966, they turned and ran down the hillside. But it was too late. Within minutes 100,000 tonnes of coal waste had hit the school at 80mph, killing almost everyone in its path.It took a little more than a year for Robens and his henchmen to face a form of justice. I sat through the public inquiry when the scale of the disgrace was unveiled, day after agonising day, and Robens was the final witness.The inquiry chairman treated his protestations of ignorance and innocence with richly deserved contempt and I remember leaping into my car to deliver a live broadcast with the sense that justice had finally been delivered.But had it? Have we really learned anything as a result of Aberfan? The horror of the Grenfell Tower inferno suggests not. The inquiry found thatthe deaths of all 72 people in 2017 were “entirely avoidable”, resulting from systemic failures, deregulation and corporate dishonesty. It added: “There is still a great deal to learn.”True, the last of the collieries in the Welsh valleys has long since gone, but can it really be true that no one deserved to face charges for criminal negligence?What is true is the extraordinary spirit of those who suffered so much and, indeed, of those who survived.I remember going to the home of a little girl who’d been one of the survivors and asking her mother why she hadn’t sent her to the new school. She answered with almost chilling simplicity: “Because I don’t want mothers who’ve lost their kiddies to see her in the street and be reminded of what they’ve lost.”John Humphrys presents The Odd Couple podcast with Matthew NormanExplore more on these topicsAberfan disasterOpinionWalescommentShareReuse this content

title: The Stone Roses showed me the power of being an introvert | Culture | The Guardian
description: At boarding school in the early 90s, quietness was seen as weakness. But then I saw the band’s guitarist John Squire making a vast noise while hiding behind a fringe – and learned the strength of understatement
Author: Henry Yates
Headline: At boarding school in the early 90s, quietness was seen as weakness. But then I saw the band’s guitarist John Squire making a vast noise while hiding behind a fringe – and learned the strength of understatement
Content: ‘I assumed Squire must be an extrovert axe hero: foot on the monitor, diamante codpiece, the works.’Illustration: Martin O’NeillView image in fullscreen‘I assumed Squire must be an extrovert axe hero: foot on the monitor, diamante codpiece, the works.’Illustration: Martin O’NeillMy cultural awakeningCultureThe Stone Roses showed me the power of being an introvertAt boarding school in the early 90s, quietness was seen as weakness. But then I saw the band’s guitarist John Squire making a vast noise while hiding behind a fringe – and learned the strength of understatementHenry YatesSat 24 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn September 1991, I had just been thrown into the meat-grinder of a Midlands boarding school. In this bear pit, there were predators and there was prey. You were either the swaggering rugby alpha, whipping a wet towel at pale bodies in the eight-boy dormitory; or the homesick ghost, keeping your guard up, endlessly braced for your toilet cubicle to be kicked open or your washbag chucked off the fire escape.My mind had always been loud, racing with opinions, stories, jokes. But by the time I adequately considered a thought, the conversation had raced on without me. Suddenly, under 24/7 social scrutiny in a world where bullhorn confidence is king, I felt dismissed.Up to that point, music hadn’t helped. Every rock star I had ever seen – Elton John, Freddie Mercury, Mick Jagger – was a showboating peacock, all hips, handclaps and absurd glasses, seeming to whisper in my ear: “This isn’t for you, bookworm.” But that September, I stumbled across the Stone Roses’ self-titled 1989 debut album. I must have seen John Squire’s genius before I heard it, on his paint-splashed, lemon-drizzled sleeve art.Hearing his cascading, iridescent guitar solos, I assumed Squire must be an extrovert axe hero: foot on the monitor, diamante codpiece, the works. But there he was on the CD inlay: pipecleaner-skinny, dressed in Manchester streetwear and inscrutable beneath a bird’s-nest fringe (until the mid-90s, I genuinely wasn’t sure if Squire had eyes), slinging a Gretsch Country Gentleman guitar but not treating it like a penis extension.Years before YouTube, it wasn’t easy to find out more. But when I dug up back issues of NME, I went from fan to disciple. A sometime model-maker who once worked on The Wind in the Willows – but also a child of 70s punk – Squire was enigmatic and otherworldly, softly spoken yet intense as a laser-cutter. Asked by one interviewer what the Roses were all about, his answer was the perfect collision of sky-scraping ambition and bone-dry Britishness: “Love and hate. War and peace. Morecambe and Wise …”In those formative weeks, for the first time, I realised that “quiet” could also mean charismatic, insolent, snarky, simmering with latent attitude and temperamentally suited for a life in the arts. Through Squire, I discovered painting (Jackson Pollock’s “drip and splash” influence was all over his sleeves and guitars), modern history (the Paris riots of May 68 referenced on Bye Bye Badman), fashion and even religion (you only had to read his lyric to 1994’s Love Spreads, a take on the Passion, with Jesus imagined as a Black woman, to sense the iconoclast claws below the still waters).Hearing the Roses at school, meanwhile, was my ticket into a secret society of indie kids that I hadn’t known existed, all swapping albums, making mixtapes, easy in each other’s company, building each other’s confidence. I picked up the guitar that same year, too, went on to write about it for the music press – and now play so loud in my own band that I can drown out a thousand braying show-offs.Squire doesn’t do many interviews, and when I drove to his Cheshire farmhouse for Guitarist Magazine, I was worried he wouldn’t actually speak. But perhaps he recognised a kindred spirit. Over an hour’s encounter in his studio, the musician who had meant so much to me proved thoughtful, witty and profound, signed the schoolboy-era guitar I’d flecked Pollock-style with paint, and even gave me a parting hug.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJohn Squire didn’t change me; he stopped me fighting myself. Under his influence, I stopped trying to turn up the volume, accepted being an introvert and held him in mind whenever anyone equated quietness with dullness. Fast-forward 35 years – to a time when influencers squeal and preen, flogging every last grain of themselves to the attention economy – and the Roses guitarist seems a few degrees cooler for existing on his own terms, leaving something to the imagination, and treating Jonathan Ross withchilly disdain. Perhaps we could all stand to be a little more Squire?Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: Healey’s first budget to include big devolution package to boost growth | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Chancellor will build on Burnham’s promise that local leaders in England will no longer have to ‘come cap in hand to Westminster’
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Chancellor will build on Burnham’s promise that local leaders in England will no longer have to ‘come cap in hand to Westminster’
Content: Burnham said Healey’s budget was about ‘shifting power out of Westminster and into the hands of the people who know their communities best’.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBurnham said Healey’s budget was about ‘shifting power out of Westminster and into the hands of the people who know their communities best’.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianBudget 2026Healey’s first budget to include big devolution package to boost growthChancellor will build on Burnham’s promise that local leaders in England will no longer have to ‘come cap in hand to Westminster’Heather StewartSat 24 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has promised that local leaders in England will no longer have to come “cap in hand to Westminster” ahead of a fresh drive to devolve spending power in next week’s budget.In his statement on Wednesday, the chancellor,John Healey, will include plans for a new £1.5bn borrowing facility, to be drawn up in collaboration with mayors over the next two years.Regional mayors have long complained that they are constrained by their limited borrowing power – in contrast to local authorities in the US and some European countries, which commonly issue their own bonds.The borrowing plan will form part of a big devolution package aimed at boosting regional economic growth. This will also include the allocation of an initial £285m “good growth” funding next year, to be spent on local leaders’ priorities – which could include housing, transport links or high street regeneration.Can curry nights and canny advisers help Healey deliver a budget for everyday people?Read moreAmid fears in the Treasury about whether some local authorities have the capacity to administer increasingly large budgets, Healey will also announce £150m of support to help them scale up and build expertise.Hailing the plans, Burnham said they would mean local leaders would no longer need to come to the Treasury for approval for each individual project. “I’m calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country. When I became prime minister, I said that if a decision can be made closer to home, it should be.“Today we’re putting that into practice, shifting power out of Westminster and into the hands of the people who know their communities best.”The £285m in “good growth” funding is intended to tide local authorities over until a new system comes into force in 2028 whereby some income tax revenue will be handed directly to their areas to give them longer-term security – an ideafirst mooted by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, earlier this year.View image in fullscreenRachel Reeves, the chancellor under Keir Starmer, first mooted the idea of a ‘good growth’ fund.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersMore details of how this will work will be announced at the budget. Local leaders are expected to be allowed to keep some of the additional revenues created by a stronger local economy, giving them an incentive to back pro-growth policies.Tax and spending in the UK is more centralised than in many other leading economies, and Burnham experienced the constraints first-hand as mayor of Greater Manchester.Healey said: “Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas.”The package has been drawn up in collaboration with No 10 North, which has been holding a weekly “situation room” meeting with local leaders, to ask them about the barriers to promoting economic growth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis resulted in an announcement this week that the Treasury has calledthe “green book”, which gives guidanceon which projects taxpayers should fund. Under the new rules, projects that can be combined to boost growth – a housing and a transport scheme, for example – can be considered together.A governmentwhite paper on “rewiring the state”, due to be published after the budget, will set out more details of how the civil service will be reshaped, as more powers are passed down from Whitehall.View image in fullscreenOil tankers stranded near the strait of Hormuz – the war in the Middle East has driven up bills for UK households.Photograph: Barry Iverson/AlamyAlongside the devolution plans, Healey’s first budget isexpected to include support for poorer householdshit by rising energy costs; and modest tax rises, including on banks. The chancellor has repeatedly said he wants to offer a “breathing space” to households and businesses that have struggled as the war in the Middle East has driven up bills.These higher costs have also pushed up the interest rates on government borrowing, making it harder for Healey to balance the books.He will set out how he plans to fully fund the four-year defence investment plan announced in the dying days of Keir Starmer’s premiership.However, Healey is not expected to say when the UK will commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence – an issue that was central to his resignation from Starmer’s cabinet. This is likely to be delayed until a spending review due at some point next year.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyAndy BurnhamDevolutionEnglandEconomic policyUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Storm Boelo: Travel disrupted and events cancelled as UK hit by wind and rain | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Fresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on Friday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on Friday
Content: People struggle to hold their umbrellas against strong winds in Liverpool on Saturday.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople struggle to hold their umbrellas against strong winds in Liverpool on Saturday.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAUK weatherStorm Boelo: Travel disrupted and events cancelled as UK hit by wind and rainFresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on FridayPol Allingham and Helen William, Press AssociationSat 24 Oct 2026 18.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmber weather warnings have come into force as the worst ofStorm Boelocould be set to hit parts of the UK.Storm Boelo’s winds will peak from Saturday evening, leaving areas in the warning zone, including Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, braced for gusts of 60-70mph and even 80mph in exposed coastal spots, the Met Office said.The forecaster’s amber warnings came into force on Saturday at 9pm.Maximum gust speeds of 75mph have already hit South Uist Range, Western Isles, Highland and Eilean Siar, Scotland on Saturday, according to the Met Office, which has also issued several yellow warnings for rain.Storm Boelofollows Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season, which brought strong winds to parts of the UK on Friday.Gusts of 76mph were recorded at St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, with 74mph at Aberporth in south-west Wales and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall.Heavy downpours since 8am on Saturday have already seen rainfall totals of 72mm in White Barrow, Wiltshire, along with 43mm in both Cwm Dyli, just south of the Snowdon range in North Wales, and Inveruglas on the west shore of Loch Lomond, Scotland.View image in fullscreenWaves crash over the lighthouse at Newhaven Harbour in East Sussex during Storm Austen on Friday.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersHundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday where the National Grid said power had been restored to 131,225 properties by Saturday at 7pm.An amber wind warning, the Met Office’s second most severe, is active across Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm on Saturday to the same time on Sunday.A further amber warning runs from 9pm on Saturday to 10am on Sunday in the north-east of Northern Ireland.Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, will bring a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves and people should stay indoors as much as possible, the forecaster said.The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings which extend south into parts of England and North Wales and cover the whole of Northern Ireland.TheEnvironment Agencyhad issued 58 alerts for spots across England where flooding is possible by 8pm on Saturday, as well as 12 warnings stating that flooding is expected.Met Office chief forecaster Jason Kelly said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north.“Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts.“People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”People should secure loose items outside, plan ahead if they are travelling and keep an eye on the latest forecast and warnings, he advised.View image in fullscreenThe wet weather did not deter shoppers in Oxford Street, central London, on Saturday.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/PAStorm Boelo has already caused widespread disruption.Boelo’s strong winds disrupted flights at Dublin airport, where as of 4pm on Saturday, nine outbound and 10 inbound flights had been cancelled by airlines because of weather issues.It also reported that six inbound flights performed go-arounds – five of which landed on the second attempt, with the other diverting to another airport before returning a short time later.Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, in a call for those living near rail lines to secure their garden furniture firmly.Visit Liverpool announced that the region’s River of Light event, featuring illuminated artwork, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”.London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations this Sunday were also cancelled on independent health and safety experts’ recommendations in light of the storm.Other attractions closed on Sunday include Edinburgh Castle and the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire, which was due to host its Fountains by Floodlight event.Explore more on these topicsUK weatherEnvironment AgencynewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November
