Content: Andy Burnham said he believed the ‘balance of migration’ had changed in recent years.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said he believed the ‘balance of migration’ had changed in recent years.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EUPrime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in NovemberPatrick DalySat 24 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean theUK goes “all the way”and rejoins the EU.Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU.In an interview with the Sunday Times he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.”The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029.The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it”, but suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade.“It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” hetold the Sunday Times.“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”Burnham will meet EU chiefs at a summit in Brussels on 20 November.He argued that there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe.The issue of migration was one of the dominant debates during the 2016Brexitreferendum campaign.Andy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EURead moreIn the 12 months to June 2016 – the month of the Brexit leave vote – net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000,according to the Office for National Statistics.Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however.Net migrationpeaked at a record 944,000in the year to March 2023 due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic.It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at171,000 last year, almost half of what it was in 2016.Burnham has said he will take the opportunity around the summit with EU leaders in November to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.But Burnham added that he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen Area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro.Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a “total betrayal” of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.The Reform UK leader added: “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamEuropean UnionBrexitMigrationEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Met says it shared allegations about Meghan’s father with her but not other forces | Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex | The Guardian
description: Scotland Yard says it shared letter about Thomas Markle Sr allegations in 2019 but did not pass claims to other agencies
Author: Harry Taylor
Headline: Scotland Yard says it shared letter about Thomas Markle Sr allegations in 2019 but did not pass claims to other agencies
Content: The Duchess of Sussex said she was ‘deeply distressed’ by allegations about her father.Photograph: Cyril Zingaro/Keystone/APView image in fullscreenThe Duchess of Sussex said she was ‘deeply distressed’ by allegations about her father.Photograph: Cyril Zingaro/Keystone/APMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMet says it shared allegations about Meghan’s father with her but not other forcesScotland Yard says it shared letter about Thomas Markle Sr allegations in 2019 but did not pass claims to other agenciesHarry TaylorSat 24 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 08.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheMetropolitan policehave confirmed they gave a letter to the Duchess of Sussex in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, after accusations arose on Friday about Thomas Markle Sr having child sexual abuse images.Scotland Yard said it had received a letter in January 2019 making a number of allegations about offending outside Britain.The police force said it had passed the information on to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s office, but it did not pass it on to “other law enforcement agencies”.The Sun newspaperpublished claims thatMeghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, claimed he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.On Friday, Meghan said she had been made aware of these allegations by the Met, and that she was “deeply distressed” by them.The duchess, who is estranged from her father said in a statement she had broken off contact to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them.Meghan and Prince Harry recently moved back to the UK from the US.Meghan’s father has denied the allegations and told the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”.The Met said it was considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office forPoliceConduct (IOPC) to review its actions.In a statement, a Metropolitan police spokesperson said: “Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS (Metropolitan Police Service) Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”In a statement on Friday, issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”She later said she had misremembered the year the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.A spokesperson for the Duchess of Sussex said: “In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months.“If the MPS holds a time-stamped record confirming that the letter was reviewed in 2019, that should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the duchess.“I think it is reasonable to recognise that she is doing her best to recall the precise timing of events that were not diarised at the time, and that any discrepancy of a few months is an understandable consequence of that passage of time.”Sources said that although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.Explore more on these topicsMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMetropolitan policeMonarchyPoliceCrimeLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing | France | The Guardian
description: Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres
Content: Demonstrators gather in Paris as fresh protests sweep FranceFranceHundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policingAlmost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centresAngelique Chrisafisin ParisSat 24 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 17.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to supportschoolchildren’s demandsfor more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.Riot police also charged a larger crowd of protesters at the end of the Paris march, using batons against them.Major protests in Paris and other French cities in challenge to Macron – in picturesRead morePolice fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police. At least two people were seriously injured, one in Clermont-Ferrand and another in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off.The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched acrossFrance. Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been almost 1,000 arrests.Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said that at various street marches across France there were what he called “high-risk groups” who “broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence”.More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France sawone of the most violent days of unrestin years, with public buildings burned,hundreds of shops destroyed and lootedand at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country.At Saturday’s protests, there was widespread anger at Macron forbanning non-union demonstrationsthat his governmentdeemed “illegitimate”and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.View image in fullscreenAt the end of the Paris demonstration, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged and threw glass bottles and stones at police.Photograph: Thibault Camus/APAt the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.”A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”The radical left presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the Paris rally, said Macron must “give in” and address France’s social malaise or face repeated protests. “Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week,” Mélenchon said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government has been facing a crisis since the start ofhigh schooldemonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesterswere maimed and injuredby explosive police weaponry.At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in thegiletsjaunesanti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from thegiletsjaunesprotest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue.NFL shutters Paris fan experience as protests overshadow first France gameRead morePierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.”Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them, and we have to stand together.”She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”In Orléans, thousands shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestEuropeEmmanuel MacronGilets jaunes protestsStudentsYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Manhunt under way to find prisoner who absconded from medical facility | UK news | The Guardian
description: Met police say Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen on Friday in south London, and ‘poses a risk to himself and the public’
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: Met police say Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen on Friday in south London, and ‘poses a risk to himself and the public’
Content: Anthony Lloyd forced his way out of a health unit in Lewisham, in south-east London, shortly after 4pm on Friday.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAAnthony Lloyd forced his way out of a health unit in Lewisham, in south-east London, shortly after 4pm on Friday.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAUK newsManhunt under way to find prisoner who absconded from medical facilityMet police say Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen on Friday in south London, and ‘poses a risk to himself and the public’Patrick Dalyand Press AssociationSat 24 Oct 2026 14.10 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 14.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA manhunt is under way to locate a prisoner who police say “poses a risk both to himself and the public” after he absconded from a medical facility inLondon.Anthony Lloyd forced his way out of a health unit in Lewisham, in south-east London, shortly after 4pm on Friday, theMetropolitan policesaid.The force warned the public not to approach Lloyd, but instead to contact 999 if he is spotted.Lloyd was seen heading in the direction of Catford, police said in a statement on Saturday.Lloyd was convicted in 2025 of actual bodily harm, according to the Press Association, relating to an incident in Nottinghamshire involving three emergency services workers.He received a 12-month custodial sentence and wassent to prison. In September he was transferred to the medical facility in Lewisham.The 38-year-old is white and about 5ft 8in, of medium build with short dark hair.He was wearing a grey-blue T-shirt, black tracksuit bottoms and white trainers when last seen at about 4.10pm on Friday, police said.Det supt Melanie Pressley, who is leading the manhunt, said: “We are conducting various significant inquiries to find Lloyd and return him to custody.“We are concerned he poses a risk both to himself and the public, and would urge anyone who sees him to call 999 immediately. Do not approach him.“If you have any information – however small – that could help us locate Lloyd, please get in touch with police as a matter of urgency.”Officers believe Lloyd could be anywhere in the capital. He also has links to Surrey, Sussex, Thames Valley, Hampshire, Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire and Merseyside.Anyone with information is asked to call 999, quoting the reference CAD4739/23Oct.Explore more on these topicsUK newsLondonMetropolitan policenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes | West Bank | The Guardian
description: PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint
Content: Israeli troops destroy Hebron neighbourhood following attack on military checkpointWest BankIsraeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homesPM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpointJulian Borgerin JerusalemSat 24 Oct 2026 09.17 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 08.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families incollective punishment for a militant attackon an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.View image in fullscreenSoldiers patrol the northern checkpoint in Hebron after Israeli forces levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/GettyPeople said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.The large-scale demolitions followan attack on Fridayon an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20-minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.Israeli elections will take place in four days and the prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.View image in fullscreenIsrael's finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, filmed himself wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersHeidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attackRead moreNetanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.View image in fullscreenA Palestinian man clears debris outside a business demolished by Israeli forces in Hebron.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/GettyA Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”The Israeli army was approached for comment on the operations and on videos showing extensive devastation.Explore more on these topicsWest BankBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelPalestineInternally displaced peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Most levelling up projects still unfinished years after funding allocated | Inequality | The Guardian
description: Data released under freedom of information laws reveals hundreds of projects unfinished despite Tory promises on regional equality
Author: Michael Goodier
Headline: Data released under freedom of information laws reveals hundreds of projects unfinished despite Tory promises on regional equality
Content: Data reviewed by the Guardian found 821 levelling up projects out of 1,347 were yet to be finalised as of May 2026.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenData reviewed by the Guardian found 821 levelling up projects out of 1,347 were yet to be finalised as of May 2026.Composite: Guardian DesignTown and countryInequalityMost levelling up projects still unfinished years after funding allocatedData released under freedom of information laws reveals hundreds of projects unfinished despite Tory promises on regional equalityCan a £5.8bn scheme help revive Grimsby and other town centres?Michael GoodierandRichard PartingtonSat 24 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost levelling up projects are not finished, years after funds were allocated, highlighting how ambitious Conservative promises of quick progress on regional equality have faltered.Data released under freedom of information laws and manually reviewed by the Guardian found 821 levelling up projects out of 1,347 were yet to be finalised as of May this year. Across the UK, 73 council areas that had a bid for a project accepted were yet to see a single one fully completed. The Guardian has identified 59 projects that were completed since the data was collected.Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have seen slower delivery in their levelling up projects, despite having fewer overall. North-west England and Yorkshire also had low project completion rates, but they were also the two regions allocated the most projects to begin with.Boris Johnson’s government swept to power in 2019 after promising to revive left-behind towns and spread opportunity as part of alevelling up agendaheaded by Michael Gove. With 57% of projects still unfinished, the figures show many communities are still waiting for those ambitions to become reality.The figures cover three of themain funds associated with the levelling up agenda: the Future High Streets Fund (launched in 2018), Town Deals (2019) and the Levelling Up Fund (2021).The Future High Streets Fund was supposed to complete in March 2024, and the official deadline for spending all of the Towns Fund and Levelling Up Fund money was March 2026. The Levelling Up Fund and Town Deals were consolidated into the Local Regeneration Fund under Labour, with a new deadline of March 2028.Labour has since also launched the Pride in Place programme. It gives places longer-term funding, with local boards deciding how it is spent, rather than making councils compete for grants.Jack Shaw, the director of Groundwork Research, which supplied the data to the Guardian, said it showed a large gap between the intentions of levelling up and what had been delivered. He said: “Despite significant funding, too many one-off commitments have failed to translate into substantive improvements in communities or local economies.“The Pride in Place programme is a step forward because it provides communities with £2m a year over 10 years, giving places the certainty and time to deliver visible, lasting improvements.“But in future the government also needs to look at how investment can reach communities more quickly, so that funding announced at this budget can improve neighbourhoods over the course of this parliament, whether that be through new social infrastructure or a better public realm.”Blackburn with Darwen council had eight projects funded through the Local Regeneration Fund, none of which have been fully completed.View image in fullscreenLayton in Blackpool was one of the areas earmarked for increased funding.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianSimilarly, all eight projects funded in Leeds are yet to close. Five arein Morley: a refurbishment of Morley town hall, the establishment of a learning and skills centre, the station gateway transport scheme, a project to make the area greener and better connected, and the Heritage Investment Programme (which has only partly been completed).Twoprojects in Holbeck– a green housing retrofit and a local centre scheme – also remain incomplete, as does the St Matthew’s community centre and Old Box Office project.Part of the reason for the delays across the UK has been inflation,which meantcouncils had to scale back or pause projects due to increased costs eating into their awarded pots.Zoë Billingham, the director of the IPPR North thinktank,said the Tories’ Town Fund failed because it had created a “begging bowl culture” where councils would need to approach Whitehall mandarins to access centrally controlled funding pots.She said: “The levelling up – the ‘hanging baskets strategy’ as it was called – was short-term pots of money that could help clean up high streets and make tangible and important improvements. But that’s different to long-term support for what high streets are and should be. No one would dismiss it [levelling up funding], but you have to have a long-term plan rather than pots of money that run out.”Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist who has advised Burnham, said the levelling up fund was “better than nothing” despite problems with it. He said: “It was in some ways the kind of worst of Whitehall. Because all the decisions were centralised. There looked to be degrees of pork barrel politics rolled into which places got it.“It was all a bit sort of unsightly and pork barrelly.”The national figures exclude 69 projects that were either cancelled or merged into another existing project. Some of the projects are broader programmes of funding, parts of which may have been completed.Sarah Longlands, the chief executive of the Centre for Local Economic Strategies, warned Labour’s Pride in Place programme could face similar pitfalls to the Tories’ towns fund. She said: “It doesn’t surprise me the [Towns Fund] projects are not finished. Capital money takes time – you just can’t throw stuff up. This is my worry with the current programme of neighbourhood boards. We’re dealing with a lot of capital money, and it can’t be done quickly sometimes.”You can look at the projects in your area and whether they have been completed or not using the map below. The government data may be missing some recent project completions. The Guardian has attempted to correct for this using published online announcements, but it is possible some completed projects may be missing from the data.Some places are yet to see a levelling up project completed.A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We are committed to driving good growth in every postcode, giving local leaders stability through long-term targeted funding.“That’s why we introduced our £5.8bn Pride in Place programme, giving the power to local people to decide how to invest this money to regenerate their own communities.“And thanks to our Local Regeneration Fund, we’re seeing more money from previous funding programmes being delivered quicker.”Explore more on these topicsInequalityTown and countrynewsShareReuse this content

title: More than one million Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoff | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro
Content: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was cheered by a huge crowd on Copacabana beach on Saturday amid hopes he can secure an historic fourth term.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersView image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva was cheered by a huge crowd on Copacabana beach on Saturday amid hopes he can secure an historic fourth term.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersBrazilMore than one million Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoffNearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio BolsonaroTom Phillipsin Rio de Janeiro andTiago Rogeroin Belo HorizonteSat 24 Oct 2026 17.10 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 14.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than one million supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival,Flávio Bolsonaro.Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonarowon the first round on 4 Octoberby 47% to 45%.On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt tohelp Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president, who was first elected in 2002, would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day.”View image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva waves to supporters on Saturday.Photograph: Dhavid Normando/AP“The people have woken up,” Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have sweptBrazilsince the leftist’s first-round defeat, many led by students.“Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again – and we don’t want dictatorship. We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career.“There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes,” Silva claimed.Polls suggest a far tighter margin and most analysts see Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, waspresident from 2019 to 2022, as the slight favourite, having sold himself to voters as someone who will tackle chronic levels of violent crime with an iron fist.However, in recent days Lula has appeared to regain the initiative and climb in the polls, amid a succession of scandals involving his rightwing foe. Last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of Brazil’s 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party attended by sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to strike a deal with the government of his father.View image in fullscreenPeople watch a televised debate between Flávio Bolsonaro and his election rival on Friday.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersSome experts speculate a Lula comeback may be possible. At the Copacabana rally –which Rio’s City Hall said attracted about 1.1 million people– activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “WE ARE GOING TO TURN THIS AROUND!”On Saturday afternoon, Lula attended an even larger rally on Paulista Avenue, in the heart of Brazil’s biggest city, São Paulo.“I’m super excited. Lula’s going to win,” said Marta Moraes, a 59-year-old restaurateur, as she joined Saturday’s demo in Rio.Moraes said the election was not about left versus right. “We’ve nothing against the right … what we’re against is Bolsonarismo,” she said, tears filling her eyes as she recalled how Flávio Bolsonaro’s fatherbotched the response to Covidduring his chaotic 2019-2022 administration.“I lost four members of my family because of Bolsonaro’s neglect,” Moraes said.View image in fullscreenLula supporters on Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersJair Bolsonaro isserving a 27-year prison sentencefor plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Many Brazilian democrats fear he will be released – and could even return to government – if his son wins. Reports in the Brazilian press suggest several of Bolsonaro’s fellow plotters – who are now in prison or hiding in exile – may be given top military and police jobs in a Bolsonaro administration.Cammy Marinho, a 49-year-old DJ and activist, said: “I’m here to prevent democracy becoming extinct – which is what the Bolsonaro family wants”.Marinho said she had spent the past fortnight fighting to persuade people who voted for Bolsonaro, or did not vote in the first round, to back Lula.Strongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in peril | George MonbiotRead more“It’s non-stop work: in the bakery, in the supermarket, on the underground – whenever you feel there is an opening to talk to someone and show to them the reality, everything that Lula has done and is doing for the people and everything that this [Bolsonaro] family has done against the people,” she said.Many marchers were part of the so-called “Lula’s Army” – a 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was created after the first round in the hope of turning the election around.“Being a soldier in Lula’s army … means fighting for Brazilian democracy. This isn’t a normal election,” said Isabella Gaze, 64, a retired teacher and one of the group’s members.“They constantly claim Lula is corrupt. But the truth is that they represent the most rotten and worst part of Brazilian politics. This is what we are fighting against now,” Gaze said of the Bolsonaros.Many of the faces on Copacabana beach were teenagers, including 14-year-old Heitor Lopes da Silva. Silva had come from the city of Duque de Caxias in his wheelchair, with a placard that said: “Lula, I’m a person with a disability and I’m here to support you.”“My whole life I’ve believed Lula was a good president. [Bolsonaro] represents the destruction of Brazil …. he represents sadness and death,” he said of the Bolsonaro-era Covid catastrophe.View image in fullscreenSome Lula supporters believe he can overturn the lead his rival secured in the first round of voting.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersLarge crowds of Bolsonaro supporters also hit the streets, including in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, which has Brazil’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo, and is a key bellwether. No presidential candidate has ever won the presidency without securing Minas Gerais, where Bolsonaro led by just under 5% in the first round.Thousands of Bolsonaristas gathered to see their candidate in a palm-lined plaza called Praça da Liberdade. To the booming sound of AI-generated funk carioca tracks praising Bolsonaro, a sea of supporters dressed in Brazil’s yellow football jersey waved Brazilian flags – and many of the United States too.“The US is a great nation. Who wouldn’t want to be aligned with them?” said 56-year-old cosmetics entrepreneur Marcos Antonio, holding a flag that merged the emblems of both countries.“I don’t want an alliance with Cuba or Venezuela. I want to move forward,” Antonio added. When reminded that Venezuela was currently aligned with the US afterDonald Trump’s January invasion, he said: “True. But for now, a fully right-wing government hasn’t been installed yet. It’s in transition.”View image in fullscreenBolsonaro supporters, some with the flags of the US, Israel and Brazil, also held last-minute rallies on Saturday.Photograph: Raquel Cunha/ReutersAntonio Carlos Costa Jr, the 59-year-old owner of a shooting club, complained: “Lula did nothing for the country.”Jair Bolsonaro relaxed gun ownership and buying laws – which security experts agree ended up diverting many firearms to criminal gangs – whereas Lula tightened regulations once again. “Jair Bolsonaro simply gave citizens the right to defend themselves, and his son will do the same,” said Costa Jr.Lula supporters scoff at the idea that Bolsonaro, who has a history of well-documented ties with members of Rio’s paramilitary “militia” groups, could rid Brazil of criminality.“If we vote the militias into power, we will be living in a dictatorship,” said Erika Cavalcante, 43, an architect who came to the march with a sign reading: “Don’t let the mobsters win.”Explore more on these topicsBrazilAmericasRio de JaneironewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Bolso shows all signs of fascism’: the journalist who predicted Brazil’s future – and paid the ultimate price | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Dom Phillips warned that Jair Bolsonaro would make life more dangerous for reporters and the Amazon rainforest, and that his sons were even more extreme
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Dom Phillips warned that Jair Bolsonaro would make life more dangerous for reporters and the Amazon rainforest, and that his sons were even more extreme
Content: Dom Phillips pictured in 2018. He predicted, correctly, that Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency would lead to more mortalities and more destruction of the Amazon rainforest.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverView image in fullscreenDom Phillips pictured in 2018. He predicted, correctly, that Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency would lead to more mortalities and more destruction of the Amazon rainforest.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverBrazil‘Bolso shows all signs of fascism’: the journalist who predicted Brazil’s future – and paid the ultimate priceDom Phillips warned that Jair Bolsonaro would make life more dangerous for reporters and the Amazon rainforest, and that his sons were even more extremeJonathan WattsSat 24 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 10.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Bolso shows all signs of fascism, as do his supporters,” the murdered British journalist Dom Phillips told me before his death. “His sons are all more extreme if anything.”These words were written in 2018 by the Guardian contributor shortly before the election of the far-right former army captainJair Bolsonaroas president of Brazil – a prospect that Dom viewed with dread.As he predicted back then, this would lead to more mortalities, more destruction of theAmazon rainforestand more danger for journalists. His own life and death were to prove the prescience of this foresight.Dom was killed four years ago alongside the Brazilian indigenous expert Bruno Pereira, but his views feel alarmingly relevant once more as Brazil braces for a presidential runoff this Sunday in which a member of the far-right Bolsonaro clan is once more a favourite to win – despite all thedangers that posesto the environment and those who seek to protect it.One year after the deaths of Bruno Pereira and Dom Phillips, their work must go onRead morePolls suggest Flávio Bolsonaro – the son of Jair Bolsonaro – is narrowly ahead of the Workers party incumbentLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Although the difference between them is within the margin of error and Lula appears to have gained momentum, the possibility of another Bolsonaro administration is likely to fill any friends of Dom and Bruno with alarm.Dom was no diehard political leftist. In an earlier election, he shocked me by expressing support for the centre-right challenger Aécio Neves because he felt the then Workers party administration had become too entangled in corruption. But while Dom eschewed ideology, he had clear ideas about the importance of sound, considerate government in the interests of people and the planet.He saw the Bolsonaro family as a menace to both. Looking back through our exchanges of WhatsApp messages, I am struck by the prescience of his observations.Some may be inclined to normalise Flávio as just another candidate, or to assume that all politicians are as bad as each other. That was certainly not how Dom saw things – and he came to pay the ultimate price for his efforts to address those concerns.“I don’t think I have ever been so negative about Brazil’s future. Spent a week in Manaus, everyone seemed to be voting for Bolsonaro,” he wrote ahead of the first-round vote in 2018. “ If he wins, what would it be like living here? It’s like a ‘carte blanche’ to attack anyone his mob disagrees with.”‘This is a lethal threat’: Indigenous groups fear Bolsonaro’s hold on voters in Brazil’s Amazon townsRead moreTwo weeks later, he observed the creeping hostility towards the media at a Bolsonaro press conference, which he said was packed with rightwing supporters who loudly booed a journalist that they considered unfriendly.This followed a physical attack on the organiser of an anti-Bolsonaro women’s group. “Chilling times here,” he wrote on 12 October of that year.“I agree that Bolso shows all signs of fascism, as do his supporters.“This is a very dark and worrying period and it is only going to get worse. My sense if [sic] that it is also going to become more dangerous for journalists.”He detailed the changes he was already seeing – the proliferation of lies, a hardening of discourse online and a rising sense that violence was acceptable. He predicted more people would die as a result of Bolsonaro’s policies, and the wider environment would also pay a heavy price.Over the following years, Dom’s reports for the Guardian confirmed his worst fears. Bolsonaro’s mismanaged response to the Covid crisis contributed to more than 704,000 deaths – the second highest toll in the world after the US.His four years in power saw the highest level of Amazon deforestation of any presidential terms. Orwellian misinformation campaignsincluded efforts toblame environmental groups for forest firesand to boast – contrary to all the evidence – that hisgovernment was saving the Amazon.In August 2019, Dom told me these claims were “staggering even by Bolsonaro standards, especially given Flávio Bolsonaro’s bill to get rid of legal reserves”, the latter a reference to a proposal by the then president’s son – and now presidential candidate – to remove one of the greatest protections for the rainforest.Dom also came under social media attack after he politely asked the president about Amazon deforestation at a press conference. Bolsonaro snapped back, “the Amazon is Brazil’s, not yours, OK?” – a reply that was instantly spread across networks to suggest the nationalist had bested the foreigner.Dom felt he had been set up. “The smile doesn’t last for long,” he observed. “Wonder how much of the Amazon will be gone by the end of Bolsonaro’s first term?”Brazil’s election and the battle for the Amazon – podcastRead moreThat answer to that question would be 45,000 sq km (17,400 sq miles) over Bolsonaro’s 2019-2022 period in office, roughly equivalent to the loss of more than a million trees a day, and 59.5% higher than the previous four years.Dom never got to report on that. He too was cut down, murdered alongside Bruno on 5 May 2022 close to the Javari Valley indigenous territory while he was researching a book titled How to Save the Amazon.The man who confessed to their killing was a fisher named Amarildo da Costa de Oliveira, who is now on trial. He apparently resented Bruno’s efforts to prevent him invading the indigenous territory, incursions that wereillegal but encouragedby the president’s weakening of protections, rhetoric against environmental groups and tacit acceptance of lawlessness. As Dom had foreseen, Bolsonaro had made life more dangerous for journalists and the forest.Jair Bolsonaro lost office later that year and was then convicted for attempting a military coup to overturn the election results. Dom had also anticipated this: “He is a criminal and I sincerely hope one day I see him being arrested by those federal police guys in the balaclavas in black,” he wrote in 2021.I am sure Dom would have been cheered bylast week’s government announcementof record low deforestation in the Amazon and the neighbouring Cerrado savanna thanks to strong enforcement during Lula’s current four-year term.Such gains look precarious now that one of Bolsonaro’s “more extreme” sons is frontrunner in the presidential runoff and has promised, if he wins, to free his father and give him any job of his choice in the government.Is there time for Lula to turn this around? How much worse could a second Bolsonaro family administration be? How much life – people, trees and other species – will die if they return to power?I wish Dom were still around to discuss that.Explore more on these topicsBrazilJair BolsonaroFlávio BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasDom Phillips and Bruno PereiraAmazon rainforestfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cuts mean jobs’: Skydance staff brace for shake-up after $110bn megamerger | Media | The Guardian
description: Battle far from over after Paramount and Warner Bros deal creates new global entertainment powerhouse
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Battle far from over after Paramount and Warner Bros deal creates new global entertainment powerhouse
Content: Skydance chief executive David Ellison described the process, which faced political and industry opposition, as ‘downright ugly’ at times.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreenSkydance chief executive David Ellison described the process, which faced political and industry opposition, as ‘downright ugly’ at times.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersMedia‘Cuts mean jobs’: Skydance staff brace for shake-up after $110bn megamergerBattle far from over after Paramount and Warner Bros deal creates new global entertainment powerhouseMark SweneySat 24 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 10.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It feels like the calm before the storm,” says an executive at Skydance, the newly minted media empire formed from the megamerger of Paramount andWarner BrosDiscovery (WBD). “David has got what he wanted, but now there is a price to pay.”Earlier this month, David Ellison, Skydance’s chief executive,sealed the $110bn (£82bn) deal, creating a global powerhouse spanning two Hollywood studios each more than a century old, the TV networks HBO, MTV and Discovery, and news outlets CBS and CNN.Havingseen off a rival bid from Netflixand faced significant political and industry opposition, in a process Ellison told employees was at times “downright ugly”, the battle is far from over for Hollywood’s newest magnate.With an aggressive target of reducing an eyewatering debt load of more than $80bn in just three years, it is what is going to be cut, sold and restructured that will be uppermost in the minds of Skydance’s more than 53,000 employees.Ellison, 43, who studied film and acted in the 2006 film Flyboys before moving into producing, is targeting $6bn in savings within three years. Executives and financial backers are steering away from the need for swingeing job losses, but a memo from management earlier this month warned that there would be “difficult decisions that affect our workforce”.“It is business as usual but, to be honest, everyone is worried about what happens next,” says another Skydance executive. “Cuts inevitably mean jobs.”View image in fullscreenParamount came under fire for cancelling the long-running Late Show with Stephen Colbert.Photograph: CBSThere are also concerns about the political direction of the new entity, given Ellison’s closeness to Donald Trump – a longtime friend of his father, Larry, who co-founded the software company Oracle. David Ellison haspushed back at such framing, stating: “We do not want to politicise the company.”Nevertheless, fears in the news division have been stoked by events at Paramount before the merger. It came under fire forcancelling the long-running Late Show with Stephen Colbertafter its host said it had paid a “big fat bribe” for settling a $16m lawsuit with Trump.Days later, US regulators agreed the$8.4bn merger of Paramount with Ellison’s Skydance Media, with Trump ally Kenneth Weinstein’s appointment as ombudsman at CBS News to root out “complaints of bias” as one of the conditions to get regulatory approval.Christiane Amanpour, CNN’s international anchor, criticised the “ideological realignment of CBS” and warned that changes and cuts could lead to the potential “destruction” of flagship news show 60 Minutes. This week, she announced she was leaving CNN after 43 years, although her exit is not thought to be tied to the new ownership.CNN staff were relieved at Skydance’s decision shortly after closing the dealto keep Mark Thompson, the former New York Times boss and BBC director general, as chair and chief executive.Many had feared that the network, which alongside MS Now and Politico had faceda now-lifted White House media banin apparent retaliation for critical coverage of Trump, might face a sweeping overhaul that could have seen the divisive Bari Weiss,the editor in chief of CBS News, installed at the top.View image in fullscreenCNN’s international anchor, Christiane Amanpour, announced she was leaving CNN this week after 43 years.Photograph: Brent Stirton/ASSOCIATED PRESSWhile Thompson has said that Skydance supports CNN’s independence, fresh concerns over rightwing influence emerged this week when it was reported that Elon Musk, a Trump ally andsupporter of far-right causesthrough his X platform, has invested $1bn for a stake in the media conglomerate.“The preservation of editorial independence is a growing concern among media consumers,” said Mike Proulx, an analyst at Forrester. “Private wealth is getting a greater foothold on public information channels.”In terms of creative television output, star performers such as HBO will be left to keep churning out the all-important hits the business needs.Ellison immediately extended the soon-to-expire contract of Casey Bloys, promoting the HBO boss to also oversee streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max, to ensure the golden goose keeps making must-watch dramas such as The White Lotus, Game of Thrones, The Pitt, Succession and The Sopranos.However, there are longer-term questions over some of the group’s cable and TV channels – such as MTV, Nickelodeon, the UK’s Channel 5 and Network 10 in Australia – which are in decline but still account for 70% of profits, according to CreditSights.“In a world where the majority of consumers can access content through a smart TV, it should be a natural consideration to sell physical broadcast assets,” said Brian Wieser, chief executive of consultancy Madison and Wall.“At a Skydance level they have made the choice to go all in on streaming. But the problem you have is maybe you don’t get offered enough to sell it, and, given the cashflow we know they make, they might be better served to hold on.”Newly filed accounts for Channel 5 show the broadcaster paid a £215m dividend to Paramount last year. In the UK, the culture secretary only cleared the takeoverafter Ellison made commitmentsincluding pledging to keep Channel 5 operating as a free-to-air, public service broadcaster until at least the end of 2034. However, according to sources, these agreements do not preclude any potential sale of Channel 5 in the future.Last month, Paramount moved its £300m TV advertising sales business from Sky’s sales team to Channel 4. That came after WBD extended its deal for Sky to handle its £90m-£100m ad sales business from January, covering TNT Sports, Discovery, Animal Planet and streaming service HBO Max. However, multiple media sources believe now the Skydance deal is done the business will eventually also move to Channel 4.The megamerger also paves the way for BT to exit its joint venture with WBD – TNT Sports – which would finally end the telecoms company’s costly foray into pay-TV sport after almost 15 years.Last year, Paramount outbid WBD for the rights to Champions League football, the flagship rights owned by TNT Sports. That blow prompted BT to write off the entire value of its stake in the joint venture.However, with Ellison intending to merge Paramount+ with HBO Max, the rights will effectively be retained, and viewers will not have to sign up to yet another streaming or pay-TV service to watch all top-flight football.View image in fullscreenWarner is enduring one of its worst box office showings for years, the most recent flop being Tom Cruise’s Digger.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/APSkydance says it will spend an estimated $30bn a year on content across all divisions, and as part of the takeover Ellison promised to release at least 30 major films a year until 2031.This promises to be a boon for the UK production industry, especially for WBD’s studio at Leavesden, which is home to all of its DC superhero franchises and theforthcoming Harry Potter TV series destined for HBO Max this Christmas.However, Warner is enduring one of its worst box office showings for years, the most recent flopbeing Tom Cruise’s Digger, prompting Ellison to put Paramount’s leadership in charge of both studios.Analysts point out that Ellison is unlikely to maintain that level of moviemaking beyond the five-year pledge, as it goes against the grain of a Hollywood trend towards fewer films and lessons from past takeovers.Since Disney’s acquisition of Rupert Murdoch’s entertainment assets in 2019, which included the then 20th Century Fox and Fox Searchlight studios, the number of film releases has broadly halved.“After the 2031 deal ends there will be fewer films, obviously,” says Tom Harrington, a media analyst at Enders. “It has never happened before when there has been a takeover that more have ended up being made.”Skydance declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsMediaParamount+Paramount PicturesWarner BrosfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My mother donated her body to science. I really wasn’t prepared for what came next | Death and dying | The Guardian
description: The process included a gala featuring medical students doing aerial yoga and singing Taylor Swift to donors’ families. In some ways, it was absolutely perfect
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The process included a gala featuring medical students doing aerial yoga and singing Taylor Swift to donors’ families. In some ways, it was absolutely perfect
Content: ‘My mom was 40 when she started physical therapy school. The year she took anatomy lab she told my sister and me … when she died, she wanted to donate her body to science, too.’Illustration: Ibrahim Rayintakath/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘My mom was 40 when she started physical therapy school. The year she took anatomy lab she told my sister and me … when she died, she wanted to donate her body to science, too.’Illustration: Ibrahim Rayintakath/The GuardianMemento mori: a series about deathDeath and dyingMy mother donated her body to science. I really wasn’t prepared for what came nextThe process included a gala featuring medical students doing aerial yoga and singing Taylor Swift to donors’ families. In some ways, it was absolutely perfectMeaghan O'ConnellSat 24 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 20.18 EDTShareWhen my mother, Erin O’Connell, was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive cancer in late 2022, one of her first thoughts was: “What will I do if I can’t work?”At the time, she was 62 years old and working as a physical therapist in Portland, Oregon, where she had recently moved to live closer to me and my family. Reluctantly, she filed for short-term disability from her job and paused her training to become a volunteer search and rescue EMT.My mom was 40 when she started physical therapy school. I was already a teenager. Despite her newfound stress, I remember how deeply it affected me to watch her fall in love with her work. The year she took anatomy lab she told my sister and me – and anyone who would listen – that dissecting a real human body was the coolest thing she had ever gotten to do, and when she died, she wanted to donate her body to science, too.I spent so much of my childhood wanting nothing more than my mother’s hard-earned approval, and here she was, utterly devoted to a dead body. On some level, I was jealous of that cadaver.The last thing I did for my mother was illegalRead moreNow here I was, 25 years later, with my mom’s illness progressing, printing out the paperwork from the nearest med school: “Enrollment Form To Bequeath a Body On Behalf of an Individual”. And all I could think was how jealous I would be of the students who would dissect my mother – who would get to do what I never could, crack her open and peek inside.This paperwork, though, was its own form of clarity. My mom was going to die, too young and against her will, but we had a plan – an easy, free, meaningful one at that.Of course, the reality ended up being more complicated and more absurd than I imagined.After her death, my mom’s body was transported to Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU), just across the river from where we had both lived in Portland.I worried that, in my grief, I might drive to campus to find out where she was. Would I be tempted to wander the halls, looking for her? Better not to dwell on it, I decided. Instead, I imagined she had been shipped elsewhere, used for something vaguely embarrassing like rectal science or dentistry.Every year, roughly 25,000 Americans sign up to donate their bodies to science after death. But demand far outstrips supply. According to Tamara Ostervoss, director of OHSU’s body donation program, “it remains an unpopular choice,” partly becauseso few people even know it’s an option. In Oregon, she told me, only about 1% of people choose to donate their bodies.For my mom, theregistration processwas simple: a two-page consent form, signed in front of two witnesses. My mom agreed that her family would not profit from the donation or any discoveries that resulted from it, and that we would have no say in how her body was used. She chose to have her remains cremated and mailed back to us. Eighteen months later, they arrived in a red, white and blue US Postal Service box marked “HUMAN REMAINS”, with an illustration of an urn on the side.By the time I spoke to Ostervoss, the remains were safely in my closet – and I had a darkly funny story about my awkward visit to the post office to prove it.Still, talking to the woman who had overseen my mom’s donation was emotionally fraught. As Ostervoss likes to say, your life dictates how you go on to teach others. Thanks to the progression of her cancer, my mom was missing so many internal organs by the end that I joked she would have given some poor anatomy student a pretty limited education.It’s a credit to Ostervoss’s professional, respectful demeanor that she didn’t laugh so much as smile warmly, with pity in her eyes.I didn’t tell her that, when my mom was still alive, I had asked her how she would feel if she ended up sold to one of those Bodies exhibits from China. Would my kids recognize her without her skin on?She laughed, then shrugged. “What do I care? I won’t be there.”But I will be,I wanted to say.You can decide what happens to your body after you die, if you’re willing to plan ahead. But that doesn’t necessarily mean that, once you’re no longer there to insist, your family will follow through with your plans.If your loved ones are firmly opposed to body donation, they can simply call a funeral home instead. Which is why, if you’re considering donating your body to science, it’s a conversation worth having while you’re still alive.Most families, though, fall somewhere in the squeamish-but-accepting middle. “We’ve had families where they might not choose it for themselves, but they really want to honor and support their loved ones’ wishes,” Ostervoss said. “So they’re more along the lines of, “I don’t want to hear anything about it, I don’t want to know about it. I just want to support my mom.”double quotation markWas it odd to feel jubilant on the same day I watched my mother take her final breath?For me, the mild unease of never knowing exactly what happened to my mom’s corpse at the university was peanuts compared with the prospect of being upsold a coffin by a funeral director while I waded through grief. According to theNational Funeral Directors Association, the average cost of burial in our home state of Oregon is $7,895 and the average cost of cremation is $5,812 – numbers that don’t even include a funeral or memorial service.With body donation, you can always do a memorial later, but in the meantime there are no grief-stricken decisions about embalming or viewings. No deciding what goes on the gravestone, no grave. What does happen is a brief phone screening (in our case, by a hospice nurse), followed by a brief, in-person physical assessment. Then, voilà, off my mom went to fulfill her destiny as, in the language of the body program, someone’s first patient.The reality is that about 25% of registered donors don’t meet the eligibility requirements at the time of death, per Ostervoss’ estimate. “It’s like medical school,” she said, “Not everyone gets in.”A common disqualifier is high or low body weight, and privately my sister and I feared my mom had lost too much to be accepted. When she was, I found myself literally jumping up in the air to cheer. “She passed her final test!” I wrote to her sibling group chat, triumphantly. “PTL!” her sister wrote back. Praise the Lord!Was it odd to feel jubilant on the same day I watched my mother take her final breath? Absolutely, but it was also a gift. It really did feel like her version of a med school acceptance, I told Ostervoss.Those 150 bodies who do “get in” are able to go on to teach approximately 5,000 learners across the state of Oregon, encompassing not just the first-year medical students you might think of, but surgical residents and practicing doctors, dentists and other healthcare workers.For students, the benefits of learning about human anatomy and practicing procedures on the real thing, with no risk of hurting them, are intuitive and obvious – the difference between a flight simulator and piloting an airplane. Think of all the variation in vasculature and body size. In reality, no surgeon would see the same internal organs twice. It’s the kind of thing that can’t be replicated, not even with advanced 3D models with haptic feedback.The emotional side of the student experience is another story. Facing your cadaver for the first time as a new med student has always been a rite of passage, but as western life expectancy increases and our end-of-life rituals become more and more sanitized, anatomy lab is more and more often students’ first encounter with a dead person.Historically, med school programs have dealt with this by cultivating what the writerMary Roachcalls “a sort of sink or swim mentality about dealing with death”, a kind of future doctor hazing ritual that encouraged future providers to desensitize themselves.Roach talked to the director of the medical anatomy program at Vanderbilt University, Art Dalley, who says that, “There was a time not all that long ago when students were taught to be insensitive, as a coping mechanism.” In the past, she writes: “Humor – at the cadaver’s expense – was tolerated, condoned, even.”Not so in our current era. Instead, I received an invitation to a gala in the mail.At OHSU, the anatomy class culminates in what Ostervoss calls, “the body ceremony”, a 25-year tradition where students plan a memorial to honor the donors and families who have made their education possible.The service was created to honor the donors, but it’s also important emotionally for the students who are encouraged to have conversations with the families at the reception afterward.After a year of almost willful dissociation on my part, it was a bizarre experience to be welcomed in. The invite explained that the service would include a slideshow of the 100 or so donors who had given their bodies that year. Students would show their gratitude through performances and reflections they had programmed themselves.It sounded bizarre but earnest, like a talent show for death. I was thrilled.Once we were in the auditorium, my eyes darted over to the section of nervous future doctors in new blazers and kitten heels. There was a kind of aura of promise about them, and I felt almost maternally proud. It was clear that families and students had a wild interest in each other and my heart raced as I scanned the rows, looking, as I imagine they did, for some glint of recognition.I leaned over to whisper to my sister, a note of hope in my voice. “Do you think they’ll recognize us?”“Meaghan,” she shushed me. “No.”“But maybe our height?” (My mother, like us, was around 5ft tall with shoes on.)Lauren just gave me a look and I went back to studying the program.In accordance with HIPAA laws, no one would tell us who dissected whom. It was clear what a bizarre human exchange we had been party to, despite never having met. It had to be acknowledged, ritualized. Otherwise, it made no sense.Not that a collective death talent show made a whole lot of sense either. As the students took the stage to share their talents – someone played Taylor Swift’s Bigger Than The Whole Sky, a member of the school of dentistry’s class of 2028 sang Sweet Creature by Harry Styles – I wanted to feel something like closure, but all I could muster was affectionate bemusement.Who were these children, I wondered, and what did they know about death?When two svelte near-adults took the stage in spandex (their leggings a respectful shade of black) and did what I can only assume was aerial yoga accompanied by Debussy, I had to avoid eye contact with my sister to avoid laughing. Still, as they balanced on each other’s shoulders and knees in midair, I had the urge to text my mom, to tell her how weird it was. I wished I believed she could see it. I know she would have thought it was cool.When a chaplain got to the podium. “We know that your loved one’s participation in this program has probably complicated your grief, and prolonged it.” She talked about how when someone dies, there is a human need for closure, and we families probably hadn’t quite gotten it yet. They wanted to acknowledge the sacrifice we had made.Truthfully, I hadn’t thought of it as a sacrifice at the time, more like a “get out of jail free” card, but I was beginning to understand. The chaplain’s words reminded me of the recurring dreams I had had after the two polite, somber men had taken my mom’s body away in a sprinter van. In real life, my sister and I had watched her take her last breath. When it happened it was so obvious, on an almost existential level, that to check her pulse would have been absurd. We didn’t need a nurse to come out. We declared her dead ourselves.In sleep, though, my subconscious had its say. In recurring dreams, my mom would show up, back from the morgue and on her doorstep again, a little worse for the wear. She would push past us to get inside, clearly miffed we had sent her away prematurely.After enough of these dreams, I came to understand why we bury our dead. Sure, no onewantsthe finality of loss but maybe the brain has a hard time moving on without it. It wasn’t until the chaplain alluded to this that that I realized that the lack of closure was exactly what I wanted. I didn’twantto move on. The ambiguity, the mystery even, meant the story of my mother wasn’t over yet.Near the end of the ceremony, families were invited up to speak. When it was my turn, I gripped the podium, shaky-voiced but not crying. I remember knowing for certain what my mom would want me to say.‘You’re honoring a life well-lived’: embalmers describe their work (in great detail)Read moreI told the students about my mom’s own experience in anatomy lab, all those years ago. The way our dining room had been overtaken by her schoolwork – the table strewn with flash cards and textbooks, colored-pencil anatomical drawings papering the walls. Those years we would find candy corn and York peppermint patty wrappers in the couch cushions – Mom’s study snack of choice.She was more scatterbrained and short-tempered than ever, but I loved watching her find something she loved, something that was only hers. She learned a kind of devotion, then, an awe that would stay with her even in the darkest days of her illness.I told them that they would have this, too.A few weeks ago, after getting up the nerve to ask Ostervoss, I signed a HIPAA form and a media release to find out how my mom’s body came to be of use after she died. Five days later, a media relations specialist from the university forwarded me the answer in the body of an email. It read:During her time with us, Erin played a crucial role in teaching spine anatomy, associated surgical techniques, and stereotactic and functional neurosurgery skills at OHSU. Through these educational experiences, neurosurgery and neurology trainees gained greater foundational knowledge that will inform their patient care throughout their careers.After supporting these learners, she went on to teach in several orthopedic residency training courses.In total, 121 learners directly benefited from your mother’s gift. Her legacy will live on through countless patients cared for by the healthcare professionals she helped educate.Reading it, I felt the thrill of new information, of something happening in the world of my mother.Then came the pang of loss, knowing that the one person who would truly appreciate this information was necessarily not available to receive it.She would think it was so cool. She would have loved to know all of it.Explore more on these topicsDeath and dyingMemento mori: a series about deathWell actuallyMedical researchAnatomy and physiologyShare

title: Outback kaleidoscope: Australia’s fabled desert lake bursts to life in rare sight | Environment | The Guardian
description: A prodigiously wet monsoon season has brought damaging floods to parts of Australia, but transformed Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre in a way not seen in decades
Author: Blake Sharp-Wiggins
Headline: A prodigiously wet monsoon season has brought damaging floods to parts of Australia, but transformed Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre in a way not seen in decades
Content: An arresting sight: green water surrounds Silcrete Island in South Australia’s vast Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn arresting sight: green water surrounds Silcrete Island in South Australia’s vast Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianEnvironmentOutback kaleidoscope: Australia’s fabled desert lake bursts to life in rare sightA prodigiously wet monsoon season has brought damaging floods to parts of Australia, but transformed Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre in a way not seen in decadesAdam Mortonwith photography byBlake Sharp-WigginsSat 24 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTShareThe Australian desert is green. Not just green – depending on where you look from above, it could also be a marbled reddy-pink and blue or yellow-brown with flecks of purple. But green is the most striking colour because the desert is not supposed to look like this.It won’t last. But for now, in late September, the deep outback – a celebrated part of the Australian continent that few people get to see – is blanketed in plant life. There is sandhill wattle, saltbush and lignum, and grasses and desert flowers. The vegetation is thickest along hundreds of twisting rivers and creeks that cut across the landscape.View image in fullscreenWater twists and turns through a lush green landscapePhotograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianThese rivers and creeks carry water from a prodigiously wet monsoon season that brought flooding rains to western Queensland. Rainfall nearly50% above the long-term averagecaused havoc, killing livestock and cutting outback tracks, some of which remain underwater. But it also filled up three major river systems – the Georgina, the Diamantina and Cooper Creek.View image in fullscreenThe outback is blanketed in colour as flood waters fill rivers and creeksView image in fullscreenSturt’s Desert Pea grows along the Oodnadatta Track.They run to one place: Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre. Local rainfall, which persisted between March and August, added to the flow. The result is that the centre of the continent is being transformed in a way that hasn’t happened since 1974.Taking offWe are flying north in a six-seater light aircraft from William Creek, a tiny outpost that operates as something like an independent kingdom in the middle of Anna Creek station, the world’s largest cattle property. At nearly 24,000 sq km, Anna Creek is bigger than Wales.View image in fullscreenThe sun sets in William Creek in South Australia.William Creek is much, much smaller. Lying on the traditional lands of the Arabana people, and owned by charter flight operator and unofficial mayor Trevor Wright, it has about a dozen buildings, huddled together in a vain attempt to shelter from the elements, about halfway along the famed Oodnadatta Track.View image in fullscreenTrevor Wright stands on a ridge overlooking William CreekKati Thanda is about 60km north-east of the town. They are separated by the Tirari Desert, which now looks more like scrubby parts of the coastal east than arid backcountry.After a few minutes the lake appears on the horizon like an ocean. Soon, mirror-like water is all we can see as the horizon disappears.View image in fullscreenThe south-west shore of Lake Eyre appears on the horizonIt’s Australia’s largest lake by surface area. Stretching 144km in length and 77km in width, it covers about 9,500 sq km – almost as much as suburban Melbourne. It includes the country’s lowest point, about 15 metres below sea level.Kati Thanda is endorheic, meaning the water it collects has nowhere to drain. Most of the water from the region’s river systems enters via the Warburton Creek. Once in the lake it becomes the Warburton Groove, a north-south geological channel that paints a dark band as it spreads across the lake for up to 90km.View image in fullscreenThe deep Warburton Groove cuts through the still water of the lake.From lake to salt plainIt empties by evaporation, sometimes at an astonishing rate, losing up to 1cm of depth a day. Given the infrequency of the sort of heavy rains experienced this year, it is empty most of the time. When it is, it turns into a vast salt plain.Its crust is estimated to be made up of 400m tonnes of salt. The salt flats not underwater, mainly in the north, shimmer with vibrant white. They are stable enough when completely dry for British driver Donald Campbell to have chosen it as the place to set a land speed record of 648 km/h in 1964.View image in fullscreenSalt lakes create unique patterns in the landscapeWhen we visit, the salinity of the lake is roughly equivalent to an ocean. Soon, as evaporation kicks in, it will be as much as seven times saltier than the Coral Sea.
