Content: An England fan holds up a sign saying ‘Harry's #1 fan’. The Bayern Munich and Three Lions striker’s consistency and longevity are compelling reasons for him to be this year’s Ballon d’Or winner.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn England fan holds up a sign saying ‘Harry's #1 fan’. The Bayern Munich and Three Lions striker’s consistency and longevity are compelling reasons for him to be this year’s Ballon d’Or winner.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesInside footballHarry KaneWhy Stanley Matthews’ Ballon d’Or triumph echoes down the years for Harry KaneJonathan WilsonIn 1956, the Blackpool great was recognised for his force of individual will, the very thing that makes the Bayern and England striker the standout candiateSat 24 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTShareSystems football began In 1963(On the hallowed turf at Wembley)With the impact of a cynical foulBy Gino Pivatelli.At that moment in the European Cup final, when the hard-working Milan forward, brought in to combat Benfica’s Mário Coluna, caught the great playmaker, football of the individual came to an end. The foul not only checked a promising break, but broke a bone in Coluna’s foot. Without substitutes, he hobbled on, diminished, and Milan won 2-1 to lift the trophy and register the first victory for a team that prioritised the system over the individual. Modern football was born.There are degrees, of course. The success of Zinedine Zidane’s Real Madrid was far more predicated on individuals than that of, say, Thomas Tuchel’s Chelsea or Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City. But, fundamentally, since that first success forcatenaccio, football has been resolutely a team game.Which is what always makes individual awards in the game such an oddity. Even in successful teams there is often a tension between the individual and the collective. That can be productive – sparks of friction are often creative. In sides that disappoint, though, the issue, whether the result of his own ego or the shortcomings of his teammates, is often an overreliance on one individual.View image in fullscreenStanley Matthews was the first Ballon d’Or winner despite his club Blackpool’s relative lack of success.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesWhen the Ballon d’Or launched in 1956, that paradox was less pronounced. If the decision back then was less contentious than Monday’s award will assuredly be, though, it can only have been because there was no social media on which the furious could vent.That the Hungarian vote was split between Ferenc Puskás, József Bozsik and Sándor Kocsis immediately highlighted a problem that successful teams still face, although given the award was made a month after the uprising was crushed by and Soviet tanks entering Budapest, with two of the three players in the process of defecting, it was probably just as well for the magazine France Football that none of the Hungarians did triumph.Still, the choice ofStanley Matthews, from today’s perspective, looks odd. While it is true Blackpool had finished second in the First Division in 1956, but they were 11 points behind Manchester United and had gone out of the FA Cup in the third round. Was there not a case for Duncan Edwards or Tommy Taylor? Or for Bert Trautmann, the goalkeeper who won the Football Writers’ player of the year in 1956 after playing on with a broken neck in the final as Manchester City lifted the Cup?Looking beyond England, what ofAlfredo Di Stéfano, who had inspired Real Madrid to the inaugural European Cup? Or one of the Athletic Bilbao players who had just won La Liga? Or Pivatelli, who had been top-scorer in Serie A? Or Giuliano Sarti, the goalkeeper who had won the Scudetto with Fiorentina? Or Nikita Simonyan, whose goals had powered Spartak Moscow to the Soviet title? Matthews was 38, and there’s a clear sense that the inaugural Ballon d’Or was something of a lifetime achievement award.Perhaps that is fine. Maybe the award should recognise longevity. What, after all, is it for? It’s certainly not just about how much a player wins in a given year. If it were, Fabián Ruiz would be a hot favourite on Monday, having won the World Cup, the Champions League and Ligue 1 this season.Yet fine player though the midfielder undoubtedly is, he would be neither Paris Saint-Germain nor Spain’s player of the season. Besides, an award for winning lots of other awards is the definition of gilding the lily. There’s perhaps even an argument that individual awards represent an opportunity to acknowledge those who strive and delight but rarely win medals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChaotic state of football in Brazil epitomises a nation where greed has conquered glory | Jonathan LiewRead moreAccording to its website, the Ballon d’Or is “awarded based on three essential pillars … individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.” The “complete” winner will be defined by a “combination of talent, sportsmanship and competitive excellence”.Team achievement is perhaps easiest to isolate. PSG have largely ditched their egos as Luis Enrique has led them to back-to-back Champions Leagues, but how do you tease out which of their exceptional front three has been the most important?Ousmane Dembélé won that battle last year. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia was arguably the standout this year, but, in a World Cup year, can a player whose country didn’t qualify be regarded as the best individual? And neither Dembélé nor the other member of the trio, Desiré Doué, had an especially notable World Cup.Given the relative level of the French league and the fact PSG can rest players for domestic games to keep them fresh for Europe, it’s arguable the greatest achievement by a European club last season came from Arsenal, as they won the Premier League and reached the Champions League final. But their strength is the collective, and only three of the 30-man shortlist are Arsenal players, but none of Gabriel, William Saliba or Declan Rice had stellar World Cups.What then of Spain? They too are a team short on star quality, certainly when Lamine Yamal is carrying an injury as he did for the first few months of this year. They won the World Cup, ultimately, because of the collective strength of their midfield. Rodri is the embodiment of their approach, but his involvement at Manchester City in the second half of last season was restricted.View image in fullscreenBayern Munich’s Harry Kane heads home against Stuttgart: 61 in 51 club games last season represents a remarkable record.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersReal Madrid have just endured one of only five trophyless seasons this century, which weakens the claims of Kylian Mbappé and Jude Bellingham and Vinícius. Lionel Messi had great moments at the World Cup but playing in MLS reduces his chances. Which perhaps means it’s time again to reward somebody who has had a good year, even if he went out of the World Cup in the semis and the Champions League in the quarters:Harry Kane.Goals in the Bundesliga may not quite have the currency they did when Karl-Heinz Rummenigge was scoring them, but 61 in 51 club games last season represents a remarkable record, and he also got six at the World Cup, winning the game against the Democratic Republic of the Congo almost by force of individual will.In a season without an obvious outstanding candidate, there seems a strong possibility that the panel, just as it did in 1956, will reward consistency and longevity.Explore more on these topicsHarry KaneInside footballEnglandBayern MunichBallon d'OrcommentShareReuse this content

title: Leicester turn up the hostility as Steward caps old-time beating of Northampton  | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Leicester scored four unanswered tries in the second half to overturn a 7-3 interval deficit and beat Northampton 28-7 in the Prem
Author: Michael Aylwin
Headline: Leicester scored four unanswered tries in the second half to overturn a 7-3 interval deficit and beat Northampton 28-7 in the Prem
Content: Try-scorer Finn Carnduff roars his approval as Leicester run riot in the second half.Photograph: Cat Goryn/INPHO/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTry-scorer Finn Carnduff roars his approval as Leicester run riot in the second half.Photograph: Cat Goryn/INPHO/ShutterstockPrem RugbyLeicester turn up the hostility as Steward caps old-time beating of NorthamptonLeicester 28-7 NorthamptonHosts score four unanswered tries after intervalMichael Aylwinat Mattioli Woods Welford RoadSat 24 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 12.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe have seen this before. It is easy to forget, amid all the tries and sunshine, that rugby has a darker side too: a wet, windy, deafening ferocity that not even the most twinkle-toed can transcend. And they practically invented it here.This is not the first timeLeicesterhave welcomed their beloved neighbours to the lair as champions and disabused them of any notions of grandeur. It took the Tigers 40 minutes to whip themselves into the necessary fervour, but when they did, all else followed: the rocking stadium at capacity, the win, the bonus point, the obliterated opposition.Will Borthwick’s autumn England squad embrace Prem chaos or prioritise prudence? | Gerard MeagherRead more“The crowd was brilliant,” said Geoff Parling, Leicester’s head coach. “The crowd is outstanding. This stadium is iconic. It’s rustic, I know it is. I’ve said it before. It’s old. But I wouldn’t change it for the world.”It was not just the 40 minutes of directionless fumbling by the home team, but a mass fracas with a number of those visiting friends, which spilled into the stand, that sparked them into life, pretty much from the moment they re-emerged from the break.The second-half Tigers showed the first-half version how a lineout and drive is executed, when Jamie Blamire scored their first try within four minutes of the restart. That earned them a one-point lead and normal service was resumed.Half-time’s highlights analysis probably centred on that, well, we can’t really call them fights these days – this is the age of the camera, after all – but certainly pushing and shoving long after the referee had brought the first half to a close.There were Alex Coles and Freddie Steward at each other’s throats. On it went, up the steps of the Crumbie Stand, where Henry Pollock, obviously, seemed more interested in tying his shoelace than getting in for an orange. Ollie Chessum and Steward, his England teammates, did not find it funny, shoving him all the way to the changing room.“These games are going to be hostile,” said Phil Dowson, theNorthamptoncoach. “In the current game, you can’t throw anything. It’s just push and shove and talk crap. That happens every derby. So I don’t think that had any impact. It’s not as if anyone got filled in. Well, you just can’t any more.”Quick GuideRoundup: Bristol battle past Exeter to climb to thirdShowBristolmoved into third place in the Prem table with a hard-fought 20-7 win overExeterin appalling conditions at Ashton Gate.It was their fifth successive league victory over Rob Baxter’s men after an old-style-rugby war of attrition in heavy rain and strong winds.Bristol took the lead when a long pass by England scrum-half Harry Randall found Gabriel Ibitoye in space on the left wing to cross in the corner.Centre James Williams slotted an excellent touchline conversion and he was also on target with a 35m penalty three minutes later.Exeter got back into the game when they kicked a penalty to the corner and Greg Fisilau was driven over in emphatic style. Henry Slade converted to make it 10-7 and the visitors chances to draw level in the last 10 minutes when they turned down two kickable penalties inside the 22. Bristol made sure of victory three minutes from time when Williams kicked his second penalty and Luka Ivanishvili added some gloss when he forced his way over moments later.On Friday night,Gloucestercontinued their resurgence to remain at the top of the Prem table with a hard-fought 23-5 victory overBathat Kingsholm.The win looked unlikely when Bath dominated for most of the first half, but Gloucester survived for a morale-boosting victory.For Bath, it was a disappointing night as they fell to their third consecutive defeat and lost both Santiago Carreras and Guy Pepper to injuries. Freddie Thomas and Max Llewellyn scored Gloucester’s tries with George Barton converting both and adding three penalties. A try from Kepueli Tuipulotu was Bath’s sole response.Christian Wade equalled Chris Ashton’s top-flight try record to inspireNewcastleto their first win of the season in the Prem. Wade made it 101 tries when he sprinted over in the 49th minute as Newcastle recovered from a 3-0 interval deficit to blowSaleaway 17-3 in a gale at Kingston Park. It drew the 35-year-old winger, capped once by England, level with former Sale wing Ashton, who was inside the stadium.The Newcastle captain, George McGuigan, grabbed the other home try with Josh Hodge adding seven points with the boot. There was little to cheer for Sale, who only had a George Ford penalty to show for their visit to the North East.Press AssociationWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Such discord was in keeping with a first half in which neither side could quite find their feet on the slippery turf. Saints seemed more in tune with the kind of rugby that has prevailed before the rains came. Theirs was the only try of the first half, early on, when Finn Smith, with an advantage, chipped in behind, where Billy Searle spilled and James Pater gathered to score.Leicester could not make anything of a stream of penalties in the first half, sending four of them to the corner in the first quarter and spilling or, often, not even securing the subsequent possession. How that was going to change.Once Blamire’s try had restored order, the Tigers tore through the Saints at set piece and high ball. The champions deteriorated in the swirling rain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCameron Henderson was next to rise to take a lineout, after a ferocious scrum had earned the penalty. Henderson then finished in the corner like a winger, sent away by Gabriel Hamer-Webb. That put Leicester six ahead and five minutes later they were more than a score clear, this time Finn Carnduff finishing after another attacking lineout.Quick GuideLeicester 28-7 Northampton: teams and scorersShowLeicesterSteward (Pearson 79); Radwan, Wand (Bailey 73), Kata, Hamer-Webb; Searle, Van Poortvliet (Whiteley 73); Van der Flier (Haffar 73), Blamire (Asiata 79), Heyes (Hurd 73), Henderson (Thompson 79), O Chessum (capt), Wainwright, Carnduff, Cracknell (Moro 73).TriesBlamire, Henderson, Carnduff, Steward.PensSteward, Searle.ConSearle.NorthamptonPater (Sleightholme 76); Freeman, Hutchinson, Dingwall (capt), Hendy; F Smith, Mitchell (McParland 58); Iyogun (Fischetti 63), Langdon (R Smith 63), Kundiona (Necolai 54), Coles, Prowse (Van der Mescht 63), Kemeny, Pearson (Lockett 58), Pollock (Chick 54).Yellow cardLockett 70.TryPater.ConF Smith.RefereeCraig Maxwell-Keys.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The bonus point came in the final 10 minutes after one of the more bizarre swings of fortune. Smith’s cross-kick had sent George Hendy away from his own 22, Adam Radwan’s slap-down earned him a yellow card. But way back earlier in the move Tom Lockett’s head had collided with Solomone Kata’s. It was another totally innocent accident, Kata not only changing direction, but rising sharply to clash with the covering Lockett.Even by rugby’s standards, the yellow card was absurd punishment. But it also meant Radwan’s was rescinded. On he came, off Lockett went, and over strolled Steward for the bonus point from the subsequent lineout.When it is not your day, it is not your day, Saints must have rued. But when it is your day, especially at this grand stadium in the wet and windy twilight, it really is.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyLeicesterNorthamptonRugby unionmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Winds of change are coming for Australia as selection storm brews in South Africa | Australia cricket team | The Guardian
description: Crushing defeat in second Test raises fresh questions about visitors’ fragile batting lineup before Cape Town decider
Author: Martin Pegan
Headline: Crushing defeat in second Test raises fresh questions about visitors’ fragile batting lineup before Cape Town decider
Content: Marnus Labuschagne is among Australia’s selection dilemmas for the third Test in Cape Town after they were humbled by South Africa in an innings defeat.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarnus Labuschagne is among Australia’s selection dilemmas for the third Test in Cape Town after they were humbled by South Africa in an innings defeat.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesSportblogAustralia cricket teamWinds of change are coming for Australia as selection storm brews in South AfricaCrushing defeat in second Test raises fresh questions about fragile batting lineup before Cape Town deciderMartin PeganSat 24 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 18.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe old adage that it is harder to get out of the Australia cricket team than into it is about to be put to the test. The horror show against South Africa in the second Test that ended indefeat for Australia by an innings and 31 runsexposed familiar fractures in the lineup that have less than a week between matches to be repaired.The Australian selectors have shown in South Africa they are prepared to change a winning formula with the ball, while they have long been reluctant to cut ties with proven performers with the bat. But the first innings capitulation asAustralia were all out for 99in Gqeberha could force their hand to make a tough call or two – or perhaps more – as a selection storm brews before the series decider in Cape Town.South Africa beat Boland and weather to force series decider against AustraliaRead moreMarnus Labuschagne remains a persistent problem though arguably not the most pressing concern with Australia forced to consider other selection dilemmas. Even with three scores in the 30s from four innings in this series against South Africa, Labuschagne’s numbers are damning. So was his decision to loft off-spinner Simon Harmer into a stiff breeze and toward the long on fence when time at the crease was Australia’s only hope of escaping St George’s Park with a series lead.The 32-year-old’s barren spell without a Test century has now extended well beyond three years and he has averaged 22.09 in 47 innings since last raising the bat against England at Old Trafford. He has not averaged more than 40 in a Test series since compiling 207 runs with three half-centuries on home turf against Pakistan in 2023-24. A Test average that sat above 61 in late 2022 has now dropped to 43.36.View image in fullscreenMarnus Labuschagne could be considered to partner Travis Head as Australia search for openers for the Test series decider against South Africa.Photograph: Themba Hadebe/APLabuschagne had been clinging on to his spot since long before he was left out of the side for three Tests against West Indies that followed the 2025 World Test Championship final. Even with the numbers stacked against him, Labuschagne could still be handedone morelast chance with a vacancy widely expected to open at the top of the order to partner Travis Head. The most likely route to another Test lifeline could therefore be for Labuschagne to open the innings in Cape Town, just as he did in the WTC final defeat last year.Cameron Green and Josh Inglis are expected to be available for the third Test after recovering from injuries sustained during the one-day leg of the tour of South Africa. Green is nearing a return after suffering an abdominal strain in the third ODI and spent time batting in the nets as the second Test played out at St George’s Park. The 27-year-old once rivalled Labuschagne as the batter most under pressure, until he earned some credits with a defiant ton and a half-century from No 5 in the drawn series against Bangladesh. Head coach Andrew McDonald has said Green is unlikely to bowl in the Test series against South Africa but his batting alone should be enough to ensure selection, if fit, with Australia needing reinforcements to help fill the top six.View image in fullscreenCameron Green tightened his grip on a spot in Australia’s Test side with a century against Bangladesh in Darwin.Photograph: James Ross/AAPInglis, on the other hand, remains far from a walk-up starter. The keeper-batter has become a mainstay of Australia’s white ball sides but has been unable to make the most of his opportunities in the longest format since a century on debut against Sri Lanka. Cooper Connolly is also back in the frame though the spin-bowling all-rounder’s hopes of adding to his one Test could rest on whether selectors are prepared to back the versatile but underperforming Beau Webster as well as the conditions at Newlands.The three batters forming a queue just as Australia weigh up their options are all best suited to the middle order, just as gaps appear to be forming at the top. The selection gamble to recall Nic Maddinson after almost a decade in the Test wilderness and more than 18 months without first-class cricket, in part while recovering from testicular cancer, has shown few signs of paying off.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 34-year-old looked out of his depth as he returned with a 33-ball duck and even a quick-fire 48 in the second innings in Durban only left a glimmer of hope that better was to come. Kagiso Rabada has troubled more established batters than Maddinson but the manner in which he was dismissed by the South Africa quick for another duck and eight in Gqeberha is likely to bring an abrupt end to the left-handed batter’s shock selection.Golden bat or ball: does cricket need an equivalent to the Ballon d’Or? | Taha HashimRead moreShifting Matt Renshaw back to the top order and letting him settle in a position where he has been comfortable at domestic level could resolve the most glaring issue. It would also open up a spot for Green to return in the middle order while leaving the door ajar to perhaps call in Inglis or Connolly for the third Test against South Africa.Australia have not lost a bilateral Test series since early 2023. They have not been defeated by a side other than India since Pakistan claimed a 1-0 series victory in the wake of “sandpapergate” in the UAE in 2018. The natural flow state of the side under captain Pat Cummins has been to ride out the highs and the lows. But the long journey through the top end of Australia, a tour of South Africa and home series against New Zealand, then the renewal of the tensest of rivalries in India and England already looks like being blown off course. Winds of change are finally coming for the Australia Test team. And this time, even Cummins’ unwavering calm might not be enough to weather the storm.Explore more on these topicsAustralia cricket teamSportblogCricketSouth Africa cricket teamAustralia sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The sexual assault scandal rocked gymnastics – but has pace of change in the sport been too slow? | Gymnastics | The Guardian
description: Former USA team doctor Larry Nassar’s 2018 conviction sparked a global reckoning in gymnastics, yet gymnasts say they are still being let down
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Former USA team doctor Larry Nassar’s 2018 conviction sparked a global reckoning in gymnastics, yet gymnasts say they are still being let down
Content: Simone Biles, Aly Raisman and Maggie Nichols are among many to have suffered abuse in the scandal that rocked gymnastics.Composite: Guardian Pictures; NurPhoto/Getty Images; Getty Images; Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSimone Biles, Aly Raisman and Maggie Nichols are among many to have suffered abuse in the scandal that rocked gymnastics.Composite: Guardian Pictures; NurPhoto/Getty Images; Getty Images; Corbis/Getty ImagesGymnasticsThe sexual assault scandal rocked gymnastics – but has pace of change in the sport been too slow?Former USA team doctor Larry Nassar’s 2018 conviction sparked a global reckoning in gymnastics, yet gymnasts say they are still being let downSuzanne Wrackin RotterdamSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 10.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been 10 years since the Indianapolis Star published allegations of sexual abuse by Larry Nassar, the former team doctor for USAGymnastics, setting off a chain of events that would lead to a reckoning for the sport. Hundreds of women came forward with their own allegations against Nassar, who also worked at Michigan State University, leading to his conviction and jailing.The exposure of his crimes sparked a wider investigation into how gymnastics had allowed predators to abuse young athletes around the world. While Nassar was the worst recorded case, it emerged many other countries had questions to answer about the failure to protect victims from not only sexual but physical and emotional abuse. But a decade later, on a large houseboat moored in Rotterdam three tram stops away from the Ahoy Arena, where the World Gymnastics Championships are taking place this week, survivors and advocates raised fears about the slow pace of change.The impact of the Nassar case was seismic, not least because of the decision of Judge Rosemarie Aquilina, on agreeing to Nassar’s plea deal, to allow his victims to have their say in her courtroom. People tuned into Aquilina’s courtroom from all over the world to watch as 169 people took to the stand across seven days, delivering blistering, emotionally charged and brave testimonies of Nassar’s abuse and the impact of that abuse. Aquilina sentenced him to up to 175 years in jail with other convictions, federal and state, making a total of 300 years to life.“I know, dealing with so many victims, that when they speak publicly you see them shed their pain and get taller. You see them have a relief, an automatic release,”says Aquilina, perched on a seat in the helm of the boat. “The most interesting thing was that at first I had a list of maybe a dozen names who wanted to speak, then it was 20, then it was 30, and then it got up to 80, 100, etc.View image in fullscreenJudge Rosemarie Aquilina (left) looks at Larry Nassar as he listens to Jennifer Rood Bedford’s victim’s impact statement.Photograph: Scott Olson/Getty Images“What happened was that one girl empowered the next, who empowered the next. It was the beginning of their healing because they felt finally heard and believed, in a safe space, and they got to tell him to his face, eyeball to eyeball: ‘You hurt me. I am not a number, I am a name, how dare you?’”“Nassar constantly wanted control. He wanted to continue to control me, to control the girls, and to say: ‘Look what I’ve done. I took the plea for you’. That was constant … Did he deserve my respect? No. Did he give me respect? No. Did he give any of the victims respect? No. He never owned it. That infuriated me. It should infuriate everyone.”‘Money and medals over safety’: Nassar judge warns gymnasts are still being failedRead moreAmong the victimsmotivated to speak after hearing others’ statements was the Olympic gold medallist Aly Raisman, who was excoriating in blaming USA Gymnastics for enabling Nassar. She was joined by fellow gold medallist Jordyn Wieber, Olympic bronze medallist Jamie Dantzscher and former US national champion Mattie Larson.The mother of the athlete who first complained about Nassar, Maggie Nichols, read out a powerful statement on her behalf.Simone Biles, the most famous gymnast of her generation, revealed she was a victim on social media and later testified publicly in front of the US Senate Judiciary Committee.Two years after Nassar’s sentencing, a documentary film named after Nichols, called Athlete A, was released, shining a spotlight on the traditional coaching system of compliance, fear and silence and how it allowed Nassar to operate. The documentary opened the global floodgates.Kim Shore, who was a gymnast in Canada in the 1980s and “experienced all forms of abuse, but also all forms of joy”, was then on the board of directors of Gymnastics Canada, the national governing body, after stepping into governance when her own experiences and direct intervention had failed to prevent the cycle of mistreatment repeating with a family member.“I absolutely love the sport. I love how it feels in my body. I love so many aspects of it. And yet I spent most of my time surviving it,” she says.View image in fullscreenMaggie Nichols performs an uneven bars routine in the documentary Athlete A.Photograph: NetflixShore, who is an independent safe sport advocate, says of the impact of the Nassar case: “I was floored, understanding: ‘OK, I wasn’t a bad kid, I wasn’t a bad gymnast, this is why I was treated that way, it’s endemic.’”Yet the reaction from the organisation was “absolutely lacking”, says Shore. “I remember I sat and watched those girls tell their story in the courtroom and I just bawled. I encouraged the board members that I was associated with to watch it as well.” She does not believe any of them did.Eloise Jotischky, 23,who in 2022 won the first civil case against British Gymnastics for the abuses she suffered in the sport, says the impact of the film was being able “to articulate what you’ve been through and find the terms to understand and talk about your experience”.“It’s very hard to explain it to people who are not within that culture, that sport,” she says. “The only way I can really describe it is that it’s sort of like a cult in a lot of ways. It’s a very closed system, you’re very isolated, in a lot of cases you’re pulled out of school, you’re removed from your friends, you’re travelling to competitions all the time and you’re deprived of a normal social life. I’d say it’s very similar to a coercively controlling relationship in a domestic setting, there’s a lot of parallels there, but you’re a child, so there’s the duty of care issue as well.”Gymnastics’ ongoing reckoning: inside fight for survivor-led reform 10 years on from Nasser caseJotischky stopped training at 14. “By the end, it wasn’t joyous. I think I hated it. You just blame yourself and you think that you’re the problem, until Athlete A comes out. That was about sexual abuse, but the underlying themes of Athlete A are about the physical and emotional abuse, the non-contact physical abuse, which made it get to that point. That’s what all resonated.”At the same time, the life of former British gymnast and athlete Claire Heafford was in transition. She was splitting from her husband, leaving her dream job and taking up wrestling. “Those major changes were partly taking place because I hadn’t yet realised I’d been so badly abused and that I had some psychiatric issues,” she says.“I got into professional wrestling when I saw it and felt very drawn to it. I didn’t really understand why, but it’s a performance art that is largely about the performance of masculinity and the violence is clear and obvious. I was really attracted to that being the inverse of my own experiences. I couldn’t understand that at the time. I was like: ‘I’ve gone mad, I’m 36, I’m learning to be a Mexican wrestler. I’m splitting up with my husband. What the fuck’s gone wrong in my life?’“It was only when Athlete A came out that the penny dropped.”The documentary made Heafford want to act; she decided to set up Gymnasts for Change, an alliance to bring about safer sport. As the head of Gymnasts for Change International, she brought together the advocates and survivors in Rotterdam.“Athlete A was seismic. It came out just as Me Too had started,” she says. “On the one hand, Athlete A showed how awful the sexual abuse was and on the other it demonstrated to everybody in the world that gymnastics was a coercively controlling environment built on control and power. It showed that was just what the sport was, that everybody in it had experienced it and that they almost believed that it was necessary.”View image in fullscreenClaire Heafford, who founded Gymnasts for Change, brought together advocates and survivors in Rotterdam.Photograph: ITVThe Nassar case triggered a series of reports and new measures in the US including the FBI acknowledging its handling of the case was “inexcusable” and Congress establishing the US Center for SafeSport. That organisation has since faced heavy criticism. USAG went through four presidents in less than two years, said it would adopt 70 of the recommendations in an independent report into preventing sexual abuse and set up an Athlete Bill of Rights. USAG now says athlete safety has been its “top priority since establishing a new board of directors and leadership team in 2018-2019”. It emphasises that “a culture of safety is something that has to be worked on every day, at every level”, requiring all adult USAG members to be trained in safeguarding. Eight members of the board are former elite athletes and one seat is dedicated to that of a survivor.The case also inspired athletes around the world to speak up about their own experiences of abuse, including in Australia, Brazil and Britain. In Britain, an independent review led by Anne Whyte QC found that physical and emotional abuse were systemic, leading British Gymnastics to launch a 40-point plan aimed at changing the sport. That included a zero tolerance approach to abuse and a gymnast-coach led environment where “both feel empowered to create safe, positive and fair experiences at every level”.Such an environment is something Aimee Boorman, who is Simone Biles’ former coach, has spent her career advocating for. Boorman channelled her anger at her own experience of negative coaching as a child gymnast into her coaching philosophy. “I knew that I never wanted to make another child feel the way that I felt as a child. So, that was the basis of everything,” she says. “So many times I was told that I wouldn’t be successful because I was too nice. I was like: ‘Well, then I guess I’m not going to be successful by your metrics, your standard, your qualifier for success’. For me, success is having happy, healthy athletes who want to put their children in gymnastics because they have such a good experience.View image in fullscreenOlympic gymnast Jamie Dantzscher (left) sits alongside Jordyn Wieber as she testifies at a Senate hearing.Photograph: Aaron P Bernstein/Reuters“Then, I went from being too nice to just being lucky that I had Simone, she’s successful and I’m successful because I was lucky that I had her. No, the reality is that Simone never would have gotten to where Simone is without the training she had from me and the other coaches that she had growing up. So, I’ve just had to hold on to my core beliefs.”Across Europe, too, gymnasts have spoken out to force change. Former Dutch gymnast Petra Witjes and Germany’s Adina Hausch document falling out of love with the sport because of their experiences.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“At the elite club in the city I moved to it wasn’t fun anymore,” says Witjes, whose book, Silenced for Gold, is a memoir about the systemic abuses within sport and her battle to expose it. “My dad taught me to let my voice be heard but in the gym it was the opposite.”View image in fullscreenCoach Aimee Boorman watches as Simone Biles (left) trains. Boorman has spent her career advocating for a gymnast-coach led environment.Photograph: Smiley N Pool/Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesWitjes was terrified of speaking to her parents, she was taught not to trust them. “I didn’t feel safe at first, because my coach always said that parents don’t understand elite gymnastics,” she says. “They push your parents away from you. We were in total isolation.”Hausch says an injury that forced her from the sport was a relief. “I was on beam and I slipped with one leg and fell with the other on to the beam and then crashed down,” she says. “The leg was pushed sideways so much that it broke. From the age of 13 I don’t think there was a week without training through pain. When I left after the injury, the worst injury I’ve ever had, I was really happy that I didn’t have to go to the gym anymore.”In Rotterdam, survivors vary in age from their 50s to their teens; it is hard not to view the issues as systemic and global. And ongoing. Charlotte Jacobs, who is only 18, quit the sport after suffering emotional abusewhen training in the UK.“It got to a point where I was like: ‘I can’t do it anymore’,” she says. “My experience was strange because it wasn’t physical, it wasn’t sexual, but it was emotional. You were ridiculed all the time, constantly. You weren’t allowed to cry, you weren’t allowed to talk, you weren’t allowed to sit down, if you were caught leaning on anything you’d have to run, you needed permission to go to the toilet, you needed permission to drink, and it’s that sort of really controlling, consistent and dismissive behaviour so that no one really felt safe that was prevalent.”Shore, who is a member of G4C Canada, argues that if a big list of cultural reforms comes from the top, that is then normalised within the national federations and then the clubs “all the way down to grassroots, then I think we would see faster reform and less resistance”.“The more I learn that the stories are consistent internationally the more it says something about the need for World Gymnastics to take a leadership role,” she says “The treatment across the world is pervasive and coaches are moving from space to space, country to country, more frequently now or they’re not even staying in this sport, they’re moving into other sports, especially if they’ve come into trouble.”World Gymnastics has moved to address the cross-border issue within the sport at least, publishing a newsafeguarding policylast week which notes that the Gymnastics Ethics Foundation, which it launched in 2019 and has handled nearly 500 reports, has the power to extend sanctions imposed by member federations providing they are compatible with the rules of the governing body and general principles of law.Among the efforts of World Gymnastics to address safeguarding concerns was the launch of the10 Golden Rules of Gymnasticsin 2021, the establishment of a safeguarding commissionin 2022 and, this year, the launch of a safeguarding newsletter and the appointment of a full-time Safeguarding Manager.Shore believes the pace of governing bodies fully engaging with the change needed has been slow, however, “because to admit that there is harm going on in the sport puts organisations into a liability risk. Also, they have been able to deflect responsibility for so long. They don’t know how to solve it and they are getting pressure from all sides. By putting their head in the sand for literally 50 years we’ve now got to a crisis.”A statement from World Gymnastics said: “Creating a safe environment for current and future generations of gymnasts is a responsibility that World Gymnastics takes extremely seriously and shares with all stakeholders across the sport. The priority for World Gymnastics is not only to strengthen safeguarding rules and policies, but to ensure that they lead to meaningful changes in everyday practice.”Heafford alleges that British Gymnastics isn’t entering into meaningful engagement and collaboration with Gymnasts for Change and other survivors in the sport and says that she finds that “extremely frustrating”. She is also hugely critical of the processes gymnasts have to go through in raising a complaint against a coach or gym and what resolution looks like, saying: “In six years, we haven’t had one outcome that we can stand by and say that was a good outcome.”View image in fullscreenWomen from Michigan-based victim advocacy groups cheer after the sentencing of Larry Nassar in January 2018.Photograph: Anthony Lanzilote/Getty ImagesBritish Gymnastics, however, insists it has engaged with the organisation regularly which has “helped shape its approach”, including a meeting with G4CI and others in Rotterdam as well as introducting a new complaints and disciplinary process“to improve transparency and fairness”.Minky Worden, of Human Rights Watch, fears the situation could worsen. “Sport is getting younger. There’s a youth Olympics about to launch in Senegal. There’s going to be thousands of athletes, every one of them 18 or younger. They’re all children and they’re at a very elite level,” she says. “These children are being monetised and they are not protected because we know the systems are not in place to protect them.”Hausch wants to see “measurable boundaries, for example increasing the competition age to 18,” she says. “I would root for Germany not to join youth international competitions. Having a 13-year-old do youth European championships is the same as doing it as an adult, it’s the same amount of work you have to put in, the same amount of pressure, it’s not a softer version, it’s the full version, and it doesn’t make sense.”All agree there needs to be more done to help athletes advocate for themselves and others. Jacobs says: “There needs to be a sort of package of what to look out for. I think there needs to be more training for coaches in terms of mental wellbeing, disability, neurodiversity, all that, alongside what are and are not best practices.“We need more regulation,” she adds of the British landscape. “Look at the new guidance that’s come out about keeping children safe in education. That’s all been updated. Where’s the guidance for anything sports-wise, extracurriculars, whether it’s swimming, gymnastics, dancing, anything like that?”British Gymnastics says that it “recognises there is always more to do” but that prevention is “at the heart of our work. We have overhauled learning and development … and set clearer policies and guidance to drive meaningful change.” It says a coach developer network, regional teams and safeguarding and welfare officers in every club support communities.Jotischky, who is now studying law off the back of her experience, says there are changes needed there too. “The legislative gap that exists is astonishing. You have the 2015 Serious Crime Act section 76, which talks about coercive control, but it’s limited to domestic and familial relationships. Then you have the 2021 Domestic Abuse Act which lists personally connected individuals as only being family members. In a coach-to-athlete relationship where you spend 30 hours a week in the gym with your coach, and some gymnasts even go and live with their coach because they’ve formed such a close relationship, of course coercive control and emotional abuse can happen but it’s not recognised within the law. So, we have very little legislative ground to deal with the most serious cases in particular.”Listening to this group of women in Rotterdam, what becomes clearer is that while federations, to differing degrees, make changes in the name of athlete safety, survivors are still being failed. Meanwhile, these survivors and knowledgeable advocates remain isolated from the very structures that should be embracing them and channelling their knowledge and understanding of their experiences into the changes necessary to ensure the future health of the sport.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available fromthe following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers supporton 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland.In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsGymnasticsSport politicsUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Premiership: Kelsy fires Rangers to emphatic win; Dundee United pip Aberdeen | Scottish Premiership | The Guardian
description: Kevin Kelsy scored two goals to help Rangers to a 4-0 win over 10-man St Johnstone in the Scottish Premiership while Dundee United beat Aberdeen 3-2
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Kevin Kelsy scored two goals to help Rangers to a 4-0 win over 10-man St Johnstone in the Scottish Premiership while Dundee United beat Aberdeen 3-2
Content: Rangers’ Ryan Naderi (right) scores their first goal at a rain-swept Ibrox.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PAView image in fullscreenRangers’ Ryan Naderi (right) scores their first goal at a rain-swept Ibrox.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PAScottish PremiershipScottish Premiership: Kelsy fires Rangers to emphatic win; Dundee United pip AberdeenRangers 4-0 St Johnstone; Dundee United 3-2 AberdeenKevin Kelsy scores two to sink 10-man SaintsPress AssociationSat 24 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 15.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDerek McInnes asked hisRangersside to be “brilliant” againstSt Johnstoneand was rewarded with a 4-0 Premiership win at Ibrox. Afterdropping two points at Dundee last Saturday, the Light Blues dominated the first half but only led at the interval through a goal in the 29th minute from the Venezuela forward Kevin Kelsy.Saints started the second half brightly but goals from the Gers striker Ryan Naderi in the 61st minute and Kelsy again five minutes later had the home side cruising. The Saints substitute Kai Fotheringham was shown a straight red card by Chris Graham in the 74th minute for his high challenge on the midfielder Nico Raskin, before the substitute Tochi Chukwuani added a fourth for the hosts with three minutes remaining.Older, calmer, but still playing the hits: Mourinho and Madrid primed for clásicoRead moreMcInnes said: “It’s quite ironic in the sense that we were so good and so brilliant at times in the first half and create so many opportunities, that we were only a goal to the good at half-time. And obviously, we don’t want to let the frustration of those missed opportunities and dominance filter into the second half.“I think half-time came at a bad time for us because, despite the conditions, some of the play was really good. I asked the players to be brilliant today, not just win the game, can we really commit to being the best we can be, as good as we can be? And I thought we were in the first half. Everything was brilliant except the result at half-time because we should have been more in in front.”Celticcan restore their four-point advantage overRangersat the top when they travel toHibernian, the bottom side, at noon GMT on Sunday.Dundee Unitedwon a rollercoaster game 3-2 againstAberdeenat Tannadice. Zidane Iqbal scored for the hosts before the visitors equalised through Nesta Guinness-Walker – both players scoring their first goals for their clubs.United took the lead once more thanks to a Dylan Tait strike, with Connor Ronan drawingAberdeenlevel after the break. Zac Sapsford secured all three points for his side, with the win moving United up to fourth – one point behindHearts, who are atMotherwellon Sunday – while Aberdeen dropped to ninth.Two own goals helpedFalkirkclimb to seventh with a 3-0 victory overKilmarnock. Centre-backs Cathal McCarthy and George Stanger scored past their own goalkeeper either side of a Jacob Murrell header.St Mirrenended their losing streak with a 2-1 victory overDundeewith goals from Calvin Ramsay and Eseosa Sule before Bradley Fink pulled one back for the visitors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis story will be updated after Sunday’s matchesExplore more on these topicsScottish PremiershipRangersSt JohnstoneDundee UnitedAberdeenFalkirkKilmarnocknewsShareReuse this content

title: 'Culture is stagnant, so politics is stuck' | Playwright James Graham – Radical Thinking – podcast | Culture | The Guardian
description: Are we doomscrolling our way into a democratic crisis? That’s what the playwright James Graham fears may be happening, as he suggests that our algorithms have led us into ‘a massive crisis of the new’ and are preventing us from imagining a different future
Author: Aditya Chakrabortty
Headline: Are we doomscrolling our way into a democratic crisis? That’s what the playwright James Graham fears may be happening, as he suggests that our algorithms have led us into ‘a massive crisis of the new’ and are preventing us from imagining a different future
Content: 46:04Politics Weekly UKCulture'Culture is stagnant, so politics is stuck' | Playwright James Graham – Radical Thinking – podcastAre we doomscrolling our way into a democratic crisis? That’s what the playwright James Graham fears may be happening, as he suggests that our algorithms have led us into ‘a massive crisis of the new’ and are preventing us from imagining a different futureAditya suggested reading (and watching) list for James GrahamJames Graham has written a shaming amount. I’ve listed below three1. Dear England: about England’s football teamhttps://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episodes/m002qktz/dear-england2. Sherwood: mentioned in the conversation, set in the village where James Graham grew up in the shadow of the miners’ strikehttps://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episodes/p0c724lz/sherwood3. Quiz: set on the British quiz show, Who wants to be a millionaire, where a contestant wins a million quidhttps://www.itv.com/watch/quiz/2a7854On cultural stagnation:A lot of people say culture is stuck, although few sketch out the political consequences of that stagnation as well as James Graham does in our chat.Many also disagree on why:For ‘it was the algorithm that did it’, read Filterworld: How algorithms flattened culture by Kyle ChaykaFor a wider ranging explantaion look at Blank Space: A Cultural History of the Twenty-First Century by W. David MarxThose two are fairly recent. Much earlier and truly magnificent is the much-missed Mark Fisher on what he called the slow cancellation of the futurehttps://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aCgkLICTskQOn the same theme this essay by Adam Mastroianni is greathttps://www.experimental-history.com/p/the-decline-of-deviancePresented byAditya ChakraborttywithJames Graham, produced byFrankie TobiandLuke John Smith, graphics byNatalie Gegan, the executive producers areMaz Ebtehaj,Kirsty MajorandJames TindaleSat 24 Oct 2026 02.45 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 05.11 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsCulturePolitics Weekly UKJames Graham

title: As Trump’s time runs out, this could be his most dangerous legacy: a world divided into three | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Content: Traditional Russian dolls on sale at a souvenir shop in St Petersburg, Russia.Photograph: Dmitri Lovetsky/APView image in fullscreenTraditional Russian dolls on sale at a souvenir shop in St Petersburg, Russia.Photograph: Dmitri Lovetsky/APOpinionDonald TrumpAs Trump’s time runs out, this could be his most dangerous legacy: a world divided into threeSteve BloomfieldWe’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystalliseSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 07.11 EDTShareIn the final two years of a US presidency, when Congress has been lost, approval ratings have sunk like a stone and their party has started to think about who’s coming next, the person occupying the Oval Office can feel their power draining away. Domestic legislation, particularly in an era where bipartisan cooperation is almost nonexistent, grinds to a halt. But as the days tick by until the end, and as presidents begin to think about their legacy, there is one part of the job where they still have power: the rest of the world.In the final weeks of his presidency in 1992 George HW Bush sent 28,000 American troops to Somalia to help end a famine. For Bill Clinton, it was a quixotic attempt to bring peace to the Middle East by ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Barack Obama restored diplomatic ties with Cuba, making a historic visit to Havana, as well as a final, successful push on the Iran nuclear deal.In 10 days,Donald Trumpwill enter his own twilight zone. He is almost certain to lose control of the House and it’s not impossible he will face a Democratic Senate too. Any hopes of passing domestic policy – not that he’s bothered with that much during his first two years – will disappear. Instead, he will face a series of investigations that could lead, once again, to impeachment.On the world stage, however, it will be a different story. And unlike Bush senior, Clinton and Obama, his ambitions won’t be peaceful. The first two years of his second term have been catastrophic; the final two could be even worse.Once the midterms are over, the US isunderstood to be planning to restart its unwinnable war with Iran, already carrying out exercises with the Israeli military and withdrawing diplomats from the region. Trump’s sellout of Ukraine is well under way. In the past week he has argued that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine”, while his envoy Steve Witkoff met with Vladimir Putin in Moscow,praising him in a televised meetingas a “humanitarian…and I salute that, I commend you and I thank you again.”On top of a reckless war in the Middle East and appeasement in Europe, the shadow of a new world order is emerging, which Trump will relentlessly pursue in his final years. Putin has proposed a summit between himself, Trump and China’sXi Jinping, to be held in China next month.The Trump-Putin love story’s next chapter: selling out Ukraine | Sidney BlumenthalRead moreSuch an unprecedented meeting, were it to take place, would have potentially devastating consequences for the rest of us. The three leaders have ambitions to transform the way the world is governed, essentially dividing it into spheres of influence. One summit wouldn’t turn an idea into reality, but it would send us down a very dangerous path. In Europe, it would have an impact beyond Ukraine if the US refused to help protect nations threatened byRussia. In east Asia, the withdrawal of the American security blanket would cause enormous problems for Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, as well as Australia.We’ve talked a lot about the end of the west over the past two years – this feels like a moment when many of those fears will crystalise.The Trump administration’s ambition to divide the world into spheres and side with dictators over democrats has long been evident. Last year’sNational Security Strategywas deeply critical of the US’s traditional allies in Europe and east Asia. But it was what it didn’t say that was most shocking. Both Russia and China avoided direct criticism. In six paragraphs describing the threat to Taiwan, China was not mentioned once. Elsewhere in the document, China was actually praised as “rich and powerful … us[ing] its wealth and power to its considerable advantage.” The section on Russia’s war in Ukraine failed to mention how it started and did not suggest that Putin should be defeated; instead it focused on how the US could help Europe and Russia mend their relationship. The 33-page document discussed the importance of the US controlling the western hemisphere, but made clear that so long as the US still had economic dominance, it cared little whether other parts of the world are protected. “The affairs of other countries,” it stated, “are our concern only if their activities directly threaten our interests.” For too long, it argued, America’s allies had “suck[ed] us into conflicts and controversies central to their interests but peripheral or irrelevant to our own”.For Putin, this is a success almost three decades in the making. He has long viewed American support for democracy in eastern Europe and central Asia as “interference” in Russia’s backyard. Now he has a US president who agrees. Trump has also placed Putin on a far higher pedestal than Russia’s economy and its technological prowess deserves.Xi, too, has welcomed the US’s rhetorical retreat from east Asia, particularly if it allowsChinagreater maritime control in the East China Sea and South China Sea. World opinion on China has dramatically improved as that of the US has slid. As Chrystia Freeland, a former Canadian foreign minister, put it this week, “there has not been a president who has been more beneficial for China than Donald Trump”.At stake is not merely territorial control. All three governments see the possibility of increasing economic ties. For the US and China, the bigger issues are future control of economic supply chains and technology platforms, while Russia’s fossil fuel resources are also a factor. All three are key players in the next space race, both in terms of commercial and military control. If these three nations begin to work together, at the expense of Europe and the rest of the world, it will fundamentally change the nature of geopolitics. A decade ago, talk of a multipolar world was based around the idea of the US, China and the European Union as the three most powerful blocs. Somehow, Brussels has been replaced by Moscow.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGiorgia Meloni is Italy’s great political survivor. Could one man be about to bring her down? | Riccardo AlcaroRead moreUntil now, the rest of the west has – on the whole – tried to muddle through. Nato still exists on paper, G7 and G20 summits may be chaotic but they still take place. Optimists in the Foreign Office point out that Trump turned up to the UN general assembly and his administration is still deeply involved in the UN’s day to day activities.Mark Carney spoke of a “rupture” and warned the old post-cold war world was not coming back, but despite warm words from Emmanuel Macron, and renewed discussion about how Europe can protect itself without the US, there is still a sense that everyone is waiting for Trump’s time in office to end. A Great Powers summit makes this harder to ignore.While US presidents seek foreign policy success in their final months, history suggests they rarely find it.Clinton’s Camp David talks collapsedafter Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat were unable to reach an agreement. Bush would argue that his initial intervention in Somalia eased a famine, but it ended in humiliation.A botched raid on a warlordled to the deaths of 18 US soldiers and several hundred Somalis. Obama’s diplomacy in Cuba and Iran succeeded, but were both promptly ripped up by Donald Trump.Trump will get his photoshoot – and maybe that’s all he wants – but there is no guarantee that this unsavoury troika becomes a permanent geopolitical fixture. Trump’s foreign policy has divided his Maga movement and has shocked traditional conservatives. The Wall Street Journal editorial board described the proposed summit as “arguably the worst idea of the second Trump term”. A President Vance or Rubio might be less willing to throw in their lot with dictators; a President Ossoff or Ocasio-Cortez certainly won’t.But just because Trump won’t win, doesn’t mean that the US won’t lose. He will be arriving in Shenzhen at the weakest moment in his presidency. An 80-year-old lame duck leader fated to limp towards the finish line unable to pass any legislation and threatened by two chaotic years of investigations into his alleged corruption. Opposite him will be two authoritarian leaders in their early 70s who believe the only thing preventing them from ruling their nations for another two decades is death. Indeed, giventheir “hot mic” discussionsabout longevity drugs last year, perhaps they both believe they can rule for even longer.If it goes ahead, this summit will bring Putin back in from the cold and reiterate Xi’s position as a global leader who cannot be ignored.The image of the three leaders will come to define this era when the rules-based international order was torn apart and a new, uncertain period began to form.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the ObserverExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS politicsXi JinpingVladimir PutinUnited NationsRussiaChinacommentShareReuse this content

title: Fine ‘headphone dodgers’ if you will, but to really tackle antisocial behaviour, Britain should look to Japan | Emily Bratt | The Guardian
description: Working in Japanese schools, I saw how teaching young people civic pride creates adults with consideration for others, says freelance journalist Emily Bratt
Author: Emily Bratt
Headline: Working in Japanese schools, I saw how teaching young people civic pride creates adults with consideration for others, says freelance journalist Emily Bratt
Content: ‘Some loudcasters are simply oblivious.’Photograph: Drazen_/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Some loudcasters are simply oblivious.’Photograph: Drazen_/Getty ImagesOpinionPublic transportFine ‘headphone dodgers’ if you will, but to really tackle antisocial behaviour, Britain should look to JapanEmily BrattWorking in Japanese schools, I saw how teaching young people civic pride creates adults with consideration for othersSat 24 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 08.11 EDTShareThere are two types of people who listen to music in public: those who wear headphones and those who … are a word I probably can’t use here. “Loudcasting” – playing audio, watching videos or talking on speakerphone in public spaces – is a form of antisocial behaviour that driveseight in 10of people in the UK crazy, and I’m gladAndy Burnham is oneof those eight. But while I welcome his policy to fine “headphone dodgers”, I’m not convinced it will solve the problem.This behaviour isn’t only a nuisance, but a grave indicator of a deeper societal issue: the erosion of empathy. You can’t legislate civic pride into an individualistic culture where feelings of social disconnection are widespread.From 2019 to 2021 I lived in Japan, where keeping the peace is paramount and you can be reprimanded just for talking on the bus. When I returned to England, I felt shock and shame at how we treat one another and our public spaces. I still do. We watch our dogs defecate in the street andwalk away. We use public bathrooms as if we’re feral two-year-olds. We inflict the soundtrack of our mindless social-media scrolling on an entire train carriage.Time’s up for tinny tunes and blaring football highlights. London’s headphone cavalry has arrived | Hugh MuirRead moreJapanese society is not without its flaws; I often chafed at the level of deference I witnessed. But living there also highlighted to me just how selfish we can be in Britain. Last week, I saw someone had smeared dog poo into the communal carpeted entrance of their own block of flats. Some on the far right love to cast other cultures as primitive, but I think we need to look at ourselves.We could learn from Japan. As a broadly collectivist society, it favours social harmony and group responsibility. One guiding principle ismeiwaku wo kakenai: the idea that you should avoid inconveniencing others.I worked in Japanese state schools and was astonished when students as young as five diligently began stacking chairs and clearing apparatus as sports day wrapped up. Nobody told them to. Additionally, Japanese schools don’t completely rely on cleaners: the students sweep the halls, wipe down desks, empty bins and even disinfect and scrub the bathrooms. This cleaning practice, a component oftokkatsu(special activities), forms part of a wider approach to holistic education and teaches children personal responsibility for, and pride in, their environment.It’s important to add that a teenager is still a teenager, no matter the country. It’s a myth that all Japanese children are innately disciplined perfect little angels. But the wider impact of these social ethics is obvious. Crime rates in Japan are (comparatively) low, public spaces are meticulously maintained and litter is a rarity. It’snota myth that Japanese streets are so clean you could lick them. Lick an English street and, bam! Dysentery.View image in fullscreenJapanese children clean their classroom after a lesson.Photograph: Aflo Co., Ltd./AlamyThe UK government’s crackdown on content-blaring can only work in conjunction with a wider effort. First, fines have to actually be imposed by those in authority – and they need to feel safe and incentivised to do so. Train managers have been hot on calling out fare dodgers for years (one made me cry when I was 19 for not having my student railcard, such was his wrath). Now they need to bring the same resolve to headphone dodgers. Burnham’s policy states that drivers would not be expected to enforce such rules – it’s a job for safety officers or the police. But unless someone is there to enforce the rules in the moment, the policy becomes little more than an empty threat.Second, we need to rebuild social norms so that consideration for others is instinctive. The word etiquette seems antiquated, but given thatalmost half of usin the UK play content from our phones without headphones – and that this behaviour bothers most of us – etiquette education is still necessary. Maybe, so we don’t feel we’re in a Jane Austen novel, we call it something else. Perhaps in schools, it’s civic responsibility class, or lessons in caring about others, or simply learning how to not be a twat. It doesn’t require major educational reform. Copying Japan’s approach to school-cleaning, for example, could be a good (and easy) place to start.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe onus, of course, isn’t only on schools – parents have to lead by example. But imagine the ripple effect if British schoolchildren were given the responsibility of caring for their classrooms and corridors.Unfortunately, there’s also a deeper issue. Some loudcasters are simply oblivious, but others are deliberately rage-baiting. The latter is a product of a disaffected society, which Burnham’s fines by themselves could exacerbate. Nobody likes being told off, but especially not angry people.We don’t need to become Japan. But in an increasingly divided world, consideration for others and respect for our surroundings are what can still hold us together.Emily Bratt is a freelance journalistExplore more on these topicsPublic transportOpinionTransport policyTransportJapanAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: What essentials to keep, what rubbish to get rid of? Burnham, Badenoch, Farage don’t know either  | Robert Hutton | The Guardian
description: After a fractious week, they probably agree that no one at all needs Liz Truss’s new book, but then the political housekeeping decisions get much harder, says author and journalist Robert Hutton
Author: Robert Hutton
Headline: After a fractious week, they probably agree that no one at all needs Liz Truss’s new book, but then the political housekeeping decisions get much harder, says author and journalist Robert Hutton
Content: Kemi Badenoch at Oil States Industries in Aberdeen, 5 June 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch at Oil States Industries in Aberdeen, 5 June 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOpinionPoliticsWhat essentials to keep, what rubbish to get rid of? Burnham, Badenoch, Farage don’t know eitherRobert HuttonAfter a fractious week, they probably agree that no one at all needs Liz Truss’s new book, but then the political housekeeping decisions get much harderSat 24 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTShareWhat are you stockpiling? Wes Streeting says we needwater and food to last 72 hoursin case of national emergency, as well as wind-up radios so that we can check in on how the apocalypse is developing in Ambridge. Personally, I have a two-week supply of jokes about the government that I can draw upon even as the zombies break down my front door.Andy Burnham, far from stockpiling, is busy chucking stuff out. This week Labour’s much cherished commitment not to allow new drilling for oil and gas in the North Seawent into the skipround the back of Downing Street, where it lies next to a complete set of European Union red lines, a plan for digital ID and a signed photograph of Peter Mandelson.Tory frontbenchers waved their hands in amazement as the prime minister explained that the government is now in favour of dashing for gas. The argument Burnham was using aboutsecurity of supplywas exactly the one they’d been throwing at the government for months.ToKemi Badenoch, it’s a sign that she’s winning the argument. But then the Tory leader’s self-confidence is so total that she sees the rising of the sun each morning as a sign that she’s winning the argument. A more thoughtful opposition leader might wonder what she will have left to throw at Burnham after he’s finished jettisoning the unpopular and hard-to-explain bits of policy that Keir Starmer left cluttering up Downing Street.Badenoch is having her own clear-out. All of us do this when we move into a new place and find that the previous occupant left something hideous behind: a phallic ornament in the garden, for instance, or a list of approved candidates featuring Grant Shapps.Of course, as anyone who’s spent a weekend driving to the local tip knows, there’s always something so toxic the council simply refuses to take it off your hands. In Badenoch’s case, it’sLiz Truss, who has a new book outnext week on how everything was someone else’s fault.That’s a line that the Tory leader has decided to recycle, as she bags up any sense of responsibility for the government in which she was a cabinet minister and leaves it out for the binmen along with a pile of “Mel Stride for chancellor” posters.On Tuesday she was asked why, if cutting taxes and welfare spending is so easy, her party didn’t do either when it was last in power. “Well, I didn’t raise those taxes,” she replied, explaining that she had disagreed with the government she was part of, but had decided to keep this to herself. Courage takes many forms.The effect of all these unwanted old positions hitting the Westminster landfill is that the electoral battleground is clearing nicely. We find ourselves in the unusual situation that both Burnham and Badenoch agree on the argument they want to have: was Margaret Thatcher right?One party that is definitely stockpiling is Reform, which continues to lay in supplies of nasty ideas about race, as though there was the slightest danger they might run out. The party’s headquarters has now been so thoroughly turned over that it’s an open question whether there’s anyone on the staff who isn’t an undercover reporter. But if you want to know what Reform thinks, you really don’t need to spend six months hiding a camera inside your lapel. Just listen to what the party’s MPs are saying.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDanny Kruger, whodefected from the Torieslast year, has usually been seen as a genial soul, certainly relative to the Slytherin tendency that is Robert Jenrick and Andrew Rosindell. But introducing Nigel Farage on Tuesday, he made a determined effort to prove that his “nice but dim” image is only half right. “The problem isn’t with individual Muslims,” he told his audience. No, the problem is Muslims as a group, “who are taught by their clerics that their loyalty isn’t to the United Kingdom, but to the global Islamic community”. It’s an argument that was applied to Catholics 200 years ago and to Jews 100 years ago: you just can’t trust them.Farage is too canny to say this stuff himself, and as an election approaches, he may find himself disavowing it, just as he’s distanced himself from his great buddy Donald Trump. But the trouble with stockpiles of the wrong stuff is that they can be hard to clear out at short notice. Just ask the Liberal Democrats: it’s weeks since they put Ed Davey on Freecycle, and they haven’t had even a nibble of interest.Robert Hutton is an author and journalistExplore more on these topicsPoliticsOpinionKemi BadenochAndy BurnhamNigel FaragecommentShareReuse this content

title: Forget the Live Aid image, Africa is only a broken continent in the minds of the west | Moky Makura | The Guardian
description: Innovators and business leaders are driving progress across the continent, but the ‘visibility gap’ prevents the rest of the world from truly seeing it
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Innovators and business leaders are driving progress across the continent, but the ‘visibility gap’ prevents the rest of the world from truly seeing it
Content: People using the M-Pesa banking service in Nairobi, Kenya, in 2013. Africa pioneered innovations in mobile money.Photograph: Trevor Snapp/Bloomberg/MDGGetty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople using the M-Pesa banking service in Nairobi, Kenya, in 2013. Africa pioneered innovations in mobile money.Photograph: Trevor Snapp/Bloomberg/MDGGetty ImagesOpinionGlobal developmentForget the Live Aid image, Africa is only a broken continent in the minds of the westMoky MakuraInnovators and business leaders are driving progress across the continent-wide, but the ‘visibility gap’ prevents the rest of the world from truly seeing itSupported byAbout this contentSat 24 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTShareThirty years ago, shortly after SouthAfricaemerged from apartheid, I left London for Johannesburg in search of a better life. Not long afterwards, a friend who was preparing to visit from the UK called with an intriguing question: do they have ATMs in South Africa?After I picked myself off the floor, I explained that not only did South Africa have ATMs, but in many respects its banking system was far more advanced than the one I had left behind in Britain. She was surprised and – dare I say – delighted that she wouldn’t have to lug a wad of cash around South Africa after all.That moment has stayed with me far longer than it should, because I’ve witnessed too many moments where the continent has persistently surprised and delighted the uninitiated. That’s because, for much of the world, the image of Africa still owes more to Live Aid’s legacy than to the reality.Astudy we commissionedby social psychologist Dr Adam Hahn at the University of Bath helps explain why. When people in Britain and the US think about Africa, they disproportionately associate it with economic and political dysfunction, harsh environments and a lack of modernity and culture. Those associations affect whether they want to visit the continent, buy its products or engage with its culture. In their minds, Africa remains a place that is broken, dependent, lacking in agency and apparently in ATMs, too.Britain may have more ATM’s and higher conventional bank-account ownership, but it was Africa that pioneered one of the biggest innovations in modern finance: mobile money. Kenya showed that millions of people could, in effect leapfrog traditional banking altogether, using their phones to store, send and receive money. Today, sub-Saharan Africa remains the centre of the global mobile-money revolution. And when it comes to new money,Nigeria now ranks third in the worldfor cryptocurrency adoption, while Britain ranks 17th.Global investors have noticed the continent’s leadership when it comes to finance and are moving in. We have produced a surprisingly high number of fintech “unicorns” – privately owned startups valued at more than $1bn (£760).Nigeriaalone has Flutterwave, OPay, Moniepoint and Interswitch. Investors are not putting billions into African financial technology out of charity; they are backing the entrepreneurs who are not waiting for help to create viable, profitable solutions.One of those is Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, who has been all over the global media for theworld-class refinery he built in Nigeria. The $20bn Dangote refinery is the largest single-train refinery in the world, built in a country that, despite being Africa’s biggest oil producer, spent decades exporting crude oil only to import much of its refined fuel.Dangote is exceptional in his wealth, the scale of his ambition and visibility he has garnered. But he is not exceptional in spirit. There are thousands of smaller “Dangotes” on the continent: entrepreneurs who see a gap, build something to fill it and, in doing so, move their country forward.Take Siny Samba, a Senegalese entrepreneur who launched an infant food brand after wondering why virtually all the baby food in her country was imported. She started in her kitchen with banana and millet and in 2018 launched Le Lionceau, creating new markets for local farmers and women’s cooperatives.In Tanzania, Diana Orembe looked at fruit and vegetables being thrown away and saw fish food. Her company, NovFeed, turns that waste into affordable feed in the agriculture sector and has worked with at least 200 farmers.In Maiduguri, northern Nigeria, Mustapha Abubakar Gajibo started by converting petrol-powered tricycles to electric. Today his company, African Motor Works, designs and builds electric vehicles, producing about 200 units a month.Samba, Orembe, Gajibo and thousands like them who are contributing to their countries’ growth, will probably never make international headlines. And that may be one of Africa’s most overlooked challenges: not the absence of progress, but the lack of visibility.Development experts talk endlessly about Africa’s many gaps – the infrastructure gap, financing gap, skills gap – but perhaps the most consequential gap is the visibility gap: the distance between the Africa today (the one that surprises and delights) and the Africa the world imagines.Addressing the visibility gap is why theOpportunity Africa initiativewas started earlier this year. Its mandate; to make the continent’s progress impossible to overlook by spotlighting the many people – such as Samba, Orembe and Gajibo – the places, the policies and the initiatives moving Africa forward.Places such as Rwanda, which has rebuilt its reputation around innovation, tourism and digital government.
