Ethiopia has transformed its agricultural sector and sharply reduced its dependence on imported wheat.Kenyanow generates up to 91% of its electricity from renewable sources.Nigeria’s big tax gamble: great in theory but people are already checking their pockets | Cheta NwanzeRead moreThen there are the policies, the unglamorous government decisions that rarely make headlines: Benin keeping more of its cashews for local processing; Namibia requiring more of its lithium to be processed at home; and Zambia removing fees from state education.And progress is happening continent-wide through ambitious initiatives. Fifty countries have ratified the African Continental Free Trade Area, making it easier for African businesses to trade with each other. A pan-African payments system now lets them settle transactions in local currencies. And 38 countries have joined the single African air transport market, helping create 108 new intra-African routes since 2022.And this is just the tip of the iceberg. If my friend was surprised by South Africa 30 years ago, imagine what else has changed and progressed. Through the recentCorrect the Map campaign led by Togo, we challenged the world to see Africa differently – quite literally. Now we are asking the world to see us as we truly are.The#NotWaitingcampaign is where you will find the proof point: stories of a continent already building, solving, producing and moving forward.Moky Makura is executive director ofAfrica No Filter, an advocacy organisation working to change how the world sees Africa and how Africa sees itselfExplore more on these topicsGlobal developmentOpinionAfricaFintechEntrepreneursNigeriaKenyaPrivate sectorcommentShareReuse this content

title: Attention LaMelo Ball: only losers boast about avoiding diaper duty | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The basketball star seems proud to leave the job to his partner. That’s so last century
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The basketball star seems proud to leave the job to his partner. That’s so last century
Content: ‘A baby doesn’t care that you signed a five-year contract extension.’Photograph: Matt Krohn/APView image in fullscreen‘A baby doesn’t care that you signed a five-year contract extension.’Photograph: Matt Krohn/APThe Week in PatriarchyParents and parentingAttention LaMelo Ball: only losers boast about avoiding diaper dutyArwa MahdawiThe basketball star seems proud to leave the job to his partner. That’s so last centurySat 24 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTShareNobody can accuse the basketball star LaMelo Ball of being bad at his job. That said, the Minnesota Timberwolves point guard doesn’t seem to be a huge fan ofdribbling.Ball has a nine-month-old son, LaOne, with his partner Ana Montana (real name: Analicia Chaves) and is apparently uninterested in dealing with all the body fluids that come with a baby.“You’re a dad now,” the sportscaster Ernie Johnson Jr said to Ball during an ESPNinterviewon Wednesday. “Are you a diaper changer?”“Nah, my girl do all that,” Ball replied. “We got a good gameplan going on. So I know what I gotta do, bring to the table, she know what she gotta do, bring to the table.”Johnson, to his credit, seemed disappointed by this answer. “Oh man, you don’t know what you’re missing, I’m telling you that.”“I did it before, you feel me? I’ve definitely did it before, [but] it’s just not my job,” Ball clarified. “You know what I’m saying? It’s not my job.”Well, actually, excuse me while I mumsplain here, but it very much is your job. A baby doesn’t care that you signed a five-year contract extension worthup to $260min 2023. Parenting is a 24/7 commitment no matter how much money you make.Ball and Montana (and, presumably, a team of hired help) are obviously free to share domestic duties however suits them. Nobody expects a professional athlete to be as hands-on as a parent with a more flexible schedule.But going on TV and boasting about how you don’t change diapers? That’s an extremely outdated look. A 1982 study based on fathers in Britain found43% of fathershad never changed a nappy (as diapers are called in the UK). By 2000, that figure had dropped to 3%.Meanwhile, the average time US dads spend caring for their offspring daily has quadrupled over the past 50 years and about 85% of dads say parenthood is one of the most important aspects of their identity. Being a hands-off dad is now very last century.Still, even though modern fathers are doing a lot more, they’re still held to different standards than mothers. Imagine if a female athlete said changing diapers wasn’t her job: the rightwing pitchforks would be instantly out for her.It doesn’t matter how accomplished a woman is in her career; there’s still an expectation that her identity as a mother comes first. Particularly under the Trump administration, which is trying to foster a whole new generation of tradwives.Ball is only 25, so I’ll give him some grace. But I hope the backlash to his comments makes him realize that only complete losers boast about not changing diapers. A case in point:Donald Trump.“I would never ask to change [Barron],”the president toldthe New York Post in 2006. “Melania probably wouldn’t let me. I’d just do it wrong.” Asked whether he’d ever changed the diapers of his four other children, he said he probably had, but couldn’t remember.There’s a phrase frequently applied to men who pretend they’re incapable of doing basic domestic chores in order to wriggle out of them:weaponized (or strategic) incompetence. In Trump’s case, however, it may not actually be weaponized incompetence. It may just be incompetence.Which leads me to present a modest proposal. In the future, we should apply the Diaper Test™ to any man in the running for a high-powered job. If he can’t clean up his own child’s mess, he’s sure to make a mess of the job.Gamblers were betting on the outcome of the Cornell 7 sexual assault caseTwo days after a New York district attorney reopened the alleged Cornell University gang-rape case, the Polymarket gambling app allowed people to bet on the results of the investigation.According to Defector, Polymarket initially said nothing about why they were letting people bet on a traumatic sexual assault case, before issuing a PR statement full of corporate gobbledegook. “Markets bring objective, data-driven insight into how a matter like this is moving through the legal system, on a topic that deserves far more transparency and honest attention,” the statement read. Monetizing sexual assault is feminism now, apparently! Polymarket then reconsidered this position. After about three weeks of being up, the bet has been removed from the platform.Trump has a weirdly homoerotic midterm strategyAdam Gabbattexamines whythe president keeps “offering unsolicited, and increasingly unhinged, assessments of men’s bodies”.Poland’s parliament votes to slightly ease abortion lawsIn 2021, anear-total banon abortion took effect in Poland. Now the lower house of parliament hasapproved two billsthat would remove some criminal penalties for people who help women access abortion care and would allow a termination if there was a foetal abnormality. While that sounds like a small step in the right direction, the draft laws are likely to bevetoedby the conservative president, Karol Nawrocki. Women are now protesting on the streets in more than 20 Polish cities demanding access to legal abortions.Liechtenstein prince uses veto to quash abortion accessIt’s not just Poland that seems determined to be at odds with the rest of Europe on abortion. The hereditary prince of Liechtenstein, who will never need an abortion himself, hasused his vetofor the first time to kill off a bill that would have eased the country’s draconian laws.The death toll since the October ‘ceasefire’ in Gaza rises to 1,538Israeli attacks killed yet another child in Gazathis weekas the territory faces a new risk of famine.Trump and JD Vance are defending an ad weaponizing sexual abuseDemocrat Amy Acton is running against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to be governor of Ohio. It’s a tight race and Ramaswamy clearly thinks he can’t win on merit because he’s stooped to putting out arevolting attack adfeaturing Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, whose former husband has been accused of sexually abusing Acton when she was a child. In the ad, Arthur accuses Acton of lying “her entire life”. There’s been bipartisan backlash to the ad, but JD Vance has mounted a vigorousdefense, saying he’s “disgusted” by fellow Republicans who have criticized it. On Thursday, Trump also endorsed the ad, calling it “very powerful”.The week in pawtriarchyRemember when the Nordic phenomenon ofslow TVwas being touted as the antidote to the frenetic nature of modern life? Well it’s back! A 24-hour Finnish TV show that follows the progress of a dog and her six newborn puppies has become a massive hit. The show has an accompanying 24-hour webcam,Pentulive(Puppy Live), which is very soothing. I recommend tuning in whenever you feel like the world’s gone barking mad.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsParents and parentingThe Week in PatriarchyBasketballFamilySexual harassmentGamblingJD VanceDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Judge rules Cornell’s ‘Jane Doe’ can use pseudonym in suit over alleged gang-rape | New York | The Guardian
description: Woman alleging frat-house rape had privacy and safety issues outweighing need to publicly identify her, judge says
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Woman alleging frat-house rape had privacy and safety issues outweighing need to publicly identify her, judge says
Content: Demonstrators march in support of ‘Jane Doe’ in Washington DC on 8 October 2026.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APView image in fullscreenDemonstrators march in support of ‘Jane Doe’ in Washington DC on 8 October 2026.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APNew YorkJudge rules Cornell’s ‘Jane Doe’ can use pseudonym in suit over alleged gang-rapeWoman alleging frat-house rape has privacy and safety issues outweighing need to publicly identify her, judge saysGuardian staff and agencySat 24 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe woman at the center ⁠ofrape allegationsagainst students at Cornell University can continue using a pseudonym in ⁠her lawsuit, a ⁠judge ​has ruled.TheNew Yorkstate judge Phaedra Perry-Bond ruled on Friday that the woman’s ⁠privacy interests – particularly concerns for her safety – outweighed any need to publicly disclose her identity ⁠in court proceedings.The woman alleges she ​was drugged and ‌raped by students at the elite Ivy Leagueuniversityin upstate New York in 2024.She has become the target of threats, ‌her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said earlier this month.‘Is this too little, too late?’: Cornell students on school’s response to gang-rape allegationsRead moreThe defendants in the lawsuit have not opposed the request for anonymity, as the woman continues to go by a generic placeholder name “Jane Doe” used in many legal or official situations, especially when a woman’s identity is protected.But Perry-Bond wrote in a ruling released on Friday that “some members of the public have made it their ‌mission to try and identify Jane Doe”.The judge warned that “cyberstalking and engaging in ​or encouraging threats across state lines, whether it be of Jane Doe, of any of the named defendants, or their attorneys, can be considered a federal ⁠crime and perpetrators of those acts may be subjecting ​themselves ​to prosecution”.The woman in the Cornell case was 20 at the time ​of the ‌alleged gang-rape at a fraternity house at the university. She filed her ​suit on 16 September, prompting prosecutorsto reopena criminal investigation they had initially closed without charges.Mass protests erupted on Cornell’s Ithaca campus earlier this month, with students criticizing officials’ handling of Jane Doe’sgang-rape allegations, demanding theuniversity president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administration building.Protestersshouted“Ban the frats” andheld signssaying “At Cornell, rapists are safer than women” and “Stop rape culture.” Some demonstrators directed their anger at Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, arguing he had failed to keep students safe andchanting, “Kotlikoff, resign!”Reuters contributed reportingInformation and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsNew YorkRape and sexual assaultLaw (US)Fraternities and sororitiesUS universitiesUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: But Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX owns Starlink, accuses Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: But Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX owns Starlink, accuses Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms
Content: Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, previously warned any restriction to Starshield system would ‘bring a lot of human losses’.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAView image in fullscreenUkraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, previously warned any restriction to Starshield system would ‘bring a lot of human losses’.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAUkraineUkraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictionsBut Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX owns Starlink, accuses Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s termsDonna FergusonSat 24 Oct 2026 17.25 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications systemwas suddenly restricted.But hours after the announcement, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink,accusedthe Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for ⁠offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in asocial media post.Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential adviser, said on the Telegram app that the country is “physically unable” to use Starlink for long- and medium-range attack drone operations.Ukraine’s general staff and defence ministry did not immediately comment.The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled.Russiawas able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.The speed restrictions coincided withthe announcementby Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on theTrump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.View image in fullscreenMusk blamed the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X that the systems were ‘owned and controlled by the US government’.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersThe US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.Ukraine’s president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming whom in the Ukraine-Starlink row?Read moreAnnouncing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomaticvideo addresson the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for ‌today is that Starlink ‌and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the ‌level we need.”The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.Whenasked by reporterswhether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUkraineTrump administrationEuropeElon MuskDonald TrumpVolodymyr ZelenskyySatellitesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sam Fender tells fans high ticket prices for Proper Massive tour are ‘getting changed’ | Sam Fender | The Guardian
description: Fender criticises stadium pricing, calling it ‘bollocks’ and says it ‘won’t be happening’ on his tour
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Fender criticises stadium pricing, calling it ‘bollocks’ and says it ‘won’t be happening’ on his tour
Content: Sam Fender said he had no idea how high ticket prices became ‘normalised’.Photograph: Thomas Jackson/AlamyView image in fullscreenSam Fender said he had no idea how high ticket prices became ‘normalised’.Photograph: Thomas Jackson/AlamySam FenderSam Fender tells fans high ticket prices for Proper Massive tour are ‘getting changed’Fender criticises stadium pricing, calling it ‘bollocks’ and says it ‘won’t be happening’ on his tourPriya BharadiaSat 24 Oct 2026 11.29 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 11.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Fender has responded to criticism by fans about ticket prices for his 2027 stadium tour by promising he would lower the cost, telling followers on Instagram: “They’re getting changed.”The 32-year-old musician announced his Proper Massive stadium tour earlier this week.Gavin Davis, an Instagram user, shared details of standing tickets for Fender’s show at Wembley, which were split into “front standing”, costing £130.75, and “standing”, priced at £98.85. Prices for seating ranged between £64.75 and £130.75.Responding to the post, Fender said he was “not happy with these prices”.He said: “It got inflated well more than I’d had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on.”In his reply, Fender also criticised the division of standing tickets into front and back tiers as “bollocks”, saying this “won’t be happening” on his tour.“I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs,” he added.Tickets at other venues were also listed at more than £100, with the highest ticket price in Newcastle at £112.90, in Cardiff £119, and in Edinburgh at £120.95. The top ticket price in Manchester was £119.60.Tickets for the tour are due to go on sale on Friday, with a presale on Wednesday morning.Fender is not the first pop star to criticise ticket prices for his own show. The Swedish pop singerZara Larssonhas also called out steep ticket prices. In a TikTok post in August, she agreed with criticism from fans that ticket prices for her show in Bangkok were “very expensive” and wished to be “more involved” with setting prices.“I hate the fact that people genuinely want to come, but they can’t because of the prices,” Larsson added.View image in fullscreenSam Fender with Olivia Dean after receiving the award for song of the year at the Brit awards in Manchester.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersFender will perform at Newcastle’s St James’s Park, Cardiff’s Principality Stadium, Dublin’s Marley Park, Murrayfield in Edinburgh and the Etihad in Manchester across summer 2027.Earlier this week, Fender also confirmed there would be a fourth album but he has yet to release the title or cover.Fender, who was born in North Shields in Tyne and Wear, is best-known for his hit songs Hypersonic Missiles, Seventeen Going Under and People Watching. He is also the winner of five Brit awards and received the Mercury prize for his 2025 album People Watching.Earlier this year, Fender rerecorded his single Rein Me In asa duetwith the English singer-songwriter Olivia Dean, which won 2026 song of the year at the Brit awards. The song spent 23 overall weeks at No 1 in the singles chart, making it the longest-running No 1 single in British history.Explore more on these topicsSam FenderPop and rockEnglandTicket pricesMusic industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: New York archdiocese finalizing $800m settlement with clergy sex abuse survivors | New York | The Guardian
description: Agreement with more than 1,300 victims of clergy members and lay leaders would resolve long legal fight
Author: Eric Berger
Headline: Agreement with more than 1,300 victims of clergy members and lay leaders would resolve long legal fight
Content: ‘It gives closure to people, many of whom are in their 60s, 70s and even into their 80s,’ said Paul Mones, who represents some of the plaintiffs.Photograph: Gerald Herbert/APView image in fullscreen‘It gives closure to people, many of whom are in their 60s, 70s and even into their 80s,’ said Paul Mones, who represents some of the plaintiffs.Photograph: Gerald Herbert/APNew YorkNew York archdiocese finalizing $800m settlement with clergy sex abuse survivorsAgreement with more than 1,300 victims of clergy members and lay leaders would resolve long legal fightEric Bergerin New YorkSat 24 Oct 2026 17.33 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 17.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Catholic archdiocese ofNew Yorkis finalizing a settlement for at least $800m with more than 1,300 people who said they were sexually abused by clergy members and lay leaders, according to one of the plaintiff’s attorneys.The agreement would resolve a long legal fight, as well as reportedly reduce the risk of the diocese going bankrupt.While the parties have not reached a final deal, just a few details remain, according to attorney Paul Mones, who represents some of the plaintiffs.“It gives closure to people, many of whom are in their 60s, 70s and even into their 80s,” Mones said in a phone interview on Saturday. “That is a significant matter in terms of closing the emotional door – or trying to – because it’s never going to be closed, but [it] at least gives some measure of justice to people who were terribly wronged.”In 2006, the New York state court of appeals refused to waive a statute of limitations concerning allegations that Catholic priests committed sexual abuse in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s, theNew York Times reported.The state then in 2019 passed theChild Victims Act, which allowed sexual abuse survivors to bring civil lawsuits against abusers until the plaintiff turned 55. Afterwards, thousands of peoplefiled lawsuitsagainst the archdiocese, theBoy ScoutsandJeffrey Epstein, among others.Then, in 2025, thearchdiocese of New Yorkstarted trying toraise $300mto pay 1,300 survivors of clergy abuse. The New York Roman Catholic district sold off assets and cut costs to settle the claims; in New Orleans, the archdiocesedeclared bankruptcyamid similar scandals.The New York survivors can now either enter into an agreement with the archdiocese in which each receives $250,000, or fill out a form detailing what happened and participate in an allocation procedure that will determine how much money they receive, Mones explained.In an email to priests, which was shared withthe New York Times, the New York archbishop, Ronald A Hicks, said: “We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors.”While the settlement would resolve the claims in New York, the Catholic church faces lawsuits concerning alleged sexual abuse in other states.Chicago attorneys filed a half dozen lawsuits this month against the city’s archdiocese alleging that the institution knew its priests were running a sex ring at a parish and did not stop it, according toWTTW News. In Baltimore, the archdiocese is in mediation with sexual abuse survivors,WBAL reported.Mones said that he is representing alleged survivors of sexual abuse in lawsuits against archdioceses across the country, including Buffalo, San Diego and San Francisco.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkCatholicismRape and sexual assaultChildrenLaw (US)ReligionUS justice systemShareReuse this content

title: ‘You need persistence’: the Norfolk couple who took on environmental regulators three times – and won | Wetlands | The Guardian
description: Tim and Geli Harris have spent more than a decade fighting to protect Catfield Fen, a rare wetland in the Norfolk Broads
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Tim and Geli Harris have spent more than a decade fighting to protect Catfield Fen, a rare wetland in the Norfolk Broads
Content: When they bought their 460-acre farm about 30 years ago, the Harrises converted arable fields to pasture.Photograph: Ali Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWhen they bought their 460-acre farm about 30 years ago, the Harrises converted arable fields to pasture.Photograph: Ali Smith/The GuardianWetlands‘You need persistence’: the Norfolk couple who took on environmental regulators three times – and wonTim and Geli Harris have spent more than a decade fighting to protect Catfield Fen, a rare wetland in the Norfolk BroadsPatrick BarkhamSat 24 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolluters and regulators who fail to stop pollution must quake in their boots when they receive a letter from the lawyers for Tim and Geli Harris. The couple, who farm 460 acres in theNorfolkBroads, have now scored a hat-trick of landmark legal victories to save an internationally important wetland after they won again in the high court this month.Lady Justice Lieven found thatNatural Englandfailed in its statutory duty to protect Catfield Fen from pollution after nitrates and phosphates washed from arable fields into one of the finest examples of calcareous fen in western Europe, home to 2,500 species including rarities such as the fen orchid, crested buckler fern, breeding bittern and swallowtail butterflies.In ascathing assessment of Natural England’s inactionsince the Harrises first reported the pollution to it in 2021, the judge said the cause of the pollution was “the most basic level of common sense” and required action by the government’s conservation watchdog.The Harrises have spent 15 years and £1.5m of their own money taking action to hold to account government agencies for failing to protect the fen, which is part of a special area of conservation (SAC), an internationally important wetland protected by law. The marshes lie within the Broads national park.“This is bigger than a little ditch in Norfolk,” says Tim. He fears that “regulatory inertia” is preventing pollution from being halted on waterways across the country. “Inertia is prevalent throughout all the regulatory bodies. It’s a landmark judgment because it says they can’t just do nothing.”View image in fullscreenCatfield Fen is an internationally important and tremendously diverse wetland.Photograph: Ali Smith/The GuardianThe couple are big fans ofDirty Business, the recent Channel 4 dramatisation of a maths professor and a retired detective’s battle against sewage pollution, the water companies and the Environment Agency.“It’s just like that film when you go to a meeting,” Tim says. “The language is from [George Orwell’s] 1984. What we call the light side doesn’t have the money. The dark side does. That’s where the money is. Of course it is.”“They are slippery snakes,” Geli adds.Tim held senior roles in the shipping industry, collecting “the wages of sin”, before turning to environmental campaigning in retirement. “She’s the greenie,” he says of Geli, who grew up near the forests around Heidelberg, Germany, and has always loved the natural world.They bought their farm, which came with a large chunk of Catfield Fen, in 1994, wanting to live closer to nature. They turned their arable fields into pasture to prevent soils and pollution from washing into the fen, and continue to tend English white park cattle, sheep and rare-breed Eriskay ponies.‘Cash to trash’ levy on house developers too low to offset damage to Norfolk Broads, say criticsRead more“It is beautiful,” Geli says of the fen, which requires a careful rotational cut to preserve its rare plants, invertebrates and birdlife. “It’s a little bit of wildness. It’s mysterious. There are places here where we’ve never been – they are pure nature.”Tim says: “It’s taken 1,000 years to create this and people could destroy it very quickly.” Geli adds: “If you water your plants with the wrong water, they die quite quickly.”View image in fullscreenThe Harrises have spent 15 years and £1.5m of their own money holding agencies to account for failing to protect the fen.Photograph: Ali Smith/The GuardianThe Harrises take conservation advice from the experts at NaturalEngland. “We get on well with Natural England, apart from suing them,” Tim says. “They all came to tea and we talked about everything but the thing [the legal case]. It was a very British occasion. They have some very good people. The trouble is too many no longer have fire in their bellies. They are apparatchiks. We respect them but we wish they had more ‘go’.”Natural England said it accepted the court’s verdict that it had not done enough to protect Catfield Fen but it would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.In 2016, the couple won a public inquiry that demonstrated that too much groundwater was being taken from the valley by water companies and local farmers, causing Catfield Fen to dry out. Theywon a second battle in 2022, forcing the Environment Agency to limit the abstraction of water close to other nature-rich sites on the Norfolk Broads.Their principles have cost them local friendships. They say National Farmers’ Union reps rejected their application for membership of the local branch, saying half their members would resign, with farmers upset at restrictions on their abstraction of water to boost lucrative crops such as potatoes. “We’re farmers, we’re not anti-farmer,” Tim says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSince their 2022 legal victory, the Harrises have noticed an improvement in the water levels and biodiversity of Catfield Fen’s dykes. Geli says: “We are a Noah’s ark until things get better and nature can spread outwards from here again.”View image in fullscreenThe couple are campaigning to limit water abstraction in the area.Photograph: Si Barber/The GuardianThe fen and its wildlife may be in a better condition under their stewardship, but they are not confident that nature is winning. “The evidence this summer was that the insect numbers are going south, according to the experts who survey here,” Tim says. “We are not complacent; we are very worried.”The judge is to make further rulings on what Natural England must do to stop the pollution of Catfield Fen. For the Harrises, the answer is simple: arable farmers must be paid to put in buffer strips of grassland between their ploughed fields and the ditches leading to the Broads to reduce the nitrate-filled soils washing from arable fields into the fen.View image in fullscreenThe couple are considering another legal challenge.Photograph: Si Barber/The GuardianMore widely, Tim argues that regulatory bodies must simply put their resources into monitoring and compliance. He fears most breaches of environmental rules go unnoticed because of a lack of both.The Harrises say they do not want to spend their time campaigning. “I don’t want any of this, believe me,” Tim says, gesturing at the box files that take up two walls of shelving. “I’m 79. I want to read books.”He believes the Broads Authority, the government agency responsible for the national park, should be leading the fight against pollution. Nevertheless, they are considering another legal challenge to stop the Broads from being polluted.Their stewardship of Catfield Fen will continue after they go. Their daughter will take on the farm, and she is a lawyer by training. So is their granddaughter. “The agencies are not getting rid of the Harrises when we die,” Tim laughs.Do they hope their example can inspire others to believe they can act to protect nature and clean water? “You need enormous persistence,” Tim says.“You need passion,” Geli adds. “Evil can happen when people do nothing.”Explore more on these topicsWetlandsConservationNatural EnglandEnvironment AgencyWaterEnvironmental activismFarmingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘False autumn’: stressed trees drop leaves early after scorching English summer | Autumn | The Guardian
description: Season will be less vibrant with trees such as birches, which usually offer a striking burst of yellow leaves, already bare
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Season will be less vibrant with trees such as birches, which usually offer a striking burst of yellow leaves, already bare
Content: A birch tree in Wisley garden, Surrey. The white branches would normally be covered in yellow leaves in mid-October.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA birch tree in Wisley garden, Surrey. The white branches would normally be covered in yellow leaves in mid-October.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianAutumn‘False autumn’: stressed trees drop leaves early after scorching English summerSeason will be less vibrant with trees such as birches, which usually offer a striking burst of yellow leaves, already bareMatthew PearceSat 24 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmong a canvas of copper, red and purple autumn leaves on display at Wisley garden inSurrey, south-east England, one tree stands conspicuously naked.“The birch has lost all its leaves,” says Guy Barter, the chief horticulturist at the Royal Horticultural Society. “That’s the effect of drought, so it’ll have no autumn colour this year.”Where a burst of sunny yellow foliage would normally brighten the display, the birch can offer only its ivory-white bark. Afterthe hottest summer on record, the tree has dropped its canopy early, stressed from months of high temperatures and choosing to not lose any more water through its leaves.This is also known as a “false autumn”, where the stress of extreme summer conditions prompts trees and plants to behave as if the season has changed.View image in fullscreenGuy Barter, the chief horticulturalist at the RHS, at Wisley garden.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianThe birch illustrates how extreme weather driven by the climate crisis is reshaping the flow of the UK’s seasons. Thousands of plant varieties at Wisley are still displaying vibrant hues, but the drought-sensitive, yellow-leafed trees such as birches, beeches and sycamores had shed their foliage by mid-October.Normally, autumn’s effect on trees is triggered by shortening daylight, dropping night-time temperatures and adequate ground moisture brought on by rain. But severe summer heat and drought has disrupted this usual cycle by forcing stressed trees into early defoliation and premature colouring, resulting in a display that kicked in earlier than expected.The majority of England and Wales remains in drought, and six areas of England weredeclared in severe droughtthis month with river and reservoir levels running low.View image in fullscreenBarter beside an oak tree – a species that has fared better than some during the extreme heat owing to its deep roots.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianUnlike deep-rooted species such as oaks, trees with shallow root systems are unable to tap into deeper groundwater, making them vulnerable to leaf drop when surface soil dries out during a drought. “Birch, beech and sycamore have been among the trees worst affected,” says Barter. “It’s at least as colourful as it is most years, but some of the trees are not giving their best, so it’s not the perfect autumn colour.”The RHS expects an earlier autumn colour peak in drought-hit areas, with intense but potentially fleeting displays. Reds, ambers and purples could stand out as some trees normally prized for yellow foliage lose their leaves.Tim Upson, the director of gardens and horticulture at the RHS, says the colour peak historically comes toward the end of October, but this year’s drought has brought some trees into colour earlier. “Quite often now it’s going into November when you get that crescendo,” he says. “So for me, this is quite unusual.”AsStorm Austenblows in, the Met Office has warned of strong winds that could damage buildings and bring down trees. Expertswarned in Septemberthat high winds brought byEl Niñocould decimate already drought-weakened trees.Although shallow-rooted and yellow-leaved trees are struggling, other species remain vibrant, including the biggest liquidambar tree in the UK with its flutter of pink, red and purple leaves. Barter says gardeners here are likely to plant fewer birches and more “trees of the future” such as liquidambar going forward.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“There are different scenarios under climate change,” he says. “The generally accepted one is that we’ll have milder, wetter winters, but we’ll still have the occasional really cold one. So it’s no good planting tender trees, because when we have a really cold winter, they’ll succumb.“We’re looking for trees that are completely hardy in cold winters and have also got deep, wide-ranging roots that can tolerate hot, dry summers.”He lists Lebanon cedars and swamp cypresses as trees that Wisley will plant more of to adapt to changing conditions.View image in fullscreenVisitors photograph the vibrant autumn displays.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianUpson says adaptation is nothing new at Wisley; it was happening when he started working in horticulture 40 years ago. “There are some wonderful Californian oaks and Mediterranean oaks which we planted as an experiment 30 years ago, and they’re thriving now.”Familiar species will still have a place as temperatures change, he says, but beech and birch could become less spotted, surviving better in sheltered or damper locations.“I think what will happen is that we won’t necessarily lose plants, but they will either become shorter-lived or they won’t grow in the most exposed and stressful situations,” he says. “It’s going to be very much a changing landscape.”Explore more on these topicsAutumnDroughtTrees and forestsClimate crisisExtreme heatSurreyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom | BBC | The Guardian
description: BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say
Author: Tara Conlan
Headline: BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say
Content: Creatures filmed in the deep ocean are ‘more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real’, said the Blue Planet III producers.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoView image in fullscreenCreatures filmed in the deep ocean are ‘more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real’, said the Blue Planet III producers.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoBBCBlue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boomBBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers sayTara ConlanSat 24 Oct 2026 04.32 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheDavid Attenborough-narrated series Blue Planet III deliberately includes cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said.Nearly a decade after Blue Planet II shone a light on plastic pollution, and 25 years since the first Blue Planet aired, the hitBBCseries is returning with more animal behaviour and cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed “stonefish” cam.Since the first Blue Planet, TVs and cameras have evolved to give viewers sharper, higher definition pictures. But the combination of the rise in AI and the extraordinary sequences and fantastical creatures captured by BBC Studios’ natural history unit for this series led producers to include what they called more “organic” footage and less polished shots, to show that the animals were not AI-generated.View image in fullscreen‘No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame,’ said the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jo HaleyThe executive producer, Elizabeth White, said AI, “makes us want to be even more authentic”, adding that the creatures filmed in the deep ocean “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real”.She said that in the past “the amount of plankton and things that are in the water in the sequences” would usually mean they might be excluded, and previously, “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’”But now such things are being left in as “we’re really leaning into that authenticity … As AI booms we will probably lean more into the more organic”, murkier and less polished footage.For the first time, the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle, assured journalists at a press screening: “No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame. It’s all real photography.”Bootle added that as we live in a “golden age of natural history-making … sometimes people feel like they’ve seen it all before [so] this series is bursting with novel behaviour”.View image in fullscreenThe hit BBC series returns with cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed ‘stonefish’.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoThat includes never-before-seen action of dolphins using sea sponges to block holes in coral to trap fish, captured using underwater CCTV – developed by the programme’s producer and director, Yoland Bosiger.Over the four years of filming across five oceans, BBC Studios “continually innovated”, said the series producer, Lara Bickerton, creating a “mini-dome” camera to follow an octopus, a “deep-sea selfie stick”, camera operators wearing leg-mounted scooters to create immersive TikTok-style diving footage and using lasers to film deep-sea creatures.Other remarkable animal behaviour captured in the programme includes grouper communicating with another species of fish; 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed; sea urchins using shells as sun hats; and footage involving penguins that echoes the Planet Earth II,‘iguana v snakes’sequence.Threats to the ocean as well as its resilience are addressed in the series. One episode shows how warmer seas caused by the climate crisis are killing off sea anemone where clown fish live and how they try to fix their homes, and the issue of plastics raised in Blue Planet II continues with a story about pollutants [and] forever chemicals, said White.Bosiger said Attenborough, who is 100 years old, was “very much involved” and made changes to scripts.White added: “What’s wonderful is he hasn’t lost his curiosity … he’s still that little boy … who gets excited … when you show him a new piece of footage.”Asked if the BBC’s£500m cost-cutting drivewould affect BBC Studios’ renowned natural history reputation, White said she could not comment on that but pointed out that Blue Planet III made savings by using more local crews on location than in previous series.Blue Planet III starts Sunday 1November on BBC1 and iPlayerExplore more on these topicsBBCNature documentariesScience and nature TVBBC OneDavid AttenboroughMarine lifeAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: British woman dies trying to save sons on Bahamas snorkelling trip | Bahamas | The Guardian
description: Mother, 36, died after current off North Bimini reportedly swept away two boys, who were later rescued, police say
Author: Harry Taylor
Headline: Mother, 36, died after current off North Bimini reportedly swept away two boys, who were later rescued, police say
Content: A marina in North Bimini. The woman was taken to a ferry dock after being rescued from the water.Photograph: Francisco Blanco/AlamyView image in fullscreenA marina in North Bimini. The woman was taken to a ferry dock after being rescued from the water.Photograph: Francisco Blanco/AlamyBahamasBritish woman dies trying to save sons on Bahamas snorkelling tripMother, 36, died after current off North Bimini reportedly swept away two boys, who were later rescued, police sayHarry TaylorSat 24 Oct 2026 05.43 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling.The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday.The force said they believed she was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island of North Bimini when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.The police said that in an attempt to rescue her boys, “the woman was also swept away”. The children were later rescued from the water.The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support.Bimini is a small island group between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland.The islands are best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and are also home to a world-leading shark research centre.In a statementposted on social media, the Royal Bahamas police force said: “According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini ferry dock.“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.“She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. Foul play is not suspected at this time.”An autopsy would be carried out to help determine the exact cause of death, the statement said.A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”Explore more on these topicsBahamasAmericasCaribbeannewsShareReuse this content

title: Storm Boelo to bring 80mph gusts and heavy rain to parts of UK | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: Second named storm will hit northern parts of UK as thousands remain without power after Friday’s Storm Austen
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Second named storm will hit northern parts of UK as thousands remain without power after Friday’s Storm Austen
Content: Storm Austen has left parts of the south-west of England without power.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenStorm Austen has left parts of the south-west of England without power.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersExtreme weatherStorm Boelo to bring 80mph gusts and heavy rain to parts of UKSecond named storm will hit northern parts of UK as thousands remain without power after Friday’s Storm AustenPriya BharadiaSat 24 Oct 2026 09.28 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 07.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK is bracing for a second storm this weekend, as strong winds and heavy rain are expected to disrupt travel and cause further power cuts in the north.Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, is expected to bring heavy, frequent showers and winds potentially exceeding 80mph to northern parts of the UK.Thousands of homes in the south-west of Englandhave already been left without power after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday.TheMet Officehas advised people to stay indoors as much as possible and said the storm will bring danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.The forecaster has issued an amber alert, its second most severe weather warning, covering Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm Saturday to the same time on Sunday. Another amber warning is also in place for the north-east ofNorthern Irelandfrom 9pm Saturday to 10am Sunday.View image in fullscreenPeople cross Westminster Bridge in London as the UK braces for more winds and heavy downpours.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAHow autumnal high pressure brings on the dark doldrumsRead moreA large yellow warning for very wet and windy weather will cover the whole of the UK’s north from midday Saturday to 9pm on Sunday. Another warning for heavy rain covers Wales and parts of western and southernEnglandfrom 11am to 11pm Saturday.Widespread travel disruption is expected on ferries and trains. TransPennine Express has warned against making all but essential train journeys on Saturday and Sunday, while Avanti West Coast has strongly advised users not to travel north of Preston on Sunday.The Met Office has also warned that power cuts across the south-west of England could be replicated across amber areas in the north this weekend.In the south-west of England, 31,000 homes were without power at one stage on Friday. More than 3,700 were still without electricity on Saturday morning, according to the National Grid map.Human-driven climate change has continued to reshape rainfall patterns and weather conditions globally. TheUK experienced its hottest summeron record this year, with five heatwaves and a record-breaking 40 days of temperatures above 30C.The Met Office meteorologist Alex Burkill said: “Storm Boelo is arriving. It’s going to bring widespread rain and some very strong winds indeed, and it’s quick on the tails of Storm Austen which is now clearing away towards the east.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s the winds that were perhaps most concerned about, they’re really going to whip up some strong gusty winds across Northern Ireland, northern parts of England and alsoScotlandthrough the day – strengthening as we head towards the evening.“Temperatures will be a little more than the seasonal average but obviously with the wind and rain it’s going to feel pretty unpleasant out there,” Burkhill added. “A very, well, different side of autumn compared with what we’ve seen through much of the season so far.”Storm Boelo’s winds are expected to peak from Saturday evening. The wet weather will clear overnight in many areas, while more rain continues to hit Scotland and northern Ireland.Attending a summit on the summer’s record wildfires on Friday, Andy Burnham warned that the UK could face“a winter of greater flooding”.The prime minister denied suggestions that the government was playing catch-up with civil preparedness, but said “we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common”.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherUK weatherEnglandNorth of EnglandMet OfficeScotlandNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: He wants to clean up the city and banish high prices. But who is ‘London’s Batman’? | London | The Guardian
description: The caped crusader is paying for hospital parking fines, giving out fuel to drivers – and sponsoring the return of cut-price Freddo bars
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: The caped crusader is paying for hospital parking fines, giving out fuel to drivers – and sponsoring the return of cut-price Freddo bars
Content: Calling himself ‘London’s Batman’, the mystery philanthropist is trying to help with the cost of living.Photograph: officiallondonsbatmanView image in fullscreenCalling himself ‘London’s Batman’, the mystery philanthropist is trying to help with the cost of living.Photograph: officiallondonsbatmanLondonHe wants to clean up the city and banish high prices. But who is ‘London’s Batman’?The caped crusader is paying for hospital parking fines, giving out fuel to drivers – and sponsoring the return of cut-priced Freddo barsSammy GecsoylerSat 24 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the harsh light of day, a caped crusader storms the streets ofLondonto tackle a crime that has long blighted the capital: littering.“When I said I wanted to save London, I meant it. I will not stop until every single bit of trash is off the streets,” he says in a viral video, narrated in his trademark deep, husky and (suspiciously) American voice, joined by a gang of hooded helpers clearing rubbish-strewn streets in Tower Hamlets.This was Batman’s first good deed for the capital and, in the month since relocating from Gotham, he has carried out many more: paying parking fines for those visiting loved ones in hospital, giving out “free fuel” to motorists and bringing back £1 chicken and chips to those who once savoured this cheap and filling after-school meal.But who is he really and what does he stand for? In a recentinterviewwith a BBC reporter, who was only given a time and location before the masked figure emerged in an alleyway, he summed up his mission: “People are struggling and I want to help them.”View image in fullscreen‘London’s Batman’ collects rubbish in an alley.Photograph: officiallondonsbatmanAs for his identity, Niko Omilana – YouTuber, prankster and fifth-placed London 2021 mayoral candidate, who has pulled off similar stunts – is the most obvious guess, though he has denied it.When asked by BBC London if he was the city’s masked mystery saviour, Omilana sent the team a voice note saying: “BBC, just to tell you, I’m not Batman.”Count Binface, who has faced off against some of the nation’s most high-profile politicians in elections across the country, is another name in the mix, though he denied the rumours.He told the Guardian: “I can see why a human might think that ‘London’s Batman’ is me, but it is actually a bit armour-ist of you. We’re not all the same.“I’m happy to make the clarification and I would like to take the opportunity to wish London’s Batman well, including with his inevitable battle on the planet Copyright.”Omilana remains the most likely suspect. His 2021 mayoral manifesto pledges included turning off all power in London once a year to “call it Londoff”, forcing then-prime minister Boris Johnson to “shush” and reducing the price of a Freddo chocolate bar to 5p.View image in fullscreenThe self-styled superhero picking up rubbish with his hooded helpers.Photograph: officiallondonsbatmanCuriously, in one of his most viral stunts, London’s Batman set up a stall in Oxford Street where a Freddo could be exchanged for a tiny, silver 5p coin. (The frog-shaped chocolate bar was never officially sold for this sum, with 2p in the 1970s and 10p in the 1990s and early 2000s being the lowest retail prices documented.)Ace Clvrk was in the area buying a guitar when he came across the stall. “I was lucky that day I had exactly 5p. It felt like fate,” said the 32-year-old musician.He was approached on the street by some “hooded, masked youths” who “seemed really friendly”. They stopped him and asked: “Do you want to buy a Freddo?”Clvrk was guided to a stall where he saw the caped crusader in the flesh. He told Clvrk he was “trying to bring attention to lowering the cost of Freddos”.Like Gotham’s caped crusader, his London doppelganger appears to have significant resources behind him. His social media videos are slickly produced and the tasks he has carried out are hardly cheap.For the “free fuel” stunt, one resident,speakingto the Times, estimated he gave away more than £3,500 to motorists throughout the day. The Guardian contacted several organisations that had benefited from London’s Batman’s good deeds who declined to speak citing confidentiality reasons.Clvrk said it looked like a well-run stunt. “Everyone that I spoke to was really friendly and the actual content came out looking great too. I don’t remember actually seeing the camera,” he said.View image in fullscreenIt’s estimated that ‘London’s Batman’ distributed more than £3,500 worth of free fuel in one day.Photograph: officiallondonsbatmanIn the video touting his bargain frog-shaped chocolates, London’s Batman featured a clip of Andy Burnham holding a Freddo whiledeclaring it the “most talked about cost of living symbol in the UK”before going on to say he “might not be able to do anything to reduce the price of these”.The caped crusader’s Freddo policy could suggest he’s vying for real power. “I’d vote for him, 100%,” said Clvrk. “5p Freddo, £1 chicken and chips and paying for fuel. What’s not to love?”There could be some weight to this, especially if two-time political candidate Omilana, who also ran against Rishi Sunak in his Richmond and Northallerton seat in 2024, is behind the mask.The message appears to be resonating. On TikTok, he has already amassed 315,000 followers in just over four weeks.“I think everything he’s doing is amazing,” said Clvrk. “Politics and prime ministers are removed from the everyday Londoner and British person on the streets who used to be able to get a Freddo for 10p or cheap chicken and chips.“With rising prices, it’s shining a light on things that seem small to those that are removed from it, but not for the everyday person.”Explore more on these topicsLondonBatmanUK cost of living crisisSuperhero moviesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: More than third of post offices in TG Jones stores to shut by early 2027 | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Closures within chain formerly under the WH Smith brand raise fears of high streets becoming ‘postal deserts’
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Closures within chain formerly under the WH Smith brand raise fears of high streets becoming ‘postal deserts’
Content: Up to 150 of the 450 stores acquired by the private equity firm Modella are expected to shut. Of the 110 announced closures, 70 contained, or contain, post offices.Photograph: Michael Kemp/AlamyView image in fullscreenUp to 150 of the 450 stores acquired by the private equity firm Modella are expected to shut. Of the 110 announced closures, 70 contained, or contain, post offices.Photograph: Michael Kemp/AlamyRetail industryMore than third of post offices in TG Jones stores to shut by early 2027Closures within chain formerly under the WH Smith brand raise fears of high streets becoming ‘postal deserts’Sarah ButlerSat 24 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTowns and even city centres face being left as “postal deserts” after it emerged that more than a third of post offices within the troubled TG Jones chain are closing.So far this year 36 branches within the high street chainformerly known as WH Smithhave closed and a further 34 are set to close by early 2027, according to Post Office records analysed by the Guardian.TG Jones was bought and renamed by Modella last year. Before the private equity group’s restructurewon approval from creditors in July, the chain operated 180 post offices and it had been feared that as many as 60 could be closed under the shake-up.Up to 150 of the 450 stores acquired by Modella are expected to shut, about 65 of which have already closed and at least another 46 are to cease operating early next year. This total of 110 announced closures include the 70 containing post offices.The larger-than-expected wave of TG Jones branch closures follows an announcement in the summer that 52 post offices will close within Morrisons Daily convenience stores this year, some of which are close to the TG Jones sites. The move forms part of a wider plan by Morrisons to close 100 loss-making small stores.The raft of closures means that towns such as Stevenage in Hertfordshire, Bracknell in Berkshire and Orpington in Greater London, and some smaller cities including Hull and York are each losing two post offices in a matter of months. Telford’s last one is due to close in January.The majority of these lost sites replaced former crown post offices, the now almost entirely closed network of more than 100 directly operated large branches, which offered a full suite of services such as identity and passport checks, driving licence and banking operations.Some regions such as Essex, the West Midlands, Wales, Suffolk and Hertfordshire have been particularly hard hit. Six post offices in TG Jones stores in Essex are going, with Clacton-on-Sea and Brentwood shutting in January after the closure of ones in Basildon, Southend-on-Sea, Harlow and East Ham. Five are closing in the West Midlands and four in Wales.ThePost Officeis trying to find new operators in these locations but so far only Stirling has reopened after a TG Jones closure, and a permanent replacement for Ipswich is set to open in November. Temporary branches are to operate after TG Jones closures in Maidenhead and Uxbridge.Such losses can be devastating to the health of local economies. As thePost Office itself pointed outto a parliamentary inquiry into revitalising high streets, almost a third of small- and medium-sized businesses use their local branch at least once a week and more than half use the network at least once a month. Many small businesses report that losing this access would threaten their viability within months.After the closure of more than 6,800 bank branches across the UK, the Post Office “plays a critical role in protecting this essential service”, according to thetstate-owned company’s evidence to the inquiry. Post office operators already run 250 banking hubs, which combine services for several banking brands, across the UK.Mole Meade, a senior member at theCWU, the largest union for postal workers, said the closures would leave some areas as “postal deserts”.Meade added: “What we are seeing with the TG Jones closures is the continuation of a long-term strategy of cutting costs and chasing profit, with little regard for the communities that depend on post office services.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The CWU believes the Post Office should be focused on protecting and expanding access to services, not presiding over a continued reduction of the network.”The Post Office said: “We fully recognise the challenging trading conditions that TG Jones and many other high street retailers are facing at the moment. We proactively sought expressions of interest from our postmasters and partners to take on post offices within TG Jones stores that may close as a result of their restructuring plan or any decisions taken by landlords.“There is interest in taking on every location where it has been confirmed that a post office within a TG Jones store will close. In some locations there are over 40 applications from our postmasters who recognise the significant footfall operating a post office brings to their store … We’re committed to replacing every branch within a TG Jones store that closes and are working to progress applications as quickly as possible.”The state-owned Post Office – which is still reeling from theHorizon IT scandal– announced the closure ofmore than 100 branches in late 2024.WH Smith travel stores in railway stations, hospitals and airports were not part of the Modella deal and remain owned by its original stock market-listed parent company.TG Jones was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsRetail industryPostal servicePost OfficePrivate equitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Suspect arrested over fire at Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ retreat in Bavaria | Germany | The Guardian
description: About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle blaze at former Nazi mountain retreat in remote part of southern Germany
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle blaze at former Nazi mountain retreat in remote part of southern Germany
Content: A still from a video of the fire sweeping through the mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, formerly Adolf Hitler's Eagle’s Nest retreat.Photograph: AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenA still from a video of the fire sweeping through the mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, formerly Adolf Hitler's Eagle’s Nest retreat.Photograph: AFP/GettyGermanySuspect arrested over fire at Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ retreat in BavariaAbout 200 firefighters deployed to tackle blaze at former Nazi mountain retreat in remote part of southern GermanyDonna Fergusonand agenciesSat 24 Oct 2026 10.28 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 02.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice have arrested a 33-year-old German citizen after a fire ripped through Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat in Bavaria, leaving the historic Nazi meeting place – known as the Eagle’s Nest – largely destroyed.About 200 firefighters were deployed on Friday night to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote, purpose-built Kehlsteinhaus residence, a protected building on the peak of Obersalzberg in southernGermany.Flames rose high into the air as firefighters approached the scene to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said, adding that nobody was injured in the fire.Lisa Maier, a police spokesperson, said firefighters struggled to tackle the blaze due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft).The building, which was one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era, was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.View image in fullscreenThe Kehlsteinhaus the morning after the fire.Photograph: Jason Tschepljakow/DPA/APBuilt by the Nazis and formally inaugurated by Hitler on his birthday in 1939, the Eagle’s Nest has been preserved as a monument to “the insanity of the regime”,according to its website.The building is only accessible via a road cut into the mountain through previously impassable terrain. Nazis would enter a tunnel and take a 124-metre brass lift buried in the mountain to get inside the building.Authorities were alerted to the fire when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.15pm, police said. When firefighters arrived on the scene at about 9.50pm, the entire building was engulfed in flames.Fire departments from six municipalities sent emergency personnel to tackle the blaze and the Bavarian Red Cross, the local mountain rescue service and the police also attended.No reason for the fire was given, but German media reported that investigators suspected it was the result of arson. Firefighters found no one inside the building.Efforts to fight the fire were hampered by a strong wind and rain, which turned into the year’s first snow, and firefighters had to pull out overnight after several hours.The blaze was reportedly still burning at 7am on Saturday but appeared to be out later in the morning, although smoke continued to rise from the building.View image in fullscreenA photograph from 2007 of the Kehlsteinhaus, or Eagle’s Nest, near Berchtesgaden, Germany.Photograph: Geir Moulson/APA police spokesperson told the German tabloid Bild: “It is damaged to a large extent. The house is unlikely to be saved.” Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an Agence France-Presse photographer.Maier said police were still investigating and would hold a news conference later on Saturday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMap of south-east Germany showing the location of KehlsteinhausThe 33-year-old suspect arrested by the police was a German citizen who had ties to the area but did not live there. Prosecutors said he showed signs of mental illness and after being questioned he was being sent to a psychiatric facility.The possibility of a political motive for the blaze would be investigated, but police said there was nothing to indicate anyone else was involved.The Eagle’s Nest was constructed between 1937 and 1938 and forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and communists in theHolocaust.It became legendary in the postwar period and was often depicted as an essential meeting place in US war films, although in reality Hitler rarely visited the complex.Since 1952 the building has housed an exhibition bythe Institute for Contemporary Historyrecounting its Nazi history, and a restaurant.Officials indicated that the building, which is owned by Bavaria’s state government, would be restored after discussions with local officials, historians and conservators.“We’re not going to leave a ruin there,” Joachim Herrmann, Bavaria’s interior minister, told reporters, adding that it was important to continue to do “the work of remembrance”.Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsGermanyAdolf HitlerEuropeNazismHolocaustSecond world warnewsShareReuse this content

title: ICC prosecutor says court making ‘significant progress’ despite US sanctions | International criminal court | The Guardian
description: Nazhat Shameem Khan claims some staff are facing ‘banking difficulties’ but their work is unaffected
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Nazhat Shameem Khan claims some staff are facing ‘banking difficulties’ but their work is unaffected
Content: ICC deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan: ‘We haven’t made any decision based on the sanctions to reduce our capability.’Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/ReutersView image in fullscreenICC deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan: ‘We haven’t made any decision based on the sanctions to reduce our capability.’Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/ReutersInternational criminal courtICC prosecutor says court making ‘significant progress’ despite US sanctionsNazhat Shameem Khan claims some staff are facing ‘banking difficulties’ but their work is unaffectedJulian BorgerSenior international correspondentSat 24 Oct 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 09.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe deputy prosecutor of the international criminal court has said new US sanctions are beginning to take effect on its staff but insisted they have not hindered the court’s work.The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, announced thesanctions this month, accusing the ICC – a frequent target of the Trump administration – of being a “rogue court” and declaring: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”Nazhat Shameem Khan, who is co-running the office pending the appointment of a new chief prosecutor, said the court was so far continuing its work.She said the Gaza war investigation and others had made “significant progress” sincewar crimes arrest warrantswere issued in November 2024 for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister, Yoav Galant. Further applications from the prosecutor were being kept secret by order of the court, she said.View image in fullscreenThe ICC issued a war crimes arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.Photograph: Amir Cohen/ReutersSome ICC staff had however encountered banking problems, she said, even though the US sanctions on the court were not due to take effect until six months from 9 October, the date of their announcement. She said the banks were “over-complying” to minimise risk while there was uncertainty over the ultimate scope of the measures.“These are sanctions imposed on the institutions and, in principle, our individual members should not be impacted directly,” the Fijian deputy prosecutor said in an interview with the Guardian. “But again, what I am hearing from members of our staff is that some of them are experiencing difficulties in banking.”The court is working on insulating itself from sanctions imposed by a hostile administration in Washington. It has switched its software from Microsoft to European ​alternatives, and is negotiating with relevant service providers over banking and health insurance.“All the investigations across all situations continue. We haven’t made any decision based on the sanctions to reduce our capability or reduce our output,” Khan said, acknowledging that it was impossible to anticipate the full impact of sanctions when they officially took effect.The new sanctions target the whole institution of the ICC, but theUS first targeted 13 ICC staffin February 2025. Khan was one of them, so is accustomed to dealing with sanctions, which affect aspects of everyday life.“Life without a credit card is inconvenient. It’s amazing how many things now we cannot do around the world, particularly in relation to travel, without a credit card,” she said, but added that her inconvenience was put into perspective when she visited refugee camps or sites of mass atrocities.“We see the faces of our victims for whom sanctions and credit cards are completely irrelevant. They just want justice.”View image in fullscreenThe former ICC chief prosecutor, Karim Khan.Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/ReutersAmerican sanctions are not the only disruption to the ICC prosecutors’ work. Formal investigations began in late November 2024 intoallegations of sexual harassmentagainst the former chief prosecutor, Karim Khan. The British jurist (who is no relation to the deputy prosecutor) denied the charges. He wasremoved in July this yearafter a vote by member states.No further charges over the Gaza war have been announced since late 2024. Khan insisted that investigative work on the Israel-Palestine file had only gone quiet because of the court’s ruling earlier this year that all charges and applications for warrants should be kept secret until the judges decide they can be made public.“Even if we reach a stage of the investigations where it might be imminent, we may not discuss it publicly,” she said. “And so while there might be an appearance that nothing is happening, I can assure you that there’s significant progress in that particular situation as well as others.”When announcing the sanctions, Rubio gave the ICC a six-month grace period “to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns” but it is unclear what would satisfy theTrump administration, which has exhibited a longstanding hostility towards the court.Rubio claimed, without evidence, this month that “globalist ‘experts’ an ocean away” wanted the ICC to prosecute US citizens. Khan said it was unclear who and what Rubio had in mind.View image in fullscreenUS secretary of state, Marco Rubio: ‘Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.’Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters/AP“It is possible that there is a mistaken belief on the part of those who are concerned that we are pursuing Americans, but we certainly haven’t brought any Americans before the court,” she said. “If his reference is to Afghanistan, then in fact the priority for the investigation is in relation to offences committed specifically against women, girls and other vulnerable groups by the Taliban and by the Islamic State Khorasan in Afghanistan.”This month, four arrest warrants were unsealed by the ICC pretrial chamber against members of the Taliban on charges of gender persecution.The court registrar for the ICC is in negotiation with the EU over blocking the US sanctions or protecting the court in other ways. There has been support for the court, and on Thursday, theEuropean parliament awarded its Sakharov prizefor freedom of thought to the court and its officials.Khan said the support was “a very important message that the staff at the court need to hear”, as were pledges from other countries to continue to contribute towards the ICC’s costs.“I think that the fact that there is so much attention on us is a reflection of how relevant we are,” Khan said. “This is a court that provides an avenue of justice for victims who have nowhere else to go, who really want to cut past politics and want their voices to be heard.”Explore more on these topicsInternational criminal courtInternational criminal justiceTrump administrationMarco RubioUS politicsIsrael-Gaza warUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits? | Spain | The Guardian
description: Established under the Franco dictatorship, the lunchtime ritual is in decline but all is not lost
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Established under the Franco dictatorship, the lunchtime ritual is in decline but all is not lost
