Content: A pedestrian walks past a board showing amenú del día, a fixed-price offering originally dreamt up in the 1960s to attract tourists.Photograph: Thomas Coex/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA pedestrian walks past a board showing amenú del día, a fixed-price offering originally dreamt up in the 1960s to attract tourists.Photograph: Thomas Coex/AFP/Getty ImagesSpain‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?Established under the Franco dictatorship, the lunchtime ritual is in decline but all is not lostSam Jonesin MadridSat 24 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlittle before lunchtime each working day acrossSpain, evidence of one of the lingering, if less notorious, legacies of the Franco dictatorship is carefully traced in chalk, marker pen and printer ink.Beckoning to hungry workers from blackboards, whiteboards and pieces of paper hastily taped to windows, the competitively pricedmenú del día,or daily set-price lunch, has been part of everyday Spanish life for more than half a century. But while4mmenúsare still servedeach weekday, Spain is slowly losing its appetite for the familiar ritual.Back in 2009, the country’s best-known chef, Ferran Adrià, went so far as topronounce it dead– a victim of changing eating habits, economic downturns and bistro-style restaurants trying to charge €20-€30 (£17-£25) for what should be a simple starter, a hearty main and a choice of pudding or coffee … with bread and a drink thrown in.Seventeen years later, however, the diagnosis seem a little premature. A new book by the Spanish food journalist Lakshmi Aguirre charts the history and evolution of themenúand argues that while the tradition is indeed in hot water, it hasn’t quite had its chips.Her book –Menú del Día:Everyday Scenes of a First Course, a Second Course and Pudding – begins with the unpalatable fact that it all began with a tourist menu dreamed up in the mid-1960s up by the Spanish dictator Francisco Franco’s information and tourism minister,Manuel Fraga.The regime was keen in the aftermath of the“years of hunger”that followed the Spanish civil war to show foreign visitors that food was plentiful, good and affordable. So it was that establishments serving food should offer “a starter of soup, a main course chosen from at least three options and based on egg, fish or meat and accompanied by a side dish, and a pudding based on fruit, something sweet, or cheese”.View image in fullscreenA selection of daily menus on chalkboards in Madrid. They typically consist of a simple starter, a hearty main and a choice of pudding or coffee with bread and a drink thrown in.The price was set at between 50 and 250 pesetas and, to stop unscrupulous restaurant owners watering down the drinks, the law stipulated that the accompanying quarter-litre ofvinohad to be “reds and whites from Spain that are pure, clean, pleasant on the palate and with an alcohol content of not less than 12%”.In the early 1970s, themenú del díawas rebaptised to make it look less like an attempt to woo – and sometimes gouge – tourists, but also to give ordinary Spaniards the idea that they, too, could indulge.It is now so ubiquitous that many in Spain have no idea of its genesis. “When I was working on the book and people asked me about themenú del día, I’d mention Manuel Fraga and lots of them would throw their hands up in shock,” Aguirre said. “Some people know, but the vast majority don’t. It says a lot about us Spaniards; we forget very quickly.”Researching the book, which includes personal reminiscences and a hefty selection of recipes, led Aguirre to consider the place of themenúin the popular consciousness.“It’s part of our history, yet it’s changed over the years, reflecting the evolution of Spanish society,” she said. “It originated from something as terrible as a dictatorship, and today it has become a deeply ingrained custom. We feel a sense of nostalgia as we realise it’s fading away.”View image in fullscreenAguirre says restaurants serving a menú del día should be a centre of community gravity ‘where families with limited financial means can afford to eat out’.Photograph: Jeffrey Isaac Greenberg/AlamyThe threats to the set lunch, whoseaverage price today is €14.70, are many. Increasingly time-poor, many Spaniards now opt for a quick lunch, eating food from home at work or popping to a supermarket for a ready meal to microwave in a soulless canteen. Rising energy and food prices are making it harder for small, family-run restaurants to offer a rotating daily selection of starters and mains.All of which explains the rise of the “dish of the day”, which offers restaurants a cheaper alternative to the traditional choice of three or four mains, and the increasing diversity of somemenús, which now feature Latin American staples as a reflection of Spain’s changing demographics.“Themenú del díapurists reject such options, but it has always been a reflection of the society that consumes it – and that’s exactly how it should be,” Aguirre said. “Spain today isn’t the same as it was in the 1980s, it is far more diverse and pluralistic, and as a result diners have changed as well. Themenú del díaexists for those who need it, for people who may come from many different backgrounds.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA daily menu at a restaurant in Palma, Mallorca. The food writer Lakshmi Aguirre says chalkboards should ideally be written by ‘someone who’s never heard of lettering’.Photograph: Ian Shaw/AlamyAguirre’smenúof choice would be a simple but well-cooked vegetable stew followed by hake in green sauce or baby squid in ink, and thenleche frita(fried custard) or rice pudding.But, as she points out in her book, the surroundings are almost as important as the cooking. Her benchmarks for a goodmenú del díaspot include simple dishes, a regularly changing menu, chips that aren’t frozen, a chorus of regulars and “a chalkboard free of any trace of words such as avocado, burrata, tartare, truffle or sourdough bread”.That chalkboard should, by preference, be written “by someone who’s never heard of lettering”, and bonus points are awarded if the child of the owners is doing their homework on a table down the end.As it hobbles slowly towards what may be its demise, themenú del díahas become something that transcends a filling and reasonably priced midday meal.“What’s being lost is a meeting point,” Aguirre said. “A centre of community gravity where families with limited financial means can afford to eat out, and where those who live alone can find some company during a meal, which remains a deeply social activity.“It’s a place where joys, sorrows and problems can be shared, or where you can simply enjoy a bit of breathing space, as well as a place for those who live far away or who don’t have the time to go home for lunch.”The true privilege of themenú, she added, lay “not just in being able to pay for a meal, but also in having the time to enjoy it”.Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropeFoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dónal Lunny, ‘colossus of Irish music’, dies aged 79 | Folk music | The Guardian
description: Founding member of Planxty, Lunny went on to play for bands such as Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Founding member of Planxty, Lunny went on to play for bands such as Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin
Content: Dónal Lunny performing on stage at the Manchester Apollo in April 1999.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDónal Lunny performing on stage at the Manchester Apollo in April 1999.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianFolk musicDónal Lunny, ‘colossus of Irish music’, dies aged 79Founding member of Planxty, Lunny went on to play for bands such as Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and CoolfinPress AssociationSat 24 Oct 2026 04.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 05.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Irish traditional musician Dónal Lunny has died at the age of 79 from cancer.Lunny rose to prominence in the trio Rakes of Kildare alongside his brother Frank and Christy Moore. He went on to play in bands such asPlanxty,Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin among others and toured the world.A post on his Facebook page confirmed that Lunny died in St James’s hospital in Dublin on Friday morning.“We are heartbroken to confirm that our beloved Dónal passed away peacefully this morning in Dublin following a short stay in St James’s hospital,” the post said. “Thank you for helping us to remember and celebrate his immense contribution to music, to culture and to so many people’s lives all over the world.”View image in fullscreenCatherine Connolly said Lunny was ‘central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music’.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAThe Irish president, Catherine Connolly, expressed her “deepest condolences to the family, friends and many musical collaborators of Dónal Lunny”.In a statement, she said: “Dónal was one of Ireland’s greatest musical figures, a wonderfully talented musician and producer who was central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music.“Dónal will be particularly remembered for his long partnerships with fellow musicians such as Christy Moore and Andy Irvine and for the innovative music he has left behind both as a musician in groups including Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts and also as a renowned producer.“This rich musical legacy, including his central role in the introduction of the bouzouki into Irish music, was appropriately recognised by his fellow artists in Dónal’s membership of Aosdána, as well as the well-deserved recognition which he received in being awarded a lifetime achievement award at the 2025 RTÉ Radio 1 Irish folk awards.“Beyond his music, Dónal will be remembered for his warmth and the strong connection which he had with audiences all over Ireland and beyond. He will be deeply missed.”The post ended in Irish, saying his likes will not be seen again: “Ní bheidh a leithéid arís ann.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Irish folk group Planxty in London in January 1973. From left: Andy Irvine, Liam O’Flynn, Dónal Lunny and Christy Moore.Photograph: Michael Putland/GettyLunny was born in Tullamore, County Offaly, and was a multi-instrumentalist but was best known for his mastery of the bouzouki. He was a talented melody writer and considered central to the revival of traditional music as he produced 17 albums under his record label Mulligan Records.The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he was “deeply saddened” to hear of Lunny’s death. “A colossus of Irish music, as a performer, songwriter and producer,” he wrote in a post on social media.“Uniquely gifted, Dónal carried traditional and folk music to new audiences through Planxty and his many other endeavours.”Sinn Féin’s president, Mary Lou McDonald, also paid tribute online, saying: “Deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Dónal Lunny. A giant of Irish traditional music, Dónal helped shape the sound of Irish music for generations, bringing our rich musical heritage to audiences at home and around the world. His contribution to Irish music and culture will never be forgotten.“Ar dheis Dé go raibh a anam[May his soul rest in peace].”Explore more on these topicsFolk musicIrelandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Lime bike jousts? Why youth culture is embracing the medieval era | Culture | The Guardian
description: From chainmail-wearing pop stars to high-fashion catwalks, the spirit of the middle ages is erupting into the zeitgeist
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: From chainmail-wearing pop stars to high-fashion catwalks, the spirit of the middle ages is erupting into the zeitgeist
Content: ‘It’s fun. It can be camp and it can be macho and it can be sexy as well.’ Lime bike jousting at London Fields in east London last week.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreen‘It’s fun. It can be camp and it can be macho and it can be sexy as well.’ Lime bike jousting at London Fields in east London last week.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPACultureLime bike jousts? Why youth culture is embracing the medieval eraFrom chainmail-wearing pop stars to high-fashion catwalks, the spirit of the middle ages is erupting into the zeitgeistEllie Violet BramleySat 24 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMedieval knights used to joust on warhorses with wooden lances, but this week in eastLondon, two men jousted on Lime bikes with PVC pipes. This contemporary spin on a medieval spectacle is just one example of the spirit of the middle ages erupting into the zeitgeist.As part of Frieze art fair, the artist Corbin Shaw staged a show called Feast of Fools. The “‘anti-Frieze” Frieze show took inspiration from a medieval festival where,as Shaw put it to GQ, “the peasant class could insult the rich”. In the video for Troye Sivan’s latest song, Party, the Australian pop star postures as a medieval knight.View image in fullscreenA model wears chainmail at the Chopova Lowena spring/summer 2026 fashion show in London.Photograph: Victor Virgile/Gamma-Rapho/GettyOn catwalks atGivenchy, Louis Vuitton and Max Mara, from wimples to chainmail, it’s been called “medievalcore”. In the new film The Uprising, actor Andrew Garfield has been leading the rabble in Paul Greengrass’s retelling of the Peasants’ Revolt. Sports Banger,the political collectivethat makes punchy T-shirts, has offerings that read: “Peasants’ Revolt 1381. Let’s finish the job”.Why is the medieval era being mined by contemporary culture? Simon Trafford, a senior lecturer in medieval history at the University of London Institute of Historical Research, says “it’s always there”, but it’s more “a matter of which particular bit of it we decide to borrow from at any one time”.View image in fullscreenThe Lime bike joust was geared towards accessibility in the week the ‘expensive and inaccessible’ Frieze art fair took place.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA“Some of the way modern artists and fashion designers are using the medieval is focused on joy and playfulness,” says Marion Turner, a professor of English literature and language at the University of Oxford. They’re not, she adds, “saying: ‘This is what I actually think the medieval world was like.’”Bridget Dalton, a semiotician and cultural analyst at Truth Consulting, says: “It’s fun. It can be camp and it can be macho and it can be sexy as well.” In the video for Party, a victorious, post-battle Sivan gallops to celebrate with a hedonistic, homoerotic knees-up in a castle. In one piece of choreography, Sivan is used like a battering ram.Dalton describes another emerging medieval strand as “wenchcore”, which offers “a more acceptable voracious sexuality, the ribald, singing, dancing, drinking, doesn’t-need-to-be-perfect idea of womanhood and of masculinity … more of just whatever goes”. It could be seen as the perfect, medieval-inflected answer to Brat. The middle ages, says Trafford, “gives us a sort of fantasy other space”.View image in fullscreenThe Australian pop star Troye Sivan poses as a medieval knight in a music video for his song Party.Photograph: YouTubeMany buzzy modern ideas feel medieval-tinged: seasonality, an emphasis on nature, folklore and locality, which take on different emphases in our technological, globalised times. Community, is a focal point in much of this contemporary medievalism. The joust in London was geared towards accessibility in the week that Frieze, described by 24-year-old jousting artist Jack Cardenas “expensive and inaccessible”, took place. “So many members of the community came out,” he says.There’s also an anti-authoritarian streak in medievalism, from Shaw to The Uprising in which a Ploughman takes his grievances to London in a move to restore egalitarianism to 14th-century England. With its own “no kings” moment, Garfieldtold the Washington Post recentlyhe saw it as “prescient and kind of predictive” of the No Kings movement in the US.There is, says Turner, an “interesting parallel” in the pandemic. “After the plague swept across Europe, there was massive social change, prompted by population decline, wage rises and new social mobility.” The peasants’ revolt “is absolutely that generation after the plague”. In the UK, in the post-Covid era, “people feel like they just don’t want to put up with what they used to put up with before the pandemic”.View image in fullscreen‘Watching youth culture embrace the medieval is a way to talk about Britain without flying a St George,’ says Bridget Dalton from Truth Consulting.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAAnother parallel could be the advent of printing then versus the advent of the internet and AI now. For Turner, “AI is more extreme in its negative effects, but again there are parallels with the squashing of individual creativity by big technology”.While rightwing politics often looks back to the middle ages for its own ends, within today’s youth-centric medievalism there’s a reclamation of the symbols of Englishness. As Shaw, whose cult-favourite T-shirt reads “Eng ‘lish’”, told GQ: “I hate the ruling classes ofEngland, but there’s a lot of reasons to be proud to be English, we have to take these symbols back.”According to Dalton, “watching youth culture embrace the medieval is a way to talk about Britain without flying a St George. It’s a very interesting route to reparative ideas about what it means to be British.”For Trafford, “you will always be able to cherrypick … the little bits that play to your cause.” Marine Le Pen might be drawing on Joan of Arc as “this massively militant Christian figure”, while “you can definitely find that more friendly, more conducive society if you happen to be a leftwing person.” There’s a medievalism for everyone.Explore more on these topicsCultureFrieze art fairEnglandLondonTroye SivanAndrew GarfieldHeritagefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Channel 4’s new social media drama has 90-second episodes – and it’s as enjoyable as watching adverts | Drama | The Guardian
description: Vertical dramas are a global phenomenon made in bite-sized addictive chunks to watch on phones. But Channel 4 has made a slow-release syrupy tale in five parts – without tension or actual drama
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Vertical dramas are a global phenomenon made in bite-sized addictive chunks to watch on phones. But Channel 4 has made a slow-release syrupy tale in five parts – without tension or actual drama
Content: Party people … the cast of the Guest List, Channel 4’s short-form phone drama.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenParty people … the cast of the Guest List, Channel 4’s short-form phone drama.Photograph: Channel 4DramaChannel 4’s new social media drama has 90-second episodes – and it’s as enjoyable as watching advertsVertical dramas are a global phenomenon made in bite-sized addictive chunks to watch on phones. But Channel 4 has made a slow-release syrupy tale in five parts – without tension or actual dramaHannah J DaviesSat 24 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVertical dramas – that is, short-form content made specifically for phones – are big business in 2026. They are particularly popular in countries such as China and India, and the global market is expected to be worth $26bn by 2030. It makes sense: much has been made of the double-screening epidemic, and of people scrolling so much thatNetflix has to remind them what is going on on their TV screensevery few seconds. Why not just cut out the middleman and ditch the telly bit altogether?Enter Channel 4, which has released its first vertical drama on social media in the UK. It’s described as “a bold, character-led series” that explores “the friendship, ambition and lives of a diverse group of intelligent young women”. The Guest List is made in partnership with the skincare brand Sol de Janeiro, and episodes are around 90 seconds to two minutes in length. The microdramas that have gripped Asia are camp and cliffhanger-heavy – one producer described them as“soap operas on cocaine”. The Guest List is less cocaine, more Coke Zero: sweet, syrupy, probably not bad for you but not especially good either. Anodyne. Sort of like watching the adverts before a YouTube video, instead of pressing the skip button at your earliest convenience.Part of the issue might be that many of these bite-size dramas release all their episodes at once, and viewers could watch 100 instalments in a day (if that sounds a lot, consider that a TikTok or Instagram user could devour many hundreds of shortform reels in 24 hours). Channel 4, however, is airing just one episode per week. If the idea is to get viewers addicted, surely 90 seconds every seven days will not cut it. Besides, I’m three episodes in and I barely know who is who. Will it be a month before I find out? There are also a mere five episodes in total; while this is the broadcaster’s first foray into the format, it does feel rather slight.That is not to say it isn’t fun. Episode one follows Amaka (Jadesola Odunjo) who – according to the publicity bumf – is “a PR guru who is bold, energetic and impossible to ignore – just like [the Sol de Janeiro perfume] Intense Mist Cheirosa 62”. It opens with her inviting friends to an exclusive boat party on the Thames ... only to have her phone snatched by a thief. She commands a passing rickshaw driver “Follow that bike!”, as she mourns the loss of “every client, every influencer, my press contact … my bank card”. (Could our reliance on our phones perhaps be bad?! Very meta). With barely 30 seconds to go and Amaka now arguing with the rickshaw driver who has realised he won’t get paid, I am hooked. Nothing else really happens, truth be told, but itcouldhave. There is youth. There is possibility. There is excellent eyeshadow. There is a woman telling Amaka that the Thames is now a 45-minute walk away.Next week’s episode finds finance intern Bella (Felicity Ali) on a work call, being patronised by her boss. She messages her mates: she won’t have time to go home and get changed before the boat party. A text pings from one of them: “ambition is your dress code”. Yes, girlboss! She fashions a dress out of a blazer, and uses her tie as a belt. (Carrie Bradshaw, eat your heart out.) Meanwhile, the episode due for release on 4 November is perhaps the most relatable for me – Mika (Mia Ito Smith) racing to collect her parcel from the corner shop then squatting in an aisle so her neighbour doesn’t see her in her sweatpants.I’m quite intrigued to find out whether the girls make it to that party, but the thought of waiting weeks to find out is the antithesis of what vertical dramas are all about. Releasing the episodes so far apart – refusing to hijack our eyeballs, glue us to our phones and make us cancel all social plans for the foreseeable future – just isn’t the microdrama way. UntilChannel 4is willing to give us the entire Guest List cinematic universe, this feels more like a gen Z Boots ad than the future of British television.The Guest List is released on 24 October on TikTok, Meta and YouTube.Explore more on these topicsDramaTelevisionChannel 4Television industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #266: The knives are out at Netflix – maybe now it will make something worth watching | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: Stalling subscriber numbers have led to a corporate bloodbath, but the streaming giant has an inherent quality problem that will be a lot harder to fix
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: Stalling subscriber numbers have led to a corporate bloodbath, but the streaming giant has an inherent quality problem that will be a lot harder to fix
Content: Lights out? ... The demise of Netflix is a story we’ve heard before.Photograph: Michael Yanow/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLights out? ... The demise of Netflix is a story we’ve heard before.Photograph: Michael Yanow/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #266: The knives are out at Netflix – maybe now it will make something worth watchingIn this week’s newsletter: Stalling subscriber numbers have led to a corporate bloodbath, but the streaming giant has an inherent quality problem that will be a lot harder to fixGwilym MumfordSat 24 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn all the fevered hype around a certainthree-hour, form-breaking documentary portrait of a disgraced tech CEO, another big Hollywood story this week has been relatively sidelined: the drama at Netflix, where sluggish subscriber numbers and a general lack of Wall Street enthusiasm has led to a remarkable spree of sackings. A thousand employees, or 6% of its entire workforce, have been laid off – including some very big names. Among a clutch of other execs, chief content officer Bela Bajaria – the figure most synonymous with Netflix’s tone and ethos over the past decade – has been fired. The company’s head of film, Dan Lin, has gone too. That shade of red on the streamer’s logo has never looked more bloody. You Can See Everything getting very messy indeed.We’ve been here before, of course. Netflix – giant, controversial, inescapable – is the sort of company people love to make grand speculations about.Pencils were sharpened in 2022when Netflix lost subscribers for the first time and saw its share price plummet as a result, before the company enjoyed a notable resurgence. Just as the obituaries written for the streamer were premature then, writing it off now would be foolish too.But a cull of this magnitude is still telling, indicating that Netflix itself thinks something has gone badly awry – particularly in terms of the actual stuff it’s been pumping out. Bajaria was the exec who famously likened the streamer’s programming to a “gourmet cheeseburger”; a premium product that was also highly snackable. Her exit suggests that recipe isn’t as appealing to viewers as it once was.It’s a question that gets asked more often than the streamer would like: when was the last time you watched a truly great new show on Netflix? Adolescence tends to be a popular answer, but that series (a limited run of only four episodes, let’s remember) was released 18 months ago. This year the cupboard has been extraordinarily bare. You might make a case for How to Get to Heaven from Belfast, or East of Eden at a push, but neither feel unmissably brilliant. And the streamer’s record with returning series is strikingly shaky, with precipitous audience drop-offs for shows’second seasons.Netflix’s quality issue is baked into its very model. The limitations of the company’s all-at-once, binge-friendly release strategy have been obvious for some time, resulting in shows that burn brightly but briefly for a week or two, before disappearing from the cultural conversation. But just as damaging, I’d argue, is a complete disinterest in cultivating shows with the potential for real staying power. Shows are often cancelled right as they are finding their voice, and flashy limited series with big names are prioritised over ones that could run and run. (Name-led series tend to takelonger to returntoo, due to their stars’ many other commitments.) With the exception of cosy heartlands romantic drama Virgin River and Black Mirror (a bit of an outlier given it is an anthology series and debuted on another platform, Channel 4), no current Netflix drama has been airing for more than four seasons.Netflix isn’t alone in its aversion to lasting, sprawling TV: in this era, post-the golden age of The Sopranos, Breaking Bad and the like, shows have tended to get shorter both in season and episode counts, with bigger gaps between seasons. TV as a whole feels less ambitious and substantial – not to mention reliably delivered – than it once did. But it is Netflix, as the chief disruptor of the old TV model, that bears the most responsibility for this shift – and that is perhaps most vulnerable as a result. It has become, for many, a platform that is clicked on to out of habit, rather than rushed to in fevered anticipation of the latest episode of a great show.Perhaps that will change in the wake of all the corporate bloodletting; the new chief content officer, British industry veteran Peter Rice, has been talked up for his excellent taste, having overseen a dynamite run of films (28 Days Later, Sideways, Juno) when he was head of the Fox Searchlight studio. Or perhaps it doesn’t really matter either way: habit is a strong drug, andNetflix equals TVfor many people. Indeed, its primary rival, in its own estimation, is not the BBC or Disney+ or the like, but YouTube, which is why it has been trying to hoover up many of the same things that are popular on that platform: influencer videos, podcasts, live sport.Netflix has long dreamed of being the “everything store”, a place that has all the content you could ever need – which is a fine ambition. I just wish there was something good to watch on it once in a while.To read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every Fridayskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSandra Hüller plays Erika, the daughter of writer Thomas Mann (played by Hanns Zischler) in the film Fatherland.Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/PAView image in fullscreenSofia Coppola on the set of Marie Antoinette.Photograph: MUBI/PAView image in fullscreenNathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.Photograph: A24/APExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: A Course Called Ireland: Bill Murray clearly hated making his new golfing show – but it’s extremely fun to binge | Bill Murray | The Guardian
description: In his rogue new travelogue, the Hollywood star tees off, has drunken pub singalongs – but mostly just proves how tired he is of fame
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: In his rogue new travelogue, the Hollywood star tees off, has drunken pub singalongs – but mostly just proves how tired he is of fame
Content: Driven … Bill Murray and Joanne McNally in A Course Called Ireland.Photograph: BBC/Stellify MediaView image in fullscreenDriven … Bill Murray and Joanne McNally in A Course Called Ireland.Photograph: BBC/Stellify MediaThe watcherBill MurrayA Course Called Ireland: Bill Murray clearly hated making his new golfing show – but it’s extremely fun to bingeIn his rogue new travelogue, the Hollywood star tees off, has drunken pub singalongs – but mostly just proves how tired he is of fameRhik SamadderSat 24 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m suspicious of travelogues, which often feature celebrities in contrived situations, serving up a sentimental postcard of a place that is tantamount to a lie. I also hate how famous people are inexorably drawn to golf: a boring game historically predicated on a rancid mix of social exclusivity and extensive land ownership. So it was perverse of me to watch a show in which author Tom Coyne drives around Ireland playing various courses with his friend, actorBill Murray. It’s the perfect intersection of none of my interests.I was, however, hooked by a strange promise in A Course Called Ireland’s introductory sequence. “This is not a show about golf,” it says. “It’s not even a show about Bill Murray.” This was immediately followed by a scene in which an Irish woman standing by the roadside misidentified the actor as Bill Cosby. OK, I thought. What are they teeing up here?There’s a hole in at least one of those promises. A Course Called Ireland (Sunday 25 October, 9.30pm, BBC Two) is intended to be a jocular road trip, in which the two friends meet colourful characters and reflect on their own Irish heritage, between spectacular rounds on the rugged links. It’s based on a journey Coyne documented in his book of the same name, in which he played every course in the country. Which again, sounds like a marriage in crisis to me – but the book is very popular.What we get is a fascinating, existential snapshot of fame. A camera crew trailing a Hollywood legend around a series of Irish villages is, unavoidably, the story. Murray can’t stop for a wee without being mobbed. The director wants as much Murray on screen as possible. The 76-year-old Ghostbuster wants to give the spotlight to anyone else who’ll take it. The wheels quickly start to come off. He rips up the itinerary, digs in his heels, grouches. He cringes at the artifice of making TV, such as pretending to meet people for the first time. He’s been famous for 50 years – and it shows.He also embodies the paradox of the reluctant celebrity, which is that most of them can’t stop doing things that perpetuate their myth. They hate the fame, they need the fame. The oddball actor is known for giving regular people “a Bill Murray story”, crashing graduation ceremonies or stepping behind the bar to pull pints. We see that here, as he hoists a groomsman on his shoulders, or gently pushes an ice-cream in a woman’s face. As he jokes, “If I wasn’t famous, I’d probably have a few more cuts and bruises to the face.”In one sequence, Murray refuses to attend a pub as scripted, and disappears to a nearby evening of folk music instead. Later, once filming has been aborted, he returns to the pub to lead the room in a drunken singalong. It’s exactly what the producers would have wanted; for Murray, such larks only have meaning if they aren’t being manufactured for the cameras. There is something heroic in his stubbornness. (Of course, someone films the whole thing on their mobile phone.)The show bends many of the format rules, by necessity or design. The BTS feeling of a crew working around a recalcitrant star is juicy. Each episode also boasts a voiceover from a supporting character – the proprietor of a tweed shop, a junior runner, Ireland’s former minister of the arts. The best is Margaret, an elderly woman outside a sweet shop who tells Murray he was the best thing in “Gorseboosters”. “Bill is 98% Irish if you look at his DNA, which I haven’t, but it says so here in the script,” she lilts. These unexpected and charming turns ground a show that otherwise feels like Lost in La Mancha set in Ballybunion.If the show fails by its own marker, it succeeds at being funny, peculiar and melancholy: a much higher bar. It’s as unconventional and highly watchable as its impish star, the one it pretends not to be hopelessly in thrall to. What’s more, I finally understand why celebrities love golf so much. They want to be as far away from other people as possible.Explore more on these topicsBill MurrayThe watcherTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It annoys people when I eat’: Siobhán McSweeney on perfect snacks, parental pressure – and the power of being ‘a delicious fatty’  | Siobhán McSweeney | The Guardian
description: The Derry Girls actor has always loved food, so who better to take over as the new presenter of the Guardian’s Comfort Eating podcast?
Author: Kitty Drake
Headline: The Derry Girls actor has always loved food, so who better to take over as the new presenter of the Guardian’s Comfort Eating podcast?
Content: Portrait: Jay Brooks/The GuardianThe Derry Girls actor has always loved food, so who better to take over as the new presenter of the Guardian’s Comfort Eating podcast?ByKitty DrakeSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSiobhán McSweeney is teaching me her preferred way to enjoy a packet of cheese and onion crisps. She has arranged two matching slabs of Cadbury’s Dairy Milk chocolate, two piles of Tayto crisps and two cans of Guinness on the table in front of us – and is issuing strict instructions. “Don’t swallow!” she booms theatrically, and I freeze, my mouth full of Taytos. The trick, McSweeney explains, is to get the crisps, chocolate and Guinness into your mouth at the same time, and then swill it all around a bit to make a kind of boozy, oniony soup. “See?” McSweeney is watching me carefully to check I am putting all the ingredients into my mouth in the correct order. “It’s delicious! Just delicious!”McSweeney burst into the public consciousness back in 2018 withDerry Girls, a comedy series about a group of Catholic schoolgirls, set against the background of the Troubles in 1990s Northern Ireland. McSweeney won a Bafta playing the girls’ headmistress, Sister Michael – a potty-mouthed, judo-loving nun – and can count Martin Scorsese as a fan. Asked for a TV recommendation during a panel discussion in 2022, thedirector name-checked Derry Girlsand then lifted his fist in the air in a kind of salute, exclaiming rapturously, “Those nuns!”I have spent so many hours watching McSweeney in character as Sister Michael that it is almost a shock to see her without a nun’s habit. We are meeting today, in a conference room in London, because McSweeney is taking over fromGrace Dent as the new host of the Guardian’s food podcast, Comfort Eating. I arrived at the interview with a multipack of Taytos, a family‑size Dairy Milk and two cans of Guinness in my bike bag, because McSweeney chose this concoction as her favourite snack when sheappeared on the podcastas a guest, back in 2021. She also told a story about eating a caterpillar that had fallen from her moth-infested ceiling into her stir‑fry, purely because she couldn’t be bothered to fish it out. “Listen: protein,” she says today, remembering that caterpillar. “Free protein where you can.”View image in fullscreenMcSweeney as Sister Michael in Derry Girls (above) and as Della Fry in Amandaland (below). Photographs: Peter Marley/Channel 4; Natalie Seery/ BBC/MermanPhotograph: Peter Marley/ Channel 4View image in fullscreenSince Derry Girls, the actor has made a habit of portraying slightly intimidating women. She plays the achingly sarcastic celebrity chef Della Fry inAmandaland, and hosts the Irish version of The Traitors, in which she commands a pack of wolfhounds and wears a lot of ruffs. But today, McSweeney’s short, silver‑grey hair is brushed back from her face and she is dressed casually, in trousers and a simple top. Sister Michael is always lolling back in her chair and surveying you sardonically across a desk – but the real McSweeney leans forward and asks a lot of questions.It is lunchtime, so I have brought a takeaway from the Indian restaurant Dishoom with me, as well as the Taytos. “I love doing this podcast because it annoys people when I eat,” McSweeney says, tucking into a fish curry. Part of the reason why she accepted the job as host of Comfort Eating, she explains, is because visibly enjoying her food – as a woman who is not stick-thin – is a kind of provocation. “They’ve been told that somebody like me should not feel good about themselves,” she says, grinning toothily at me. “Being a delicious fatty.”Ever since she first arrived at drama school, in the early 2000s, people have been telling McSweeney to lose weight. “Agents, casting directors, teachers” – McSweeney checks the list off for me now, almost breezily. “I have been different sizes but it’s never been an acceptable size,” she says. “‘Unruly’ I call it – there’s sort of an unruliness that has been forced upon my body that I don’t feel about it, but other people feel it’s unruly and it doesn’t behave.” All the other girls at her drama college were starving themselves, McSweeney remembers now. “They were starving in secondary school as well – it was the 90s! I don’t know how I managed to escape it.” She is grinning at me again. “I don’t think I have the willpower to not eat. I don’t really have much discipline.”It strikes me that continuing to like yourself and your body, in the face of such vicious scrutiny, is not so much a failure of will as its opposite – proof that McSweeney has a will of absolute iron. Responding to a particularly poisonous bout of online criticism of her looks back in 2023, McSweeney delivered a kind of masterclass in the art of self-worth, tweeting: “I’m really lovely. I like my hair. And I like food. And I’m not sorry I’m loud. I thought feminism fights for me to be loud. And my accent is gorgeous. My teeth are yellow and wonky that’s true. But I sorta don’t care. And sure are you perfect?”double quotation markI taught, I waitressed, I pulled pints, I went on the dole, I worked at music festivals. And I was shit at every single one of themView image in fullscreenPortrait: Jay Brooks/The GuardianMcSweeney says she wouldn’t even bother to respond to online abuse like that these days, because “it’s so insane now on social media. There is no honesty to it because we don’t know if they are bots or not.” But when I push her on the willpower point, and suggest that there is something inherently political about refusing to lose weight in her industry, she agrees with me. “I do get perverse pleasure in [responding to those] people who expect me to feel bad – by insulting me, by calling me ‘fat’ – by going, ‘And?’”McSweeney also credits her mother, who she describes as “the kind of mam who would be round the back having a cigarette reading Dostoevsky”, with teaching her to aspire to a version of womanhood that wasn’t about appealing to men. “She wasn’t interested in me having boyfriends that much – she was, like, men will come, men will go; it’s fine.”“She just instilled this utter independence in me that didn’t centre in any way on a romantic relationship.” McSweeney pauses for a moment here, and seems to reconsider. “I mean … she wasn’t completely immune to all that. No one is strong enough to combat that, you know? And there would be a bit of, ‘Would you not brush your hair?” McSweeney is putting on her mother’s voice now and making pleading motions. “Please, just briefly! Just give it a quick brush!”Siobhán McSweeney grew up in County Cork, Ireland. Her father was a civil servant and her mother ran a cottage industry baking bread and cakes to sell to local shops, so the young Siobhán woke up every day to the smell of fresh soda bread. But, like any teenager worth their salt, McSweeney only wanted what she couldn’t have. “I went to the neighbours at one point because they had white sliced pan and red jam, and I thought, they’re so lucky, I have to go home now and have my freshly baked brown soda bread and my local butter,” she says. Her mother would make her school lunch every day with bread so fresh it was still warm. McSweeney remembers looking at her lunchbox and thinking “no one suffers more than me”.McSweeney knew from an early age that she wanted to act. She says that as a child she would wish on a star every night that she would become an actor, and tells me that she once spent an entire day at school pretending she was in a sitcom, pausing every now and again to play the laugh track in her head. “Or I’d look to the camera” – she mimes whirling her head around to lock eyes with an imaginary film crew. “How obnoxious! What a pest to be around.”double quotation markThe really sad thing about illness is that it often takes your appetite away – I want a lovely big bellyView image in fullscreenPortrait: Jay Brooks/The GuardianMcSweeney’s parents, however, had other plans for her. “We didn’t know anyone who was an actor. People on the telly didn’t look like me, didn’t sound like me,” she says. “My parents were, like, so what would that mean? You would do the panto once a year? You’re meant to work!”Speaking to the Irish Times in August, McSweeney said that anybody in the creative industries has “an angel and a devil on your shoulder, and the devil quite often is your parents going, ‘Don’t embarrass us.’” Did she feel as if her parents were embarrassed about her? “Yeah, absolutely yeah – it’s embarrassing to have your child standing up there making a tit of themselves,” she says. “Also, Ireland in the 80s, you blend in – the idea of standing out is quite … ” she tails off thoughtfully. “I think it was a protective idea – when you are in the open you are open to abuse and people taking advantage. All these things are true and I understand fully why any parent wouldn’t want that for their child.”McSweeney was virtually unknown before the release ofDerry Girls, which came out after her 40th birthday. She tells me that in a strange way she is pleased that fame came later in life for her, because she knows people “who have achieved success very early on in their career and their heads are turned”. But the years she spent trying and failing to get parts were gruelling. “I taught, I waitressed, I pulled pints, I went on the dole, I worked at music festivals,” she says. “And I was shit at every single one of them.”She remembers being particularly “shit” at the waitressing. “Sure, I didn’t know anything about food. I was pouring the wine the way my parents would drink wine, which would be wine right up to the top of the glass, and I didn’t know about al dente,” she says. “I thought, who is this Al Dente?”There was a point in the 2010s when she considered giving up acting completely. “I hadn’t worked in over a year and I had just got a litany of nos,” she remembers. “And now it’s getting harder and harder for not-rich people to be an actor.” McSweeney had received grants from the EU and a scholarship to study drama at the Central School of Speech and Drama – and that kind of funding literally doesn’t exist any more. “I get really panicky thinking about the other Siobháns who don’t get what they’re meant to do,” she says, and her face is unusually serious for a moment – but then she looks at me and her eyes begin to twinkle. “I mean it should be better, it should be a bit more useful than being a clown – but, you know, it’s what I’m meant to do.”Part of the struggle when she was being rejected at auditions was the lack of decent roles available for women. In previous interviews, McSweeney has said that casting directors explicitly told her that even though she was the funniest person in the audition room, they were going to give the part to a “prettier, younger, less funny” woman. “I graduated into a world where I really hoped somebody had a girlfriend because there was no way on earth a programme was going to centre on a woman,” she says to me now. But she wouldn’t even be in the running for the girlfriend part because “they wanted somebody who was more ‘girlfriend material’, ie, more acceptable – so, bland and pretty”.McSweeney says she would never be considered for the main character, “always the satellite”. She rolls her eyes. “And now I’m the mother.”McSweeney tells me that sheis deliberately taking on more presenting work because properly meaty, complex acting roles for women on TV are still so rare. As well as The Traitors Ireland, McSweeney hostsThe Great Pottery Throw Down.She landed the job after an appearance on a Great British Bake Off festive special in which she had a meltdown over making a trifle and ended up sitting on a bench with Sandi Toksvig, drinking champagne (“They went, that’s who we want”).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWith presenter Sandi Toksvig in the 2020 Great Festive Bake Off (above) and on the set of The Great Pottery Throw Down in 2023 (below). Photographs: Mark Bourdillon/Love ProductionsView image in fullscreenMcSweeney is also an acclaimed theatre actor. She played opposite her Derry Girls co-star Nicola Coughlan last year inThe Playboy of the Western Worldat the National Theatre, andsays that being onstage is what she has always enjoyed the most (she remembers being a child and “seeing red curtains on the telly and having a funny feeling in my belly”). But presenting is “work I find interesting – and it also pays more than the theatre”, she says, with characteristic honesty.Presenting jobs pay better than TV shows do, too – even the most successful ones. McSweeneyhas said publicly“I think I got 40 quid” in residuals when Derry Girlssold to Netflix. The programme has beenviewed for a total of 17.3m hourson the platform. Can that figure possibly be true? McSweeney nods enthusiastically. “When Netflix bought it we got fuck all!”When she was 27, McSweeney lost her mother, who never saw her daughter succeed as an actor. In herBafta acceptance speech, which has been viewed 467,000 times on YouTube, McSweeney told a story about how, as her mother lay dying, she pleaded with her to retrain as a teacher. “If she could see me now, winning a Bafta for playing a teacher,” she said, wearing a red vinyl dress and laughing, lifting her bare arm above her head to punch the air with her award: “Joke’s on you, Mam!”Would her mother feel pride, if she could see her daughter now? Or relief? “Er, relief,” says McSweeney, quick as a flash. Then she pauses for a second. “And I think she would like … I have a lot of opinions and she would like the way I speak about certain opinions.” In the same Bafta speech, McSweeney thanked the people of Derry, calling out the “ignorance and stupidity” of their political leadership, and she is a vocal critic of both English and Irish policy. Last year she was among those who campaigned successfully for the thousands of UK-based survivors of the work camps for “fallen women” that were in operation until the 90s in Ireland – known as the Magdalene laundries –to be given compensationwithout losing their rights to benefits.Would her mother have been proud of her feminism? “I think she would have been as close to proud as I would allow her to be,” says McSweeney, almost shyly. “And my dad, too … He was a natural feminist rather than a learned one – couldn’t think of anything I couldn’t do because of my gender, that would make no sense to him.”View image in fullscreenMcSweeney accepts the female performance in a comedy programme award for Derry Girls at the 2023 Bafta Television Awards.Photograph: Stuart Wilson/Bafta/Getty Images for BaftaHer father died in 2018. McSweeney moved back into the family home to live with him during his final illness. She drew on those experiences to makeSpudin 2024, a beautiful, surprisingly funny short film about a middle-aged woman caring for her dying father (McSweeney summarises the plot, with fabulous bluntness, as being about “an unfuckable woman who is rural and who cleans her daddy in a bath”).In one particularly tender scene, the father and the daughter, who is played by McSweeney herself, sit eating rice pudding together in front of the telly. Was that drawn from life? Was food a comfort for them both during that time? “The really sad thing about illness is that it often takes your appetite away,” she says. “I found it with my mum, too: her appetite went towards the end.” She tells me a story about sneaking a carbonara into the hospital to give to her mother, and the sadness of her not being able to eat it. “She was so beautiful and everybody’s mam is beautiful, but she ended up with a flat belly – and I was, like, what use is a flat belly? I want a lovely big belly.”Right at the end of Spud, McSweeney’s character finds out her father has died, and the camera closes in on her face. There is pain there but there is also something else: she is smiling slightly. It’s a great moment because it is so unexpected – and so honest. You can see in the daughter’s expression that, on some level, her father’s death has come as a relief. “I remember when my dad died, I was sort of manic for about six months because I suddenly was free, and I was grieving, but I was also free,” McSweeney says. In the immediate aftermath of her father’s death, McSweeney was bursting with ideas for new projects. “With no parents, you don’t feel like you’re letting the entire family down if you say or do something.”Comfort Eating with Grace Dent is backRead moreBetween 2018 and 2021, McSweeney went through a period that she has described – in a moment of understatement worthy of Sister Michael herself – as containing lots of “life stuff”. Her aunt, who had been a kind of surrogate mother to her, died the year after she lost her father. In 2019, her London flat burned down because of a faulty plug adaptor. Then, in 2021, in the middle of filming a Kathy Burke-directed crime drama,Holding, she broke her leg so badly that at one point the doctors thought they would have to amputate it.How did she cope? “We place romantic and biological relationships at the heart of our sort of experience,” says McSweeney, but it was her friends who got her through it. She tells me that when she was struggling the most, she became furious with one of her friends and accused him of talking about her behind her back with the rest of the group. “I was, like, ‘Are you all talking about me?’” She puts her hands on her hips here and mimes outrage, and then she switches characters so she can play her friend’s role: “And he was, like, ‘Yeah! We’remeantto do that! We care about you! We’re making sure you’re OK, we’re asking each other, how do you think she’s doing?’”McSweeney talks about this being a moment of realisation. She saw that friendship has an elasticity and a resilience that no romantic relationship can ever really have. “You have a fight with your boyfriend and that could destroy the relationship, right?” she says. “You have a fight with your friend, you go into your respective corners, you sulk. You call other friends. You bitch about each other. Then you go back, you have a coffee, you get drunk!”McSweeney’s friends are annoyed with her at the moment, because she is getting her kitchen redone in her new flat, and she is refusing to install a dishwasher – as a way of preventing them from popping in for meals. “I don’t want you coming over and eating my food,” she says. She has described herself as a “sociable misanthrope” in previous interviews. As much as she loves her friends, she is not that fond of cooking and cleaning for them. I tell her I like going to other people’s homes and letting them cook for me, and then leaving without doing any washing up at all. “I bet you do!” she says. “It’s horrible for the other person – get out of my house!”So who does she cook for? “Myself!” she says, looking me right in the eye – and for the first time there is a kind of challenge in her voice. She doesn’t like to talk about any romantic partners.She lives alone in a flat she recently bought in London. What does she cook for herself? “It’s so boring, but I’ve been working so hard for the last five years that all my food is comfort food and I try to make it as healthy as possible,” she says. She makes a lot of bone broth and a lot of ramen. “Also, I like white bread toasted till it’s nearly black, with Kerrygold butter” – but the butter has to be sliced extremely thickly, she specifies. It has to be “sliced like cheese”.We’re nearly out of time – and Dair y Milk. McSweeney has been hospitably breaking off slabs of chocolate and handing them to me every few minutes for the last half hour, so I can keep making Guinness-crisp soup in my mouth. I’ve got time for just one final question, so I ask McSweeney what she is looking forward to. “I’ve got my first day off for 26 days tomorrow,” she says, “but I’ve got nothing in the fridge.” She plans to go to a bakery round the corner and buy some freshly made soda bread. Ironically, after all that teenage rebellion, she likes it now. Would her mother be pleased to look down on her doing that? “Yes,” she says. “And I’m going to buy it with the money I earned being a clown.”The new series of Comfort Eating, hosted by Siobhán McSweeney, launches on 11 November.Explore more on these topicsSiobhán McSweeneyFoodThe Great Pottery Throw DownThe TraitorsThe Great British Bake OffDerry GirlsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Unlike anything we’ve experienced’: fans swarm San Francisco for BTS star’s art exhibition | Exhibitions | The Guardian
description: K-pop star RM gave a boost to the previously struggling SFMOMA with an exhibition of over 100 pieces from his collection
Author: Soo Youn
Headline: K-pop star RM gave a boost to the previously struggling SFMOMA with an exhibition of over 100 pieces from his collection
Content: Portrait of RM, member of K-pop band BTS.Photograph: Courtesy of HYBEView image in fullscreenPortrait of RM, member of K-pop band BTS.Photograph: Courtesy of HYBEExhibitions‘Unlike anything we’ve experienced’: fans swarm San Francisco for BTS star’s art exhibitionK-pop star RM gave a boost to the previously struggling SFMOMA with an exhibition of over 100 pieces from his collectionSoo YounSat 24 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo years ago, RM of the wildly popular K-pop boybandBTSwas serving as a soldier in the South Korean military when he received an offer from América Castillo, a museum curator in San Francisco: would he consider an exhibition of his private art collection?‘Taylor Swift tells us to take the lead!’ Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula?Read more“I loved it,” said RM (real name: Kim Namjoon) at the media preview ofRM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me, a new exhibition that opened in San Francisco earlier this month and is co-curated by SFMOMA’s Castillo and Hyoeun Kim. “There aren’t many things that show a person more honestly than a collection they’ve built over a long period of time.”The result is a multi-dimensional exhibition of 142 works of RM’s private collection of mostly Korean works, including paintings, calligraphy, sculpture and even a Pokémon animation cel, in conversation with 36 of the museum’s pieces. The show has been a blockbuster success, with over 66,000 tickets sold and advance sales that were six times higher than any previous exhibition at the museum.RM has been an evangelist for modern Korean art: asongfrom his 2022 solo album Indigo samples a conversational snippet from the Korean painter Yun Hyong-keun. At the SFMOMA show, Yun’s monochrome Umber-Blue sits juxtaposed next to MarkRothko’s No. 24 in the show. There’s also an audio guide and playlist by RM.View image in fullscreenInstallation View of RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me.Photograph: Matthew Millman“I’ve always dreamed of seeing different places, times, boundaries and backgrounds all mixed together in harmony,” RM said at the preview, before adding lightly: “It could be a mess – I never formally studied art history, and I’m not a curator.“Sometimes an outsider can bring in a new breeze,” he added.While his celebrity looms large over the show, the collection and the curation of the show are formidable. In South Korea, gallery owners and art dealers who have met RM have told me their nickname for him is “bakhsa” (professor) owing to the depth of his knowledge. “It is especially meaningful to bring the depth and richness of his collection to a wider audience,” says Kim, assistant curator of painting and sculpture.View image in fullscreenChang Ucchin, Road, 1986. Collection of RM.Photograph: © Chang Ucchin Foundation, courtesy Seoul AuctionSome of the art is displayed with a scholarly arc, while other curation feels more intuitive. One room is titled “I Don’t Know, But I Like It.”“I started this with an innocent heart,” RM said at the preview. “I just didn’t know that this innocence would eventually make me write, erase and rewrite hundreds of labels.” His text that accompanies the pieces combines historical context with diaristic personal reflections, in a break from museum convention.In a placard that accompanies a Lee Ungno painting of the Gwangju uprising in 1980, a brutal crackdown on protesters by a military dictatorship, RM writes: “He painted these crowds until the day he died. Strange, isn’t it. These people are not falling. Arms raised, legs wide, they are dancing.”Last year, as US museums grappled with the lingering effects of the pandemic on attendance, funding challenges under the current administration and lower tourism rates in many cities, SFMOMA laid off 7.5% of its workforce amid a $5m deficit. Its new director Christopher Bedford wrote that the museum would adjust its programming and budget to reflect “a reduced annual attendance normal in the range of 600,000 visitors”.Since the RM show opened, the museum has seen an undeniable financial boost. Its success, and whether it ushers in a direction toward celebrity exhibitions, is something officials and other museums seem to already be considering. In 2024, Brooklyn Museum staged a majorexhibitionshowcasing the private collection of Swizz Beatz and Alicia Keys, while other recent shows have focused on art made by musicians likeJack WhiteandPaul McCartney.View image in fullscreenInstallation View of RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me.Photograph: Matthew MillmanYet the dedication ofBTSfans, who call themselves Army, may prove to make this show a one-off. On the day of the media preview and opening reception, a couple hundred fans lined up outside the museum entrance, one holding a sign saying she came from London for RM. Another handed journalists small bags of gifts including custom-made bookmarks, key chains and cake pops along with thank you notes for covering the exhibition.Exhibition merch available at the SFMOMA Museum Store andweb storesold out within three hours. “It’s different in so many ways,” store director Shane Salvata says of the exhibition, adding that it is important for visitors to commemorate “how special it is that he curated this show”.“It’s unlike anything we’ve ever experienced, and probably will experience ever again,” he says.For Castillo, who originally conceived the show, success has a different measure. “To actually see it in the galleries … people are crying in front of you,” she says. “You’re never going to expect that. It’s a beautiful surprise.”RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Meis on view at SFMOMA until 7 February 2027Explore more on these topicsExhibitionsBTSMuseumsArtPop and rockK-popSan FranciscofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Blind date: ‘We overstayed our welcome – the waiters were shaking the cutlery drawer really loudly’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Alexandrea, 32, a lawyer, meets Pardis, 32, a doctor
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Alexandrea, 32, a lawyer, meets Pardis, 32, a doctor
Content:
Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘We overstayed our welcome – the waiters were shaking the cutlery drawer really loudly’Alexandrea, 32, a lawyer, meets Pardis, 32, a doctorSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlexandrea on PardisView image in fullscreenWhat were you hoping for?A fun date and to hopefully meet the one!First impressions?Handsome and relaxed.What did you talk about?The sports we do. Books. Family. Friends. Our jobs. Travelling and travelling mishaps. Vermin infestations. Stocks and shares. ISAs.Most awkward moment?We both arrived at the restaurant on time but there was a big queue which resulted in me sitting at the table alone for about 10 minutes – I got a bit nervous.Good table manners?No faux pas so all good.Best thing about Pardis?He is very sincere. He asked lots of questions, seemed interested in what I was saying and was a great listener. I also loved how laid-back he was – he went with the flow when I proposed the tasting menu.Would you introduce Pardis to your friends?Of course – he’s interesting and really good company.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Describe Pardis in three wordsEasygoing, kind, engaging.What do you think Pardis made of you?A ray of sunshine, akin to what everyone else thinks of me!Did you go on somewhere?No, but we did overstay our welcome at the restaurant, to the point where the waiters were shaking the cutlery drawer really loudly.And … did you kiss?A lady never tells … But no.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?I would have loved it to be in Paris. Pardis in Paris!Marks out of 10?8.Would you meet again?Pardis is a lovely guy but I think we’re better suited as friends.View image in fullscreenPardis and Alexandrea on their date.Pardis on AlexandreaView image in fullscreenWhat were you hoping for?The scene in About Time where the protagonist meets Rachel McAdams in that dark dining restaurant. (I appreciate that isn’t quite the same concept as a blind date.)First impressions?I was a few places behind her in the queue to get in the restaurant. I could only see the back of her head but thought: nice hair, good fashion sense.What did you talk about?There was a healthy amount of chat on the life cycle of a fly and the declining quality of mousetraps. We’ve both had minor pest issues recently – a perk of living in London.Most awkward moment?Probably mistaking her Irish accent for a Scottish one. Not my finest hour.Good table manners?Excellent, a picture of sophistication.Best thing about Alexandrea?Very down to earth, clearly adventurous and a great dinner party guest.Would you introduce Alexandrea to your friends?I wouldn’t put the poor girl through the trauma of meeting my rabble …Blind date: ‘He asked if my disco ball tattoo was an onion’Read moreDescribe Alexandrea in three wordsAdventurous, kind, intelligent.What do you think she made of you?I think she enjoyed my chat. Either that or she’s great at acting entertained (or I’m completely oblivious).Did you go on somewhere?No, I was on early morning uncle duty the next day, so had to call it a night.And … did you kiss?No, a good wholesome hug.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?I’d brush up on my accent recognition beforehand.Marks out of 10?8 (for a friendship connection, otherwise it would have been higher).Would you meet again?Sure, as friends I’d be happy to.Alexandrea and Pardis ate atMildreds,London W1. Fancy a blind date? Emailblind.date@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsDatingBlind dateRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A theatrical dancer on a pristine limestone mountain in East Java: Mohammad Nur Nasikin’s best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: The photographer hopes his image of a father and son practising a traditional Indonesian artform will go some way towards preserving it
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: The photographer hopes his image of a father and son practising a traditional Indonesian artform will go some way towards preserving it
Content: Leap of Tradition: The Energy of Bujang Ganong, 2026, shot on Huawei Pura 80 Pro.Photograph: Mohammad Noor NasikinView image in fullscreenLeap of Tradition: The Energy of Bujang Ganong, 2026, shot on Huawei Pura 80 Pro.Photograph: Mohammad Noor NasikinSmart shotPhotographyA theatrical dancer on a pristine limestone mountain in East Java: Mohammad Nur Nasikin’s best phone pictureThe photographer hopes his image of a father and son practising a traditional Indonesian artform will go some way towards preserving itGrace HollidaySat 24 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarly this summer, in a pristine, limestone mountain range in the East Java province of Indonesia, Mohammad Nur Nasikin met with the father and son pictured here. His aim was to capture a character from a treasured Indonesian theatrical dance and art form called Reog Ponorogo.‘I wanted to show children playing under the open sky – and the joy of Sundays’: Monojit Dutta’s best phone pictureRead more“Bujang Ganong is one of the characters in the dance; a young regent who is agile, skilful and clever,” Nasikin explains, “Mr Hanafie, on the left, is a true artist, skilled in many Javanese arts. He’s wearing the traditional costume worn by a Bujang Ganong dancer: a wooden ganong mask, and a bright red waistcoat, a shoulder cloth known as a sembong, and loose‑fitting trousers called katok panji. At his feet is his drummer – his son Tirta, which means ‘water’ in Javanese.”The energetic movements of the character made it easy to capture a range of shots, Nasikin notes. When he returned home, Nasikin showed his own 12-year-old son, and explained the importance of preserving culture passed from ancestors.“We must continue to safeguard it for generations to come,” he says. “My hope is that viewers will be interested in learning more about this art form, and our culture, and in that way I will have formed a link between the past and the future.”Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jackson Boxer’s vegetarian recipe for brown butter pumpkin soup | Food | The Guardian
description: This easy roast pumpkin soup is rich, nutty, Halloween heaven
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This easy roast pumpkin soup is rich, nutty, Halloween heaven
Content: Jackson Boxer’s brown butter pumpkin soup.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenJackson Boxer’s brown butter pumpkin soup.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.FoodJackson Boxer’s vegetarian recipe for brown butter pumpkin soupThe base of this easy roast pumpkin soup is rich, nutty, Halloween heaven –  you can go wild with the garnishesJackson BoxerSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlot of my early life in professional kitchens was spent making vegetable purees, which I find rather tiresome, not least because they can often lapse into baby food: creamy, bland and flattened by a cosseting blanket of dairy. With a judicious and considered approach, however, they can also be incredibly vivid, explosive and concentrated expressions of the very essence of the vegetable in question. I love this seasonal (not to mention Halloween-appropriate) soup for its simplicity of approach – essentially, you just roast a beautiful pumpkin with caramelised butter – and the remarkable complexity of its result.Brown butter pumpkin soupWhen browning butter, always bear in mind that it has a high water content, and that the initial seething cook is done to evaporate this – until all the water has cooked out, you won’t get the butter high enough above 100C for the milk solids and sugars to caramelise. That’s why browning butter happens two ways, like Hemingway’s bankruptcy – gradually, then suddenly. And pay close attention, or it will burn and you’ll have to start again.Prep5 minCook1 hrServes4250ml vegetable bouillon(homemade, ideally; seemy recipe last week)1 delica pumpkin(800g), cut in half, deseeded and peeled (I don’t bother peeling it, but cooked pumpkin skin is an acquired taste)250g butter10g flaky sea salt(about 2 tsp)Sherry vinegar, to tasteTo finishCreme fraicheChilli oilToasted pumpkin seedsGround black pepperA squeeze of lemonHeat the oven to 195C (175C fan)/385F/gas 5½. Pour the bouillon into a roasting tray large enough to hold both pumpkin halves, then put them cut side up in the tray.In a frying pan, simmer the butter on a high heat until it stops foaming, then turn down the heat and cook until it’s rich, brown and nutty. Immediately pour the scalding butter evenly into the pumpkin halves, then lay a sheet of greaseproof paper over the top of the pumpkins and tightly cover the whole tray in foil. Bake for 45 minutes, until the tip of a sharp knife meets no resistance and comes out clean.Cut the cooked pumpkin into chunks, put these and the bouillon from the tray in a food processor and blitz to a smooth puree. Add the salt and vinegar, then taste and adjust the seasoning. If the puree is too tight, add more vegetable broth just to loosen – it will depend on the water content of the pumpkin and how airtight the seal was on the foil tray.Transfer the mix to a large saucepan and reheat gently without boiling. Check and adjust for seasoning and acidity, then ladle into bowls – I serve this soup topped with creme fraiche, chilli oil, toasted pumpkin seeds, black pepper and a squeeze of lemon; other nice garnishes might include toasted croutons, fried sage leaves, chilli and garlic butter, and salsa verde, any and all of which would be very fine additions.Jackson Boxer is chef/owner ofBrunswick House,VesperandDove, all in London, and culinary director ofCowley Manornear Cheltenham andthe Henriettain LondonExplore more on these topicsFoodPumpkinHalloweenSoupVegetarian food and drinkVegetablesStarterrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: why did I buy an electric car? Because I wanted a medal | Family | The Guardian
description: Lunch with my agent is going nowhere, so I decide to share my latest motoring anecdote
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: Lunch with my agent is going nowhere, so I decide to share my latest motoring anecdote
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: why did I buy an electric car? Because I wanted a medalLunch with my agent is going nowhere, so I decide to share my latest motoring anecdoteTim DowlingSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 06.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m having lunch with my agent – an infrequent occurrence, because neither of us ever has any good news for the other. This lunch is no different.“Sorry to make you come all this way,” she says, “but I had to be near the office today.” She hints at some complex contractual negotiations involving an author for whom, I suspect, she always has good news.“That’s OK,” I say.“Did you come on the tube?” she says. “Did it take for ever?”“I drove, actually,” I say. “Because I have an electric car.”People sometimes ask why I bought an electric car. What did I want from it? To save money? To help the environment? To guard myself against future fuel shortages, or toxic emissions, or both?double quotation markThe official honours bestowed on electric car owners are paltry: you get no credit for being the green part of a traffic jamThe truth is: I wanted a medal. I wanted people to see the little green rectangle on my number plate and think: there goes a great guy, doing his best; let’s slow down and give him plenty of room to pull into our lane.This does not happen. The official honours bestowed on electric car owners are actually pretty paltry: a discount on the London congestion charge and a slightly abbreviated MOT test. And you get no credit for being the green part of a traffic jam.A few days earlier my wife and I had been invited to have lunch with the older one and his girlfriend, on the other side of town. In the morning, my wife declares that she will drive.Traffic is light on the way, and we arrive ahead of schedule. There is, however, absolutely nowhere to park. Every available space is occupied.On a second trawl through the neighbourhood a sudden gap appears ahead of us. “What about there?” my wife says, slowing down. I look up at the sign as we pass.“It’s for electric cars only,” I say. “Hey, wait! That’s us!”“Finally,” my wife says, braking.“But wait,” I say. “It’s actually a charging point. You have to be actively charging the car while you’re in it.”“Fine, we’ll do that then,” she says. “It can’t be more expensive than parking.”“But it’s broken,” I say. “The outlet thing is all taped up.”“Well, it’s not our fault it doesn’t work, is it?” she says, pulling in.I get out of the car and look at the sign and the broken plug, and my wife.“What do you think?” she says.double quotation markMy wife reverses down the road, leaving me on the pavement. So, I think. This is how it ends“I think that if I were a parking warden, I would love to give this car a ticket.”“Oh, for fuck’s sake,” my wife says, choosing, on this occasion, to shoot the messenger.We make two more wide circles of the area, varying the route slightly each time until we are a little lost.“There!” my wife says, pointing. “What’s wrong with that one?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s also for electric cars,” I say.Tim Dowling: could the new dog’s tricks make her into a star?Read moreBehind us a man in a car beeps, his impatience unmodulated by the green band on our number plate. My wife pulls over to let him pass. I have to open my door to examine the plug situation more closely.“It appears to be operable,” I say, leaning out for a better look.“Do we have the right cable?” she says.“Yeah, but our socket’s on the other side,” I say. “It won’t reach unless we’re facing the other way.”“That’s fine, I can turn around,” she says.“And also,” I say, craning my neck, “this particular charging point seems to be part of a local scheme. Like, you need a special parking permit from the borough to even use it.”“Get out of the car,” my wife says.“Sorry, but I am just reading what it …”“Get out of the car!”I stand up and shut the door. My wife reverses down the road, leaving me on the pavement. So, I think.
