This is how it ends.But it turns out my wife has noticed that the man who beeped at us had just vacated a parking space half a dozen car lengths back.“That was lucky,” she says, all smiles now.Two days later a waitress comes to the table, and my agent and I order.“So,” I say. “If you get the right tariff and you only charge at night, it is a lot cheaper. But don’t expect special treatment. There’s no medal.”“I think we’ve had enough about electric cars now,” my agent says.A brief silence follows – neither of us willing, for the moment, to be the first bearer of bad news.Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was so magical’: the 33-year-old who made history swimming the length of California | California | The Guardian
description: Ultra-endurance swimmer Catherine Breed navigated waves, wildlife and pollution to become the first person to swim from state’s northern-most tip to Mexico border
Author: Lois Beckett
Headline: Ultra-endurance swimmer Catherine Breed navigated waves, wildlife and pollution to become the first person to swim from state’s northern-most tip to Mexico border
Content: Left: Catherine Breed reaches the beach at Coronado, California, on 19 October. Right: Breed at Coronado on 19 October.Composite: Nelvin C Cepeda/The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLeft: Catherine Breed reaches the beach at Coronado, California, on 19 October. Right: Breed at Coronado on 19 October.Composite: Nelvin C Cepeda/The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty ImagesCaliforniaInterview‘It was so magical’: the 33-year-old who made history swimming the length of CaliforniaLois Beckettin Los AngelesUltra-endurance swimmer Catherine Breed navigated waves, wildlife and pollution to become the first person to swim from state’s northern-most tip to Mexico borderSat 24 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly four months ago, Catherine Breed, a 33-year-old from the San Francisco Bay Area, set out to become the first person to swim theentire coastline of California– from its northern-most tip to the border with Mexico. She and her support team prepared for encounters with sharks and storms. They hadn’t anticipated completing the marathon swim during a year of historicsuper El Niño weather.But after dodging hurricanes, wildlife and 8ft waves in an unusually volatile Pacific Ocean, Breed finally celebrated the end of her journey on a beach in San Diego on Monday.Breed joins a group of elite ultra-endurance swimmers who continue to set new records for long-distance swims, including swimming the entire coastlines ofIrelandandIcelandand one side ofNew Zealand’s North Island– all journeys of close to 1,000 miles (1,600km).Breed spoke to the Guardian this week about living onboard the Catalyst, the sailboat that accompanied her, her physical and mental preparations for her 111-day swim, and what she thought about while spending more than 15 weeks in the water. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.View image in fullscreenCatherine Breed reaches the beach at Coronado, California, on 19 October.Photograph: Nelvin C Cepeda/The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty ImagesOn yourwebsite, you talk about the desire to be part of “an elite group of humans who have been the first to accomplish a monumental feat”. What does that feel like now that you’ve done it?It is a little bit of an out-of-body experience. Like, I know I’m the one who did it, but there are parts of me where I feel like I’m along with the audience, watching this thing happen. I think I’m still trying to grasp what I’ve done.How did you get the idea to swim the full length ofCalifornia, which no one has ever done before?Other people showed me that the model was possible. Ross Edgleyswam around Great Britain.Sean ConwayandJasmine Harrisonswam the length of Britain. [In 2022] I did a swim down the California coast from the Golden Gate Bridge to Half Moon Bay, and it made me realize how much fun I had during that, and I was like: I want to try to do this with the coast.What did you think about while you were swimming four to five hours a day?In college, my coach used to say you only get so many energy units per day. Overthinking or excessive thinking or negative thinking – that can take some of that energy you have. During these marathon swims, I try to keep my thoughts very focused on the task at hand. Coaching myself to get to the next 30 minutes, coaching myself to do the next 2 miles, and kind of like celebrating those little moments. When the conditions were really rough, there was a lot of thought around my technique, because I really had to adjust how I was swimming to not wreck my shoulders in the big waves.What could you hear as you were swimming?I had earplugs on, so I couldn’t hear the crew. But one thing I could hear very clearly was dolphins. And so there were many occasions where I would hear the dolphins before the crew could see them. And I would look up and I’d be like, you guys, incoming, there’s dolphins.At points, you were swimming through6-8ft waves, which you have described as feeling like you were in a washing machine. What is it like to swim in those conditions?If I’m swimming into the swell, it feels like you’re swimming up a hill. But if it’s behind me, then it’s actually very fun because it feels like I’m surfing. So it really depended on the conditions. When you’ve got a lot of wind and a lot of swell, the waves can crash on you from the back or the side or the front. And it does take a lot of effort to keep my body in the right position. One day a wave picked me up, and I landed on my butt.View image in fullscreenCatherine Breed in Coronado, California, on 19 October.Photograph: Nelvin C Cepeda/The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty ImagesHow do you train for swimming in those kinds of waves?I’ve been marathon swimming for 10 years. I grew up swimming, I grew up sailing. So my whole life has been in the ocean. So those moments, they’re difficult, but I’m comfortable. I surf a lot. And so I think surfers are comfortable with waves and they understand kind of just wave mechanics and moving with the ocean.I think the challenging part of the swell was not so much as swimming, but that there’s no chance of recovery [with living on a boat]. Getting ready to swim is really hard – like you’re trying to make breakfast and you’re falling over, your coffee’s spilling. Even putting my wetsuit on is a challenge in itself.Were there days when you woke up and did not want to get in the water?Yes. Many days. [She laughs.] But for myself, I committed to this goal, and my team committed to being part of it. And so, the days I didn’t want to get in it, it didn’t matter what my emotions were, because this project is bigger than just me.You swam the English Channel in 2018 and the North Channel crossing betweennorth Ireland and Scotland in 2019. How was preparing for this California challenge different from preparing for those classic marathon swims?For my other swims, I did follow English Channel rules: it was just one cap, bathing suit, goggles. So that preparation required a lot of cold adaptation, and spending hours in the San Francisco Bay being comfortable to be in those conditions for a long time. In California, I’m wearing a wetsuit, so I didn’t have to focus so much on the cold training. I focused more on putting on muscle, and ensuring my body composition was going to benefit me for the swim. So the training was a little less swimming than my other marathon swims, and more time in the gym.What were some of the hardest moments of the past four months?Swimming down in San Diego by the Imperial Beach and Tijuana River and knowing about thesewage pollution crisis[where billions of gallons ofraw sewage and toxic chemicalsflow from the river into the ocean] – that was probably the most nerve-wracking, because, though we were 3 miles offshore and I was taking prophylactic antibiotics, I still was so scared about my health. And then, you know, any moments that the team spotted a shark fin.What did you do when your crew saw a shark in the distance?The team just says: “Shark!” And within five seconds – definitely less than 10 seconds – I’m out of the water. Then we observe the situation. And if we see the shark again, then we were just done for the day. That only happened once in four months. So it really was the most insignificant part of the trip.Our biggest shark deterrent is the fact that I was swimming right next to a 52ft sailboat. And on the other side of me, I had a tender in the water. Ultimately, the sharks just really weren’t interested in me.You’ve spoken out on your social media accounts about the assumption that sharks are the biggest threats to your swim. Why do you think that’s the wrong focus?The pollution definitely made me more uncomfortable than any shark sightings ever did. It’s so interesting how people focus so much on sharks when sharks have been in the water with humans for a really long time. We’re so concerned about them, but we should be more concerned about what damage we’re causing to our planet and our home.Outside populated cities like San Diego and Los Angeles, we saw trash and plastic pollution every day, all day. It was astounding. I think we picked up over 10 Mylar balloons in one day. I had no idea there were that many in the ocean.You did not plan to do this swim during a year of extremesuper El Niño weather, but that’s what happened. How did that change your experience?The California coastal current historically goes north to south. That’s why we picked the direction. But with the super El Niño, all of the tropical storms and hurricanes that happened this year, instead we were fighting this insane current that is pushing against us. We had to do a lot of problem-solving and pivoting to make forward progress: some of our sections, we did the opposite way. [Breed swam some daily segments of the journey backwards, south to north, allowing her to go with the current, rather than against it.]View image in fullscreenCatherine Breed (left), enjoys a moment with her nephew, Leon, age 2, and her sister, Alexandra Breed, on 19 October.Photograph: Nelvin C Cepeda/The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty ImagesYou were swimming down the coast during a summer of massive tropical storms in the Pacific, with giant waves that have wrecked havoc onsouthern California’s beaches. How did you handle that?We had some days where we knew there was going to be really bad weather, and so we just didn’t even go out that day. I can think of four or five days where we started to swim – for example, during Hurricane Rachel, we were supposed to be able to swim until 2.30pm. But then the wind went from about 10 knots to 25 knots (11mph to 29mph) in about seven minutes. And so the team was like: we’ve got to get out. We need to get to harbor.What were some of your most memorable animal encounters?I’ve had manta rays swim around me. In Morro Bay, a humpback whale and her calf swam right next to me. I could see them diving. It was so magical. In Santa Barbara, a pod of bottlenose dolphins came and played with us for about 10 minutes. It really felt like the ocean was welcoming us.From Humboldt [county] all the way to Point Concepción, we probably saw anywhere from five to 10 whales a day. I think the most we saw on a day maybe was like 50. We would have whales come swim right under the boat.Is it lonely doing these long-distance swims?No, it’s not lonely. It’s absolutely the opposite of a solo expedition. It requires a huge team and it requires a team that I literally trust with my life. Yes, I was in the water for four to five hours a day by myself. But when I got out, I was surrounded by just this incredible team of women. And through the difficult, through the tough, we still found moments to connect with laughter and just bring some lightness to the whole swim.Does it feel weird not to be swimming?Yeah. It feels very weird to wake up this morning and just get to relax.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaSwimmingWest CoastinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Fast track to the slopes: 12 European ski resorts by train – in less time than you may think | Ski resorts | The Guardian
description: For skiers looking to reduce their carbon footprint, rail travel from the UK to the Alps has never been quicker or easier. Here’s how to get there
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: For skiers looking to reduce their carbon footprint, rail travel from the UK to the Alps has never been quicker or easier. Here’s how to get there
Content: The Railjet from Zurich to St Anton am Arlberg in Austria passes through snowy valleys and over dramatic Alpine passes.Photograph: Harald EisenbergerView image in fullscreenThe Railjet from Zurich to St Anton am Arlberg in Austria passes through snowy valleys and over dramatic Alpine passes.Photograph: Harald EisenbergerSki resortsFast track to the slopes: 12 European ski resorts by train – in less time than you may thinkFor skiers looking to reduce their carbon footprint, rail travel from the UK to the Alps has never been quicker or easier. Here’s how to get thereDaniel Elkan and Robert ThorneSat 24 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpeeding effortlessly towards the slopes by train, you might wonder why you ever flew to a ski resort. On paper, it seems a short hop by plane; in reality, airport queues, cramped flights and long transfers can mean the journey eats up a whole day.Measured door-to-door, daytime rail travel from London can be as fast as flying, while taking a sleeper train gets you extra time on the slopes. And with Alpine glaciers suffering significant loss of snow cover as global temperatures rise, rail travel constitutes the biggest emissions saving a skier can make.An exciting recent development is the arrival of a dedicated sleeper train for skiers, theTravelski Night Express(TNE), launched last winter and with an additional new route for the coming one. Each carriage has couchette berths, but the train’s crowning glory is its large, speakeasy-cafe-bar-restaurant, with retro decor, soft lighting and music – you get the romance of overnight rail travel with the potential for two extra days’ skiing thrown in.The TNE has two routes: one from Paris, the other from Amsterdam and Brussels, going out on Fridays and returning on Saturdays. Both routes access Moûtiers, Aime-la-Plagne and Bourg-Saint-Maurice – stations in the popular Tarentaise region of the French Alps. UK-based skiers can connect to the TNE by Eurostar to Paris or Brussels.Overnight journeys to Austria are also possible, with a Eurostar to Paris or Brussels and then aNightjetsleeper train to the Salzburgerland region; or, for Innsbruck and the Tirol, a Nightjet from Amsterdam and Cologne.An array of resorts in France and beyond can be reached every day of the week by taking the Eurostar to Paris Nord, getting a taxi or the RER for the short transfer to Gare de Lyon, and from there catching a fast TGV train south.The most direct daytime option is Eurostar’s flagship ski service,Eurostar Snow, which carries snowboards and skis free of charge on top of the usual luggage allowance. Skiers take it from London to Lille, then switch to an adjacent platform for the onward train to Bourg-Saint-Maurice.double quotation markThe most direct daytime option is the flagship ski service Eurostar Snow, which carries snowboards and skis free of chargeUnfortunately, the final outbound departure for this coming season is on 20 February, leaving the ski industry frustrated. Eurostar’s explanation is that it needs to “deploy rolling stock to where it best meets customer demand. Historically, March has not always been the strongest period for Eurostar Snow.”Iain Martin, founder of sustainable ski-travel campaignSki Flight Free, says: “It’s ridiculous for Eurostar to curtail their flagship service and blame lack of demand. If Eurostar worked effectively with the ski industry and ski tour operators to market the train, they could sell it out many times over.”Ski tour operators are certainly hungry for more train seats. “We’re keen on promoting rail travel to the French Alps and we know clients want this,” says Alison Willis, managing director of French ski specialistPeak Retreats. “While changing in Paris is straightforward, we know that direct services are an even more compelling alternative for those who usually fly. March ski holidays, with longer days and excellent conditions, are really popular. So, we’d welcome more direct rail options across as much of the ski season as possible.”It’s a view echoed by ski tour operatorInghams, which has increased its range of rail-inclusive packages to include 75% of its French destinations, as well as some in Switzerland, Italy and Austria. “There’s a genuine appetite among skiers to travel to the mountains by train,” says head of sustainability Krissy Roe.Here are 12 resorts you can reach easily by rail.St Anton am Arlberg, AustriaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Roger Cracknell Photography/Getty Images“The cradle of skiing”, St Anton is consistently ranked among the best resorts in the world. While its slopes are known for being challenging and exhilarating (the mighty Valluga being the pinnacle), there are plenty of gentler areas, too. St Anton isn’t just about skiing, either: this delightful village offers a host of activities, including swimming, bowling, indoor rock climbing and some of the best toboggan runs in the Alps. Completing its ski-hard, party-hard image, the resort is renowned for its après-ski, with a long list of celebrated terraces where visitors can dance to live music while knocking back schnapps.By train: 10h 30minDepart London St Pancras on the 07.31 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 12.22 TGV to Zurich; then the 16.40 Railjet to St Anton, arriving at 19.01.Where to staySki Solutionsoffers seven nights at the Hotel Post from £1,870pp half-board, including return rail travel.Alpbach, AustriaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ski JuwelComprising antique, chocolate-box chalets, Alpbach is perhaps the prettiest village on this list, with fantastic skiing to boot. Despite its low altitude, the resort’s north-facing slopes protect fresh powder, with the best off-piste and snowboarding terrain being on the far side of the Wiedersbergerhorn. Alpbach has gone to great lengths to preserve its rustic character. The main lifts are a short shuttle ride away from the village, and you’ll find gorgeous Tyrolean dishes at mountain hut restaurants such asBöglalm, torchlit walking trails, horse-drawn carriage rides and an Alpine coaster. Pick up a freeAlpbachtal Cardfor access to local activities.By train: 16h 49minDepart London St Pancras on the 15.04 Eurostar to Brussels-Midi; then catch the 18.25 ICE to Cologne; get on the 21.45 Nightjet to Jenbach, arriving at 08.53. From there, it’s 20 minutes by bus or taxi.Where to staySTC Skioffers the four-starHotel Alphof, with doubles from £955pp for seven nights’ half-board.Sainte-Foy-Tarentaise, FranceView image in fullscreenSainte-Foy, the smallest resort on this list, is highly regarded among ski writers as a “hidden gem”.Just 25 minutes from Bourg-Saint-Maurice station, it has retained its cosy, quiet ambience, thanks to bigger nearby names drawing the crowds. Yet Sainte-Foy has truly excellent skiing: powder that lasts on its untracked, north-facing slopes, and fantastic provisions for children and beginners. Despite some development, the village has remained rustic, with traditional dishes served in 16th-century farmhouses and glasses of local rosé downed on sunny terraces. The quiet pine woods are perfect for snowshoeing, while adrenaline junkies can try their hand at paragliding high above the Tarentaise.By train: 7h 58minEurostar Snow departs London St Pancras at 09.01 to Lille Europe; switch to the 11.35 Eurostar Snow continental train to Bourg-Saint-Maurice, arriving at 17.45. From there, it’s 25 minutes by bus or taxi.Where to stayPremiere Neigeoffers seven nights’ self-catering in the three-bedroom Panorama apartment from €600pp, based on six people sharing.La Rosière, FranceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Real Image/AlamyCommanding spectacular views of the Tarentaise valley, La Rosière is as beautiful as it is convenient. Its position on the Franco-Italian border allows skiers to choose between south- and north-facing slopes (in neighbouring La Thuile), while its two core villages are relaxed and compact, in classic chalet style. La Rosière has kept up an excellent pace of development, exemplified by the new high-speed Petit-Bois chair, ensuring a high-quality experience all-round. Sledging is popular, including the new sunset toboggan run from the top of the Les Eucherts lift. While fairly quiet, you’ll find some decent après-ski and DJ sets atLe Comptoir, too.By train:7h 44minEurostar Snow departs London St Pancras at 09.01 to Lille Europe; switch to the 11.35 Eurostar Snow continental train to Bourg-Saint-Maurice, arriving at 17.45. From there, it’s 40 minutes by bus or taxi to the resort centre.Where to stayTraditional chalet-hotelL’Accroche-Cœurhas double rooms from €240 a night B&B.Les Menuires, FranceView image in fullscreenPart of the famous Three Valleys, Les Menuires is one of the best value-for-money resorts in the Alps: 600km of piste but without the high price tag of Méribel or Courchevel. Unsurprisingly, it’s very popular with families who love the resort’s early-access ski patrol lessons withESF Club Piou-Piou. Dining is similarly family-oriented: expect hearty, locally sourced Savoyard meals at restaurants such asChez Pépé Nicolas. Finally, in March, Les Menuires hosts a seasonal silly slalom,Complètement à la Masse, open to all ages.By train: 13h 5minDepart London St Pancras on the 17.31 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 22.52 Travelski Night Express to Moûtiers, arriving at 07.36. From there it’s 45 minutes by bus or taxi.Where to stayTravelskioffers seven nights at Hôtel Les Menuires Les Bruyères from £1,356pp B&B, including rail travel from Paris, transfers and seven-day ski pass. The Eurostar to Paris needs to be booked independently.Montgenèvre, FranceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Michele D’Ottavio/AlamyFrance’s oldest ski resort, Montgenèvre was the stomping ground of the Parisian set before British skiers started arriving in the 90s, attracted by its bargain prices and easy access to Italy. Pleasantly old world and fully pedestrianised, “Monty” is the ideal family resort, with an extensive beginners’ zone and affordable accommodation. Intermediates will enjoy the network of red and blue runs, while experts can plough through off-piste powder in the Gondrans bowl and off the Col de l’Alpet. Over the past year, the resort has extensively redeveloped its lift system to dramatically improve speed and ease – in time for hosting the 2030 Winter Olympics.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBy train: 8h 20minDepart London St Pancras on the 08.01 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 12.46 TGV to arrive at Oulx at 17.21. From there it’s 35 minutes by bus or taxi.Where to stayPeak Retreatsoffers seven nights B&B in a suite in Hôtel Anova from £1,046pp, including rail travel, based on four sharing.Peisey-Vallandry, FranceView image in fullscreenPeisey-Vallandry offers a wealth of activities, including skijoring – skiers being pulled across the snow by a horse.Peisey-Vallandry occupies a prime position between Les Arcs and La Plagne, connecting to both via the immense Paradiski domain. Its sunny, west-facing piste offers something for everyone: a high-altitude beginners’ area, picturesque intermediate tree runs to the Chapelle Notre-Dame, and two challenging blacks (plus some fairly gnarly freeriding and all 425km of Paradiski). Thanks to its golden child, Olympic championÉric Perrot, the resort has a strong reputation for cross-country, including a new Nordic centre, shooting range and 43km of high-quality trails (open for ages 3+). For something more unusual, trySummit Bike’s electric snow-biking sessions or skijoring (putting on skis and being pulled across the snow by a horse).By train: 7h 47minEurostar Snow departs London St Pancras at 09.01 to Lille Europe; switch to the 11.35 Eurostar Snow continental train to Landry, arriving at 17.34. From there, it’s 25-35 minutes by bus or taxi.Where to stayThe ski-in-ski-out, fully renovatedHotel Émeraudehas doubles from €130 B&B.Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, FranceView image in fullscreenLe Topo, a climbing facility in Saint-Gervais-les-Bains.Photograph: Arthur DelicqueSaint-Gervais has been a popular tourist destination since the middle ages, owing to its natural hot springs. Today, the resort’s state-of-the-art thermal baths are still a huge draw for skiers seeking the ultimate wellness holiday. Combined with more than 455km of quiet piste and the best views of Mont Blanc in France, Saint-Gervais is a must-visit. In 2022, the resort opened a world-class indoor climbing facility,Le Topo. Dining, meanwhile, remains suitably traditional, including Savoyard platters, fondue and local craft beer. It’s also perfect for holidaying by rail, with a station-to-village gondola,Le Valléen, plus the Mont-Blanc tramway, one of the highest in Europe.By train:8h 45minDepart London St Pancras on the 09.31 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 14.18 TGV to Bellegarde; then the 17.15 TER to Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, arriving at 19.16. From there, it’s five minutes by the Valléen gondola to the village centre.Where to staySeven nights’ self-catering in a two-bedroom apartment in Les Sources de Canopée in Saint-Gervais, withPeak Retreats, costs from £645pp, including rail travel, based on four sharing.Val Cenis, FranceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sebastien TachetVal Cenis recently invested €25m in sustainable development and infrastructure, and the results are showing. The resort has successfully created a second “recycled” chairlift, Combe de l’Ours, using secondhand seats, pylons and cables to reduce new materials tenfold. A new panoramic treetop walkway and energy-efficient gondola will greet guests this winter, giving easy access to its 125km of high-quality, north-facing piste. As a year-round working community, the resort comprises several well-stocked villages with a wide variety of shops, restaurants and bars, as well as a bowling alley. Off-piste snowshoeing in the spectacular Vanoise national park is a popular activity; locals Thierry Bardagi and Hélène Degano offer a combinedsnowshoeing and mountain refuge package, with a cooked breakfast overlooking the mountain sunrise.By train: 7h 47minDepart London St Pancras on the 08.01 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; change to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 12.46 TGV to arrive at Modane at 16.48. From there, it’s 30 minutes by bus or taxi.Where to stayErna Lowoffers seven nights’ self-catering in a one-bedroom apartment in Les Balcons de Val Cenis Village, from £132pp, based on four sharing, travel not included.Villars-sur-Ollon, SwitzerlandView image in fullscreenLes Bains de Villars in Villars-sur-Ollon.Photograph: Riton/Henri-Ravise NoelVillars is one of French-speaking Switzerland’s quieter and (relatively) affordable resorts, perfect for an active holiday. Its respectable 130km of piste spreads across neighbouring Les Diablerets and Gryon, providing something for all ages and abilities, as well as cross-country, touring and toboggan trails. Plus, there’s a spectacular 1,500-metre off-piste descent from Les Diablerets glacier to the village. After a long day’s skiing, book in for a spa massage atLes Bains de Villarsor a dip in the hot springs atLavey, before a night of music and malt whisky in the bar at LesMazots du Clos.By train: 8h 49minDepart London St Pancras on the 09.31 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 14.18 TGV to Geneva; then the 18.05 InterRegio train to Aigle, arriving at 19.20. From there, it’s 20 minutes by bus or taxi.Where to stayAlpe Fleurie Hotel & Residencehas double rooms from £193 B&B.Grandvalira, AndorraView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zuzana Dolezalova/AlamyAndorra’s duty-free status makes Grandvalira particularly attractive to visitors looking for shopping and high-quality, low-cost accommodation. Spread across three high-altitude villages, the resort is by far the largest in the Pyrenees, with 215km of piste best suited to intermediates. The village of Pas de la Casa has garnered a reputation for its après-ski, while further along, Soldeu is home to some swanky four- and five-star hotels. The ace up Grandvalira’s sleeve, however, is its unique Catalan cuisine, quite unlike traditional Alpine fare, with an emphasis on flame-grilled meats and hearty vegetable stews.By train: 15h 12minDepart London St Pancras on the 17.31 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare d’Austerlitz and take the 22.14 Intercités de Nuit to Andorre-L’Hospitalet, arriving at 09.43. From there, it’s 35-55 minutes by bus or taxi.Where to stayAlpine Answersoffers seven nights in a double room (with balcony) at the four-star Sport Hotel Village, from £1,030pp B&B.Sestriere, ItalyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Michele D’Ottavio/AlamyEurope’s first purpose-built ski resort remains cheap and cheerful, catering best to families and young adults on a budget. Sestriere’s slopes are some of the best in the Via Lattea domain (which includes France’s Montgenèvre and neighbouring Sauze d’Oulx), ranging from sprawling nursery meadows to the steep Col de Sises Olympic giant slalom. Local amenities are well-organised and non-ski activities abundant, including a sizable leisure centre and swimming pool, open-air ice rink and dog-sledding. Après-ski is also surprisingly lively for a family-focused resort, with several popular pubs in the centre of town, alongside a good, old-fashioneddiscoteca,Tabata.By train: 8h 20minDepart London St Pancras on the 08.01 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 12.46 TGV to arrive at Oulx at 17.21. From there, it’s 35 minutes by bus or taxi.Where to stayInghamsoffers seven nights at Grand Hotel Sestriere, from £1,134pp, including rail travel and transfers.Accommodation prices are for the 2026/27 season and were correct at the time of publicationExplore more on these topicsSki resortsSkiing holidaysFrance holidaysAustria holidaysSwitzerland holidaysAndorra holidaysItaly holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Young country diary: A red squirrel examines a nut, right in front of me | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Brownsea Island, Dorset: I’ve been here lots of times to see the squirrels, so I know exactly where to find them – behind the church in the woods
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brownsea Island, Dorset: I’ve been here lots of times to see the squirrels, so I know exactly where to find them – behind the church in the woods
Content: A red squirrel on Brownsea Island. ‘They stay still when they spot us, waiting to see if we are friend or foe.’Photograph: Colin Waite/AlamyView image in fullscreenA red squirrel on Brownsea Island. ‘They stay still when they spot us, waiting to see if we are friend or foe.’Photograph: Colin Waite/AlamyYoung country diaryWildlifeYoung country diary: A red squirrel examines a nut, right in front of meBrownsea Island, Dorset:I’ve been here lots of times to see the squirrels, so I know exactly where to find them – behind the church in the woodsSat 24 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 06.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery October my family have an annual trip to Brownsea Island. We go in autumn because this is a good time to see the red squirrels. In the other seasons, they are high up, hidden in the trees. We catch the ferry from Poole Harbour, and we know we are close when we can see the castle come into view. When we arrive we’re greeted by nosy chickens and attention-seeking peacocks on the lawns.We go behind the little church into the woods. It is a different world there. There is a mix of crunchy and soggy brown leaves on the ground and little mushrooms popping up from the earth. Some mushrooms are sprouting from rotting logs.View image in fullscreenA video still of the red squirrel Tom encountered.Photograph: Family handoutThe red squirrels scurry at high speed. If we are at a distance or very quiet then we get good views of them. We were lucky that they stopped right in front of us on a dead log to examine a nut. A beam of sunlight hit a squirrel giving its body a golden outline. They stay still when they spot us, waiting to see if we are friend or foe. Then they continue their busy work when they realise we are just watching.Red squirrels enjoy eating seeds from pine cones, nuts, bugs and berries. Although they don’t hibernate, they do slow down in winter and stay in their dreys (homes) to avoid the bad weather and eat all food they stockpiled. I think red squirrels are smart and resilient creatures. I love watching them get their winter food while keeping watch for any predators nearby. This shows how clever they are.Tom, 10Read today’s other YCD, by Ned, 14: ‘These birds are ‘common’, but they’re special to me’.
