title: As a divided Israel prepares to go to the polls, can Netanyahu pull off his greatest political trick yet? | Israel | The Guardian
description: The prime minister has defined and dominated his country’s politics for three decades and is putting his rivals on the defensive before Tuesday’s general election
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The prime minister has defined and dominated his country’s politics for three decades and is putting his rivals on the defensive before Tuesday’s general election
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu first become prime minister 30 years ago and has held the office for more than 19 years.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFPView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu first become prime minister 30 years ago and has held the office for more than 19 years.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFPThe Saturday readIsraelAs a divided Israel prepares to go to the polls, can Netanyahu pull off his greatest political trick yet?The prime minister has defined and dominated his country’s politics for three decades and is putting his rivals on the defensive before Tuesday’s general electionJonathan Freedlandin Modi’inSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTShareThey chant his name, they cheer and clap – and yet he is not the most dominant person in the room. Looming over the crowd that has gathered to hear Gadi Eisenkot, the former general who is the lead opposition challenger in Tuesday’s Israeli election, is a man who is not there. It is the man Eisenkot seeks to replace as prime minister, the man who first served in that role three decades ago and who has held it, on and off, for 19 of the past 30 years. It isBenjamin Netanyahu.Naturally, the warm-up speakers at this evening rally in the modest city of Modi’in, halfway between Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, stress the virtues of Eisenkot, a son of working-class Moroccan Jews who rose through the ranks to become chief of staff of theIsraelDefense Forces and entered politics only four years ago. But every sentence might as well end with two words that go unspoken:unlike Bibi.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, delivers an address on the campaign trail. In an obvious reference to Benjamin Netanyahu, he has called for a ‘country without lies’.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesEven the name of Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, meaning straight or direct, carries the implied contrast with Netanyahu, who is regarded by friends and enemies alike as a maestro of the darkest political arts. When Eisenkot calls for “a country without lies”, when he calls for “responsibility and leading by example”, when he suggests US-style term limits for the role of prime minister, “because power corrupts”, everyone knows what – and who – he means.None of this comes with rhetorical fire or theatrical panache. But the lack of charisma serves only to emphasise that Eisenkot is every inch the un-Bibi. “I think that’s an advantage,” Noa Sadeh, 56, told me after Wednesday night’s rally. “I’m fed up with people who know how to talk – like Bibi. We need someone who will do the doing part.”Spotting a journalist with a notebook, David Nadler, 74, a retired colonel who served under Eisenkot, insisted I write down the word “integrity”, meaning “he says something, he means it, he will do it”. Another sentence ending with those silent words:unlike Bibi.View image in fullscreenEisenkot shakes hands with Netanyahu at a swearing-in ceremony in Jerusalem in 2015 attended by the then defence minister, Moshe Ya’alon. Eisenkot has pledged to wipe out Hamas.Photograph: Menahem Kahana/AFP/Getty ImagesIt’s hard to overstate Netanyahu’s dominance not only over this campaign but over Israeli politics and political culture. The two blocs in this election are not left and right but Bibi and anti-Bibi. The latter camp includes at least two figures – the former PM Naftali Bennett and the Moldova-born Avigdor Lieberman – whose natural home is on the nationalist right and who both once worked closely with Netanyahu, only to fall out with him spectacularly.Almost every political figure is defined, or defines themselves, in relation to Netanyahu. Eisenkot offers himself as the antidote, but listen to the pitch made by the far right and it too is all about the prime minister.Netanyahu is like a shopping trolley, says Yishai Fleisher, of Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, to a group of about 30 orthodox voters in a study hall in Bet Shemesh on Thursday evening. “He has a tendency to go left, so you have to pull him to the right.” Fleischer makes the case foryet more Jewish settlementsin the West Bank, to say nothing of settling Gaza; for a “ministry of emigration” that will encourage the “voluntary” departure of Palestinians; for the death penalty; for ever harsher treatment of Palestinian prisoners; for putting more guns and more ammunition into the hands of Jewish Israeli civilians – but all in the context of strengthening the resolve of a new Netanyahu-led coalition. On the right, Ben-Gvir is a moon that is rising, but Netanyahu is still the sun.View image in fullscreenItamar Ben-Gvir, centre, the leader of the Jewish Power party, on the campaign trail in Ramla. The far-right politician is calling for more Jewish settlements in the West Bank and harsh measures against Palestinians.Photograph: Amir Cohen/ReutersPartly, that’s a function of sheer longevity. But it’s also down to Netanyahu’s undimmed ability to set the political agenda. Even in this election, he has demarcated the terrain on which battle is fought. Hislatest poster campaignoffers voters a rhyming choice ofYamin, meaning the right, orFalastin, meaning Palestine. On the right side is, of course, his own face and the Israeli flag; on the other, the leaders of the opposition parties, including Bennett and Lieberman who are adamantly opposed to a Palestinian state, all of them surrounding two heads of parties that represent Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the country’s population. The message is not subtle: vote for me, or you’ll get the Arabs.View image in fullscreenNetanyahu campaign posters are put on display in Jerusalem. The prime minister is pitching the election as a choice between himself and the Arabs.Photograph: Kevin Coombs/ReutersIndeed, the closing weeks of the campaign have centred on the question of whether the anti-Netanyahu bloc of Jewish Israeli parties – currently forecast to do better than the Netanyahu bloc but to fall short of an overall majority in the Knesset – will do some kind of parliamentary deal with the mainly Arab parties, most of which have, historically, both refused to join Israeli governments and not been invited. Backed by that chunk of the media that is loudly and vociferously pro-Netanyahu, most notably the Fox News wannabe Channel 14, Netanyahu has succeeded in putting his opponents on the defensive.A rare exception to that pattern came just this week when a Netanyahu uber-loyalist, Channel 14’s Yinon Magal,characterised Eisenkot as a Moroccan “monkey”. The racial slur was so crude that had it been used by the left to describe a politician of the right, it would have had Netanyahu denouncing Ashkenazi elitism from the rooftops (even though Netanyahu is, of course, a privileged scion of the Ashkenazi elite).Tellingly, while the warm-up speakers in Modi’in mentioned the “monkey” remark, Eisenkot himself did not. To his admirers, that was the mark of a decent man reluctant to follow his opponents into the gutter. To the doubters, it was a sign of a politician still playing by Marquess of Queensbury rules – one who doesn’t quite appreciate what, or rather who, he is up against.For an outside observer, the most puzzling question about this Israeli election is: how is this even close? How can the polls be showing the two blocs, pro- and anti-Netanyahu, neck and neck? Abroad, many will be baffled that Netanyahu can still be in contention given the devastation his government brought down uponGaza, flattening much of the territory and killing more than 70,000 Palestinians, even if, as Israel says, one-third of them were Hamas combatants.But even inside Israel, where the impact of the war on the people of Gaza is all too rarely discussed, it is no less of a riddle that Netanyahu is a serious candidate in these elections, let alone one who could emerge on top.View image in fullscreenEisenkot, who entered politics only four years ago, is defining himself as the anti-Netanyahu candidate in Tuesday’s election.Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty ImagesTo start with the most elemental fact, the biggest disaster in the country’s history happened on his watch. The massacres inflicted on civilian Israel on 7 October 2023, at the Nova music festival and at a string of southern kibbutzim, are still fresh in the memory. Stickers depicting the faces of those killed on that day adorn bus stops and railway platforms from one end of the country to the other. As Oded Levi, who voted for Netanyahu in 2022 but was in the Modi’in crowd for Eisenkot, put it: “Whoever was prime minister [then] is responsible. He has to go. For this reason alone, we need a change.”But it hardly ends there. Netanyahu promised a war that would destroy and eradicate Hamas. That didn’t happen. Instead, Israel destroyed its own international reputation, leaving the country isolated and fast becoming a pariah state. Netanyahu promised to destroy Iran’s nuclear threat and that too didn’t happen.View image in fullscreenRaz Zarfati at a memorial to her sister, Ron, who was killed in the 7 October attacks. Netanyahu has shifted blame for the disaster.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APAdd to that the “judicial coup” in the months before 7 October, where Netanyahu tried to weaken the restraint on his power represented by the supreme court, thereby splitting Israel in two, and the Qatargate scandal, in which his closest aides stand accused of taking money from Doha in return for boosting Qatar’s image. Along with his ongoing corruption trial, it all adds up to the mystery of why Netanyahu was not counted out long ago.Any explanation begins with the loyalty of his base, built over three decades. Their support for him is unshakeable, unmoved even by reports that Netanyahureceived credible warningsof a Hamas attack on 7 October and failed to act. They are kept on side by the PM’s enduring skill in crafting a narrative, in the case of 7 October, that everyone else is to blame except him, that he was kept in the dark by army and intelligence chiefs acting out of incompetence or something more sinister, a baseless claim advanced by his “poison machine” of media and online outriders. And he remains a consummate political operator, so gifted in the business of divide and rule that many can foresee him playing the coalition arithmetic on Wednesday morning far better than any of his rivals.Still, that prospect has prompted a fierce reaction, one whose intensity can be felt thousands of miles from Israel. In the departure lounges of airports around the globe, you can find expat Israelis, many of them liberal and secular, heading home to vote on Tuesday. I saw it for myself as I travelled in a plane packed with those who felt it their duty to fly back and cast a vote to remove Netanyahu. That’s a group not picked up by pollsters and, who knows, in a contest that could turn on the fate of just one of the Knesset’s 120 seats, it may make a difference.Some of that same determination was visible at the state ceremony in Jerusalem on Thursday marking the anniversary of the assassination in 1995 of the former prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, remembered still as a would-be peacemaker gunned down before a lasting accord with the Palestinians could be struck. It was not well attended – Netanyahu stayed away and sent a low-ranking minister – and it was tempting to view it as further evidence of how far to the right Israel has shifted in these past three decades, in this age of Bibi. Here were the luminaries of the old Israeli left, gathered in a burial ground.And yet, Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats, successor party of Rabin’s, was dismissive of such talk. A former general who served with Eisenkot, and a hero of 7 October who drove south to rescue people in his own car that fateful day, Golan told me: “I’m optimistic. I never went into battle thinking ‘all right, I’m going to be killed, I’m going to be wounded’. No, I’m going to win, and we are going to win.”View image in fullscreenYair Golan, centre, leader of the Democrats, attends a memorial service for Yitzhak Rabin in Tel Aviv on Thursday. Golan, a former general, says he is confident of success on Tuesday.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty ImagesGolan even believes he and his fellow opposition leaders can agree on the beginnings of “some sort of a regional, strategic process in order to bring security for the long run”. He didn’t use the words “peace process”, but it’s clear what he meant.The word “peace” became tainted for many Israelis, associated with moves such as the 2005 withdrawal from Gaza which Netanyahu and his allies have succeeded in casting as an early step on the road to 7 October. And yet it has not vanished. Avideo went viral earlier in the weekshowing scores of young Israelis at a Negev music festival dancing and singing to Shir LaShalom, the song for peace, the anthem of those 1990s peace efforts and the last song Rabin sang before he was shot leaving a peace rally 31 years ago.Yes, the polls are deadlocked and, yes, Netanyahu is a political magician, but the sight and sound of those young people, like the queues for planes home, have given at least some Israelis the hope that change might be coming – that the age of Bibi might, at last, be drawing to a close.Explore more on these topicsIsraelThe Saturday readBenjamin NetanyahuGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaShare

title: More than one million Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoff | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro
Content: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was cheered by a huge crowd on Copacabana beach on Saturday amid hopes he can secure an historic fourth term.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersView image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva was cheered by a huge crowd on Copacabana beach on Saturday amid hopes he can secure an historic fourth term.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersBrazilMore than one million Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoffNearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio BolsonaroTom Phillipsin Rio de Janeiro andTiago Rogeroin Belo HorizonteSat 24 Oct 2026 17.10 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 14.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than one million supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival,Flávio Bolsonaro.Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonarowon the first round on 4 Octoberby 47% to 45%.On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt tohelp Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president, who was first elected in 2002, would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day.”View image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva waves to supporters on Saturday.Photograph: Dhavid Normando/AP“The people have woken up,” Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have sweptBrazilsince the leftist’s first-round defeat, many led by students.“Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again – and we don’t want dictatorship. We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career.“There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes,” Silva claimed.Polls suggest a far tighter margin and most analysts see Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, waspresident from 2019 to 2022, as the slight favourite, having sold himself to voters as someone who will tackle chronic levels of violent crime with an iron fist.However, in recent days Lula has appeared to regain the initiative and climb in the polls, amid a succession of scandals involving his rightwing foe. Last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of Brazil’s 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party attended by sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to strike a deal with the government of his father.View image in fullscreenPeople watch a televised debate between Flávio Bolsonaro and his election rival on Friday.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersSome experts speculate a Lula comeback may be possible. At the Copacabana rally –which Rio’s City Hall said attracted about 1.1 million people– activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “WE ARE GOING TO TURN THIS AROUND!”On Saturday afternoon, Lula attended an even larger rally on Paulista Avenue, in the heart of Brazil’s biggest city, São Paulo.“I’m super excited. Lula’s going to win,” said Marta Moraes, a 59-year-old restaurateur, as she joined Saturday’s demo in Rio.Moraes said the election was not about left versus right. “We’ve nothing against the right … what we’re against is Bolsonarismo,” she said, tears filling her eyes as she recalled how Flávio Bolsonaro’s fatherbotched the response to Covidduring his chaotic 2019-2022 administration.“I lost four members of my family because of Bolsonaro’s neglect,” Moraes said.View image in fullscreenLula supporters on Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersJair Bolsonaro isserving a 27-year prison sentencefor plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Many Brazilian democrats fear he will be released – and could even return to government – if his son wins. Reports in the Brazilian press suggest several of Bolsonaro’s fellow plotters – who are now in prison or hiding in exile – may be given top military and police jobs in a Bolsonaro administration.Cammy Marinho, a 49-year-old DJ and activist, said: “I’m here to prevent democracy becoming extinct – which is what the Bolsonaro family wants”.Marinho said she had spent the past fortnight fighting to persuade people who voted for Bolsonaro, or did not vote in the first round, to back Lula.Strongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in peril | George MonbiotRead more“It’s non-stop work: in the bakery, in the supermarket, on the underground – whenever you feel there is an opening to talk to someone and show to them the reality, everything that Lula has done and is doing for the people and everything that this [Bolsonaro] family has done against the people,” she said.Many marchers were part of the so-called “Lula’s Army” – a 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was created after the first round in the hope of turning the election around.“Being a soldier in Lula’s army … means fighting for Brazilian democracy. This isn’t a normal election,” said Isabella Gaze, 64, a retired teacher and one of the group’s members.“They constantly claim Lula is corrupt. But the truth is that they represent the most rotten and worst part of Brazilian politics. This is what we are fighting against now,” Gaze said of the Bolsonaros.Many of the faces on Copacabana beach were teenagers, including 14-year-old Heitor Lopes da Silva. Silva had come from the city of Duque de Caxias in his wheelchair, with a placard that said: “Lula, I’m a person with a disability and I’m here to support you.”“My whole life I’ve believed Lula was a good president. [Bolsonaro] represents the destruction of Brazil …. he represents sadness and death,” he said of the Bolsonaro-era Covid catastrophe.View image in fullscreenSome Lula supporters believe he can overturn the lead his rival secured in the first round of voting.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersLarge crowds of Bolsonaro supporters also hit the streets, including in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, which has Brazil’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo, and is a key bellwether. No presidential candidate has ever won the presidency without securing Minas Gerais, where Bolsonaro led by just under 5% in the first round.Thousands of Bolsonaristas gathered to see their candidate in a palm-lined plaza called Praça da Liberdade. To the booming sound of AI-generated funk carioca tracks praising Bolsonaro, a sea of supporters dressed in Brazil’s yellow football jersey waved Brazilian flags – and many of the United States too.“The US is a great nation. Who wouldn’t want to be aligned with them?” said 56-year-old cosmetics entrepreneur Marcos Antonio, holding a flag that merged the emblems of both countries.“I don’t want an alliance with Cuba or Venezuela. I want to move forward,” Antonio added. When reminded that Venezuela was currently aligned with the US afterDonald Trump’s January invasion, he said: “True. But for now, a fully right-wing government hasn’t been installed yet. It’s in transition.”View image in fullscreenBolsonaro supporters, some with the flags of the US, Israel and Brazil, also held last-minute rallies on Saturday.Photograph: Raquel Cunha/ReutersAntonio Carlos Costa Jr, the 59-year-old owner of a shooting club, complained: “Lula did nothing for the country.”Jair Bolsonaro relaxed gun ownership and buying laws – which security experts agree ended up diverting many firearms to criminal gangs – whereas Lula tightened regulations once again. “Jair Bolsonaro simply gave citizens the right to defend themselves, and his son will do the same,” said Costa Jr.Lula supporters scoff at the idea that Bolsonaro, who has a history of well-documented ties with members of Rio’s paramilitary “militia” groups, could rid Brazil of criminality.“If we vote the militias into power, we will be living in a dictatorship,” said Erika Cavalcante, 43, an architect who came to the march with a sign reading: “Don’t let the mobsters win.”Explore more on these topicsBrazilAmericasRio de JaneironewsShareReuse this content

title: British woman dies trying to save sons on Bahamas snorkelling trip | Bahamas | The Guardian
description: Mother, 36, died after current off North Bimini reportedly swept away two boys, who were later rescued, police say
Author: Harry Taylor
Headline: Mother, 36, died after current off North Bimini reportedly swept away two boys, who were later rescued, police say
Content: A marina in North Bimini. The woman was taken to a ferry dock after being rescued from the water.Photograph: Francisco Blanco/AlamyView image in fullscreenA marina in North Bimini. The woman was taken to a ferry dock after being rescued from the water.Photograph: Francisco Blanco/AlamyBahamasBritish woman dies trying to save sons on Bahamas snorkelling tripMother, 36, died after current off North Bimini reportedly swept away two boys, who were later rescued, police sayHarry TaylorSat 24 Oct 2026 05.43 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling.The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday.The force said they believed she was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island of North Bimini when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.The police said that in an attempt to rescue her boys, “the woman was also swept away”. The children were later rescued from the water.The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support.Bimini is a small island group between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland.The islands are best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and are also home to a world-leading shark research centre.In a statementposted on social media, the Royal Bahamas police force said: “According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini ferry dock.“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.“She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. Foul play is not suspected at this time.”An autopsy would be carried out to help determine the exact cause of death, the statement said.A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”Explore more on these topicsBahamasAmericasCaribbeannewsShareReuse this content

title: Rubio tells Cubans ‘now is the time’ to act to see political change | Marco Rubio | The Guardian
description: US secretary of state makes comments after Trump tells US rally warships could intervene on return from Iran
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US secretary of state makes comments after Trump tells US rally warships could intervene on return from Iran
Content: Marco Rubio in Mumbai, India, on 21 October.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreenMarco Rubio in Mumbai, India, on 21 October.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Pool Reuters/APMarco RubioRubio tells Cubans ‘now is the time’ to act to see political changeUS secretary of state makes comments after Trump tells US rally warships could intervene on return from IranGuardian staff and agenciesFri 23 Oct 2026 20.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 22.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change in their country to act, saying “now is the time” moments afterDonald Trumptold a Friday rally for candidates in south Florida that US warships could intervene in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.The US secretary of state, in hissocial media postaddressed “to those who seek to create positive change”, urged Cubans to capitalize on Trump’s plans. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said.The top US diplomat, whose parents leftCubafor the United States before the socialist revolution there, seemed to mistakenly use the word “discrete”, meaning separate, rather than “discreet”, meaning private or secret.Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days before midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the US war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to sendMarco Rubioin to finish up the deal.”Havana on Friday mocked the “desperation” of the US following the comments made by Rubio and Trump.“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban deputy foreign minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would “be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of US military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it”.Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba had been a national security threat for years because of its ties to US adversaries and that Trump was intent on addressing it. While saying theTrump administrationwanted to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the US could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a 29 September interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing. We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the US side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.During his address to the United Nations general assembly last month, Trump said Rubio – son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership – was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”, saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep”.Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal”, adding: “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk , and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have immigrated, many to the United States.Explore more on these topicsMarco RubioCubaDonald TrumpUS foreign policyUS politicsTrump administrationAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kim Jong-un crosses newly opened bridge into China  | North Korea | The Guardian
description: North Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party member
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: North Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party member
Content: Wang Huning (front right), a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party accompanied Kim Jong-un (front left) to the bridge.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenWang Huning (front right), a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party accompanied Kim Jong-un (front left) to the bridge.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockNorth KoreaKim Jong-un crosses newly opened bridge into ChinaNorth Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party memberRaphael Rashidin SeoulSat 24 Oct 2026 09.34 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 05.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKim Jong-un has visited China, inaugurating a bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hopes to expand cooperation with his neighbour.The North Korean leader arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday after crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, according to South Korea’s unification ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua news agency.He met Wang Huning, a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party. The pair toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship.Kim said his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries”, according to Xinhua.Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, Xinhua said.North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?Read moreThe visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of Kim’s ties with Beijing ahead of the 25 October anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean war, which came days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River intoNorth Koreain October 1950.Japan’sKyodo news agency saidon Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum about China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.The 3km bridgeopened in mid-October, 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russiaopened the first road bridgeacross their own short border, leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when heattended a military paradein Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xivisited Pyongyang in June, his first trip there in seven years.Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans toresume loudspeaker broadcastsat the border within days.Xi will host theAsia PacificEconomic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.Reutersreported on Friday, however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsNorth KoreaChinaKim Jong-unAsia PacificSouth KoreanewsShareReuse this content

title: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China | Taiwan | The Guardian
description: Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Content: A structure built for a traditional Taoist religious ceremony in Keelung lies collapsed due to strong winds from Typhoon Champi.Photograph: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA structure built for a traditional Taoist religious ceremony in Keelung lies collapsed due to strong winds from Typhoon Champi.Photograph: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty ImagesTaiwanTyphoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to ChinaSuper typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelledReutersFri 23 Oct 2026 22.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTyphoon Champi swept pastTaiwanon Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southernJapan.View image in fullscreenWaves generated by Typhoon Champi crash against a seawall in Keelung.Photograph: Ann Wang/ReutersTaiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.Explore more on these topicsTaiwanAsia PacificChinaJapannewsShareReuse this content

title: Embattled Greens senator Jordon Steele-John confirms leave from parliament after allegations against him made public | Australian Greens | The Guardian
description: WA politician says he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be ‘unacceptable’
Author: Sarah Basford Canales
Headline: WA politician says he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be ‘unacceptable’
Content: Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he has taken leave from parliament.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenGreens senator Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he has taken leave from parliament.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAustralian GreensEmbattled Greens senator Jordon Steele-John confirms leave from parliament after allegations against him made publicWA politician says he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be ‘unacceptable’Get ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastSarah Basford CanalesFri 23 Oct 2026 20.52 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 04.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament next week as the embattled Greens senator apologises for publicly releasing the letter outlining the claims against him.On Saturday afternoon, Steele-John removed a social media post containing a three-page letter marked as “confidential” sent to the Greens leader,David Shoebridge, earlier this month. The letter urged an investigation into allegations he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.Steele-John has denied all allegations made against him.The Western Australian senator said he’d heard the full letter had been circulating online and “didn’t want to be seen as hiding from it”.“I’m now not sure that was the right call and I’ve taken it down. I am really sorry for any additional stress it caused,” he said on social media.Jordon Steele-John’s position remains in limbo as Greens prepare for moment in spotlightRead moreAfter days of confusion following historical complaints about alleged misconduct were publicly aired in the media, the now-deleted statement posted to social media late Friday night said he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be “unacceptable”.He would instead focus on seeing through an independent investigation to its conclusion, he said.“Over the past few days there has been a growing chorus calling on me not to attend parliament next week. I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable,” Steele-John said.Steele-John said a precedent of keeping parliamentarians out of parliament after “allegations of allegations” were made had now been set.“Had an allegation or complaint been made against me, I would have taken these actions immediately,” he said.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThe 32-year-old senator’s attendance in parliament for the remainder of the year had been uncertain after a public stoush with Shoebridge over whether he was on leave during the investigation.The complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens and have been referred to theIndependent Parliamentary Standards Commission.Shoebridge claimed Steele-John had requested leave and he accepted it last week after seven party members penned a letter to the leader urging an investigation into the claims.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe three-page letter sent on 13 October, and first published by the Nine newspapers, said the authors had been “made aware of multiple allegations of serious misconduct” against Steele-John about his “behaviour in the presence of women”.The letter referred to an allegation of sexual harassment at a Greens campaign event in 2024 that the alleged victim had not reported out of fear of backlash. The letter provided no further detail.In another, the authors referred to an allegation of “serious sexual misconduct” in 2025. Steele-John later responded this was alleged by a former partner and was investigated by Western Australian police with a finding of “no charges”.Guardian Australia has confirmed the WA police told Steele-John the investigation was closed in May with no charges.Also contained in the letter was a reference to a disparaging nickname for Steele-John – “feels on wheels” – which the authors said implied he had a reputation for acting inappropriately.“To be clear, all signatories to this letter know that an allegation does not equate to a fact and/or guilt. We simply believe that it is in the party’s best interests to ensure that every allegation is investigated thoroughly, in alignment with community and member expectations,” the letter’s authors wrote.Steele-John wasdefiant in a lengthy statement last Sunday, rejecting the allegations against him, denying he agreed to take leave from parliament and accusing an internal faction within the Greens of playing “nasty political games” in their decision to release the letter to the media.Steele-John said any claims of his alleged behaviour should be investigated “fairly and thoroughly” but accused an “unofficial faction” within the WA branch of releasing the complaint letter to the media in a bid to oust him from the Senate.Explore more on these topicsAustralian GreensDavid ShoebridgeAustralian politicsWestern AustralianewsShareReuse this content

title: Helen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attack | Helen Haines | The Guardian
description: Independent MP now serious but stable, according to update from Melbourne’s Alfred hospital
Author: Adeshola Ore
Headline: Independent MP now serious but stable, according to update from Melbourne’s Alfred hospital
Content: Flowers left outside Member for Indi Helen Haines’s electorate office.Photograph: Mridula Amin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFlowers left outside Member for Indi Helen Haines’s electorate office.Photograph: Mridula Amin/The GuardianHelen HainesHelen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attackIndependent MP now serious but stable, according to update from Melbourne’s Alfred hospitalGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAdeshola OreFri 23 Oct 2026 20.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 16.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndependent MP Helen Haines’s condition has been downgraded to serious but stable after she lost both legs following an alleged attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria on Monday afternoon.The Alfred hospital in Melbourne provided an update on Haines’s condition on Saturday morning.“The patient is in a serious but stable condition at The Alfred on Saturday morning,” a spokesperson for the hospital said.Haines, the federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying tosave her right legbut both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.The MP’s husband, Phil Haines, provided an update at the Alfred hospital on Wednesday, saying “both her heart and her mindare in good shape.”“I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind,” he said.“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her – her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.”The alleged attack on Helen Haines shocked the nation. It shouldn’t haveRead morePolice on Tuesday charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Police have since charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailNugent appeared at the Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday and did not apply for bail.On Friday, an update on Haines’s social media accounts said her staff were working to reopen her electorate offices next Thursday.“What happened on Monday has deeply affected Helen’s family and all of her staff. Many of us witnessed the incident and some were among the first to come to her aid,” the post read.“As Helen takes the time she needs to recover, we will take time to look after ourselves and one another, too. Healing will take time, and we ask for your understanding as we navigate the days and weeks ahead.”Haines’ staff said they had been overwhelmed with kindness shown by the local community in Indi and across Australia and the globe. They said more than $730,000 had been raised for Save the Children in Haines’ honour after her husband directed people to donate to the special appeal as his wife recovered.“We are deeply moved by the extraordinary generosity of so many people,” the post read.The alleged attack on Haines has reverberated through Australian politics, prompting conversations about thetemperature of political debate,security risks for MPs andmental health servicesin regional Victoria.WA Police charged a 56-year-old man afterallegedly threatening staff and wielding nunchucksat the electoral office of the the state’s local government minister, Hannah Beazley, days after the alleged attack on Haines.A community vigil was held for Haines in Wodonga on Wednesday evening after it was revealed the MP had lost both her legs following Monday’s alleged attack.Haines’s predecessor as the federal member for Indi, Cathy McGowan, said on the sidelines of the event the community was grappling with “mixed emotions”.Explore more on these topicsHelen HainesAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November
Content: Andy Burnham said he believed the ‘balance of migration’ had changed in recent years.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said he believed the ‘balance of migration’ had changed in recent years.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EUPrime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in NovemberPatrick DalySat 24 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean theUK goes “all the way”and rejoins the EU.Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU.In an interview with the Sunday Times he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.”The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029.The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it”, but suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade.“It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” hetold the Sunday Times.“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”Burnham will meet EU chiefs at a summit in Brussels on 20 November.He argued that there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe.The issue of migration was one of the dominant debates during the 2016Brexitreferendum campaign.Andy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EURead moreIn the 12 months to June 2016 – the month of the Brexit leave vote – net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000,according to the Office for National Statistics.Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however.Net migrationpeaked at a record 944,000in the year to March 2023 due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic.It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at171,000 last year, almost half of what it was in 2016.Burnham has said he will take the opportunity around the summit with EU leaders in November to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.But Burnham added that he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen Area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro.Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a “total betrayal” of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.The Reform UK leader added: “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamEuropean UnionBrexitMigrationEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: But Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX owns Starlink, accuses Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: But Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX owns Starlink, accuses Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms
Content: Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, previously warned any restriction to Starshield system would ‘bring a lot of human losses’.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAView image in fullscreenUkraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, previously warned any restriction to Starshield system would ‘bring a lot of human losses’.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAUkraineUkraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictionsBut Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX owns Starlink, accuses Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s termsDonna FergusonSat 24 Oct 2026 17.25 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications systemwas suddenly restricted.But hours after the announcement, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink,accusedthe Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for ⁠offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in asocial media post.Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential adviser, said on the Telegram app that the country is “physically unable” to use Starlink for long- and medium-range attack drone operations.Ukraine’s general staff and defence ministry did not immediately comment.The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled.Russiawas able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.The speed restrictions coincided withthe announcementby Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on theTrump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.View image in fullscreenMusk blamed the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X that the systems were ‘owned and controlled by the US government’.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersThe US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.Ukraine’s president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming whom in the Ukraine-Starlink row?Read moreAnnouncing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomaticvideo addresson the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for ‌today is that Starlink ‌and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the ‌level we need.”The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.Whenasked by reporterswhether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUkraineTrump administrationEuropeElon MuskDonald TrumpVolodymyr ZelenskyySatellitesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing | France | The Guardian
description: Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres
Content: Demonstrators gather in Paris as fresh protests sweep FranceFranceHundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policingAlmost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centresAngelique Chrisafisin ParisSat 24 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 17.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to supportschoolchildren’s demandsfor more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.Riot police also charged a larger crowd of protesters at the end of the Paris march, using batons against them.Major protests in Paris and other French cities in challenge to Macron – in picturesRead morePolice fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police. At least two people were seriously injured, one in Clermont-Ferrand and another in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off.The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched acrossFrance. Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been almost 1,000 arrests.Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said that at various street marches across France there were what he called “high-risk groups” who “broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence”.More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France sawone of the most violent days of unrestin years, with public buildings burned,hundreds of shops destroyed and lootedand at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country.At Saturday’s protests, there was widespread anger at Macron forbanning non-union demonstrationsthat his governmentdeemed “illegitimate”and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.View image in fullscreenAt the end of the Paris demonstration, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged and threw glass bottles and stones at police.Photograph: Thibault Camus/APAt the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.”A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”The radical left presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the Paris rally, said Macron must “give in” and address France’s social malaise or face repeated protests. “Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week,” Mélenchon said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government has been facing a crisis since the start ofhigh schooldemonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesterswere maimed and injuredby explosive police weaponry.At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in thegiletsjaunesanti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from thegiletsjaunesprotest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue.NFL shutters Paris fan experience as protests overshadow first France gameRead morePierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.”Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them, and we have to stand together.”She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”In Orléans, thousands shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestEuropeEmmanuel MacronGilets jaunes protestsStudentsYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Suspect arrested over fire at Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ retreat in Bavaria | Germany | The Guardian
description: About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle blaze at former Nazi mountain retreat in remote part of southern Germany
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle blaze at former Nazi mountain retreat in remote part of southern Germany
Content: A still from a video of the fire sweeping through the mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, formerly Adolf Hitler's Eagle’s Nest retreat.Photograph: AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenA still from a video of the fire sweeping through the mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, formerly Adolf Hitler's Eagle’s Nest retreat.Photograph: AFP/GettyGermanySuspect arrested over fire at Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ retreat in BavariaAbout 200 firefighters deployed to tackle blaze at former Nazi mountain retreat in remote part of southern GermanyDonna Fergusonand agenciesSat 24 Oct 2026 10.28 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 02.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice have arrested a 33-year-old German citizen after a fire ripped through Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat in Bavaria, leaving the historic Nazi meeting place – known as the Eagle’s Nest – largely destroyed.About 200 firefighters were deployed on Friday night to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote, purpose-built Kehlsteinhaus residence, a protected building on the peak of Obersalzberg in southernGermany.Flames rose high into the air as firefighters approached the scene to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said, adding that nobody was injured in the fire.Lisa Maier, a police spokesperson, said firefighters struggled to tackle the blaze due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft).The building, which was one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era, was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.View image in fullscreenThe Kehlsteinhaus the morning after the fire.Photograph: Jason Tschepljakow/DPA/APBuilt by the Nazis and formally inaugurated by Hitler on his birthday in 1939, the Eagle’s Nest has been preserved as a monument to “the insanity of the regime”,according to its website.The building is only accessible via a road cut into the mountain through previously impassable terrain. Nazis would enter a tunnel and take a 124-metre brass lift buried in the mountain to get inside the building.Authorities were alerted to the fire when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.15pm, police said. When firefighters arrived on the scene at about 9.50pm, the entire building was engulfed in flames.Fire departments from six municipalities sent emergency personnel to tackle the blaze and the Bavarian Red Cross, the local mountain rescue service and the police also attended.No reason for the fire was given, but German media reported that investigators suspected it was the result of arson. Firefighters found no one inside the building.Efforts to fight the fire were hampered by a strong wind and rain, which turned into the year’s first snow, and firefighters had to pull out overnight after several hours.The blaze was reportedly still burning at 7am on Saturday but appeared to be out later in the morning, although smoke continued to rise from the building.View image in fullscreenA photograph from 2007 of the Kehlsteinhaus, or Eagle’s Nest, near Berchtesgaden, Germany.Photograph: Geir Moulson/APA police spokesperson told the German tabloid Bild: “It is damaged to a large extent. The house is unlikely to be saved.” Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an Agence France-Presse photographer.Maier said police were still investigating and would hold a news conference later on Saturday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMap of south-east Germany showing the location of KehlsteinhausThe 33-year-old suspect arrested by the police was a German citizen who had ties to the area but did not live there. Prosecutors said he showed signs of mental illness and after being questioned he was being sent to a psychiatric facility.The possibility of a political motive for the blaze would be investigated, but police said there was nothing to indicate anyone else was involved.The Eagle’s Nest was constructed between 1937 and 1938 and forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and communists in theHolocaust.It became legendary in the postwar period and was often depicted as an essential meeting place in US war films, although in reality Hitler rarely visited the complex.Since 1952 the building has housed an exhibition bythe Institute for Contemporary Historyrecounting its Nazi history, and a restaurant.Officials indicated that the building, which is owned by Bavaria’s state government, would be restored after discussions with local officials, historians and conservators.“We’re not going to leave a ruin there,” Joachim Herrmann, Bavaria’s interior minister, told reporters, adding that it was important to continue to do “the work of remembrance”.Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsGermanyAdolf HitlerEuropeNazismHolocaustSecond world warnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nine killed and 40 injured after gunmen open fire at church funeral in Jordan | Jordan | The Guardian
description: Footage broadcast on state TV shows three attackers approaching Greek Orthodox church and firing shots
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Footage broadcast on state TV shows three attackers approaching Greek Orthodox church and firing shots
Content: A police officer stands guard outside the Greek Orthodox church attended by Christian minority worshippers in Hamoud, Jordan.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA police officer stands guard outside the Greek Orthodox church attended by Christian minority worshippers in Hamoud, Jordan.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockJordanNine killed and 40 injured after gunmen open fire at church funeral in JordanFootage broadcast on state TV shows three attackers approaching Greek Orthodox church and firing shotsReuters in Al-MushairfehSat 24 Oct 2026 10.24 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 21.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNine people have been killed after gunmen opened fire at a funeral at a church inJordanin a rare attack ⁠on the country’s Christian minority.Authorities described the attack on Friday as a terrorist act by extremists.Maj gen Abdallah al-Maaytah, the head of Jordan’s ⁠Public Security Directorate, said most of those injured in the shooting at St George’s Greek Orthodox church in Hamoud, in Karak governorate, were receiving treatment, and that the ⁠hunt for the attackers was continuing. Jordan’s health minister said 40 people were injured.Map of Jordan-Israeli border area showing where the church shootings took placeThe interior minister, Mazin Al Farrayeh, said the attack had been carried out by “extremists”, but it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups ⁠inside or outside Jordan.Such attacks are rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable, though authorities in the US say in recent years they have repeatedly ​foiled attempted attacks by Islamist militants.There was no immediate claim of responsibility.View image in fullscreenThe scene at St George’s Greek Orthodox church in Hamoud on Saturday, where gunmen opened fire during a funeral.Photograph: Alaa Al Sukhni/ReutersA ‌video, aired on Jordan’s state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station ‌that appeared to be from a security camera on the church, showed three people firing at it from a pavement and hiding behind trees and a ‌low wall. It then showed the attackers running towards the church’s entrance. Reuters was able to verify the video from the entry path and wall surrounding the church, as well as other details.In a post on X, Jordan’s prime minister, Jafar Hassan, said: “This is a result of a terrorist ideology and blind extremism and we will not allow society to go down this path.”A priest described how he and ‌others ordered people to ‌get to the ground at the church. “A sense of panic took hold among those present,” Theodoros Soueiss said. “The gunfire was indiscriminate, and you never knew where a bullet might land.”Khaled Burqan, who was at the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were present and the gunmen opened fire on them for several minutes.Ihab Ammareen, another witness, told the station he saw bloodied people collapse ‌on the floor after the attack. “People were crying, wailing, screaming – it’s hard to describe,” he said.Jordan’s King Abdullah, a leading US partner in the fight against militant Islamist groups, visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would ​be punished “with an iron fist”.View image in fullscreenKing Abdullah, centre, visits victims of the church attack at a military hospital in Karak on Friday.Photograph: Balkis Press/Abaca/Shutterstock“The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. Those who delude themselves into thinking they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity,” he said in a statement.Reuters footage from the church after the attack showed blood smeared on the floor near its entrance, where security forces were deployed.Security has been ⁠stepped up at malls, ⁠foreign embassies ​and other locations across Jordan, the US embassy in Amman said on Saturday.In a post on X, the UN secretary general, António Guterres, condemned the violence and said attacks against civilians and places of ⁠worship were unacceptable.People who gathered at a Karak government hospital to support the injured expressed shock. “What happened today has ​left people unable to speak or raise our voices. ​But our only reproach to the state is that ​it must investigate these dark ideas – where they come from and how they enter the minds of our children,” said Hani Al-Mbaydeen, who was outside the hospital.Christians make up ‌a minority of Jordan’s population. ​The country is home to several ​biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world. The US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, described it on X as a “depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship”. Jordan was among the US allies in the region to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.Explore more on these topicsJordanMiddle East and north AfricaChristianityReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes | West Bank | The Guardian
description: PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint
Content: Israeli troops destroy Hebron neighbourhood following attack on military checkpointWest BankIsraeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homesPM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpointJulian Borgerin JerusalemSat 24 Oct 2026 09.17 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 08.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families incollective punishment for a militant attackon an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.View image in fullscreenSoldiers patrol the northern checkpoint in Hebron after Israeli forces levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/GettyPeople said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.The large-scale demolitions followan attack on Fridayon an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen.
