After a 20-minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.Israeli elections will take place in four days and the prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.View image in fullscreenIsrael's finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, filmed himself wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersHeidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attackRead moreNetanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.View image in fullscreenA Palestinian man clears debris outside a business demolished by Israeli forces in Hebron.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/GettyA Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”The Israeli army was approached for comment on the operations and on videos showing extensive devastation.Explore more on these topicsWest BankBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelPalestineInternally displaced peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: No unions, low taxes: why some of Britain’s top chefs are opening outposts in Gulf states | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: Leading restaurateur says Gulf countries actively help businesses set up, while east Asia has a better work ethic
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Leading restaurateur says Gulf countries actively help businesses set up, while east Asia has a better work ethic
Content: Fallow in St James's Market, London. The restaurant’s owners have signed a deal to open a branch in the Gulf.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverView image in fullscreenFallow in St James's Market, London. The restaurant’s owners have signed a deal to open a branch in the Gulf.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverRestaurantsNo unions, low taxes: why some of Britain’s top chefs are opening outposts in Gulf statesLeading restaurateur says Gulf countries actively help businesses set up, while east Asia has a better work ethicHelena HortonSat 24 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur.James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf.Other restaurants have opened inDubai, including the celebrity hotspot Scott’s in Mayfair, the two Michelin-starred Indian venue Gymkhana, and the upmarket Chinese restaurant Park Chinois. Isabel’s, a Mayfair institution enjoyed by politicians, has opened in Abu Dhabi. And the trendy Borough Market bakery Bread Ahead has branched out in Dubai.Despite conflicts in the Middle East, including the US-Israeli war in Iran which caused Dubai to face bombardment and an exodus of expats earlier this year, restaurants continue to open in the emirate.Speaking from Hong Kong, where he is looking at opportunities in Asia, Robson said: “East Asia, the States and the Gulf are key growth targets for us. America champions business, the Gulf actively encourages and assists, whilst east Asia has a work ethic and taxation system that puts the UK to shame. I’m incredibly keen to start working in these regions over the next few years.”Fallow has risen to fame partially through Instagram, where it has 650,000 followers, and its striking dishes including a whole cod’s head drenched in a spicy butter sauce.Restaurateurs have complained of the VAT rate for hospitality in the UK, which at 20% is one of the highest rates in Europe. The European average for restaurants is about 12%. In Italy, it is set at 10% for food sold in restaurants. Chefs are calling for Andy Burnham to use next week’s budget to cut the VAT rate.View image in fullscreenTwo-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of several London establishments that has opened in DubaiPhotograph: Sophia Evans/The Observer“We have had a tsunami of taxes that have got to the point where taking business risk simply does not make sense in the UK,” Robson said, “Sadly the country has sleepwalked into multiple anti-growth taxations the last two budgets and likely more will be forthcoming next week.”The entrepreneur has asked for VAT to be put more in line with Europe. “Add 25% corporation tax and 40%-plus dividend tax, then you start to question why do businesses any more.”Jason Atherton, a Michelin-starred chef,spends a third of his timeat his Dubai restaurant now and says it is easier to make a profit abroad than in London.But human rights experts have warned of exploitation and poor worker protections in the Gulf. Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s director of campaigns, said: “Dubai might look like an attractive place to do business, but the UAE has a very poor record on workers’ rights and protection from labour exploitation. The UAE has spent heavily on polishing its image in the UK, not least through Manchester City, but that glamour shouldn’t distract from how the people who keep its economy running are treated.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Migrant workers, who make up the majority of the UAE’s population, remain bound by a sponsorship system that ties them to their employers and exposes them to labour abuse. They are denied the right to form trade unions, leaving them few ways to challenge unfair treatment.“Any UK business expanding into the Gulf has a responsibility to carry out proper human rights due diligence, to make sure the people working in its kitchens are treated fairly, paid properly and able to raise concerns without fear of losing their job or visa.”View image in fullscreenThe British Michelin-starred chef Jason Atherton has previously spoken out about high taxes and the UK’s struggling hospitality sector.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianSome restaurants in Dubai are struggling: Dinner by Heston is temporarily closed and has been since the fallout from the war in the Middle East. The Michelin guide came under fire earlier this month because it included 16 restaurants that were either permanently or temporarily closed. It appears that some visits were undertaken by inspectors at the beginning of the year, before the war started.Robson said he had no resentment paying UK tax. “I am incredibly proud of the taxes I pay and feel privileged that I can contribute to our country’s deficit and will continue to do so,” he said. “My point is UK growth simply does not have any risk-reward balance any more, therefore it’s play incredibly safe here and focus overseas.”Explore more on these topicsRestaurantsDubaiUnited Arab EmiratesTax and spendingLondonMiddle East and north AfricaWorkers' rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: As a divided Israel prepares to go to the polls, can Netanyahu pull off his greatest political trick yet? | Israel | The Guardian
description: The prime minister has defined and dominated his country’s politics for three decades and is putting his rivals on the defensive before Tuesday’s general election
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The prime minister has defined and dominated his country’s politics for three decades and is putting his rivals on the defensive before Tuesday’s general election
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu first become prime minister 30 years ago and has held the office for more than 19 years.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFPView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu first become prime minister 30 years ago and has held the office for more than 19 years.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFPThe Saturday readIsraelAs a divided Israel prepares to go to the polls, can Netanyahu pull off his greatest political trick yet?The prime minister has defined and dominated his country’s politics for three decades and is putting his rivals on the defensive before Tuesday’s general electionJonathan Freedlandin Modi’inSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTShareThey chant his name, they cheer and clap – and yet he is not the most dominant person in the room. Looming over the crowd that has gathered to hear Gadi Eisenkot, the former general who is the lead opposition challenger in Tuesday’s Israeli election, is a man who is not there. It is the man Eisenkot seeks to replace as prime minister, the man who first served in that role three decades ago and who has held it, on and off, for 19 of the past 30 years. It isBenjamin Netanyahu.Naturally, the warm-up speakers at this evening rally in the modest city of Modi’in, halfway between Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, stress the virtues of Eisenkot, a son of working-class Moroccan Jews who rose through the ranks to become chief of staff of theIsraelDefense Forces and entered politics only four years ago. But every sentence might as well end with two words that go unspoken:unlike Bibi.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, delivers an address on the campaign trail. In an obvious reference to Benjamin Netanyahu, he has called for a ‘country without lies’.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesEven the name of Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, meaning straight or direct, carries the implied contrast with Netanyahu, who is regarded by friends and enemies alike as a maestro of the darkest political arts. When Eisenkot calls for “a country without lies”, when he calls for “responsibility and leading by example”, when he suggests US-style term limits for the role of prime minister, “because power corrupts”, everyone knows what – and who – he means.None of this comes with rhetorical fire or theatrical panache. But the lack of charisma serves only to emphasise that Eisenkot is every inch the un-Bibi. “I think that’s an advantage,” Noa Sadeh, 56, told me after Wednesday night’s rally. “I’m fed up with people who know how to talk – like Bibi. We need someone who will do the doing part.”Spotting a journalist with a notebook, David Nadler, 74, a retired colonel who served under Eisenkot, insisted I write down the word “integrity”, meaning “he says something, he means it, he will do it”. Another sentence ending with those silent words:unlike Bibi.View image in fullscreenEisenkot shakes hands with Netanyahu at a swearing-in ceremony in Jerusalem in 2015 attended by the then defence minister, Moshe Ya’alon. Eisenkot has pledged to wipe out Hamas.Photograph: Menahem Kahana/AFP/Getty ImagesIt’s hard to overstate Netanyahu’s dominance not only over this campaign but over Israeli politics and political culture. The two blocs in this election are not left and right but Bibi and anti-Bibi. The latter camp includes at least two figures – the former PM Naftali Bennett and the Moldova-born Avigdor Lieberman – whose natural home is on the nationalist right and who both once worked closely with Netanyahu, only to fall out with him spectacularly.Almost every political figure is defined, or defines themselves, in relation to Netanyahu. Eisenkot offers himself as the antidote, but listen to the pitch made by the far right and it too is all about the prime minister.Netanyahu is like a shopping trolley, says Yishai Fleisher, of Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, to a group of about 30 orthodox voters in a study hall in Bet Shemesh on Thursday evening. “He has a tendency to go left, so you have to pull him to the right.” Fleischer makes the case foryet more Jewish settlementsin the West Bank, to say nothing of settling Gaza; for a “ministry of emigration” that will encourage the “voluntary” departure of Palestinians; for the death penalty; for ever harsher treatment of Palestinian prisoners; for putting more guns and more ammunition into the hands of Jewish Israeli civilians – but all in the context of strengthening the resolve of a new Netanyahu-led coalition. On the right, Ben-Gvir is a moon that is rising, but Netanyahu is still the sun.View image in fullscreenItamar Ben-Gvir, centre, the leader of the Jewish Power party, on the campaign trail in Ramla. The far-right politician is calling for more Jewish settlements in the West Bank and harsh measures against Palestinians.Photograph: Amir Cohen/ReutersPartly, that’s a function of sheer longevity. But it’s also down to Netanyahu’s undimmed ability to set the political agenda. Even in this election, he has demarcated the terrain on which battle is fought. Hislatest poster campaignoffers voters a rhyming choice ofYamin, meaning the right, orFalastin, meaning Palestine. On the right side is, of course, his own face and the Israeli flag; on the other, the leaders of the opposition parties, including Bennett and Lieberman who are adamantly opposed to a Palestinian state, all of them surrounding two heads of parties that represent Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the country’s population. The message is not subtle: vote for me, or you’ll get the Arabs.View image in fullscreenNetanyahu campaign posters are put on display in Jerusalem. The prime minister is pitching the election as a choice between himself and the Arabs.Photograph: Kevin Coombs/ReutersIndeed, the closing weeks of the campaign have centred on the question of whether the anti-Netanyahu bloc of Jewish Israeli parties – currently forecast to do better than the Netanyahu bloc but to fall short of an overall majority in the Knesset – will do some kind of parliamentary deal with the mainly Arab parties, most of which have, historically, both refused to join Israeli governments and not been invited. Backed by that chunk of the media that is loudly and vociferously pro-Netanyahu, most notably the Fox News wannabe Channel 14, Netanyahu has succeeded in putting his opponents on the defensive.A rare exception to that pattern came just this week when a Netanyahu uber-loyalist, Channel 14’s Yinon Magal,characterised Eisenkot as a Moroccan “monkey”. The racial slur was so crude that had it been used by the left to describe a politician of the right, it would have had Netanyahu denouncing Ashkenazi elitism from the rooftops (even though Netanyahu is, of course, a privileged scion of the Ashkenazi elite).Tellingly, while the warm-up speakers in Modi’in mentioned the “monkey” remark, Eisenkot himself did not. To his admirers, that was the mark of a decent man reluctant to follow his opponents into the gutter. To the doubters, it was a sign of a politician still playing by Marquess of Queensbury rules – one who doesn’t quite appreciate what, or rather who, he is up against.For an outside observer, the most puzzling question about this Israeli election is: how is this even close? How can the polls be showing the two blocs, pro- and anti-Netanyahu, neck and neck? Abroad, many will be baffled that Netanyahu can still be in contention given the devastation his government brought down uponGaza, flattening much of the territory and killing more than 70,000 Palestinians, even if, as Israel says, one-third of them were Hamas combatants.But even inside Israel, where the impact of the war on the people of Gaza is all too rarely discussed, it is no less of a riddle that Netanyahu is a serious candidate in these elections, let alone one who could emerge on top.View image in fullscreenEisenkot, who entered politics only four years ago, is defining himself as the anti-Netanyahu candidate in Tuesday’s election.Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty ImagesTo start with the most elemental fact, the biggest disaster in the country’s history happened on his watch. The massacres inflicted on civilian Israel on 7 October 2023, at the Nova music festival and at a string of southern kibbutzim, are still fresh in the memory. Stickers depicting the faces of those killed on that day adorn bus stops and railway platforms from one end of the country to the other. As Oded Levi, who voted for Netanyahu in 2022 but was in the Modi’in crowd for Eisenkot, put it: “Whoever was prime minister [then] is responsible. He has to go. For this reason alone, we need a change.”But it hardly ends there. Netanyahu promised a war that would destroy and eradicate Hamas. That didn’t happen. Instead, Israel destroyed its own international reputation, leaving the country isolated and fast becoming a pariah state. Netanyahu promised to destroy Iran’s nuclear threat and that too didn’t happen.View image in fullscreenRaz Zarfati at a memorial to her sister, Ron, who was killed in the 7 October attacks. Netanyahu has shifted blame for the disaster.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APAdd to that the “judicial coup” in the months before 7 October, where Netanyahu tried to weaken the restraint on his power represented by the supreme court, thereby splitting Israel in two, and the Qatargate scandal, in which his closest aides stand accused of taking money from Doha in return for boosting Qatar’s image. Along with his ongoing corruption trial, it all adds up to the mystery of why Netanyahu was not counted out long ago.Any explanation begins with the loyalty of his base, built over three decades. Their support for him is unshakeable, unmoved even by reports that Netanyahureceived credible warningsof a Hamas attack on 7 October and failed to act. They are kept on side by the PM’s enduring skill in crafting a narrative, in the case of 7 October, that everyone else is to blame except him, that he was kept in the dark by army and intelligence chiefs acting out of incompetence or something more sinister, a baseless claim advanced by his “poison machine” of media and online outriders. And he remains a consummate political operator, so gifted in the business of divide and rule that many can foresee him playing the coalition arithmetic on Wednesday morning far better than any of his rivals.Still, that prospect has prompted a fierce reaction, one whose intensity can be felt thousands of miles from Israel. In the departure lounges of airports around the globe, you can find expat Israelis, many of them liberal and secular, heading home to vote on Tuesday. I saw it for myself as I travelled in a plane packed with those who felt it their duty to fly back and cast a vote to remove Netanyahu. That’s a group not picked up by pollsters and, who knows, in a contest that could turn on the fate of just one of the Knesset’s 120 seats, it may make a difference.Some of that same determination was visible at the state ceremony in Jerusalem on Thursday marking the anniversary of the assassination in 1995 of the former prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, remembered still as a would-be peacemaker gunned down before a lasting accord with the Palestinians could be struck. It was not well attended – Netanyahu stayed away and sent a low-ranking minister – and it was tempting to view it as further evidence of how far to the right Israel has shifted in these past three decades, in this age of Bibi. Here were the luminaries of the old Israeli left, gathered in a burial ground.And yet, Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats, successor party of Rabin’s, was dismissive of such talk. A former general who served with Eisenkot, and a hero of 7 October who drove south to rescue people in his own car that fateful day, Golan told me: “I’m optimistic. I never went into battle thinking ‘all right, I’m going to be killed, I’m going to be wounded’. No, I’m going to win, and we are going to win.”View image in fullscreenYair Golan, centre, leader of the Democrats, attends a memorial service for Yitzhak Rabin in Tel Aviv on Thursday. Golan, a former general, says he is confident of success on Tuesday.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty ImagesGolan even believes he and his fellow opposition leaders can agree on the beginnings of “some sort of a regional, strategic process in order to bring security for the long run”. He didn’t use the words “peace process”, but it’s clear what he meant.The word “peace” became tainted for many Israelis, associated with moves such as the 2005 withdrawal from Gaza which Netanyahu and his allies have succeeded in casting as an early step on the road to 7 October. And yet it has not vanished. Avideo went viral earlier in the weekshowing scores of young Israelis at a Negev music festival dancing and singing to Shir LaShalom, the song for peace, the anthem of those 1990s peace efforts and the last song Rabin sang before he was shot leaving a peace rally 31 years ago.Yes, the polls are deadlocked and, yes, Netanyahu is a political magician, but the sight and sound of those young people, like the queues for planes home, have given at least some Israelis the hope that change might be coming – that the age of Bibi might, at last, be drawing to a close.Explore more on these topicsIsraelThe Saturday readBenjamin NetanyahuGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaShare

title: Storm Boelo: Travel disrupted and events cancelled as UK hit by wind and rain | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Fresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on Friday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on Friday
Content: People struggle to hold their umbrellas against strong winds in Liverpool on Saturday.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople struggle to hold their umbrellas against strong winds in Liverpool on Saturday.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAUK weatherStorm Boelo: Travel disrupted and events cancelled as UK hit by wind and rainFresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on FridayPol Allingham and Helen William, Press AssociationSat 24 Oct 2026 18.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmber weather warnings have come into force as the worst ofStorm Boelocould be set to hit parts of the UK.Storm Boelo’s winds will peak from Saturday evening, leaving areas in the warning zone, including Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, braced for gusts of 60-70mph and even 80mph in exposed coastal spots, the Met Office said.The forecaster’s amber warnings came into force on Saturday at 9pm.Maximum gust speeds of 75mph have already hit South Uist Range, Western Isles, Highland and Eilean Siar, Scotland on Saturday, according to the Met Office, which has also issued several yellow warnings for rain.Storm Boelofollows Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season, which brought strong winds to parts of the UK on Friday.Gusts of 76mph were recorded at St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, with 74mph at Aberporth in south-west Wales and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall.Heavy downpours since 8am on Saturday have already seen rainfall totals of 72mm in White Barrow, Wiltshire, along with 43mm in both Cwm Dyli, just south of the Snowdon range in North Wales, and Inveruglas on the west shore of Loch Lomond, Scotland.View image in fullscreenWaves crash over the lighthouse at Newhaven Harbour in East Sussex during Storm Austen on Friday.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersHundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday where the National Grid said power had been restored to 131,225 properties by Saturday at 7pm.An amber wind warning, the Met Office’s second most severe, is active across Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm on Saturday to the same time on Sunday.A further amber warning runs from 9pm on Saturday to 10am on Sunday in the north-east of Northern Ireland.Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, will bring a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves and people should stay indoors as much as possible, the forecaster said.The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings which extend south into parts of England and North Wales and cover the whole of Northern Ireland.TheEnvironment Agencyhad issued 58 alerts for spots across England where flooding is possible by 8pm on Saturday, as well as 12 warnings stating that flooding is expected.Met Office chief forecaster Jason Kelly said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north.“Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts.“People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”People should secure loose items outside, plan ahead if they are travelling and keep an eye on the latest forecast and warnings, he advised.View image in fullscreenThe wet weather did not deter shoppers in Oxford Street, central London, on Saturday.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/PAStorm Boelo has already caused widespread disruption.Boelo’s strong winds disrupted flights at Dublin airport, where as of 4pm on Saturday, nine outbound and 10 inbound flights had been cancelled by airlines because of weather issues.It also reported that six inbound flights performed go-arounds – five of which landed on the second attempt, with the other diverting to another airport before returning a short time later.Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, in a call for those living near rail lines to secure their garden furniture firmly.Visit Liverpool announced that the region’s River of Light event, featuring illuminated artwork, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”.London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations this Sunday were also cancelled on independent health and safety experts’ recommendations in light of the storm.Other attractions closed on Sunday include Edinburgh Castle and the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire, which was due to host its Fountains by Floodlight event.Explore more on these topicsUK weatherEnvironment AgencynewsShareReuse this content

title: Healey’s first budget to include big devolution package to boost growth | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Chancellor will build on Burnham’s promise that local leaders in England will no longer have to ‘come cap in hand to Westminster’
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Chancellor will build on Burnham’s promise that local leaders in England will no longer have to ‘come cap in hand to Westminster’
Content: Burnham said Healey’s budget was about ‘shifting power out of Westminster and into the hands of the people who know their communities best’.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBurnham said Healey’s budget was about ‘shifting power out of Westminster and into the hands of the people who know their communities best’.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianBudget 2026Healey’s first budget to include big devolution package to boost growthChancellor will build on Burnham’s promise that local leaders in England will no longer have to ‘come cap in hand to Westminster’Heather StewartSat 24 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has promised that local leaders in England will no longer have to come “cap in hand to Westminster” ahead of a fresh drive to devolve spending power in next week’s budget.In his statement on Wednesday, the chancellor,John Healey, will include plans for a new £1.5bn borrowing facility, to be drawn up in collaboration with mayors over the next two years.Regional mayors have long complained that they are constrained by their limited borrowing power – in contrast to local authorities in the US and some European countries, which commonly issue their own bonds.The borrowing plan will form part of a big devolution package aimed at boosting regional economic growth. This will also include the allocation of an initial £285m “good growth” funding next year, to be spent on local leaders’ priorities – which could include housing, transport links or high street regeneration.Can curry nights and canny advisers help Healey deliver a budget for everyday people?Read moreAmid fears in the Treasury about whether some local authorities have the capacity to administer increasingly large budgets, Healey will also announce £150m of support to help them scale up and build expertise.Hailing the plans, Burnham said they would mean local leaders would no longer need to come to the Treasury for approval for each individual project. “I’m calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country. When I became prime minister, I said that if a decision can be made closer to home, it should be.“Today we’re putting that into practice, shifting power out of Westminster and into the hands of the people who know their communities best.”The £285m in “good growth” funding is intended to tide local authorities over until a new system comes into force in 2028 whereby some income tax revenue will be handed directly to their areas to give them longer-term security – an ideafirst mooted by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, earlier this year.View image in fullscreenRachel Reeves, the chancellor under Keir Starmer, first mooted the idea of a ‘good growth’ fund.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersMore details of how this will work will be announced at the budget. Local leaders are expected to be allowed to keep some of the additional revenues created by a stronger local economy, giving them an incentive to back pro-growth policies.Tax and spending in the UK is more centralised than in many other leading economies, and Burnham experienced the constraints first-hand as mayor of Greater Manchester.Healey said: “Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas.”The package has been drawn up in collaboration with No 10 North, which has been holding a weekly “situation room” meeting with local leaders, to ask them about the barriers to promoting economic growth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis resulted in an announcement this week that the Treasury has calledthe “green book”, which gives guidanceon which projects taxpayers should fund. Under the new rules, projects that can be combined to boost growth – a housing and a transport scheme, for example – can be considered together.A governmentwhite paper on “rewiring the state”, due to be published after the budget, will set out more details of how the civil service will be reshaped, as more powers are passed down from Whitehall.View image in fullscreenOil tankers stranded near the strait of Hormuz – the war in the Middle East has driven up bills for UK households.Photograph: Barry Iverson/AlamyAlongside the devolution plans, Healey’s first budget isexpected to include support for poorer householdshit by rising energy costs; and modest tax rises, including on banks. The chancellor has repeatedly said he wants to offer a “breathing space” to households and businesses that have struggled as the war in the Middle East has driven up bills.These higher costs have also pushed up the interest rates on government borrowing, making it harder for Healey to balance the books.He will set out how he plans to fully fund the four-year defence investment plan announced in the dying days of Keir Starmer’s premiership.However, Healey is not expected to say when the UK will commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence – an issue that was central to his resignation from Starmer’s cabinet. This is likely to be delayed until a spending review due at some point next year.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyAndy BurnhamDevolutionEnglandEconomic policyUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manhunt under way to find prisoner who absconded from medical facility | UK news | The Guardian
description: Met police say Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen on Friday in south London, and ‘poses a risk to himself and the public’
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: Met police say Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen on Friday in south London, and ‘poses a risk to himself and the public’
Content: Anthony Lloyd forced his way out of a health unit in Lewisham, in south-east London, shortly after 4pm on Friday.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAAnthony Lloyd forced his way out of a health unit in Lewisham, in south-east London, shortly after 4pm on Friday.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAUK newsManhunt under way to find prisoner who absconded from medical facilityMet police say Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen on Friday in south London, and ‘poses a risk to himself and the public’Patrick Dalyand Press AssociationSat 24 Oct 2026 14.10 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 14.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA manhunt is under way to locate a prisoner who police say “poses a risk both to himself and the public” after he absconded from a medical facility inLondon.Anthony Lloyd forced his way out of a health unit in Lewisham, in south-east London, shortly after 4pm on Friday, theMetropolitan policesaid.The force warned the public not to approach Lloyd, but instead to contact 999 if he is spotted.Lloyd was seen heading in the direction of Catford, police said in a statement on Saturday.Lloyd was convicted in 2025 of actual bodily harm, according to the Press Association, relating to an incident in Nottinghamshire involving three emergency services workers.He received a 12-month custodial sentence and wassent to prison. In September he was transferred to the medical facility in Lewisham.The 38-year-old is white and about 5ft 8in, of medium build with short dark hair.He was wearing a grey-blue T-shirt, black tracksuit bottoms and white trainers when last seen at about 4.10pm on Friday, police said.Det supt Melanie Pressley, who is leading the manhunt, said: “We are conducting various significant inquiries to find Lloyd and return him to custody.“We are concerned he poses a risk both to himself and the public, and would urge anyone who sees him to call 999 immediately. Do not approach him.“If you have any information – however small – that could help us locate Lloyd, please get in touch with police as a matter of urgency.”Officers believe Lloyd could be anywhere in the capital. He also has links to Surrey, Sussex, Thames Valley, Hampshire, Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire and Merseyside.Anyone with information is asked to call 999, quoting the reference CAD4739/23Oct.Explore more on these topicsUK newsLondonMetropolitan policenewsShareReuse this content

title: Sam Fender tells fans high ticket prices for Proper Massive tour are ‘getting changed’ | Sam Fender | The Guardian
description: Fender criticises stadium pricing, calling it ‘bollocks’ and says it ‘won’t be happening’ on his tour
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Fender criticises stadium pricing, calling it ‘bollocks’ and says it ‘won’t be happening’ on his tour
Content: Sam Fender said he had no idea how high ticket prices became ‘normalised’.Photograph: Thomas Jackson/AlamyView image in fullscreenSam Fender said he had no idea how high ticket prices became ‘normalised’.Photograph: Thomas Jackson/AlamySam FenderSam Fender tells fans high ticket prices for Proper Massive tour are ‘getting changed’Fender criticises stadium pricing, calling it ‘bollocks’ and says it ‘won’t be happening’ on his tourPriya BharadiaSat 24 Oct 2026 11.29 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 11.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Fender has responded to criticism by fans about ticket prices for his 2027 stadium tour by promising he would lower the cost, telling followers on Instagram: “They’re getting changed.”The 32-year-old musician announced his Proper Massive stadium tour earlier this week.Gavin Davis, an Instagram user, shared details of standing tickets for Fender’s show at Wembley, which were split into “front standing”, costing £130.75, and “standing”, priced at £98.85. Prices for seating ranged between £64.75 and £130.75.Responding to the post, Fender said he was “not happy with these prices”.He said: “It got inflated well more than I’d had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on.”In his reply, Fender also criticised the division of standing tickets into front and back tiers as “bollocks”, saying this “won’t be happening” on his tour.“I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs,” he added.Tickets at other venues were also listed at more than £100, with the highest ticket price in Newcastle at £112.90, in Cardiff £119, and in Edinburgh at £120.95. The top ticket price in Manchester was £119.60.Tickets for the tour are due to go on sale on Friday, with a presale on Wednesday morning.Fender is not the first pop star to criticise ticket prices for his own show. The Swedish pop singerZara Larssonhas also called out steep ticket prices. In a TikTok post in August, she agreed with criticism from fans that ticket prices for her show in Bangkok were “very expensive” and wished to be “more involved” with setting prices.“I hate the fact that people genuinely want to come, but they can’t because of the prices,” Larsson added.View image in fullscreenSam Fender with Olivia Dean after receiving the award for song of the year at the Brit awards in Manchester.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersFender will perform at Newcastle’s St James’s Park, Cardiff’s Principality Stadium, Dublin’s Marley Park, Murrayfield in Edinburgh and the Etihad in Manchester across summer 2027.Earlier this week, Fender also confirmed there would be a fourth album but he has yet to release the title or cover.Fender, who was born in North Shields in Tyne and Wear, is best-known for his hit songs Hypersonic Missiles, Seventeen Going Under and People Watching. He is also the winner of five Brit awards and received the Mercury prize for his 2025 album People Watching.Earlier this year, Fender rerecorded his single Rein Me In asa duetwith the English singer-songwriter Olivia Dean, which won 2026 song of the year at the Brit awards. The song spent 23 overall weeks at No 1 in the singles chart, making it the longest-running No 1 single in British history.Explore more on these topicsSam FenderPop and rockEnglandTicket pricesMusic industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Northern Olympics campaign to get £7m in Healey’s budget | Olympic Games | The Guardian
description: Fund will support feasibility study for potential bid to host Games in 2040s, backed by northern mayors and top athletes
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Fund will support feasibility study for potential bid to host Games in 2040s, backed by northern mayors and top athletes
Content: Laura and Jason Kenny are among the top athletes backing the northern Games campaign.Photograph: David Davies/PAView image in fullscreenLaura and Jason Kenny are among the top athletes backing the northern Games campaign.Photograph: David Davies/PAOlympic GamesNorthern Olympics campaign to get £7m in Healey’s budgetFund will support feasibility study for potential bid to host Games in 2040s, backed by northern mayors and top athletesSammy GecsoylerSat 24 Oct 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 11.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey is to announce a £7m fund to examine a potential future bid to host the Olympics in northern England in his first budget as chancellor.The fund will be used to carry out a full feasibility study for a northern Games, which, if successful, would be held in the north ofEnglandin the 2040s.In May, before Andy Burnham entered No 10, the government commissioned an assessment by UK Sport which could inform a bid for the international sporting event in the 2040s. If the campaign were successful, it would be the first time theOlympic Gamesand Paralympics were hosted in Britain since London 2012.There was further momentum behind the idea in June when mayors from across the north of England met in Sheffield to discuss the possibility of a northern Olympic bid.More than 40 Olympians, Paralympians and elite athletes, including Laura Kenny, Jason Kenny, Sarah Storey, Beth Tweddle and Tom Pidcock, have signed a joint statement “to express our strong and united support” for the idea to hold a “box office Games” in the north of England.Announcing the fund, Burnham said an Olympics bid would “unlock opportunity across our towns and cities” and that “we can put on the greatest show on Earth”.He continued: “Few things bring a country together quite like the Olympics. I want people to feel that sense of excitement again, and to experience it in their own towns and communities, not just watch it on the telly.“The Games would unlock opportunity across our towns and cities for the whole country. From north to south, it would be something everyone could get behind and be proud of.“We know we can put on the greatest show on earth. Now we want to explore how we can do it again, with the whole country behind it.”The full feasibility study will look in greater detail at how the Games would work in practice, including types of venues and transport links needed and the prospects of developing a winning bid. It will also look into how much it could cost and examine the chances of a bid succeeding.View image in fullscreenMo Farah winning the men’s 5000m at the 2012 Olympic Games.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe work will involve the government, UK Sport, the northern mayors and the British Olympic and Paralympic Associations, who would ultimately be responsible for a bid.Healey said: “The north hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable.“Britain’s experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I’m picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious Games.“It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost.”The British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport released a joint statement welcoming the news.“Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements,” they said.Sydney, Tokyo and London are among the mega-cities that have played host to the Olympics in recent years but Brisbane, Australia’s third-largest city, will be hosting the 2032 Games.The Mayor of London Sadiq Khan has previouslycriticisedplans to explore a bid to host the Olympics in northern England, saying that excluding London would be a “missed opportunity”.Explore more on these topicsOlympic GamesNorth of EnglandOlympic legacyJohn HealeyEnglandSport politicsBudgetnewsShareReuse this content

title: Six Flags to reopen Goliath rollercoaster – but now with seatbelts after recent rider death | Georgia | The Guardian
description: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem fell from ride earlier this month, spurring amusement park to temporarily shut it down
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem fell from ride earlier this month, spurring amusement park to temporarily shut it down
Content: The Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia.Photograph: Christopher Oquendo/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia.Photograph: Christopher Oquendo/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockGeorgiaSix Flags to reopen Goliath rollercoaster – but now with seatbelts after recent rider deathHassan Jihad Ibn Kariem fell from ride earlier this month, spurring amusement park to temporarily shut it downUwa Ede-OsifoSat 24 Oct 2026 15.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSix Flags will install seatbelts on its Goliath rollercoaster inGeorgia, after ariderplummeted to his death earlier this month.Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old father and educator, was thrown from his seat on the Goliath, a coaster that plunges riders down 165ft, before a second drop of 180ft. On his way down, he collided with the ride’s other cars.Georgia authorities have launched a probe into Kariem’s death. The gruesome fall prompted the park to temporarily close the Goliath and eight rides at five other parks.Family of US man who died on Six Flags ride question if death was preventableRead more“What happened has deeply affected all of us at Six Flags. Safety has always been fundamental to the experience we provide for our guests,” the theme park’s CEO, John Reilly, wrote on Friday.Seatbelts will also be added to coasters with a similar restraint, he announced, although an exact list remains unclear. The Goliathfeaturesa lap bar that locks over a rider’s waist, a design from Bolliger & Mabillard.The park has also commissioned an independent review of the safety procedures for all of its attractions.“I know trust is earned through actions and not words,” Reilly said. “We will continue to communicate about our progress and hold ourselves accountable to our commitments to you.”The Six Flags Over Georgia fatal incident comes as the theme park is being sued over alleged bodily harm from its X2 ride at Magic Mountain. A recent CNN investigation uncovered a long history of brain injuries and at least two deaths linked to the ride.A group of past riders who say they sustained brain injuries on X2 has accused the park of having a defective coaster and negligence for allowing its continued operation, according to court documents.Six Flags permanently shut down the embattled X2 coaster in September.Explore more on these topicsGeorgiaTheme parksnewsShareReuse this content

title: Additional 178 cases of measles reported by US health authorities amid outbreak | US healthcare | The Guardian
description: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 4,588 cases across the country, more than double the tally in 2025
Author: Jessica Glenza
Headline: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 4,588 cases across the country, more than double the tally in 2025
Content: A vial of the combination measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.Photograph: Matt Rourke/APView image in fullscreenA vial of the combination measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.Photograph: Matt Rourke/APUS healthcareAdditional 178 cases of measles reported by US health authorities amid outbreakCenters for Disease Control and Prevention reported 4,588 cases across the country, more than double the tally in 2025Jessica GlenzaSat 24 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFederal health authorities reported an additional 178 cases of measles in the US this week, as the vaccine-preventable illness continues to sicken people across at least 43 outbreaks.The new data reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) comes as experts criticize the agency for lack of transparency, and as health secretaryRobert F Kennedy Jrtakes steps to further upend US vaccine infrastructure.The CDC reported 4,588 cases of measles across the country in 2026 as of Friday – more than double the tally for 2025. Pennsylvania alone reported 1,338 cases on the same day. The CDC also reported large outbreaks inSouth Carolinaand Utah, both of which are reporting more than 500 cases.CDC denies approval for high-volume measles test, citing ‘other priorities’Read moreIn spite of rising measles numbers, official tallies represent an undercount of the disease. Measles is widely regarded as one of themost contagious diseasesknown to medicine. Its most common symptoms – rash, runny nose, fever and cough – may not immediately send the infected to a doctor.Measles sends one in five unvaccinated people who become infected to the hospital, and one to three people in 1,000 die of disease-related complications. The measles vaccine is97% effectiveat preventing the disease. Vaccineside effectsinclude injection-site soreness and low-grade fever. The measles vaccine has been a focal point of anti-vaccine activism for decades.In Pennsylvania, which has had the worst outbreak in the nation for months, state authorities have reported five measles-associated deaths and are investigating a sixth. The CDC has reported three measles deaths nationally, but hasrefused to saywhere the third death took place, obscuring whether it is counting a death in Pennsylvania or elsewhere.Kennedy reportedly asked senior CDC officials in September to remove a measles death from the official tally after he questioned whether the disease contributed to the death, according toReuters.In addition to criticism of how the CDC has tallied measles deaths, Health and Human Services (HHS) this weekannounced changesto vaccine injury reporting systems. A proposal will allow doctors to bill for reporting suspected vaccine injuries, among other changes.The “vaccine adverse event reporting system”, or VAERS, has been along-time fixationof the anti-vaccine movement. The system has proved useful for researchers tracking rare vaccine safety issues. However, it has also become a source of misinformation for anti-vaccine activists, who point to VAERS to make claims, however unfounded, about safety.All vaccines have risks –a fact acknowledged by vaccinologists. Before Kennedy’s appointment to the health department, an expert panel considered each vaccine change individually to decide whether benefits outweigh risks. Kennedy fired all17 sitting membersof that board. He replaced them with members with whom he ideologically aligned. Acourt blockedthe members’ appointment in March.In his time as secretary, Kennedy also misleadingly claimed children get more than90 vaccine doses;linked vaccines to autismin spite ofextensive evidenceto the contrary; directed the CDC toremove claimsthat vaccines do not cause autism from its website; claimed the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine contains “aborted fetal debris”; and stated thatvitamin A and cod liver oilmay help children with measles, which leading physicians described as misleading.Explore more on these topicsUS healthcareMMRRobert F Kennedy JrHealthSouth CarolinaPennsylvaniaRepublicansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Epstein files take back seat in midterms but experts say issue has not gone away | US politics | The Guardian
description: Other voter concerns have prevailed but return of Congress likely to see renewed focus on late sex offender’s activities
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: Other voter concerns have prevailed but return of Congress likely to see renewed focus on late sex offender’s activities
Content: A protester holds a poster featuring Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein at the Texas state capitol building in Austin on 21 September 2026.Photograph: Rafael Lopez/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA protester holds a poster featuring Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein at the Texas state capitol building in Austin on 21 September 2026.Photograph: Rafael Lopez/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesUS politicsEpstein files take back seat in midterms but experts say issue has not gone awayOther voter concerns have prevailed but return of Congress likely to see renewed focus on late sex offender’s activitiesVictoria BekiempisSat 24 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs US voters head to the polls for crucial and fraught midterm elections, some survivors’ advocates in theJeffrey Epsteininvestigation have expressed concern that the scandal could recede into the background.Political experts believe, however, the Epstein issue is not going away permanently and that many voters can balance day-to-day concerns such as affordability and AI with the scandal involving the late financier and accused sex trafficker whose social circle was widespread among America’s elite.“My greatest concern is not that the public will forget Jeffrey Epstein, but that the politicians and institutions responsible for accountability will use the chaos of world events as an excuse to move on,” said Spencer Kuvin of Goldlaw, who has represented multiple Epstein survivors.Kuvin added: “Wars, economic crises and political controversies may dominate the headlines, but they do not erase the suffering of the victims or the unanswered questions about how Epstein and his powerful associates were allowed to operate for decades.“Justice should not have an expiration date, and it certainly should not be dictated by the news cycle. We cannot allow the Epstein scandal to become yesterday’s news simply because today’s headlines are more urgent.”Epstein’s attorney and accountant accused of ‘facilitating and concealing’ his crimes in lawsuitRead moreKuvin called for the US government to continue releasing Epstein files – which many have said were excluded from allegedly incomplete disclosures – and for Congress to demand accountability.“It has been disappointing to have seen attention diverted from Jeffrey Epstein in the past year,” said Jennifer Freeman of Marsh Law, who represents numerous Epstein survivors in litigation surrounding his sexual abuse of teenage girls.Freeman, however, expressed optimism about the long-term prospects of justice for survivors, saying: “While public attention may have shifted from the Epstein case, given the electoral cycle, I am confident it will command concentration and accountability shortly again.”Freeman noted that she was continuing to pursue a lawsuit against the US government for alleged negligence “in repeatedly, for decades, dropping the ball on investigating and prosecuting Epstein”. She is also litigating a class-action lawsuit against his estate related to his collection and production of child sex abuse images.Political experts said that Epstein might get less attention from campaigning politicians and voters, but that it was probably a temporary dip, not a permanent drop-off.“It really does feel like everything is on fire. I think people can care about several things at once, but what’s directly affecting their lives tends to take priority,” Brittany Martinez, a Republican strategist who works as acting director of Principles First, said. “When they’re worried about gas prices, living costs and whether their government is working for them, that can push Epstein out of the immediate conversation.“I don’t think the questions or the demand for answers have gone away; they’re just competing for attention. So I’d expect to hear less about it for stretches, rather than see it disappear altogether.”“There’s just something every day with Trump,” said Shawn Donahue, clinical associate professor in the University at Buffalo’s department of political science.For Donahue, timing also plays a key role. The US Congress has been in recess and without members on the House floor, so there’s not any discussion of the Epstein Files Transparency Act’s proposed new iteration. This bill, theEpstein Files Transparency Act II, seeks to address what advocates have said are shortfalls in the present EFTA – such as an absence of enforcement mechanisms.“It kind of feels like whenever Congress comes back into session, this probably starts to become more of an issue again, and especially if Democrats are looking at being in control of one or maybe both chambers of Congress,” Donahue said.Should Democrats win the house, as polls project, Donahue expects they will swiftly “put Republicans on the spot” with Epstein. “Democrats are ready to start on the investigation from day one.”For Julie Roginsky, who co-founded the non-profitLift Our Voicesand pursued a sexual harassment lawsuit against the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes, the significance of Epstein among voters has not gone away.“I think Epstein is part of the reason that Trump’s numbers are atrecord lows. I think it’s something that was one of the issues where even Maga Republicans broke with him,” Roginsky said. “I think that if Democrats do get control of at least one house of Congress this year, then starting next year, you’re going to see a lot more conversation about survivors and about Epstein.”Congressional supporters of survivors said they would keep fighting for truth and justice.“This is bigger than a moment. It’s a reckoning, and Americans are ready to have this conversation about power, abuse, and who gets protected,” the Democratic New Mexico representative Teresa Leger Fernández said in a statement. “Of course, Americans will vote with their pocketbooks. They’re worried about groceries, gas, and making rent. But they won’t forget that this president was Epstein’s friend and tried to hide the truth from them.“The survivors have fought for decades to be heard. Our responsibility is to keep fighting alongside them, get the truth out, and hold those responsible accountable. That responsibility doesn’t disappear when the headlines change.”The Massachusetts Democratic representative Ayanna Pressley said in a statement: “Justice for survivors of Epstein’s abuse has been a prominent issue amongst the electorate because people of conscience see through the cover-ups of the Trump Administration and demand accountability – that won’t change no matter how much they try to flood the zone and distract us.”Pressley and fellow representatives Leger Fernández and Deborah Ross recentlyintroduced legislationto address survivors’ financial burdens.The New Mexico Democratic senator Ben Ray Luján similarly commented that whatever might be unfolding, he would keep pushing for the files to be released in full despite the Department of Justice insisting they have released all Epstein investigative files required under the law.“We cannot lose sight of the need to release the full Epstein files, hold those responsible accountable, and ensure survivors receive the justice they deserve,” Luján said.Asked for comment, the White House insisted Trump had advocated for survivors.“Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein. And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him,” the White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement.The statement then claimed that several Democrats had yet to explain why they were soliciting money and meetings from Epstein after he was a convicted sex offender.As for the Department of Justice, the department maintains they have complied with disclosure requirements under the original EFTA. They also rejectedclaimsby New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, that the justice department had not been helping the state’s investigation.“The Epstein Files Transparency Act does not require, and the protective orders in place in the Southern District of New York do not permit, disclosure of victim-identifying information carte blanche, and New Mexico has provided no lawful basis to justify such sweeping disclosures,” the department said in a statement. “Protecting victim privacy remains a top priority for the Department, and neither [legal] requests nor a desire to cooperate outweighs that privacy. DOJ remains available to assist New Mexico’s investigation consistent with the law and binding court orders.”Explore more on these topicsUS politicsJeffrey EpsteinUS midterm elections 2026Trump administrationUS CongressnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kimi Antonelli seizes F1 US GP pole and chance to seal first world title | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Kimi Antonelli claimed pole position for the US Grand Prix with a hugely impressive lap at the Circuit of the Americas as he closes in on a first world title
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Kimi Antonelli claimed pole position for the US Grand Prix with a hugely impressive lap at the Circuit of the Americas as he closes in on a first world title
Content: Kimi Antonelli celebrates pole as he edges closer to his first world championship title.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli celebrates pole as he edges closer to his first world championship title.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAFormula One 2026Kimi Antonelli seizes F1 US GP pole and chance to seal first world titleAntonelli has 102-point lead over George RussellNeeds to be 125 points in front after Sunday’s raceGiles Richardsat the Circuit of the AmericasSat 24 Oct 2026 18.52 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 19.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKimi Antonelli claimed pole position for the US Grand Prix with a hugely impressive lap for Mercedes at the Circuit of the Americas. In beating Red Bull’s Max Verstappen into second place, Antonelli did exactly what was required to give him the chance to close out his first world championship title this weekend.Isack Hadjar did well to secure third for Red Bull, with Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton in fourth and fifth for Ferrari, and Antonelli’s Mercedes teammate George Russell in sixth.United States Grand Prix: Kimi Antonelli takes pole – liveRead moreAntonelli’s first pole since the Belgian GP in July could not have been better timed as he attempts to take his first title. The Italian has a 102-point lead over Russell and needs to be 125 points in front after this race. To take the title he must win on Sunday and have Russell finish outside the top eight, with Hamilton outside the top four. The win certainly looks to be a strong prospect but he still needs his rivals to stumble on Sunday.He can only do his best and knows that even should the title not be secured here, on this form it will surely be done and dusted by the next round in Mexico.“We got pole, so we’ll try to win tomorrow,” Antonelli said. “Max has been very quick and did an incredible job in qualifying so it’s not going to be easy. Hopefully we’ll be leading into turn one and we’ll try to set the pace, even though it’s going to be very tight. Very happy with qualifying today, Q3 was very tough with the wind, gusty, unpredictable but happy to stick it on pole.”It is another striking achievement from the Italian, not least because the Mercedes upgrades applied in Malaysia have made the car more of a handful to drive. Indeed, Russell was a full four-tenths off his teammate, and it was a strong return to form for Antonelli as he looks to become the youngest F1 world champion at just 20 years old.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli has a 102-point lead over George Russell.Photograph: Kaylee Greenlee/ReutersHe was flawless for the lap that proved unbeatable in the Texas sunshine but it was a performance by which Mercedes, too, will be buoyed given they were hoping to extract the maximum from their recent upgrades which had not delivered as expected on their opening salvos in Malaysia and Singapore. With the team having found a way to exploit them, Antonelli gave a reminder of just what a formidable opponent he is.His engineer, Pete Bonnington, admitted it was somewhat unexpected given both the team’s work on their upgrades and the form of the recently resurgent Red Bull, with Verstappen taking pole and the win at the last two rounds. A sentiment echoed by the beaming Antonelli.“It was unexpected, we felt it would be close but it was a good surprise,” he said. “I am happy because we have been working very hard on this package and since Singapore we have taken a big step further. The team have done a tremendous job and finally we are seeing the results.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor the first runs in Q3 in what had been a tightly contested session, with both Red Bull and Ferrari looking to be very much in the mix, it was Antonelli who set the pace. He put in a blistering lap with a time of 1minute 34.035seconds, almost two-tenths up on Verstappen, with the Italian hooking up what was one of his very best laps of the weekend.On the final runs Verstappen gave his all but could not improve and, although Antonelli too could not go quicker, he had done enough. His time was not bettered and a somewhat unexpected pole was secured with no little style. “Yes man, it’s good to be back,” he said.For Antonelli, in a season of milestones, including eight wins, his first pole in Austin is his seventh of the season and the first for Mercedes here since Valtteri Bottas last took the top spot in 2019, from which he went on to win – a feat Antonelli will hope to emulate.The Italian looked very much at his best and has given himself the chance to potentially finish the job. But as Verstappen observed, if not here on Sunday, then at the next round or the round after. The hard yards are over.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Kimi AntonelliMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Valkyries hold off Dream comeback to win Game 4 and level WNBA finals at 2-2 | WNBA | The Guardian
description: Golden State squander most of a 16-point lead but survive Atlanta’s second-half fightback to level the best-of-seven championship series at 2-2
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Golden State squander most of a 16-point lead but survive Atlanta’s second-half fightback to level the best-of-seven championship series at 2-2
Content: Valkyries guard Gabby Williams shoots over Dream guard Jordin Canada during the third quarter of Game 4 of the WNBA finals on Saturday at State Farm Arena in Atlanta.Photograph: Kevin C Cox/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenValkyries guard Gabby Williams shoots over Dream guard Jordin Canada during the third quarter of Game 4 of the WNBA finals on Saturday at State Farm Arena in Atlanta.Photograph: Kevin C Cox/Getty ImagesWNBAValkyries hold off Dream comeback to win Game 4 and level WNBA finals at 2-2Gabby Williams leads Golden State with 17 pointsValkyries survive late rally after leading by 16Angel Reese held to eight points as series heads westAgenciesSat 24 Oct 2026 15.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGabby Williams scored 17 points and Golden State played stellar defense to beat theAtlanta Dream67-62 on Saturday and even the WNBA finals at 2-2.The best-of-seven series moves back to California on Monday for Game 5.The Valkyries stymied Atlanta starAngel Reese, holding her to just eight points. She had dominated the previous two games, averaging 25.5 points and 14 rebounds in the Dream victories. Reese struggled in Game 4, missing 10 of her 12 shots, including a few layups in the fourth quarter, after having double-doubles in each of the first three games.Quick GuideWNBA finals 2026ShowScheduleBest-of-seven series. All times Eastern.Sat 17 OctGame 1:Golden State 68, Atlanta 64Mon 19 OctGame 2:Atlanta 79, Golden State 65Wed 21 OctGame 3:Atlanta 97, Golden State 71Sat 24 OctGame 4:Golden State 67, Atlanta 62Mon 26 OctGame 5: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm (USA/CNBC)Thu 29 OctGame 6: Golden State at Atlanta, 8pm (USA/CNBC)Sat 31 OctGame 7: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm* (USA/CNBC)*-if necessaryHow to watchIn the US, the series will air on NBC, USA Network and CNBC, with all games streaming on Peacock. In the UK, it will be carried by Sky Sports. In Australia, fans can watch through WNBA League Pass, with selected coverage also available through ESPN.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Atlanta trimmed a 16-point halftime deficit to 61-55 midway through the fourth quarter, bringing fans in the sellout crowd of over 17,000 to their feet. Golden State answered with a three-pointer by Veronica Burton to briefly silence them.The Dream then scored seven of the next nine points, including a three-point play by Rhyne Howard with 28 seconds left to get within 66-62.Burton then made the first of two free throws a second later and Atlanta couldn’t convert on the other end.Howard finished with 19 points for Atlanta, who shot just 33.3% overall and four for 23 from three-point range.Golden State players had said betweenthe 26-point Game 3 lossand Game 4 that they were confident they could win on Saturday and just needed to be more physical and play harder. They showed that grit on both ends of the court.Defensively, they challenged Atlanta shots led by Kiah Stokes and limited the Dream to few second-chance opportunities. Stokes finished with three blocks and now has aWNBAfinals record of 14 in the four games, surpassing the old record of 12 by Brittney Griner and Sylvia Fowles.View image in fullscreenAtlanta’s Angel Reese shoots over Golden State’s Kiah Stokes and Veronica Burton during the fourth quarter of Game 4 of the WNBA finals on Saturday at State Farm Arena in Atlanta.Photograph: Colin Hubbard/Getty ImagesOffensively, they limited turnovers, which had led to easy points for Atlanta in their two victories. The Valkyries also crashed the offensive boards, rebounding their own misses to give themselves more chances to score. Stokes had eight offensive rebounds of her 16 total.Coach Natalie Nakase also made a change in the starting lineup, inserting Tiffany Hayes and Kaila Charles for Kayla Thornton and Cecilia Zandalasini. While the Valkyries got off to a slow start again in the early afternoon tip-off with the Atlanta Hawks playing their home opener at night, when Thornton and Zandalasini entered the game they paid immediate dividends.The two helped a key first-quarter run that gave Golden State their first lead since the third quarter of Game 2. Atlanta got within 24-20 on Reese’s basket – her lone one of the first half – but the Valkyries responded with an 18-6 run to close the half.The 42-26 deficit at the break was the largest that the Dream had faced all play-offs.Atlanta had dominated the third quarter in the WNBA finals, outscoring Golden State 60-35 in the first three games. The Valkyries wouldn’t let them do that in Game 4.Explore more on these topicsWNBAGolden State ValkyriesAtlanta DreamBasketballAngel ReeseShareReuse this content

title: The World Series of the have-nots is here. But baseball’s money problem isn’t going away | World Series | The Guardian
description: Baseball’s two best regular-season teams are also among its lowest spenders. But their unlikely World Series comes with a warning about the sport’s future
Author: Tom Dart
Headline: Baseball’s two best regular-season teams are also among its lowest spenders. But their unlikely World Series comes with a warning about the sport’s future
Content: Milwaukee pitcher Jacob Misiorowski delivers against Tampa Bay during Game 1 of the World Series at American Family Field on Friday night.Photograph: Rob Tringali/MLB Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMilwaukee pitcher Jacob Misiorowski delivers against Tampa Bay during Game 1 of the World Series at American Family Field on Friday night.Photograph: Rob Tringali/MLB Photos/Getty ImagesWorld SeriesThe World Series of the have-nots is here. But baseball’s money problem isn’t going awayBaseball’s two best regular-season teams are also among its lowest spenders. But their unlikely World Series comes with a warning about the sport’s futureTom DartSat 24 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe best pitcher in baseball led the best team to victory over the second-best team? Weird.A World Series that makes the logical feel novel began on Friday as the Milwaukee Brewersbeat the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 in Game 1. Of course the Brewers, with their MLB-topping 103 regular-season victories, should be facing the 98-win Rays on the grandest stage. But of course, since these are two of the smallest and lowest-budget franchises in the sport, they shouldn’t.That this best-of-seven title decider is at once a shocking cold shower and a comforting warm bath is largely explained by the absence of the two-time defending champions, the Los Angeles Dodgers, whowere swept 4-0 by the Brewersin the National League Championship Series.Quick GuideWorld Series 2026ShowScheduleBest-of-seven series. All times US Eastern Daylight Time (EDT).Fri 23 OctGame 1:Milwaukee 3, Tampa Bay 2Sat 24 OctGame 2: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8pm (Fox)Mon 26 OctGame 3: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8pm (Fox)Tue 27 OctGame 4: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8pm (Fox)Wed 28 OctGame 5: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8pm* (Fox)Fri 30 OctGame 6: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8pm* (Fox)Sat 31 OctGame 7: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8pm* (Fox)*-if necessaryHow to watchIn the US, all World Series games will air on Fox and Fox Deportes, with streaming available through Fox One. In the UK, the series will be carried by TNT Sports. In Australia, fans can watch on ESPN, with streaming available through Disney+ and Kayo Sports.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.That was a philosophical battle with a drop-mic ending: the revenge of the nerds. Analytics over affluence, a triumph for the teams who scrimp and strategize rather than simply lobbing money at the best free agents each offseason.The Dodgers have parlayedfinancial dominanceinto winning the National League West division in 13 of the past 14 years. At the start of this season there was every reason to expect they would win their third World Series in succession. But instead of spending this title fight lamenting the Dodgers’ dominance and fretting that money has made baseball dull and dynastic, we have the first match-up in 46 years – and second since 1920 – between two teams that have never won a World Series.A country where the world’s richest person has reportedly made political donationsin excess of $442min this election cycle is culturally conditioned to believe that wealth wins. Yet baseball is, after all, still a sport where the won-lost standings and thesalary trackerare not fully interchangeable.View image in fullscreenBrewers pitcher Jacob Misiorowski delivers against the Rays during Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night.Photograph: Jamie Squire/Getty ImagesHere are successful teams, boasting talents as luminous as Rays third baseman Junior Caminero and Brewers catcher William Contreras, withpayrollsless than half the size of the most lavish spenders. Milwaukee’s annual outlay ($146m according to Spotrac) ranks 19th in the 30-team league with Tampa Bay ($96m) in 28th position. And the Rays reached this point by beating the Cleveland Guardians, who have MLB’s smallest payroll, in the American League Championship Series.Only the Dodgers, Brewers, Atlanta Braves and New York Yankees have more regular-season wins in the2020sthan the Rays, who are in their third World Series. Tampa Bay, founded as an expansion franchise in 1998, reached the final in 2008 (where they lost to the Philadelphia Phillies) and in the Covid-wracked 2020 season,losing to the Dodgersat the makeshift site of Globe Life Field in Texas.The Brewers’ only otherWorld Seriesappearance was a loss to the St Louis Cardinals in 1982. Though there are suspicions that national television audiences will be meager for a series between small-market teams lacking superstars, the games in Milwaukee are some of the hottest tickets in World Series history. On one resale site the asking price for standing-room only tickets to Saturday’s Game 2 in Milwaukee was north of $3,000.The first clash held moderate value for the neutral spectator. It was a night with a fast start, a false finish and some messy, unmemorable baseball in the middle. Where ordinary pitchers throw fastballs, Jacob Misiorowski, MLB’s strikeout leader in the regular season, hurlsfireballs. Pitching on 11 days’ rest, the 24-year-old started his night with the quickest pitch ever recorded in a World Series, a 103.5mph screamer to leadoff hitter Yandy Díaz.View image in fullscreenFans fill American Family Field in Milwaukee before Friday night’s World Series opener between the Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays. The matchup marks the first World Series in 46 years between two franchises that have never won the title.Photograph: Jamie Squire/Getty ImagesMisiorowski surrendered one run in five innings’ of work. “Not perfect, but good enough to get a win,”he said. Milwaukee led 3-1 after the seventh but Tampa Bay mounted a late rally, scoring a run in the ninth to induce a tense, if gauche, finish. The visitors loaded the bases but catcher Liam Hicks appeared to hit into a game-ending double play. The Brewers celebrated but the fireworks and high-fives were premature.The Rays challenged the decision, which was overturned on review. This confirmed that shortstop Cooper Pratt had taken his foot off second base too early as he threw to first, and also that Milwaukee fans can boo almost as loudly as they cheer.Still, there was more than enough air left in the lungs of the fans at American Family Field to reboot the celebrations after the teams returned to the field and closer Trevor Megill struck out outfielder Jonny DeLuca for the win, for real. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after. You know, you kind of have that emotional dump and then you have to get back on it.” Brewers slugger Christian Yelich told Fox Sports.
