title: Championship roundup: Southampton beat West Ham; QPR put five past Swansea | Championship | The Guardian
description: Southampton announced themselves in the promotion race with a statement 3-2 win at West Ham, QPR thrashed high-flying Swansea, and Burnley’s latest defeat led to the sacking of manager Nicky Hayen
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Southampton announced themselves in the promotion race with a statement 3-2 win at West Ham, QPR thrashed high-flying Swansea, and Burnley’s latest defeat led to the sacking of manager Nicky Hayen
Content: Kuryu Matsuki (left) celebrates putting Southampton ahead against West Ham.Photograph: Steven Paston/PAView image in fullscreenKuryu Matsuki (left) celebrates putting Southampton ahead against West Ham.Photograph: Steven Paston/PAChampionshipChampionship roundup: Southampton beat West Ham; QPR put five past SwanseaHammers humbled at home; Swansea thrashed 5-0Burnley sack manager Hayen after 4-1 loss at LincolnPress AssociationSat 24 Oct 2026 14.11 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 10.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouthamptonannounced themselves in the promotion race with a statement 3-2 win at the pre-season title favourites,West Ham. Kuryu Matsuki, James Bree and Lewis Dobbin were all on target in a chaotic first half, while Kyle Walker-Peters and Tomas Soucek replied for the Hammers.Burnley sack Nicky Hayen after Lincoln rout leaves them in bottom threeRead moreNuno Espírito Santo’s side would have gone top with a win but instead saw their nine-match unbeaten run halted. There were thousands of empty seats by the end at the London Stadium, with those who stayed booing the Hammers off. Southampton, deducted four points at the start of the season, are now just two points behind West Ham.“We started not the way we wanted,” said Nuno. “We were looking at the situations with hesitation, bouncing balls, too many chances for Southampton to have a second phase, third phase and achieve a goal. But the reaction was good in the second half. The boys fought until the end.”Richard Kone made an emphatic return to form by scoring a hat-trick inside 15 minutes asQPRthrashed high-flyingSwansea5-0 at Loftus Road. Jimmy Dunne struck twice for Rangers, who were four up at half-time, as the Swans – who were top of theChampionshipuntil Friday night – suffered their second defeat in a row. The Welsh side remain second in the table, while QPR’s resounding victory moved them back into the playoff positions in eighth.View image in fullscreenRichard Kone reacts after putting QPR ahead against Swansea.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PANicky Hayen’s spell asBurnleymanager was brought to an end after his side slumped to a 4-1 defeat atLincoln.Burnleywent in front through Andréas Hountondji but Ben House equalised on the stroke of half-time. Hayen’s side then fell apart in the second half, with Mikkel Ladefoged scoring twice, either side of a goal from Dom Jefferies. With their team in the bottom three, Burnley fans targeted Hayen and the board with banners and chants.Beforehis dismissal was announced by the club, Hayen said: “It’s frustrating for everyone, especially the fans. I want to apologise to them, but I know it doesn’t matter because it’s another hard defeat for them and I can understand their criticism. I will keep on working hard as long as I have the chance.”Adam Armstrong ended his goal drought with a milestone strike to give dominantWolvesa 1-0 win againstWatfordat Molineux. The 29-year-old striker, returning after a back injury, scored only his second league goal of the season, while it was his first Championship home goal for Wolves, all on his 450th league appearance.Wolves, though, failed to turn their overwhelming superiority into goals, and the unease around Molineux was evident when the 78th-minute double substitution of Tommy Doyle and Tawanda Chirewa for Jordan James and Armstrong was met with chants of “you don’t know what you’re doing” aimed at the head coach, César Peixoto.Quick GuideLeague One roundup: Huddersfield top; Foxes lose againShowHuddersfieldwent top of League One after their 2-1 win over bottom sideWiganin the early game was followed by Stockport dropping points. Ilias Bronkhorst and Derensili Sanches Fernandes scored for the Terriers in the first half, with Christian Saydee’s consolation coming in added time.AlthoughStockportsecured a 1-1 draw atNotts Countyafter Adama Sidibeh’s 81st-minute equaliser cancelled out Scott Robertson’s opener, it was not enough to return them to the top.Plymouthmoved into fourth, just a point behind Stockport, with a 3-2 win seeing them leapfrog hostsCambridgeafter Louis Appere’s own goal was followed by strikes from Xavier Amaechi and Aribim Pepple.Leicesterdramatically fell to their fourth defeat of the season to increase pressure on manager Russell Martin.Luton’sCallum Marshall scored deep into added time after Liam Cullen had levelled in the 90th minute, just after Leicester’s John Lundstram was sent off for a second yellow card following Nahki Wells’ first-half opener.Martin said: “We did so well to get ourselves back in the game with 10 men, it’s so disappointing. Within a couple of minutes, the feeling can be so different. It can feel like a win almost, down to 10 men, a battling draw, brilliant goal and then we concede a goal and it’s frustration. It was the only time they entered our box really, and we gave a goal away. We gave away two poor goals today and that’s frustration.”Doncaster’sOwen Bailey scored twice in the first 14 minutes to win the South Yorkshire derby 2-0 againstSheffield Wednesday.Press AssociationWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The substitute Aune Heggebo struck late forWest Bromto denyPrestona first win under Graham Alexander in a 1-1 draw at a wind-swept Deepdale. The Norwegian came off the bench on the hour and rifled home an 82nd-minute leveller just four minutes after Andrew Hughes hooked North End into the lead from a corner.CardiffhaltedBirmingham’swinning run as Yousef Salech secured a 1-0 victory to continue the Bluebirds’ climb up the table. Salech was named among the home substitutes initially, but the defender Krystian Bielik suffered an injury in the warm-up and had to drop out on an afternoon of relentless rain in the Welsh capital. Cardiff have now recorded three straight home wins as they continue to show real signs of adapting to life in the second tier following promotion from League One.Andri Gudjohnsen’s second double in a week earnedBlackburna clinical 2-0 win overWrexham. The Icelandic striker’s return from injury has coincided with an upturn in Rovers’ results as goals in each half delivered a third win in five games that moves Tony Mowbray’s side to within two points of the playoff spots.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAndri Gudjohnsen puts Blackburn ahead against Wrexham at Ewood Park.Photograph: Nigel French/PAChris Wilder was critical of hisSheffield Unitedside’s “annoying” first-half performance after they had to settle for a point from a 1-1 draw with struggling Derby. Bobby Clark gave the Rams a first-half lead with Patrick Bamford equalising in the closing stages, whileDerbyhad Dion Sanderson sent off in the 66th minute after he received a second booking. Wilder said: “We gave them the game that they wanted. Everybody’s brother was playing first half apart from Kalvin [Phillips] and Coops [Michael Cooper].”John Mousinho admittedPortsmouthdid not deserve to win after coming from behind to beatMillwall2-1 in a game of freak goals at a blustery Fratton Park. Jenson Metcalfe put Millwall ahead on six minutes after a calamitous pass forward from the Pompey goalkeeper, Nicolas Schmid, and, 10 minutes later, Lyndon Dykes turned the ball into his own net for 1-1. Then, eight minutes from time, an attempted clearance from Millwall’s captain, Jake Cooper, ricocheted off the substitute Thomas Waddingham and into the net for the winner.Quick GuideLeague Two roundup: Barnet held; Cheltenham go thirdShowBarnetmissed the chance to cut the gap to League Two leaders Salford to a point afterOldham’sMike Fondop’s header in the fourth minute of added time cancelled out Kabongo Tshimanga’s opener in a 1-1 draw.Cheltenhammoved into third, a point behind the Bees, with Charlie McCann’s fifth-minute goal enough to endNewport’snine-game unbeaten run.Rotherhammoved out of the bottom two in an incident-packed 3-3 draw after playing over an hour with 10 men against aShrewsburyside who also had Kian McMahon-Brown sent off late on. Paul Mullin scored twice before Kian Spence was shown a red card, allowing Josh Davison, Josh Ruffels and Will Boyle to put the visitors ahead with 23 minutes remaining. However, substitute Tom Bradshaw scored the Millers’ third before Brown was dismissed for an off-the-ball incident with Joe Rafferty.Press AssociationWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“This is the first time this season we’ve got away with one,” said Mousinho. “We were lucky to nick the win off a poor start to the second half and the defending in the first half. But we stuck in it and did everything else really well.”Philippe Clement saluted the never-say-die attitude of hisNorwichplayers after a 3-1 comeback win atCharlton. The Canaries, on a run of six straight defeats in league and cup heading to the Valley, fell behind to a Charlie Kelman goal. But Paris Maghoma equalised and Mathias Kvistgaarden fired them ahead, before Ivan Mesik’s own goal completed the turnaround.StokeandBristol Cityplayed out a 0-0 draw in wet and windy conditions, while on Friday, Will Lankshear scored twice as aMiddlesbroughbatteredBolton5-1. Aidan Morris, in-form Lankshear and a Lewis Brunt own goal before half-time set the Teessiders on the way to a 10th successive win over their hosts in a run stretching back to 2014.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipCharlton AthleticNorwich CityPortsmouthMillwallSheffield UnitedDerby CountynewsShareReuse this content

title: The sexual assault scandal rocked gymnastics – but has pace of change in the sport been too slow? | Gymnastics | The Guardian
description: Former USA team doctor Larry Nassar’s 2018 conviction sparked a global reckoning in gymnastics, yet gymnasts say they are still being let down
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Former USA team doctor Larry Nassar’s 2018 conviction sparked a global reckoning in gymnastics, yet gymnasts say they are still being let down
Content: Simone Biles, Aly Raisman and Maggie Nichols are among many to have suffered abuse in the scandal that rocked gymnastics.Composite: Guardian Pictures; NurPhoto/Getty Images; Getty Images; Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSimone Biles, Aly Raisman and Maggie Nichols are among many to have suffered abuse in the scandal that rocked gymnastics.Composite: Guardian Pictures; NurPhoto/Getty Images; Getty Images; Corbis/Getty ImagesGymnasticsThe sexual assault scandal rocked gymnastics – but has pace of change in the sport been too slow?Former USA team doctor Larry Nassar’s 2018 conviction sparked a global reckoning in gymnastics, yet gymnasts say they are still being let downSuzanne Wrackin RotterdamSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 10.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been 10 years since the Indianapolis Star published allegations of sexual abuse by Larry Nassar, the former team doctor for USAGymnastics, setting off a chain of events that would lead to a reckoning for the sport. Hundreds of women came forward with their own allegations against Nassar, who also worked at Michigan State University, leading to his conviction and jailing.The exposure of his crimes sparked a wider investigation into how gymnastics had allowed predators to abuse young athletes around the world. While Nassar was the worst recorded case, it emerged many other countries had questions to answer about the failure to protect victims from not only sexual but physical and emotional abuse. But a decade later, on a large houseboat moored in Rotterdam three tram stops away from the Ahoy Arena, where the World Gymnastics Championships are taking place this week, survivors and advocates raised fears about the slow pace of change.The impact of the Nassar case was seismic, not least because of the decision of Judge Rosemarie Aquilina, on agreeing to Nassar’s plea deal, to allow his victims to have their say in her courtroom. People tuned into Aquilina’s courtroom from all over the world to watch as 169 people took to the stand across seven days, delivering blistering, emotionally charged and brave testimonies of Nassar’s abuse and the impact of that abuse. Aquilina sentenced him to up to 175 years in jail with other convictions, federal and state, making a total of 300 years to life.“I know, dealing with so many victims, that when they speak publicly you see them shed their pain and get taller. You see them have a relief, an automatic release,”says Aquilina, perched on a seat in the helm of the boat. “The most interesting thing was that at first I had a list of maybe a dozen names who wanted to speak, then it was 20, then it was 30, and then it got up to 80, 100, etc.View image in fullscreenJudge Rosemarie Aquilina (left) looks at Larry Nassar as he listens to Jennifer Rood Bedford’s victim’s impact statement.Photograph: Scott Olson/Getty Images“What happened was that one girl empowered the next, who empowered the next. It was the beginning of their healing because they felt finally heard and believed, in a safe space, and they got to tell him to his face, eyeball to eyeball: ‘You hurt me. I am not a number, I am a name, how dare you?’”“Nassar constantly wanted control. He wanted to continue to control me, to control the girls, and to say: ‘Look what I’ve done. I took the plea for you’. That was constant … Did he deserve my respect? No. Did he give me respect? No. Did he give any of the victims respect? No. He never owned it. That infuriated me. It should infuriate everyone.”‘Money and medals over safety’: Nassar judge warns gymnasts are still being failedRead moreAmong the victimsmotivated to speak after hearing others’ statements was the Olympic gold medallist Aly Raisman, who was excoriating in blaming USA Gymnastics for enabling Nassar. She was joined by fellow gold medallist Jordyn Wieber, Olympic bronze medallist Jamie Dantzscher and former US national champion Mattie Larson.The mother of the athlete who first complained about Nassar, Maggie Nichols, read out a powerful statement on her behalf.Simone Biles, the most famous gymnast of her generation, revealed she was a victim on social media and later testified publicly in front of the US Senate Judiciary Committee.Two years after Nassar’s sentencing, a documentary film named after Nichols, called Athlete A, was released, shining a spotlight on the traditional coaching system of compliance, fear and silence and how it allowed Nassar to operate. The documentary opened the global floodgates.Kim Shore, who was a gymnast in Canada in the 1980s and “experienced all forms of abuse, but also all forms of joy”, was then on the board of directors of Gymnastics Canada, the national governing body, after stepping into governance when her own experiences and direct intervention had failed to prevent the cycle of mistreatment repeating with a family member.“I absolutely love the sport. I love how it feels in my body. I love so many aspects of it. And yet I spent most of my time surviving it,” she says.View image in fullscreenMaggie Nichols performs an uneven bars routine in the documentary Athlete A.Photograph: NetflixShore, who is an independent safe sport advocate, says of the impact of the Nassar case: “I was floored, understanding: ‘OK, I wasn’t a bad kid, I wasn’t a bad gymnast, this is why I was treated that way, it’s endemic.’”Yet the reaction from the organisation was “absolutely lacking”, says Shore. “I remember I sat and watched those girls tell their story in the courtroom and I just bawled. I encouraged the board members that I was associated with to watch it as well.” She does not believe any of them did.Eloise Jotischky, 23,who in 2022 won the first civil case against British Gymnastics for the abuses she suffered in the sport, says the impact of the film was being able “to articulate what you’ve been through and find the terms to understand and talk about your experience”.“It’s very hard to explain it to people who are not within that culture, that sport,” she says. “The only way I can really describe it is that it’s sort of like a cult in a lot of ways. It’s a very closed system, you’re very isolated, in a lot of cases you’re pulled out of school, you’re removed from your friends, you’re travelling to competitions all the time and you’re deprived of a normal social life. I’d say it’s very similar to a coercively controlling relationship in a domestic setting, there’s a lot of parallels there, but you’re a child, so there’s the duty of care issue as well.”Gymnastics’ ongoing reckoning: inside fight for survivor-led reform 10 years on from Nasser caseJotischky stopped training at 14. “By the end, it wasn’t joyous. I think I hated it. You just blame yourself and you think that you’re the problem, until Athlete A comes out. That was about sexual abuse, but the underlying themes of Athlete A are about the physical and emotional abuse, the non-contact physical abuse, which made it get to that point. That’s what all resonated.”At the same time, the life of former British gymnast and athlete Claire Heafford was in transition. She was splitting from her husband, leaving her dream job and taking up wrestling. “Those major changes were partly taking place because I hadn’t yet realised I’d been so badly abused and that I had some psychiatric issues,” she says.“I got into professional wrestling when I saw it and felt very drawn to it. I didn’t really understand why, but it’s a performance art that is largely about the performance of masculinity and the violence is clear and obvious. I was really attracted to that being the inverse of my own experiences. I couldn’t understand that at the time. I was like: ‘I’ve gone mad, I’m 36, I’m learning to be a Mexican wrestler. I’m splitting up with my husband. What the fuck’s gone wrong in my life?’“It was only when Athlete A came out that the penny dropped.”The documentary made Heafford want to act; she decided to set up Gymnasts for Change, an alliance to bring about safer sport. As the head of Gymnasts for Change International, she brought together the advocates and survivors in Rotterdam.“Athlete A was seismic. It came out just as Me Too had started,” she says. “On the one hand, Athlete A showed how awful the sexual abuse was and on the other it demonstrated to everybody in the world that gymnastics was a coercively controlling environment built on control and power. It showed that was just what the sport was, that everybody in it had experienced it and that they almost believed that it was necessary.”View image in fullscreenClaire Heafford, who founded Gymnasts for Change, brought together advocates and survivors in Rotterdam.Photograph: ITVThe Nassar case triggered a series of reports and new measures in the US including the FBI acknowledging its handling of the case was “inexcusable” and Congress establishing the US Center for SafeSport. That organisation has since faced heavy criticism. USAG went through four presidents in less than two years, said it would adopt 70 of the recommendations in an independent report into preventing sexual abuse and set up an Athlete Bill of Rights. USAG now says athlete safety has been its “top priority since establishing a new board of directors and leadership team in 2018-2019”. It emphasises that “a culture of safety is something that has to be worked on every day, at every level”, requiring all adult USAG members to be trained in safeguarding. Eight members of the board are former elite athletes and one seat is dedicated to that of a survivor.The case also inspired athletes around the world to speak up about their own experiences of abuse, including in Australia, Brazil and Britain. In Britain, an independent review led by Anne Whyte QC found that physical and emotional abuse were systemic, leading British Gymnastics to launch a 40-point plan aimed at changing the sport. That included a zero tolerance approach to abuse and a gymnast-coach led environment where “both feel empowered to create safe, positive and fair experiences at every level”.Such an environment is something Aimee Boorman, who is Simone Biles’ former coach, has spent her career advocating for. Boorman channelled her anger at her own experience of negative coaching as a child gymnast into her coaching philosophy. “I knew that I never wanted to make another child feel the way that I felt as a child. So, that was the basis of everything,” she says. “So many times I was told that I wouldn’t be successful because I was too nice. I was like: ‘Well, then I guess I’m not going to be successful by your metrics, your standard, your qualifier for success’. For me, success is having happy, healthy athletes who want to put their children in gymnastics because they have such a good experience.View image in fullscreenOlympic gymnast Jamie Dantzscher (left) sits alongside Jordyn Wieber as she testifies at a Senate hearing.Photograph: Aaron P Bernstein/Reuters“Then, I went from being too nice to just being lucky that I had Simone, she’s successful and I’m successful because I was lucky that I had her. No, the reality is that Simone never would have gotten to where Simone is without the training she had from me and the other coaches that she had growing up. So, I’ve just had to hold on to my core beliefs.”Across Europe, too, gymnasts have spoken out to force change. Former Dutch gymnast Petra Witjes and Germany’s Adina Hausch document falling out of love with the sport because of their experiences.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“At the elite club in the city I moved to it wasn’t fun anymore,” says Witjes, whose book, Silenced for Gold, is a memoir about the systemic abuses within sport and her battle to expose it. “My dad taught me to let my voice be heard but in the gym it was the opposite.”View image in fullscreenCoach Aimee Boorman watches as Simone Biles (left) trains. Boorman has spent her career advocating for a gymnast-coach led environment.Photograph: Smiley N Pool/Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesWitjes was terrified of speaking to her parents, she was taught not to trust them. “I didn’t feel safe at first, because my coach always said that parents don’t understand elite gymnastics,” she says. “They push your parents away from you. We were in total isolation.”Hausch says an injury that forced her from the sport was a relief. “I was on beam and I slipped with one leg and fell with the other on to the beam and then crashed down,” she says. “The leg was pushed sideways so much that it broke. From the age of 13 I don’t think there was a week without training through pain. When I left after the injury, the worst injury I’ve ever had, I was really happy that I didn’t have to go to the gym anymore.”In Rotterdam, survivors vary in age from their 50s to their teens; it is hard not to view the issues as systemic and global. And ongoing. Charlotte Jacobs, who is only 18, quit the sport after suffering emotional abusewhen training in the UK.“It got to a point where I was like: ‘I can’t do it anymore’,” she says. “My experience was strange because it wasn’t physical, it wasn’t sexual, but it was emotional. You were ridiculed all the time, constantly. You weren’t allowed to cry, you weren’t allowed to talk, you weren’t allowed to sit down, if you were caught leaning on anything you’d have to run, you needed permission to go to the toilet, you needed permission to drink, and it’s that sort of really controlling, consistent and dismissive behaviour so that no one really felt safe that was prevalent.”Shore, who is a member of G4C Canada, argues that if a big list of cultural reforms comes from the top, that is then normalised within the national federations and then the clubs “all the way down to grassroots, then I think we would see faster reform and less resistance”.“The more I learn that the stories are consistent internationally the more it says something about the need for World Gymnastics to take a leadership role,” she says “The treatment across the world is pervasive and coaches are moving from space to space, country to country, more frequently now or they’re not even staying in this sport, they’re moving into other sports, especially if they’ve come into trouble.”World Gymnastics has moved to address the cross-border issue within the sport at least, publishing a newsafeguarding policylast week which notes that the Gymnastics Ethics Foundation, which it launched in 2019 and has handled nearly 500 reports, has the power to extend sanctions imposed by member federations providing they are compatible with the rules of the governing body and general principles of law.Among the efforts of World Gymnastics to address safeguarding concerns was the launch of the10 Golden Rules of Gymnasticsin 2021, the establishment of a safeguarding commissionin 2022 and, this year, the launch of a safeguarding newsletter and the appointment of a full-time Safeguarding Manager.Shore believes the pace of governing bodies fully engaging with the change needed has been slow, however, “because to admit that there is harm going on in the sport puts organisations into a liability risk. Also, they have been able to deflect responsibility for so long. They don’t know how to solve it and they are getting pressure from all sides. By putting their head in the sand for literally 50 years we’ve now got to a crisis.”A statement from World Gymnastics said: “Creating a safe environment for current and future generations of gymnasts is a responsibility that World Gymnastics takes extremely seriously and shares with all stakeholders across the sport. The priority for World Gymnastics is not only to strengthen safeguarding rules and policies, but to ensure that they lead to meaningful changes in everyday practice.”Heafford alleges that British Gymnastics isn’t entering into meaningful engagement and collaboration with Gymnasts for Change and other survivors in the sport and says that she finds that “extremely frustrating”. She is also hugely critical of the processes gymnasts have to go through in raising a complaint against a coach or gym and what resolution looks like, saying: “In six years, we haven’t had one outcome that we can stand by and say that was a good outcome.”View image in fullscreenWomen from Michigan-based victim advocacy groups cheer after the sentencing of Larry Nassar in January 2018.Photograph: Anthony Lanzilote/Getty ImagesBritish Gymnastics, however, insists it has engaged with the organisation regularly which has “helped shape its approach”, including a meeting with G4CI and others in Rotterdam as well as introducting a new complaints and disciplinary process“to improve transparency and fairness”.Minky Worden, of Human Rights Watch, fears the situation could worsen. “Sport is getting younger. There’s a youth Olympics about to launch in Senegal. There’s going to be thousands of athletes, every one of them 18 or younger. They’re all children and they’re at a very elite level,” she says. “These children are being monetised and they are not protected because we know the systems are not in place to protect them.”Hausch wants to see “measurable boundaries, for example increasing the competition age to 18,” she says. “I would root for Germany not to join youth international competitions. Having a 13-year-old do youth European championships is the same as doing it as an adult, it’s the same amount of work you have to put in, the same amount of pressure, it’s not a softer version, it’s the full version, and it doesn’t make sense.”All agree there needs to be more done to help athletes advocate for themselves and others. Jacobs says: “There needs to be a sort of package of what to look out for. I think there needs to be more training for coaches in terms of mental wellbeing, disability, neurodiversity, all that, alongside what are and are not best practices.“We need more regulation,” she adds of the British landscape. “Look at the new guidance that’s come out about keeping children safe in education. That’s all been updated. Where’s the guidance for anything sports-wise, extracurriculars, whether it’s swimming, gymnastics, dancing, anything like that?”British Gymnastics says that it “recognises there is always more to do” but that prevention is “at the heart of our work. We have overhauled learning and development … and set clearer policies and guidance to drive meaningful change.” It says a coach developer network, regional teams and safeguarding and welfare officers in every club support communities.Jotischky, who is now studying law off the back of her experience, says there are changes needed there too. “The legislative gap that exists is astonishing. You have the 2015 Serious Crime Act section 76, which talks about coercive control, but it’s limited to domestic and familial relationships. Then you have the 2021 Domestic Abuse Act which lists personally connected individuals as only being family members. In a coach-to-athlete relationship where you spend 30 hours a week in the gym with your coach, and some gymnasts even go and live with their coach because they’ve formed such a close relationship, of course coercive control and emotional abuse can happen but it’s not recognised within the law. So, we have very little legislative ground to deal with the most serious cases in particular.”Listening to this group of women in Rotterdam, what becomes clearer is that while federations, to differing degrees, make changes in the name of athlete safety, survivors are still being failed. Meanwhile, these survivors and knowledgeable advocates remain isolated from the very structures that should be embracing them and channelling their knowledge and understanding of their experiences into the changes necessary to ensure the future health of the sport.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available fromthe following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers supporton 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland.In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsGymnasticsSport politicsUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Brewers survive chaotic ninth-inning replay drama to beat Rays in World Series opener | World Series | The Guardian
description: Christian Yelich drove in a run and scored another as Milwaukee held off a ninth-inning rally to beat Tampa Bay 3-2 in their first home World Series game since 1982
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Christian Yelich drove in a run and scored another as Milwaukee held off a ninth-inning rally to beat Tampa Bay 3-2 in their first home World Series game since 1982
Content: The Rays’ Junior Caminero celebrates after a call is overturned during the ninth inning of Friday’s World Series opener against the Brewers.Photograph: David J Phillip/APView image in fullscreenThe Rays’ Junior Caminero celebrates after a call is overturned during the ninth inning of Friday’s World Series opener against the Brewers.Photograph: David J Phillip/APWorld SeriesBrewers survive chaotic ninth-inning replay drama to beat Rays in World Series openerBrewers claim 3-2 victory in Game 1 of World SeriesYelich triples home a run and scores in first inningMisiorowski and Megill hold off late Rays fightbackAgenciesFri 23 Oct 2026 23.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 00.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrevor Megill struck out Jonny DeLuca with runners on second and third to escape a ninth-inning jam as theMilwaukee Brewersheld on for a 3-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night.DeLuca’s strikeout came after Tampa Bay’s Liam Hicks had grounded into an apparent game-ending double play that was overturned after a video review. Replays showed that Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt’s right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang.“You have a big range of emotions,” Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich said. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after you have that emotional dump and then have to get back on it.”Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run and four hits over five innings to earn the victory.“Not perfect, but good enough to get a win,” he said.Quick GuideWorld Series 2026ShowScheduleBest-of-seven series. All times US Eastern Daylight Time (EDT).Fri 23 OctGame 1:Milwaukee 3, Tampa Bay 2Sat 24 OctGame 2: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8pm (Fox)Mon 26 OctGame 3: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8pm (Fox)Tue 27 OctGame 4: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8pm (Fox)Wed 28 OctGame 5: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8pm* (Fox)Fri 30 OctGame 6: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8pm* (Fox)Sat 31 OctGame 7: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8pm* (Fox)*-if necessaryHow to watchIn the US, all World Series games will air on Fox and Fox Deportes, with streaming available through Fox One. In the UK, the series will be carried by TNT Sports. In Australia, fans can watch on ESPN, with streaming available through Disney+ and Kayo Sports.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Yelich hit a run-scoring triple to spark a two-run rally in the first inning that put the Brewers ahead for good and delighted a sellout crowd reveling in Milwaukee’s firstWorld Seriesgame since 1982. Jackson Chourio and William Contreras each had two hits, including an RBI single. Contreras also threw out two runners trying to steal.It was the first World Series featuring two teams seeking their first championship since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league clubs without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners.World Series 2026 predictions: will the Rays or Brewers claim their first title?Read moreThe Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time.Tampa Bay trailed 3-1 and had not put a runner on base since the sixth inning until mounting a comeback attempt in the ninth.Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson hit consecutive one-out singles off Megill. A double steal involving pinch-runner Jorge Mateo and Simpson put the potential tying run in scoring position with Rays slugger Junior Caminero at the plate. Caminero walked on a 3-2 pitch in the dirt to load the bases.Hicks hit a grounder to the right side, and Turang ranged well to his left to field the ball before throwing to Pratt to start what was initially ruled a game-ending double play.Fireworks went off, players poured onto the field and Milwaukee fans roared – before the crowd hushed as it watched the play again on the videoboard.A replay review determined Pratt’s right foot came off the bag as he caught Turang’s throw. Hicks was still out at first, but the Rays now had runners at second and third with the score 3-2.“I thought Coop had him, and obviously I was wrong,” Misiorowski said.Megill finally sealed the win as DeLuca struck out swinging.“You just have to lock it back in,” Yelich said. “It’s the World Series – you have to do what you have to do to make things happen.”By sweeping the two-time defending World Series champions, the Los Angeles Dodgers, in the National League Championship Series, the Brewers had time to set up their rotation the way they wanted by handing the Game 1 start to Misiorowski, the hard-throwing NL Cy Young Award favorite.Misiorowski opened the game by throwing the fastest pitch ever delivered in a World Series, a 103.5mph ball to Yandy Díaz. The right-hander finished with a season-low three strikeouts.While Milwaukee started with their ace, Tampa Bay countered with Nick Martinez to give two-time All-Star pitchers Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta an extra day of rest. Martinez struck out five and allowed two runs over five innings, but a slow start proved costly.Chourio lined a single to right field on Martinez’s first pitch, and Yelich drove him home with a one-out triple to centre. DeLuca covered 85ft to track down Yelich’s drive but just missed making a diving catch as the ball glanced off his glove.Yelich was batting third in the lineup for the first time since 3 August. The three-time All-Star and 2018 NL MVP posted the lowest on-base percentage (.315) and OPS (.692) of his career, but he has stepped up his game since being named the first team captain in franchise history during the final week of the regular season.View image in fullscreenTampa Bay reliever Kevin Kelly pitches during the seventh inning of Friday’s World Series opener against Milwaukee.Photograph: Kayla Wolf/APHe was the seventh player to triple in his first World Series plate appearance, and the first since Kansas City’s Lynn Jones in 1985, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.Contreras knocked home Yelich with a line-drive single to left that was deflected by shortstop Taylor Walls with the infield playing in.Tampa Bay got a run back in the fourth.Aranda drew a leadoff walk and advanced to third when Caminero doubled on a one-out liner with a 112.7mph exit velocity that sailed over centre fielder Garrett Mitchell and off his outstretched glove. Aranda came home on Hicks’ groundout to the right side.Milwaukee extended their lead to 3-1 in the seventh. Pratt drew a leadoff walk from Steven Matz and scored from second when Chourio greeted Kevin Kelly with a two-out single.That insurance run proved critical.“The guys settled in right away and did a great job,” Yelich said. “We still have a ways to go, but it’s nice to get that first one.”Explore more on these topicsWorld SeriesMilwaukee BrewersTampa Bay RaysBaseballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: The AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting back
Author: Tom Wall
Headline: The AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting back
Content: A house in the shadow of a datacentre in Newport, south Wales. All photographs: Joel Redman/The GuardianThe AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting backByTom Wall. Photographs: Joel RedmanSat 24 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDale Johnston opens the gate to his neat suburban garden on the western fringes of Newport in SouthWales. There’s a trampoline and a slide on the lawn for his grandchildren, and chairs for him and his wife. He should be enjoying the light draining from the perfect autumnal sky – but almost his entire view is blotted out by a vast expanse of prefabricated panels.The 23 metre-high grey hulk looming over him and his neighbours is a hyperscale datacentre. It is heralded by the area’s Labourpoliticiansas a job creator, yet all Johnston can think about is what he has lost: “Before, the sun used to come around here and it was lovely.” The way residents have been treated is “disgusting”.Johnston, who used to work for a chemical company in the city, worries what their lives will be like when the centre is switched on: the 36 sets of air blast coolers, needed to stop the chips inside overheating, most likely generate a constant drone, while regular testing of 60 back-up diesel generators, to prevent costly interruption to the flow of data, could produce harmful fumes. He already has to keep his bathroom window closed to stop the low hum from another facility on the rapidly expanding 46-acre datacentre campus that borders the small enclave of 27 houses. His wife, a nurse who works night shifts, can barely sleep already. He shakes his head in despair: “We just don’t know what’s going to happen.”View image in fullscreen‘The MPs backing the development won’t come round here to see what they’ve done’: Dale Johnston in his gardenJohnston can talk about little else, but he feels no one in authority is listening. He’s invited councillors and MPs backing the development to visit his garden. But “they won’t come around here to see what they’ve done”.This is the frontline of Britain’s datacentre boom, which is pitting residents against giant US tech firms seeking to build a network of facilities capable of providing the immense computing muscle for powerful AI models. There are315 hyperscale datacentreswaiting to connect to the national grid, which carries electricity from power plants to homes and businesses (hyperscale typically means facilities with at least 5,000 servers and 10,000 sq ft in size). Combined, these new centres will require 73GW of power, 28GW higher than the typical peak energy demand of 45GW on a cold winter’s day.Wales is one of the main development hotspots outside London. It already has the largest datacentre capacity beyond the capital, with new hyperscale facilities planned for former industrial and urban sites. The Keir Starmer-led Labour government viewed this as aninevitable revolution, which the country must embrace or be left behind. It establishedfive AI growth zonesto push more datacentres through the planning system and speed up connections to the national grid. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has signalled little will change,turning down calls for a moratoriumand insisting datacentres bring economic benefits. But anti-datacentre groups springing up in villages, towns and cities across the country see it rather differently: as the imposition of a resource-hungry, polluting industry that increases profits for often US big tech, with little tangible benefit to local people or the country as a whole.Digital storage is nothing new. The first home PC users saved files on floppy discs and hard drives; businesses used their own server rooms in the 80s and 90s, then moved to off-site facilities as their needs grew. But the development of cloud computing services in the 2010s, such as Google Drive, and AI chatbots in the 2020s, like ChatGPT, led to even greater information and processing demands, which the tech industry insists can only be met by larger and larger datacentres. This has driven huge speculative bets on hyperscale hubs, which investors and tech firms hope will one day reap the rewards of an AI-led transformation of the economy. Globally, it isestimatedspending on new facilities could reach $7tn by 2030 –morethan double the cost of the New Deal, the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe after the second world war and the Apollo space programme combined, even allowing for inflation.The US is at the forefront of the boom, already hosting roughlyhalfof the world’s hyperscale capacity. But the industry is facing afuriousbacklash, with three- quarters of Americans now opposed to datacentre development and blaming it forincreasingenergy bills,threateningwater supplies in drought-hit areas andspewingout toxic fumes. More than 500 counties and municipalities have passed permanent or temporarydatacentre bans.‘This is not an anti-tech town’: backlash to datacenter in city once home to IBMRead moreLoudoun County in northern Virginia sits in what is known as Data Center Alley because it ishometo more facilities than anywhere else in the world. Greg Pirio’s life was turned upside down when a gas-powered datacentre opened 150 metres from his home last year. “This neighbourhood was calm and peaceful, and it’s turned into this nightmare,” he says on a video call. “Our quality of life has been degraded so much.”The noise from the centre’s eight gas turbines is “like being at an airport with all these engines roaring,” Pirio says. “It has given many of my neighbours headaches. It has kept children up at night.” Pirio, who used to work for the Voice of America radio station, has also developed health problems since it opened, including dry eyes and chest tightness. Once he had to leave his house because he was struggling to breathe: “I know whenever the diesel generators are on, because I feel it in my lungs.”View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the datacentre in Newport …View image in fullscreen… and the outside of the buildingThe UK has not yet seen the same level of opposition as the US. But anti-datacentre groups are gathering momentum. Residents in east London are waging a high-profile campaign against a new datacentre on Brick Lane, including protesting outside the offices of Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, whooverturned a council decisionblocking the scheme.Seasoned campaigner Owen Espley, who works for environmental charity Global Action Plan, is helping scores of residents’ groups organise against planned datacentres. “This summer has been wild. Every other week a new group has popped up. Petitions are getting thousands of signatures in days,” he says. “Communities are in uproar, and most politicians are playing catch-up.”Espley has been taken aback by the gulf between the government’s conviction that there is no alternative and ordinary people’s deepening understanding of the complex issues at stake. “There has been a real grassroots questioning of datacentres that connects British Bangladeshis in Brick Lane with Hertfordshire villagers and communities in Northumberland, who want good jobs to come back,” he says. “It is astounding.”In fact, there are many alternative pathways to market-­led expansion – from tougher regulation to prioritising publicly-owned data infrastructure – which serve communal goals, such as theheart diseaseanddementiaresearch powered by Bristol University’s new Isambard-AIfacility. “First, we need strong standards for private datacentres,” Espley says. “Second, we need industrial strategy to deliver our own public computer, rather than an assumption that US big tech building and owning everything is the only way forward.”On the deprived eastern edges of Cardiff, the early morning sunshine is warming a car park dotted with scraggly weeds. The perimeter fence is overgrown with brambles, with patches of singed, blackened grass from a recent wildfire visible just beyond. It looks abandoned but soon cars carrying doctors, nurses and other NHS staff start arriving. They are here to catch free buses to Cardiff’s Heath hospital, the largest in Wales.Hundreds are said to use the park and ride every day, but it is under threat because Labour-controlled Cardiff council wants to sell the land to a property developer, Curtis Hall, to build a hyperscale data facility. The centre will use up to 150 megawatts (MW) of electricity a year, more than triple the demand of a city the size of Cardiff.The development is one of the most controversial in Wales. Council meetings have been disrupted and more than 1,200 planning objections lodged. Last month, the new Plaid Cymru-led government ordered the council to put the application on hold while it considered whether to take the decision out of councillors’ hands.Campaigners are determined to keep up the pressure on the Welsh government. Sue Elias, a retired librarian with seemingly endless reserves of energy, dashes back and forth reattaching her “Ditch the datacentre” banner to the car park fence and taping leaflets to the bus stop glass. “What is going to happen to all the people who use the park and ride? It’s bonkers,” she says.View image in fullscreenSue Elias rallying opposition to the building of a datacentre on the local park and ride …View image in fullscreen… which Abi George, a midwife, uses it every day to get to workElias has leafleted the park and ride every Wednesday morning for six weeks. Today she is collecting signatures for an open letter to prove it is well used – so far she has added the names of 1,300 staff and patients. “I’ve not done anything like this before but I’m told I’m a natural,” she says with a mischievous smile, before breaking off to speak to staff arriving for the next bus.She belongs to community-based union Acorn, which has campaigned against the scheme, and has taken part inprotests, including bursting into a council planning meeting in July. “We’d sent emails, done petitions, but we’d had nothing back – tumbleweed. They’re our elected representatives … They should be talking with us.”It is hard to find anyone in support of the plan in the queue for the bus, which runs three times an hour. “I use it every day. Without it, I probably wouldn’t continue working at the hospital,” says Ami George, a midwife. “Parking there causes that much stress.”Across Cardiff’s Rhymney River, which curves around the proposed datacentre development, the area’s newest residents have only recently moved into 100 homesbuiltunder the city council’s flagship house-building programme. Nick Richards, a freelance filmmaker and skateboarder, and his wife arrived in November. “It felt like the stars had aligned because there is a brand new skate park up the road … the best in Cardiff. It’s amazing,” he says. “I never pictured myself living in suburbia but when we came we saw kids playing outside and thought, this is a really nice area.”double quotation markI feel trapped. I couldn’t look prospective buyers in the eye and not tell themView image in fullscreenNick Richards, who moved to a new estate two months before a datacentre planning application was submittedLike many other residents on the estate, Richards had no idea the council was planning to sell the park and ride to a datacentre developer. They moved in two months before the planning application was submitted. Instead of enjoying their new life, they now fear they will never be able to sell. Their home is 300 metres from what the plans describe as the temporary energy centre, which includes seven giant gas turbines. They are expected to power the facility around the clock for five years, according to documents filed by the developer. “I feel trapped,” Richards says, pacing his kitchen. “I couldn’t look prospective buyers in the eye and not say there’s going to be seven gas turbines right next to them.”Richards has pored over the planning documents and leafleted every house on the new estate, including a care home, which will be just 150 metres from the turbines. “This datacentre will be powered by gas turbines,” he says. “They will pump nitrogen dioxide into our atmosphere. There will also be fine particulate matter and formaldehyde. All these toxins cause health conditions, such as asthma, COPD and heart disease.”Air quality assessments commissioned by the developer estimate the emissions will be within safe levels. Curtis Hall says the scheme cannot proceed without 100% compliance with all environmental and public health regulatory requirements.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are more than100 other planned UK datacentresaiming to use gas turbines due to the long wait to be connected to the grid. Richards doesn’t want his estate to be a test case. “Within a mile of this datacentre are 30,000 people. But the people building this centre don’t live here ... They don’t give two shits about Welsh people.”Astone’s throw away is Llanrumney Hall, once the home of privateer and slave trader Sir Henry Morgan, who gave his name to Captain Morgan rum. It is now a thriving community centre, with a cafe, recording studio and creche. Labour councillor Lee Bridgeman is vaping on an outdoor table, dressed in a hoodie and baseball cap. He ran the local youth centre until it was lost to austerity-era cuts, and though he’s a high-ranking councillor, jointly responsible for housing and communities, he does regular youth work shifts in the area, one of the poorest in Cardiff.“Llanrumney runs through my veins,” he says. “I’m not your usual politician. I don’t go to conferences. I got into politics to help the community.”Bridgeman is charming and friendly – but he is not afraid of a fight. He is one of the few public figures in the area who has spoken out in support of the development, sometimes clashing with anti-datacentre campaigners on local Facebook groups. “Some of the information being spread is scaremongering,” he says. “They are telling residents their electricity bills will go up … the river and reservoir will be drained … It’s false information.”View image in fullscreenLabour councillor Lee Bridgeman, who supported plans for a datacentre in Cardiff …View image in fullscreen… until local residents, like those at this public meeting in a boxing club, changed his mindMany of these fears stem from the US, where the rapid expansion of hyperscale facilities has been linked to rising electricity bills, water shortages and toxic air pollution. Bridgeman argues that “planning processes are totally different in the UK. So whereas [US authorities] turn a blind eye to some of the environmental impacts of those monstrosities, that would never happen in the UK.” He “wouldn’t be comfortable” if the gas turbines were running for five years but thinks they might not be needed if the datacentre can connect to the grid sooner.The backlash has caught him by surprise, but he blames outside activists. “I didn’t see it coming. I didn’t think there would be this much interference,” he says.Emotions are running high in the city. Some residents say they have been blocked by councillors when trying to question them on Facebook. Planning committee members have received threatening emails, Bridgeman says. “Threats like ‘I will come after you ... we will make your life hell.’ That shouldn’t happen.”Although the datacentre will employ only up to125people when it is built, Bridgeman believes it could encourage other big companies to east Cardiff: “I’m told the knock-on effect could lead to thousands of jobs.”Later that day, residents squeeze into the local boxing club for a public meeting about the datacentre plan. It is standing room only, with people lining the walls. Bridgeman repeats his claim that few locals have complained: “I have hundreds of emails from residents ... So far I’ve had two emails with regards to the datacentre.”Some in the audience react angrily. There are shouts of, “We don’t know you, that’s why” and, “Have you heard of social media?” One woman stands up and says, “Don’t tell me you haven’t been privy to the meetings … or things online.” In a show of hands, roughly three-quarters of the 80 to 100 people in the room indicate they are from Llanrumney, almost all opposed. There are cries of, “There you are … you don’t need emails!” and, “That’s every person!” Almost three weeks later, Bridgeman performs a sudden about-turn, submitting a formal letter of objection to the scheme, noting that he has heard from a large number of residents.The UK hyperscale buildout has been focused on London, but datacentre developers are increasingly targeting areas outside the south-east, to escape severe electrical grid capacity limits. Wales already has the largest datacentre capacity of anywhere outside the capital. Many more could be coming: five of Wales’s largest new and proposed datacentres will consume more electricity than all Welsh homes put together. While the previous Welsh Labour administrationwelcomedthe building spree, claiming giant tech firms’ investment would generate thousands of jobs, the Plaid Cymru-led government has been more circumspect, with ministers emphasising it must benefit Wales.In the light and airy Welsh parliament building, which overlooks Cardiff Bay, opposition is growing. Plaid Cymru’s Nick Carter, who is the Senedd member for Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, which includes Cardiff East, worries that the surging market will benefit developers and US tech firms rather than the public. “As a party, we’re not going to want to see a proliferation of datacentres, haphazardly being built across the country, on what may be an opportunistic basis,” he says.double quotation markThey could be a front for someone else: Google, Microsoft, whoeverView image in fullscreenPlaid Cymru’s Nick Carter, who fears datacentres benefit only developers and US tech firmsCarter, who has a background in commercial property, has examined the Cardiff plans in detail. He says the developer, Curtis Hall, has no track record in datacentres; “They could be a front for someone else: Google, Microsoft, whoever. I can understand why these operators need datacentres, but I’m not sure members of the public share the need.” In response, Curtis Hall says it never claimed it would operate the facility itself, adding it had been working on datacentre projects for five years.Carter is glad the Welsh government has intervened in Cardiff. But he doesn’t believe Wales needs to follow Scotland by imposing amoratoriumon new datacentres: “The Welsh government is developing a strategy for datacentres nationally. We’ll see what comes out of that.”However, it is not clear how the Welsh government can meet its goal to reach net zero by 2040 without limiting datacentre expansion. Carter admits, “It’s massively problematic.” In Westminster, similar questions have been asked. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology tells me the government will enable the development of datacentres by generating unprecedented amounts of clean power.Asoft autumnal dusk descends on the residents living beside the new datacentre in Newport. Its sleek industrial-grey walls cast shadows across the closest gardens and homes. Much of the anger and frustration that met the original proposals has given way to weariness and resignation. Some residents talk of moving away, while others are mollified by meetings with the US-based data campus operator, Vantage.Yet their troubles may only just be beginning – right now, only one of the three Vantage datacentres is operational. Microsoft will be opening its own nearby soon. When all are running, there could be upwards of 500 air handling units working at the same time, with back-up diesel generators needing regular testing, so they can immediately fire up if there is a power cut.Newport council’s chief scientific officer warned during the planning process that the fumes from all the generators had the “potential to cause unacceptable air pollution levels under use, and testing needs to be understood and mitigation proposed, if needed”.The council tells me it doesn’t have a duty to monitor emissions from generators, but says its officers check air quality management plans, and ask managers to minimise the impact of generator tests. Vantage says all its facilities operate in accordance with noise and air quality controls. It says it will monitor impacts and investigate concerns when the new centre opens.Some residents have already given up on democratic process. Johnston fought the proposals through the planning process but felt he was ignored. “We’ve been let down by all of them. I’ve had electoral roll cards come through my door. But I’m voting for none of them … I can’t trust them. They don’t care about any of us.”Over the road are older homes, where staff working on a nearby wealthy estate once lived. Sonia Thomas, a retired teacher, has lived in the same housekeeper’s cottage since 1969. She can remember when orchards and fields fanned out in front of their gardens but now she doesn’t even know if the sun is shining. “From inside you see grey, not blue,” she says, glancing at the datacentre filling the sky. “It’s horrible.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Big dataWalesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Synthetic twin’: Why Socceroo Cristian Volpato is the latest footballer to license his AI clone | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Athletes’ scramble to control – and monetise – their digital identities at the cutting edge of AI rights deals
Author: Henry Belot
Headline: Athletes’ scramble to control – and monetise – their digital identities at the cutting edge of AI rights deals
Content: These AI-generated images of Cristian Volpato were produced as part of the Socceroos star’s new deal with California-based Callandor to license his AI likeness.Computer-generated: Cristian Volpato/Callandor Group/Instagram/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenThese AI-generated images of Cristian Volpato were produced as part of the Socceroos star’s new deal with California-based Callandor to license his AI likeness.Computer-generated: Cristian Volpato/Callandor Group/Instagram/Guardian DesignAI (artificial intelligence)‘Synthetic twin’: Why Socceroo Cristian Volpato is the latest footballer to license his AI cloneAthletes’ scramble to control – and monetise – their digital identities at the cutting edge of AI rights dealsGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastHenry BelotandJack SnapeSat 24 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Socceroos star stares at the camera as he strides through an enormous atrium, the sound of his football boots on polished concrete echoing around him. Suddenly, he spawns four digital clones that peel off out of view to re-emerge in different settings around the world.This scene from a social media video is fake and generated by artificial intelligence. But it has been authorised by the very real 22-year-old footballer, Cristian Volpato, the latest professional athlete to licence and monetise his AI likeness.Draped in a white linen suit with his feet on the sand, Volpato’s “synthetic twin” turns towards a photographer as the limestone stacks of the Twelve Apostles tower behind him. Another dominates a large digital billboard wearing a football jersey. One smiles into a mirror while adjusting a sharp grey suit.AFL tells Sportsbet to stop using players in AI-generated contentRead moreThis video was produced by a new company that acts as an AI licensing agent for professional athletes. Experts believe it is one small part of a nascent online industry that could transformthe future of image rightsand sports content.As bookmakers, broadcasters and brands increasingly use athletes’ images in AI generated content without their permission, some players are fighting back.Digital twinsIn mid-September, Volpato, who plays for Italian Serie A club, Sassuolo, struck a deal with the California-based company Callandor to license his AI image.As part of the deal, Callandor was given exclusive rights to Volpato’s digital likeness, voice, biometric profiles and performance data. The company will monetise his AI image by landing brand deals, taking a cut, and help restrict content that does not have his approval.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailFrom Los Angeles, Callandor’s co-founder, Michael Fisk, tells Guardian Australia he’s in the business of making “synthetic twins”.“Cristian is constantly training,” Fisk says. “He’s constantly out there playing. If he has any free time whatsoever, he’ll probably want to spend it with family and friends, so he loses on a lot of opportunities on brand placements.“A synthetic twin could be used 24-7, year-round by brands. Assuming it’s approved, right?”Founded in February, Callandor has a small stable of athletes, including Brazilian footballer Jorginho and American sailor Chris Poole. Its campaigns are only in the pilot phase, but Callandor is pursuing an array of opportunities beyond traditional advertising.Fisk, a former executive at Sony Pictures and MGM, talks of creating AI-generated book voiceovers with foreign language editions. His team is also plotting apps that offer fans a personal relationship with a synthetic twin.“Ultimately, the holy grail of an athlete is to have that one-on-one interaction with fans,” Fisk says.He raises the prospect of creating an app that monitors how people play football. A digital clone of Volpato would give real-time instructions.“He’s realising I’m not handling the ball well [so] his synthetic twin can tell me, ‘Hey, you should be doing this and this and this’,” says Fisk.“Volpato would never be able to do that one-on-one with [them].”Volpato’s deal with Callandor is at the cutting edge of AI rights deals, but he isn’t the first to embrace the technology. In June, Brazilian superstar Neymar licensed his AI likeness to a Chinese-owned entertainment platform that created short videos published during the FIFA World Cup.These projects are being launched as governments across the world consider basic regulation of AI. At the moment, player contracts with major Australian sporting leagues make no mention of AI.But technology isn’t waiting for regulation to catch up and Fisk says his synthetic twin clients are blurring the lines between real and fake.“It’s becoming almost impossible to detect, that look and feel, the difference, particularly when you see it on a mobile device,” he says.‘We’re watching a race’William Saunders leads a small Sydney based start-up, Hyperknown, that’s trying to cut similar deals. He says athletes are beginning to realise that if they don’t monetise their AI image, others will.Earlier this month, theAFL told its gambling partner Sportsbet to stop using AI images of playerswithout their consent. This was prompted by a complaint from the players’ union, which is considering whether stricter rules should be negotiated.“Sportsbet shows us what happens when companies and technology get ahead of consent,” Saunders says.“Volpato represents the counter-move: people establishing their rights before others start making decisions about their identities.“We’re watching a race between what technology can do and what people have actually authorised.”Many in the Australian sports industry, including content creators, bookmakers, broadcasters and athletes themselves, have started embracing the technology.Earlier this month, Australian cricketer Travis Head personally appeared in an ad for the broadcaster Kayo. He joked that his AI clone had already finished filming the ad, before throwing tovision of him riding a flying kookaburra.Brand deals and endorsements have become major money makers for athletes, with some securing multimillion dollar contracts. It remains unclear whether brands will be willing to pay as much for an AI clone, as opposed to the real deal.But Saunders, whose company has only just launched, says the opportunities are enormous. He talks of AI clones selling products in foreign languages in nations athletes have never visited.“The next trust signal won’t just say ‘made with AI’,” he says, referencing a tag often used by social media companies. “It will say ‘made with this person’s permission’.“AI can make content abundant. It can’t manufacture someone’s permission. That’s becoming a new commercial requirement.”‘A tangle of different interests’Jonathan Harlen, an expert in intellectual property law at Southern Cross University, says the rise of AI brokers is “the obvious next step” in a “supercharged global market”.From a legal perspective, he says this new industry presents “a tangle of different interests and rights” that need to be carefully negotiated.“Whilecopyright already subsistsin voice recordings, artistic works and cinematographic images, it is only recognised where there has been human authorship, as well as a degree of independent or creative human effort involved in the making of the work,” Harlen says.“It doesn’t apply to AI reproductions.”Celebrities and athletes do have some protection against AI-generated content using their image and voice without consent. But these “passing off” laws only apply when public figures can prove they have suffered an economic loss.This has not slowed an explosion of deepfakes generated by increasingly sophisticated off-the-shelf software.In the UK last month, a campaign was launched by some the world’s top footballers, including Cole Palmer and Lucy Bronze, which highlighted their concerns about deepfakes and the inability for regulation to slow their explosion. This campaign was backed by the global player union, Fifpro.One offshore casinoused a deepfake video of Manchester United player Bruno Fernandes in advertising earlier this year.Not all unauthorised deepfakes will be unwanted, however. Fisk says a heavy-handed crackdown on “fan art” using AI tools might be counterproductive.“You don’t want fans to use your image and put you in [content] using brands that you don’t use, or saying something that you would never say,” he says.“Obviously, anything with religion and drugs, or whatever it might be, you have to be very, very careful. So it does complicate things a bit, but the opportunities are phenomenal.”But in this emerging realm, the consequences may be hard to predict.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Australia sportFootball AustraliaComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom | BBC | The Guardian
description: BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say
Author: Tara Conlan
Headline: BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say
Content: Creatures filmed in the deep ocean are ‘more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real’, said the Blue Planet III producers.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoView image in fullscreenCreatures filmed in the deep ocean are ‘more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real’, said the Blue Planet III producers.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoBBCBlue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boomBBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers sayTara ConlanSat 24 Oct 2026 04.32 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheDavid Attenborough-narrated series Blue Planet III deliberately includes cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said.Nearly a decade after Blue Planet II shone a light on plastic pollution, and 25 years since the first Blue Planet aired, the hitBBCseries is returning with more animal behaviour and cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed “stonefish” cam.Since the first Blue Planet, TVs and cameras have evolved to give viewers sharper, higher definition pictures. But the combination of the rise in AI and the extraordinary sequences and fantastical creatures captured by BBC Studios’ natural history unit for this series led producers to include what they called more “organic” footage and less polished shots, to show that the animals were not AI-generated.View image in fullscreen‘No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame,’ said the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jo HaleyThe executive producer, Elizabeth White, said AI, “makes us want to be even more authentic”, adding that the creatures filmed in the deep ocean “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real”.She said that in the past “the amount of plankton and things that are in the water in the sequences” would usually mean they might be excluded, and previously, “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’”But now such things are being left in as “we’re really leaning into that authenticity … As AI booms we will probably lean more into the more organic”, murkier and less polished footage.For the first time, the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle, assured journalists at a press screening: “No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame. It’s all real photography.”Bootle added that as we live in a “golden age of natural history-making … sometimes people feel like they’ve seen it all before [so] this series is bursting with novel behaviour”.View image in fullscreenThe hit BBC series returns with cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed ‘stonefish’.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoThat includes never-before-seen action of dolphins using sea sponges to block holes in coral to trap fish, captured using underwater CCTV – developed by the programme’s producer and director, Yoland Bosiger.Over the four years of filming across five oceans, BBC Studios “continually innovated”, said the series producer, Lara Bickerton, creating a “mini-dome” camera to follow an octopus, a “deep-sea selfie stick”, camera operators wearing leg-mounted scooters to create immersive TikTok-style diving footage and using lasers to film deep-sea creatures.Other remarkable animal behaviour captured in the programme includes grouper communicating with another species of fish; 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed; sea urchins using shells as sun hats; and footage involving penguins that echoes the Planet Earth II,‘iguana v snakes’sequence.Threats to the ocean as well as its resilience are addressed in the series. One episode shows how warmer seas caused by the climate crisis are killing off sea anemone where clown fish live and how they try to fix their homes, and the issue of plastics raised in Blue Planet II continues with a story about pollutants [and] forever chemicals, said White.Bosiger said Attenborough, who is 100 years old, was “very much involved” and made changes to scripts.White added: “What’s wonderful is he hasn’t lost his curiosity … he’s still that little boy … who gets excited … when you show him a new piece of footage.”Asked if the BBC’s£500m cost-cutting drivewould affect BBC Studios’ renowned natural history reputation, White said she could not comment on that but pointed out that Blue Planet III made savings by using more local crews on location than in previous series.Blue Planet III starts Sunday 1November on BBC1 and iPlayerExplore more on these topicsBBCNature documentariesScience and nature TVBBC OneDavid AttenboroughMarine lifeAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Opposition deepfake video of Spanish PM’s wife sparks outrage before election | Spain | The Guardian
description: Video shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoing
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Video shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoing
Content: Pedro Sánchez and his wife at a campaign rally in Fuenlabrada last weekend.Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPAView image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez and his wife at a campaign rally in Fuenlabrada last weekend.Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPASpainOpposition deepfake video of Spanish PM’s wife sparks outrage before electionVideo shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoingAshifa Kassamin MadridSat 24 Oct 2026 02.51 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA political ad from Spain’s main opposition party that used a deepfake video of the prime minister’s wife has sparked outrage and set off a wider debate on AI, as the deeply polarised country gears up for general elections next month.Launchedthis weekacross the social media channels of the conservative People’s party (PP), the video used artificial intelligence to manipulate the likenesses of various people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party and appeared to show them admitting to acts such as soliciting prostitutes and taking kickbacks.An AI-generated version of Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, for example, speaks aboutreceiving a university postthanks to her husband’s job, while a deepfake of the former Socialist president José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero speaks abouthiding jewelleryin a safe. Both lines are nods to ongoing investigations in which Gómez and Zapatero have denied any wrongdoing.View image in fullscreenA still from the People’s party AI-generated video featuring a deepfake of Begoña Gomez.Computer-generated: @ppopular/XThe Socialist party was swift to respond to the video, which by Friday had racked up nearly 2m views. “It’s telling people a colossal lie, and for a party to do it on its official accounts seems intolerable to me,” Óscar López, Spain’s digital transformation minister,told the broadcaster TVEon Friday.While the video noted at the bottom – in tiny, nearly transparent font – that it had been created with AI, López pointed to the wider risk. “It’s very easy for anyone who isn’t used to AI to confuse that video with reality,” he said. “And call me crazy, but that seems extremely serious to me.”On Friday, one of those whose likeness was used in the video filed a legal challenge against the PP, calling on the party to immediately take down the campaign advert. In a court complaint, Leire Díez, a former Socialist party member, reportedly accused the PP of defamation and digital identity theft, after the video used her likeness to hint at accusations that she worked to undermine judicial and law enforcement in order to help the Socialists.A majority of the nine legal expertsconsulted by the newspaper El Paísconcurred that what the PP had done was not illegal, given that the video was labelled as AI-generated and that the overall tone was one of political satire. “Given the context, everyone knows those people didn’t say those things,” Íñigo Navarro, a former dean of the faculty of law at Madrid’s Comillas Pontifical University, told the paper.But the legality of the video was just one aspect, said Juan Antonio Lascuraín, a professor of criminal law at the Autonomous University of Madrid. “It’s quite another matter to ask whether it’s appropriate, exemplary or ethically and politically correct.”Many sought to contextualise the videos within the wider effort – under way by officials across much of the world – tocrack downon the impact of disinformation.“It’s truly regrettable that the official account of a party that claims to want to govern and revitalise democracy is using AI-generated deepfakes in its campaign,” said José Javier Olivas, an associate professor who researches populism, conspiracy theories and AI biases at Spain’s National University for Distance Education.He pointed to the wider backdrop of the election campaign, in which both mainstream parties have sought to rally voters by stoking emotions and attacking the morality of their rivals, but he said the video was a “red line” in terms of how campaigns normally unfolded.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“You’re using the images of other people,
