putting words in their mouths that they’re not saying, [and] this qualifies for disinformation,” he said.The use of AI to generate or enhance political ads has also become a talking point in the US ahead of next month’s midterm elections. A recent report by a research group based at Wesleyan University in Connecticutidentified more than 200such ads, the vast majority of them tied to the Republicans.“AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year,” said Erika Franklin Fowler, a co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project. “For comparison, we identified less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 cycle. Much of the AI use is not disclosed through any type of disclaimer.”In Spain, the PP has brushed off criticism. “If there had been malicious intent to make people believe that the characters who appear there are real, then we’d have a problem,” Borja Sémper, of the party, told reporters. “But everyone can see that this is a way of using digital tools to highlight the hypocrisy in which the Socialist party operates.”Most polls suggest the PP will win the 29 November general election but will need to rely on the support of the far-right Vox party to form a government.Explore more on these topicsSpainPedro SánchezAI (artificial intelligence)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: John Healey pledges to use budget to harness power of AI to bolster Britain’s security | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Chancellor says government to commit hundreds of millions to develop ‘distinctively British’ approach to AI
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Chancellor says government to commit hundreds of millions to develop ‘distinctively British’ approach to AI
Content: Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, aims to harness the opportunities of AI to raise living standards and boost UK’s economic growth.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAView image in fullscreenChancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, aims to harness the opportunities of AI to raise living standards and boost UK’s economic growth.Photograph: Paul Reid/PABudget 2026John Healey pledges to use budget to harness power of AI to bolster Britain’s securityChancellor says government to commit hundreds of millions to develop ‘distinctively British’ approach to AIRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey has pledged to use Wednesday’s budget to harness the power of artificial intelligence to bolster Britain’s security and prosperity against the risks in the accelerating global technology arms race.As he prepares for his debut budget, the chancellor said that Andy Burnham’s government would commit hundreds of millions of pounds to develop a “distinctively British” approach to AI that would capitalise on the benefits of the frontier technology.At a fork in the road as AI developments pose bothexistential threatsand transformative economic potential, Healey said he would be making the biggest ever investment to guard against cyber risks and the disruptive potential of the technology.As part of the measures in his tax and spending statement, he promised fresh investment for Britain’s AI Security Institute and other critical institutions, alongside allocating public money to support the use of the technology for good.“AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school and every aspect of our economy can benefit,” Healey said.“I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI – one that doesn’t leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country.”Three months into Burnham’s premiership, Healey is poised to deliver a budget against an increasingly volatile backdrop as the war in the Middle East sends shock waves through the global economy, putting pressure on public finances and reigniting the cost of living crisis.The chancellor has vowed to use his first budget to provide households and businesses with“breathing space”as the global surge in energy costs triggered by the war hits millions of families this winter. On Friday, the latest tensions in the Gulf sent the oil price to its highest level for six months, risingabove $117 a barrelat one point.However he will also use the opportunity afforded by the critical speech to the Commons to flesh out Burnham’s policy priorities for government after he replaced Keir Starmer this summer, and to spell out a vision for Britain amid the increasingly turbulent global economic outlook.Aiming to harness the opportunities of AI to raise living standards, back UK businesses and support economic growth, the chancellor said he wanted to seize the opportunities of the technology as a central plank of Labour’s plan for growth.It comes after official figures show AI investment has helped the UK outperform gloomy economic forecasts as the Iran war pushes up inflation and drags down business confidence, powering the country to the strongest growth performance in the G7 in the first half of this year.However, there are growing fears over the security of the nation and critical industries as the technology opens up the danger of cyber-attacks, IT systems turning rogue and devastating job losses as companies invest in machines rather than humans.It comes as websites around the globe went dark this week aftera serious vulnerabilitywas found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web, in a development made possible by rapid AI advances. It also emerged this week thatBarclays is cutting 5,000 jobsas part of cost-saving plans identified by bosses as the rollout of AI across the bank helps it make efficiency gains.Healey said he wanted to use his budget to protect against risks while also nurturing homegrown businesses and talent, in order to cut Britain’s dependency on other countries that were also making strides in AI technology.New investments would be made in AI chip design capability in Edinburgh, alongside a new AI Centre of Excellence in Manchester that it said would enable the UK to harness the technology’s benefits.The government would also spend £10m a year to lead the UK’s work on understanding how AI will reshape jobs and industry, aiming to address concerns about potential job disruption.As part of the plan the Treasury said it would back up to £300m in public-private investment in a new AI Biosecurity Lab, designed to serve as a world-leading institution bringing together scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats.It comes after the defence secretary, Wes Streeting,warned on Thursdaythat UK households should make preparations against the mounting risks from weather, cyber or other serious emergencies.The advice to stock up on supplies to last 72 hours, in a campaign calledBe Ready, comes as Silicon Valley bosses sound the alarm over the increasingly existential threats AI could pose, and amid growing official concern over the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said: “I’m proud the UK has repeatedly been at the forefront of global efforts to use AI for the benefit of humankind.“Today’s investment will help the UK seize the opportunities AI presents to strengthen our national security, while staying one step ahead of those who seek to use AI to do us harm.”Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026EnglandJohn HealeyAI (artificial intelligence)Economic policyTax and spendingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Attention LaMelo Ball: only losers boast about avoiding diaper duty | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The basketball star seems proud to leave the job to his partner. That’s so last century
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The basketball star seems proud to leave the job to his partner. That’s so last century
Content: ‘A baby doesn’t care that you signed a five-year contract extension.’Photograph: Matt Krohn/APView image in fullscreen‘A baby doesn’t care that you signed a five-year contract extension.’Photograph: Matt Krohn/APThe Week in PatriarchyParents and parentingAttention LaMelo Ball: only losers boast about avoiding diaper dutyArwa MahdawiThe basketball star seems proud to leave the job to his partner. That’s so last centurySat 24 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTShareNobody can accuse the basketball star LaMelo Ball of being bad at his job. That said, the Minnesota Timberwolves point guard doesn’t seem to be a huge fan ofdribbling.Ball has a nine-month-old son, LaOne, with his partner Ana Montana (real name: Analicia Chaves) and is apparently uninterested in dealing with all the body fluids that come with a baby.“You’re a dad now,” the sportscaster Ernie Johnson Jr said to Ball during an ESPNinterviewon Wednesday. “Are you a diaper changer?”“Nah, my girl do all that,” Ball replied. “We got a good gameplan going on. So I know what I gotta do, bring to the table, she know what she gotta do, bring to the table.”Johnson, to his credit, seemed disappointed by this answer. “Oh man, you don’t know what you’re missing, I’m telling you that.”“I did it before, you feel me? I’ve definitely did it before, [but] it’s just not my job,” Ball clarified. “You know what I’m saying? It’s not my job.”Well, actually, excuse me while I mumsplain here, but it very much is your job. A baby doesn’t care that you signed a five-year contract extension worthup to $260min 2023. Parenting is a 24/7 commitment no matter how much money you make.Ball and Montana (and, presumably, a team of hired help) are obviously free to share domestic duties however suits them. Nobody expects a professional athlete to be as hands-on as a parent with a more flexible schedule.But going on TV and boasting about how you don’t change diapers? That’s an extremely outdated look. A 1982 study based on fathers in Britain found43% of fathershad never changed a nappy (as diapers are called in the UK). By 2000, that figure had dropped to 3%.Meanwhile, the average time US dads spend caring for their offspring daily has quadrupled over the past 50 years and about 85% of dads say parenthood is one of the most important aspects of their identity. Being a hands-off dad is now very last century.Still, even though modern fathers are doing a lot more, they’re still held to different standards than mothers. Imagine if a female athlete said changing diapers wasn’t her job: the rightwing pitchforks would be instantly out for her.It doesn’t matter how accomplished a woman is in her career; there’s still an expectation that her identity as a mother comes first. Particularly under the Trump administration, which is trying to foster a whole new generation of tradwives.Ball is only 25, so I’ll give him some grace. But I hope the backlash to his comments makes him realize that only complete losers boast about not changing diapers. A case in point:Donald Trump.“I would never ask to change [Barron],”the president toldthe New York Post in 2006. “Melania probably wouldn’t let me. I’d just do it wrong.” Asked whether he’d ever changed the diapers of his four other children, he said he probably had, but couldn’t remember.There’s a phrase frequently applied to men who pretend they’re incapable of doing basic domestic chores in order to wriggle out of them:weaponized (or strategic) incompetence. In Trump’s case, however, it may not actually be weaponized incompetence. It may just be incompetence.Which leads me to present a modest proposal. In the future, we should apply the Diaper Test™ to any man in the running for a high-powered job. If he can’t clean up his own child’s mess, he’s sure to make a mess of the job.Gamblers were betting on the outcome of the Cornell 7 sexual assault caseTwo days after a New York district attorney reopened the alleged Cornell University gang-rape case, the Polymarket gambling app allowed people to bet on the results of the investigation.According to Defector, Polymarket initially said nothing about why they were letting people bet on a traumatic sexual assault case, before issuing a PR statement full of corporate gobbledegook. “Markets bring objective, data-driven insight into how a matter like this is moving through the legal system, on a topic that deserves far more transparency and honest attention,” the statement read. Monetizing sexual assault is feminism now, apparently! Polymarket then reconsidered this position. After about three weeks of being up, the bet has been removed from the platform.Trump has a weirdly homoerotic midterm strategyAdam Gabbattexamines whythe president keeps “offering unsolicited, and increasingly unhinged, assessments of men’s bodies”.Poland’s parliament votes to slightly ease abortion lawsIn 2021, anear-total banon abortion took effect in Poland. Now the lower house of parliament hasapproved two billsthat would remove some criminal penalties for people who help women access abortion care and would allow a termination if there was a foetal abnormality. While that sounds like a small step in the right direction, the draft laws are likely to bevetoedby the conservative president, Karol Nawrocki. Women are now protesting on the streets in more than 20 Polish cities demanding access to legal abortions.Liechtenstein prince uses veto to quash abortion accessIt’s not just Poland that seems determined to be at odds with the rest of Europe on abortion. The hereditary prince of Liechtenstein, who will never need an abortion himself, hasused his vetofor the first time to kill off a bill that would have eased the country’s draconian laws.The death toll since the October ‘ceasefire’ in Gaza rises to 1,538Israeli attacks killed yet another child in Gazathis weekas the territory faces a new risk of famine.Trump and JD Vance are defending an ad weaponizing sexual abuseDemocrat Amy Acton is running against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to be governor of Ohio. It’s a tight race and Ramaswamy clearly thinks he can’t win on merit because he’s stooped to putting out arevolting attack adfeaturing Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, whose former husband has been accused of sexually abusing Acton when she was a child. In the ad, Arthur accuses Acton of lying “her entire life”. There’s been bipartisan backlash to the ad, but JD Vance has mounted a vigorousdefense, saying he’s “disgusted” by fellow Republicans who have criticized it. On Thursday, Trump also endorsed the ad, calling it “very powerful”.The week in pawtriarchyRemember when the Nordic phenomenon ofslow TVwas being touted as the antidote to the frenetic nature of modern life? Well it’s back! A 24-hour Finnish TV show that follows the progress of a dog and her six newborn puppies has become a massive hit. The show has an accompanying 24-hour webcam,Pentulive(Puppy Live), which is very soothing. I recommend tuning in whenever you feel like the world’s gone barking mad.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsParents and parentingThe Week in PatriarchyBasketballFamilySexual harassmentGamblingJD VanceDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: As Trump’s time runs out, this could be his most dangerous legacy: a world divided into three | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Content: Traditional Russian dolls on sale at a souvenir shop in St Petersburg, Russia.Photograph: Dmitri Lovetsky/APView image in fullscreenTraditional Russian dolls on sale at a souvenir shop in St Petersburg, Russia.Photograph: Dmitri Lovetsky/APOpinionDonald TrumpAs Trump’s time runs out, this could be his most dangerous legacy: a world divided into threeSteve BloomfieldWe’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystalliseSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 07.11 EDTShareIn the final two years of a US presidency, when Congress has been lost, approval ratings have sunk like a stone and their party has started to think about who’s coming next, the person occupying the Oval Office can feel their power draining away. Domestic legislation, particularly in an era where bipartisan cooperation is almost nonexistent, grinds to a halt. But as the days tick by until the end, and as presidents begin to think about their legacy, there is one part of the job where they still have power: the rest of the world.In the final weeks of his presidency in 1992 George HW Bush sent 28,000 American troops to Somalia to help end a famine. For Bill Clinton, it was a quixotic attempt to bring peace to the Middle East by ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Barack Obama restored diplomatic ties with Cuba, making a historic visit to Havana, as well as a final, successful push on the Iran nuclear deal.In 10 days,Donald Trumpwill enter his own twilight zone. He is almost certain to lose control of the House and it’s not impossible he will face a Democratic Senate too. Any hopes of passing domestic policy – not that he’s bothered with that much during his first two years – will disappear. Instead, he will face a series of investigations that could lead, once again, to impeachment.On the world stage, however, it will be a different story. And unlike Bush senior, Clinton and Obama, his ambitions won’t be peaceful. The first two years of his second term have been catastrophic; the final two could be even worse.Once the midterms are over, the US isunderstood to be planning to restart its unwinnable war with Iran, already carrying out exercises with the Israeli military and withdrawing diplomats from the region. Trump’s sellout of Ukraine is well under way. In the past week he has argued that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine”, while his envoy Steve Witkoff met with Vladimir Putin in Moscow,praising him in a televised meetingas a “humanitarian…and I salute that, I commend you and I thank you again.”On top of a reckless war in the Middle East and appeasement in Europe, the shadow of a new world order is emerging, which Trump will relentlessly pursue in his final years. Putin has proposed a summit between himself, Trump and China’sXi Jinping, to be held in China next month.The Trump-Putin love story’s next chapter: selling out Ukraine | Sidney BlumenthalRead moreSuch an unprecedented meeting, were it to take place, would have potentially devastating consequences for the rest of us. The three leaders have ambitions to transform the way the world is governed, essentially dividing it into spheres of influence. One summit wouldn’t turn an idea into reality, but it would send us down a very dangerous path. In Europe, it would have an impact beyond Ukraine if the US refused to help protect nations threatened byRussia. In east Asia, the withdrawal of the American security blanket would cause enormous problems for Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, as well as Australia.We’ve talked a lot about the end of the west over the past two years – this feels like a moment when many of those fears will crystalise.The Trump administration’s ambition to divide the world into spheres and side with dictators over democrats has long been evident. Last year’sNational Security Strategywas deeply critical of the US’s traditional allies in Europe and east Asia. But it was what it didn’t say that was most shocking. Both Russia and China avoided direct criticism. In six paragraphs describing the threat to Taiwan, China was not mentioned once. Elsewhere in the document, China was actually praised as “rich and powerful … us[ing] its wealth and power to its considerable advantage.” The section on Russia’s war in Ukraine failed to mention how it started and did not suggest that Putin should be defeated; instead it focused on how the US could help Europe and Russia mend their relationship. The 33-page document discussed the importance of the US controlling the western hemisphere, but made clear that so long as the US still had economic dominance, it cared little whether other parts of the world are protected. “The affairs of other countries,” it stated, “are our concern only if their activities directly threaten our interests.” For too long, it argued, America’s allies had “suck[ed] us into conflicts and controversies central to their interests but peripheral or irrelevant to our own”.For Putin, this is a success almost three decades in the making. He has long viewed American support for democracy in eastern Europe and central Asia as “interference” in Russia’s backyard. Now he has a US president who agrees. Trump has also placed Putin on a far higher pedestal than Russia’s economy and its technological prowess deserves.Xi, too, has welcomed the US’s rhetorical retreat from east Asia, particularly if it allowsChinagreater maritime control in the East China Sea and South China Sea. World opinion on China has dramatically improved as that of the US has slid. As Chrystia Freeland, a former Canadian foreign minister, put it this week, “there has not been a president who has been more beneficial for China than Donald Trump”.At stake is not merely territorial control. All three governments see the possibility of increasing economic ties. For the US and China, the bigger issues are future control of economic supply chains and technology platforms, while Russia’s fossil fuel resources are also a factor. All three are key players in the next space race, both in terms of commercial and military control. If these three nations begin to work together, at the expense of Europe and the rest of the world, it will fundamentally change the nature of geopolitics. A decade ago, talk of a multipolar world was based around the idea of the US, China and the European Union as the three most powerful blocs. Somehow, Brussels has been replaced by Moscow.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGiorgia Meloni is Italy’s great political survivor. Could one man be about to bring her down? | Riccardo AlcaroRead moreUntil now, the rest of the west has – on the whole – tried to muddle through. Nato still exists on paper, G7 and G20 summits may be chaotic but they still take place. Optimists in the Foreign Office point out that Trump turned up to the UN general assembly and his administration is still deeply involved in the UN’s day to day activities.Mark Carney spoke of a “rupture” and warned the old post-cold war world was not coming back, but despite warm words from Emmanuel Macron, and renewed discussion about how Europe can protect itself without the US, there is still a sense that everyone is waiting for Trump’s time in office to end. A Great Powers summit makes this harder to ignore.While US presidents seek foreign policy success in their final months, history suggests they rarely find it.Clinton’s Camp David talks collapsedafter Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat were unable to reach an agreement. Bush would argue that his initial intervention in Somalia eased a famine, but it ended in humiliation.A botched raid on a warlordled to the deaths of 18 US soldiers and several hundred Somalis. Obama’s diplomacy in Cuba and Iran succeeded, but were both promptly ripped up by Donald Trump.Trump will get his photoshoot – and maybe that’s all he wants – but there is no guarantee that this unsavoury troika becomes a permanent geopolitical fixture. Trump’s foreign policy has divided his Maga movement and has shocked traditional conservatives. The Wall Street Journal editorial board described the proposed summit as “arguably the worst idea of the second Trump term”. A President Vance or Rubio might be less willing to throw in their lot with dictators; a President Ossoff or Ocasio-Cortez certainly won’t.But just because Trump won’t win, doesn’t mean that the US won’t lose. He will be arriving in Shenzhen at the weakest moment in his presidency. An 80-year-old lame duck leader fated to limp towards the finish line unable to pass any legislation and threatened by two chaotic years of investigations into his alleged corruption. Opposite him will be two authoritarian leaders in their early 70s who believe the only thing preventing them from ruling their nations for another two decades is death. Indeed, giventheir “hot mic” discussionsabout longevity drugs last year, perhaps they both believe they can rule for even longer.If it goes ahead, this summit will bring Putin back in from the cold and reiterate Xi’s position as a global leader who cannot be ignored.The image of the three leaders will come to define this era when the rules-based international order was torn apart and a new, uncertain period began to form.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the ObserverExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS politicsXi JinpingVladimir PutinUnited NationsRussiaChinacommentShareReuse this content

title: The tragic events of the past week have shown Australians who we are – and it’s a long way from our image of ourselves | Julianne Schultz | The Guardian
description: How can we attempt to understand the climate in which the hideous alleged attack on Helen Haines occurred?
Author: Julianne Schultz
Headline: How can we attempt to understand the climate in which the hideous alleged attack on Helen Haines occurred?
Content: Floral tributes outside the office of Australian MP Helen Haines, who was critically wounded in an alleged attack outside her electoral office in Wangaratta on 21 October.Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFloral tributes outside the office of Australian MP Helen Haines, who was critically wounded in an alleged attack outside her electoral office in Wangaratta on 21 October.Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionHelen HainesThe tragic events of the past week have shown Australians who we are – and it’s a long way from our image of ourselvesJulianne SchultzHow can we attempt to understand the climate in which the hideous alleged attack on Helen Haines occurred?Sat 24 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTShareImmediately after news of the alleged attack on Helen Haines was revealed, the prime minister and others werequick to say,this is not who we Australians are, this is not the way we behave.The data from the Australian federal police, Asio and theexperience of individual MPssuggested this may in fact be what a disappointingly significant number of us have become over the past decade.Nonetheless it was a comforting and reassuring message, reinforced by the outpouring of goodwill and best wishes for the critically injured MP.Australian democracy is usually peaceful. But there’s a homegrown history of political violence | Joshua Black and Frank BongiornoRead moreBut these words had hardly entered the public domain before the backlash began online.The same thing should happen to more women; the perpetrator was a political activist,and on and on, filling the comments space in platform after platform.Other female MPs, their faces stretched tight with grief and streaked with tears, told of the threats they had received, of letters pushed under their doors, of angry people, usually men, arriving in their offices to shout abuse and make threats, to watching over their shoulder as they walked back to their car park or office at night – and of course the endless stream of online invective with expletives, caps and exclamation marks.Even the governor general, Sam Mostyn, only the second woman to hold that office, commented afterreceiving abusive commentsfollowing her call for kindness and respect. “Women across the country know that there are certain things that are reserved for women … that go to our gender and they are often vicious and just despicable.”At this point one can’t presume to guess details of what may have been in the mind of the man who has been charged with the alleged attack that led to Haines’ grievous injuries. That will be for the court to determine.double quotation markOver time the virus has mutated, increased its lethality and infected manyBut we can attempt to understand the climate in which this hideous attack occurred. It is a human and interpersonalclimate that has been heating for years– and just like the real heating climate, not one with easy, cost-free ways of cooling.This climate won’t be on trial, but it forms a backdrop that touches us all and needs to be addressed head-on.In this broader context it is demonstrable that angry, unstable men particularly hate capable, intelligent and gracious women.By contrast, good men adore them.Personally, I hold the “leader of the free world” to account for fostering and enabling an environment in which the once unthinkable has almost become the new normal.Once it wouldn’t have mattered all that much if the leader of a country in another hemispherelacked characterand said outrageous things. But in the global village it matters a great deal.Positive, personal relations between people have been undermined with vicious words and actions, and trust in institutions corroded with lies and disinformation.The thin end of this wedge was a dagger directed at women, the original “other” since Eve picked the apple in the Garden of Eden. That a person of such statureshould wield itadded weight.This virus was unleashed at precisely the moment when after decades of struggle, gender equality was becoming a reality, here, and in many other countries.Women and their allies, at least initially, successfully fought back with huge rallies and legal action. But others did all they could to put women back in home-shaped boxes, ditch witches with too much power and belittle and demean the rest. Over time the virus has mutated, increased its lethality and infected many. Even good men have found it hard to successfully push back and protect both their sons and their daughters.The consequences are dire. From increasing rates ofdomestic violenceand murder, to tolerance of intolerable treatment of the most vulnerable, and increasing communal and political violence online andin life.Female political leaders areparticular targets.The vector carrying the virus that has done so much damage is a global form of “communication” that amplifiesanger and outrage, removes national control over public discourse and corrodes humanity and decency. Click by click.I knew one of us could get hurt eventually. I never thought it would be my friend Helen Haines | Zoe DanielRead moreThis is what the new normal looks like. It is a long way from our image of ourselves. It is a new normal manufactured by a system of “communication” that amplifies hate and anger, that profits from engagement and is unconcerned about consequences.It has been brewing for a while.While the transmission medium is dressed in the clothes offreedom of speech, it is hard to combat. But as the case settled betweenMeta and dozens of USstates showed, this is not about freedom of expression, it is about hateful engagementby design. As Aaron Sorkin’s movieThe Social Reckoningshows in painful detail, this has little to do with free expression and everything to do with maximising profits through poisonous engagement.In Australia we still couch talk about what happens on these platforms in terms of freedom of speech (even though we lack it as a full constitutional right).Saying we need to be nicer, do better, is important, but not enough. Serious regulation and penalties are essential.In the 1940s American media leaders were warned that unless they lifted their game, stopped spreading lies, building up divisive and dishonourable politicians, spiking public opinion to pump profits, they might be subjected to draconian regulation – thateven the first amendmentmight be at risk.The threat was sufficient for them to respond by building professional practices that sought toraise, not lower, the level of civilisation.It needs to happen again with their successors. Public and political communication is not just another business; transmission of the virus must be stopped.Explore more on these topicsHelen HainesOpinionAustralian security and counter-terrorismAustralian politicsSocial mediaViolence against women and girlscommentShareReuse this content

title: Fine ‘headphone dodgers’ if you will, but to really tackle antisocial behaviour, Britain should look to Japan | Emily Bratt | The Guardian
description: Working in Japanese schools, I saw how teaching young people civic pride creates adults with consideration for others, says freelance journalist Emily Bratt
Author: Emily Bratt
Headline: Working in Japanese schools, I saw how teaching young people civic pride creates adults with consideration for others, says freelance journalist Emily Bratt
Content: ‘Some loudcasters are simply oblivious.’Photograph: Drazen_/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Some loudcasters are simply oblivious.’Photograph: Drazen_/Getty ImagesOpinionPublic transportFine ‘headphone dodgers’ if you will, but to really tackle antisocial behaviour, Britain should look to JapanEmily BrattWorking in Japanese schools, I saw how teaching young people civic pride creates adults with consideration for othersSat 24 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 08.11 EDTShareThere are two types of people who listen to music in public: those who wear headphones and those who … are a word I probably can’t use here. “Loudcasting” – playing audio, watching videos or talking on speakerphone in public spaces – is a form of antisocial behaviour that driveseight in 10of people in the UK crazy, and I’m gladAndy Burnham is oneof those eight. But while I welcome his policy to fine “headphone dodgers”, I’m not convinced it will solve the problem.This behaviour isn’t only a nuisance, but a grave indicator of a deeper societal issue: the erosion of empathy. You can’t legislate civic pride into an individualistic culture where feelings of social disconnection are widespread.From 2019 to 2021 I lived in Japan, where keeping the peace is paramount and you can be reprimanded just for talking on the bus. When I returned to England, I felt shock and shame at how we treat one another and our public spaces. I still do. We watch our dogs defecate in the street andwalk away. We use public bathrooms as if we’re feral two-year-olds. We inflict the soundtrack of our mindless social-media scrolling on an entire train carriage.Time’s up for tinny tunes and blaring football highlights. London’s headphone cavalry has arrived | Hugh MuirRead moreJapanese society is not without its flaws; I often chafed at the level of deference I witnessed. But living there also highlighted to me just how selfish we can be in Britain. Last week, I saw someone had smeared dog poo into the communal carpeted entrance of their own block of flats. Some on the far right love to cast other cultures as primitive, but I think we need to look at ourselves.We could learn from Japan. As a broadly collectivist society, it favours social harmony and group responsibility. One guiding principle ismeiwaku wo kakenai: the idea that you should avoid inconveniencing others.I worked in Japanese state schools and was astonished when students as young as five diligently began stacking chairs and clearing apparatus as sports day wrapped up. Nobody told them to. Additionally, Japanese schools don’t completely rely on cleaners: the students sweep the halls, wipe down desks, empty bins and even disinfect and scrub the bathrooms. This cleaning practice, a component oftokkatsu(special activities), forms part of a wider approach to holistic education and teaches children personal responsibility for, and pride in, their environment.It’s important to add that a teenager is still a teenager, no matter the country. It’s a myth that all Japanese children are innately disciplined perfect little angels. But the wider impact of these social ethics is obvious. Crime rates in Japan are (comparatively) low, public spaces are meticulously maintained and litter is a rarity. It’snota myth that Japanese streets are so clean you could lick them. Lick an English street and, bam! Dysentery.View image in fullscreenJapanese children clean their classroom after a lesson.Photograph: Aflo Co., Ltd./AlamyThe UK government’s crackdown on content-blaring can only work in conjunction with a wider effort. First, fines have to actually be imposed by those in authority – and they need to feel safe and incentivised to do so. Train managers have been hot on calling out fare dodgers for years (one made me cry when I was 19 for not having my student railcard, such was his wrath). Now they need to bring the same resolve to headphone dodgers. Burnham’s policy states that drivers would not be expected to enforce such rules – it’s a job for safety officers or the police. But unless someone is there to enforce the rules in the moment, the policy becomes little more than an empty threat.Second, we need to rebuild social norms so that consideration for others is instinctive. The word etiquette seems antiquated, but given thatalmost half of usin the UK play content from our phones without headphones – and that this behaviour bothers most of us – etiquette education is still necessary. Maybe, so we don’t feel we’re in a Jane Austen novel, we call it something else. Perhaps in schools, it’s civic responsibility class, or lessons in caring about others, or simply learning how to not be a twat. It doesn’t require major educational reform. Copying Japan’s approach to school-cleaning, for example, could be a good (and easy) place to start.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe onus, of course, isn’t only on schools – parents have to lead by example. But imagine the ripple effect if British schoolchildren were given the responsibility of caring for their classrooms and corridors.Unfortunately, there’s also a deeper issue. Some loudcasters are simply oblivious, but others are deliberately rage-baiting. The latter is a product of a disaffected society, which Burnham’s fines by themselves could exacerbate. Nobody likes being told off, but especially not angry people.We don’t need to become Japan. But in an increasingly divided world, consideration for others and respect for our surroundings are what can still hold us together.Emily Bratt is a freelance journalistExplore more on these topicsPublic transportOpinionTransport policyTransportJapanAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: What essentials to keep, what rubbish to get rid of? Burnham, Badenoch, Farage don’t know either  | Robert Hutton | The Guardian
description: After a fractious week, they probably agree that no one at all needs Liz Truss’s new book, but then the political housekeeping decisions get much harder, says author and journalist Robert Hutton
Author: Robert Hutton
Headline: After a fractious week, they probably agree that no one at all needs Liz Truss’s new book, but then the political housekeeping decisions get much harder, says author and journalist Robert Hutton
Content: Kemi Badenoch at Oil States Industries in Aberdeen, 5 June 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch at Oil States Industries in Aberdeen, 5 June 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOpinionPoliticsWhat essentials to keep, what rubbish to get rid of? Burnham, Badenoch, Farage don’t know eitherRobert HuttonAfter a fractious week, they probably agree that no one at all needs Liz Truss’s new book, but then the political housekeeping decisions get much harderSat 24 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTShareWhat are you stockpiling? Wes Streeting says we needwater and food to last 72 hoursin case of national emergency, as well as wind-up radios so that we can check in on how the apocalypse is developing in Ambridge. Personally, I have a two-week supply of jokes about the government that I can draw upon even as the zombies break down my front door.Andy Burnham, far from stockpiling, is busy chucking stuff out. This week Labour’s much cherished commitment not to allow new drilling for oil and gas in the North Seawent into the skipround the back of Downing Street, where it lies next to a complete set of European Union red lines, a plan for digital ID and a signed photograph of Peter Mandelson.Tory frontbenchers waved their hands in amazement as the prime minister explained that the government is now in favour of dashing for gas. The argument Burnham was using aboutsecurity of supplywas exactly the one they’d been throwing at the government for months.ToKemi Badenoch, it’s a sign that she’s winning the argument. But then the Tory leader’s self-confidence is so total that she sees the rising of the sun each morning as a sign that she’s winning the argument. A more thoughtful opposition leader might wonder what she will have left to throw at Burnham after he’s finished jettisoning the unpopular and hard-to-explain bits of policy that Keir Starmer left cluttering up Downing Street.Badenoch is having her own clear-out. All of us do this when we move into a new place and find that the previous occupant left something hideous behind: a phallic ornament in the garden, for instance, or a list of approved candidates featuring Grant Shapps.Of course, as anyone who’s spent a weekend driving to the local tip knows, there’s always something so toxic the council simply refuses to take it off your hands. In Badenoch’s case, it’sLiz Truss, who has a new book outnext week on how everything was someone else’s fault.That’s a line that the Tory leader has decided to recycle, as she bags up any sense of responsibility for the government in which she was a cabinet minister and leaves it out for the binmen along with a pile of “Mel Stride for chancellor” posters.On Tuesday she was asked why, if cutting taxes and welfare spending is so easy, her party didn’t do either when it was last in power. “Well, I didn’t raise those taxes,” she replied, explaining that she had disagreed with the government she was part of, but had decided to keep this to herself. Courage takes many forms.The effect of all these unwanted old positions hitting the Westminster landfill is that the electoral battleground is clearing nicely. We find ourselves in the unusual situation that both Burnham and Badenoch agree on the argument they want to have: was Margaret Thatcher right?One party that is definitely stockpiling is Reform, which continues to lay in supplies of nasty ideas about race, as though there was the slightest danger they might run out. The party’s headquarters has now been so thoroughly turned over that it’s an open question whether there’s anyone on the staff who isn’t an undercover reporter. But if you want to know what Reform thinks, you really don’t need to spend six months hiding a camera inside your lapel. Just listen to what the party’s MPs are saying.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDanny Kruger, whodefected from the Torieslast year, has usually been seen as a genial soul, certainly relative to the Slytherin tendency that is Robert Jenrick and Andrew Rosindell. But introducing Nigel Farage on Tuesday, he made a determined effort to prove that his “nice but dim” image is only half right. “The problem isn’t with individual Muslims,” he told his audience. No, the problem is Muslims as a group, “who are taught by their clerics that their loyalty isn’t to the United Kingdom, but to the global Islamic community”. It’s an argument that was applied to Catholics 200 years ago and to Jews 100 years ago: you just can’t trust them.Farage is too canny to say this stuff himself, and as an election approaches, he may find himself disavowing it, just as he’s distanced himself from his great buddy Donald Trump. But the trouble with stockpiles of the wrong stuff is that they can be hard to clear out at short notice. Just ask the Liberal Democrats: it’s weeks since they put Ed Davey on Freecycle, and they haven’t had even a nibble of interest.Robert Hutton is an author and journalistExplore more on these topicsPoliticsOpinionKemi BadenochAndy BurnhamNigel FaragecommentShareReuse this content

title: At Aberfan, I saw fathers digging for their missing children. And the lessons society should have learned, it hasn’t | John Humphrys | The Guardian
description: Each of those 144 deaths was entirely avoidable, but nobody was held to account. We still don’t know how to get justice for ordinary people, says journalist John Humphrys
Author: John Humphrys
Headline: Each of those 144 deaths was entirely avoidable, but nobody was held to account. We still don’t know how to get justice for ordinary people, says journalist John Humphrys
Content: Rescue workers digging in the wreckage of the school in Aberfan, 21 October 1966.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenRescue workers digging in the wreckage of the school in Aberfan, 21 October 1966.Photograph: PAOpinionAberfan disasterAt Aberfan, I saw fathers digging for their missing children. And the lessons society should have learned, it hasn’tJohn HumphrysEach of those 144 deaths was entirely avoidable, but nobody was held to account. We still don’t know how to get justice for ordinary peopleSat 24 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 12.41 EDTShareAberfan taught us a lot. Mostly, of course, that those in power cannot be trusted. Correction: must not be trusted.Too sweeping?I might have thought so until 60 years ago this week when I stood alongside mothers weeping and praying as they watched their husbands digging for the bodies of their children who lay crushed beneath the ruins oftheir little school.The parents’ faces were black, save for the streaks of white from their tears. Two hours earlier those men had been digging coal from deep beneath the ground. With the coal, of course, came the waste that would have to be separated to become the great mounds that disfigured every mining valley.My best friend’s father was a miner. I had been a reporter on the local paper and I once went down the mine to watch him at work. I begged to return to the surface after no more than an hour of breathing in the deadly coal dust. I tried to imagine every working hour trapped in that living hell and failed.This, surely, was the most dangerous and demanding job in the land. Few miners escaped serious lung damage. I never once spoke to a Valleys mother who wanted her son to follow his father down the pit. But what I witnessed that day was something even the toughest miners, let alone their wives, could not have dreamed of in their darkest nightmares.Every so often, one of the diggers would shout for silence. He thought he had heard a child cry out. We stood and prayed, hardly daring to breathe. Sometimes our prayers were answered. I watched a little girl handed to a policeman. She was unconscious but, thank God, she was breathing. She would live. Most did not.I did my best to tell the outside world what was happening from a phone in the local pub overlooking the school. But what I failed to report until many hours later was the terrible truth that this was a disaster that need never have happened.Correction: a disaster thatshouldnever have happened.In Wales, we’re one more flood away from another disaster like Aberfan | Aaron ThierryRead moreWhat every miner in that village and every miner’s wife had always known was that the massive waste tip that was to destroy their lives should never have been built. Or at least, should never have been built on that spot. This was not one of those disasters that might eventually be written off as part of the price society was reconciled to paying if we were to enjoy the benefits of what we once called “black gold”.Every miner knew he faced danger from the moment he stepped into the cage that would drop him a couple of thousand feet below ground. Until the nightmare of Aberfan, the most painful job I was ordered to do as a teenage reporter on the Merthyr Express was knocking on the door of a miner’s cottage a few hours after his wife had been told she was now a widow.The first time I was scared. Surely I would be ordered by the newly bereaved widow to clear off? But I learned quickly that they almost always wanted to talk about their dead husbands. And there was seldom any anger. They had always known – even if it was never talked about – that he might never come home. Accidents were inevitable.But what happened in Aberfan was no accident.View image in fullscreenA young John Humphrys reporting from Aberfan in October 1966.Photograph: Archif Ddarlledu Cymru/Wales Broadcast Archive/ITV WalesIt was the result of grotesque indifference on the part ofthe men who ran the National Coal Board(NCB) and were responsible for the location of every waste tip of every nationalised colliery in the land. Above all, of the man who chaired that board: Alfred Robens.Such was his unbelievable disregard for the hell that had been visited on that little Welsh village that he couldn’t even spare a few hours to share their grief. While they were still digging through the filth that had choked the lives from so many children, His lordship was being chauffeured to a new university for a ceremony where he was to be made chancellor. And the year of the disaster, he also accepted an honorary degree for his services to the mining industry.His “services”? Has ever the English language been more abused?What Lord Robens had always known – if only because he would have been briefed by his team of senior officials – was that to build a massive tip on that particular spot on the hillside was the equivalent of lighting a bonfire in a dynamite factory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI can state that as an absolute fact after all these years, because even as those brave miners and their wives were trying so desperately to deal with their grief, they were showing me copies of the letters they had written over and over again warning the NCB that it was criminally reckless to site the tip on that spot.There was a simple reason that even an ignoramus such as me could understand. It rains a lot in the Welsh valleys and there are many springs beneath the surface of the hills. The spot the officials chose for the tip was notorious for its springs. But it was directly above the village. And Pantglas junior school.Local journalism made me what I am today. Without it, we’ll all be the poorer | John HumphrysRead moreEvery morning two miners would trudge up the hillside of their own volition to examine the state of the tip. When they saw what was happening on 21 October 1966, they turned and ran down the hillside. But it was too late. Within minutes 100,000 tonnes of coal waste had hit the school at 80mph, killing almost everyone in its path.It took a little more than a year for Robens and his henchmen to face a form of justice. I sat through the public inquiry when the scale of the disgrace was unveiled, day after agonising day, and Robens was the final witness.The inquiry chairman treated his protestations of ignorance and innocence with richly deserved contempt and I remember leaping into my car to deliver a live broadcast with the sense that justice had finally been delivered.But had it? Have we really learned anything as a result of Aberfan? The horror of the Grenfell Tower inferno suggests not. The inquiry found thatthe deaths of all 72 people in 2017 were “entirely avoidable”, resulting from systemic failures, deregulation and corporate dishonesty. It added: “There is still a great deal to learn.”True, the last of the collieries in the Welsh valleys has long since gone, but can it really be true that no one deserved to face charges for criminal negligence?What is true is the extraordinary spirit of those who suffered so much and, indeed, of those who survived.I remember going to the home of a little girl who’d been one of the survivors and asking her mother why she hadn’t sent her to the new school. She answered with almost chilling simplicity: “Because I don’t want mothers who’ve lost their kiddies to see her in the street and be reminded of what they’ve lost.”John Humphrys presents The Odd Couple podcast with Matthew NormanExplore more on these topicsAberfan disasterOpinionWalescommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘It annoys people when I eat’: Siobhán McSweeney on perfect snacks, parental pressure – and the power of being ‘a delicious fatty’  | Siobhán McSweeney | The Guardian
description: The Derry Girls actor has always loved food, so who better to take over as the new presenter of the Guardian’s Comfort Eating podcast?
Author: Kitty Drake
Headline: The Derry Girls actor has always loved food, so who better to take over as the new presenter of the Guardian’s Comfort Eating podcast?
Content: Portrait: Jay Brooks/The GuardianThe Derry Girls actor has always loved food, so who better to take over as the new presenter of the Guardian’s Comfort Eating podcast?ByKitty DrakeSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSiobhán McSweeney is teaching me her preferred way to enjoy a packet of cheese and onion crisps. She has arranged two matching slabs of Cadbury’s Dairy Milk chocolate, two piles of Tayto crisps and two cans of Guinness on the table in front of us – and is issuing strict instructions. “Don’t swallow!” she booms theatrically, and I freeze, my mouth full of Taytos. The trick, McSweeney explains, is to get the crisps, chocolate and Guinness into your mouth at the same time, and then swill it all around a bit to make a kind of boozy, oniony soup. “See?” McSweeney is watching me carefully to check I am putting all the ingredients into my mouth in the correct order. “It’s delicious! Just delicious!”McSweeney burst into the public consciousness back in 2018 withDerry Girls, a comedy series about a group of Catholic schoolgirls, set against the background of the Troubles in 1990s Northern Ireland. McSweeney won a Bafta playing the girls’ headmistress, Sister Michael – a potty-mouthed, judo-loving nun – and can count Martin Scorsese as a fan. Asked for a TV recommendation during a panel discussion in 2022, thedirector name-checked Derry Girlsand then lifted his fist in the air in a kind of salute, exclaiming rapturously, “Those nuns!”I have spent so many hours watching McSweeney in character as Sister Michael that it is almost a shock to see her without a nun’s habit. We are meeting today, in a conference room in London, because McSweeney is taking over fromGrace Dent as the new host of the Guardian’s food podcast, Comfort Eating. I arrived at the interview with a multipack of Taytos, a family‑size Dairy Milk and two cans of Guinness in my bike bag, because McSweeney chose this concoction as her favourite snack when sheappeared on the podcastas a guest, back in 2021. She also told a story about eating a caterpillar that had fallen from her moth-infested ceiling into her stir‑fry, purely because she couldn’t be bothered to fish it out. “Listen: protein,” she says today, remembering that caterpillar. “Free protein where you can.”View image in fullscreenMcSweeney as Sister Michael in Derry Girls (above) and as Della Fry in Amandaland (below). Photographs: Peter Marley/Channel 4; Natalie Seery/ BBC/MermanPhotograph: Peter Marley/ Channel 4View image in fullscreenSince Derry Girls, the actor has made a habit of portraying slightly intimidating women. She plays the achingly sarcastic celebrity chef Della Fry inAmandaland, and hosts the Irish version of The Traitors, in which she commands a pack of wolfhounds and wears a lot of ruffs. But today, McSweeney’s short, silver‑grey hair is brushed back from her face and she is dressed casually, in trousers and a simple top. Sister Michael is always lolling back in her chair and surveying you sardonically across a desk – but the real McSweeney leans forward and asks a lot of questions.It is lunchtime, so I have brought a takeaway from the Indian restaurant Dishoom with me, as well as the Taytos. “I love doing this podcast because it annoys people when I eat,” McSweeney says, tucking into a fish curry. Part of the reason why she accepted the job as host of Comfort Eating, she explains, is because visibly enjoying her food – as a woman who is not stick-thin – is a kind of provocation. “They’ve been told that somebody like me should not feel good about themselves,” she says, grinning toothily at me. “Being a delicious fatty.”Ever since she first arrived at drama school, in the early 2000s, people have been telling McSweeney to lose weight. “Agents, casting directors, teachers” – McSweeney checks the list off for me now, almost breezily. “I have been different sizes but it’s never been an acceptable size,” she says. “‘Unruly’ I call it – there’s sort of an unruliness that has been forced upon my body that I don’t feel about it, but other people feel it’s unruly and it doesn’t behave.” All the other girls at her drama college were starving themselves, McSweeney remembers now. “They were starving in secondary school as well – it was the 90s! I don’t know how I managed to escape it.” She is grinning at me again. “I don’t think I have the willpower to not eat. I don’t really have much discipline.”It strikes me that continuing to like yourself and your body, in the face of such vicious scrutiny, is not so much a failure of will as its opposite – proof that McSweeney has a will of absolute iron. Responding to a particularly poisonous bout of online criticism of her looks back in 2023, McSweeney delivered a kind of masterclass in the art of self-worth, tweeting: “I’m really lovely. I like my hair. And I like food. And I’m not sorry I’m loud. I thought feminism fights for me to be loud. And my accent is gorgeous. My teeth are yellow and wonky that’s true. But I sorta don’t care. And sure are you perfect?”double quotation markI taught, I waitressed, I pulled pints, I went on the dole, I worked at music festivals. And I was shit at every single one of themView image in fullscreenPortrait: Jay Brooks/The GuardianMcSweeney says she wouldn’t even bother to respond to online abuse like that these days, because “it’s so insane now on social media. There is no honesty to it because we don’t know if they are bots or not.” But when I push her on the willpower point, and suggest that there is something inherently political about refusing to lose weight in her industry, she agrees with me. “I do get perverse pleasure in [responding to those] people who expect me to feel bad – by insulting me, by calling me ‘fat’ – by going, ‘And?’”McSweeney also credits her mother, who she describes as “the kind of mam who would be round the back having a cigarette reading Dostoevsky”, with teaching her to aspire to a version of womanhood that wasn’t about appealing to men. “She wasn’t interested in me having boyfriends that much – she was, like, men will come, men will go; it’s fine.”“She just instilled this utter independence in me that didn’t centre in any way on a romantic relationship.” McSweeney pauses for a moment here, and seems to reconsider. “I mean … she wasn’t completely immune to all that. No one is strong enough to combat that, you know? And there would be a bit of, ‘Would you not brush your hair?” McSweeney is putting on her mother’s voice now and making pleading motions. “Please, just briefly! Just give it a quick brush!”Siobhán McSweeney grew up in County Cork, Ireland. Her father was a civil servant and her mother ran a cottage industry baking bread and cakes to sell to local shops, so the young Siobhán woke up every day to the smell of fresh soda bread. But, like any teenager worth their salt, McSweeney only wanted what she couldn’t have. “I went to the neighbours at one point because they had white sliced pan and red jam, and I thought, they’re so lucky, I have to go home now and have my freshly baked brown soda bread and my local butter,” she says. Her mother would make her school lunch every day with bread so fresh it was still warm. McSweeney remembers looking at her lunchbox and thinking “no one suffers more than me”.McSweeney knew from an early age that she wanted to act. She says that as a child she would wish on a star every night that she would become an actor, and tells me that she once spent an entire day at school pretending she was in a sitcom, pausing every now and again to play the laugh track in her head. “Or I’d look to the camera” – she mimes whirling her head around to lock eyes with an imaginary film crew. “How obnoxious! What a pest to be around.”double quotation markThe really sad thing about illness is that it often takes your appetite away – I want a lovely big bellyView image in fullscreenPortrait: Jay Brooks/The GuardianMcSweeney’s parents, however, had other plans for her. “We didn’t know anyone who was an actor. People on the telly didn’t look like me, didn’t sound like me,” she says. “My parents were, like, so what would that mean? You would do the panto once a year? You’re meant to work!”Speaking to the Irish Times in August, McSweeney said that anybody in the creative industries has “an angel and a devil on your shoulder, and the devil quite often is your parents going, ‘Don’t embarrass us.’” Did she feel as if her parents were embarrassed about her? “Yeah, absolutely yeah – it’s embarrassing to have your child standing up there making a tit of themselves,” she says. “Also, Ireland in the 80s, you blend in – the idea of standing out is quite … ” she tails off thoughtfully. “I think it was a protective idea – when you are in the open you are open to abuse and people taking advantage. All these things are true and I understand fully why any parent wouldn’t want that for their child.”McSweeney was virtually unknown before the release ofDerry Girls, which came out after her 40th birthday. She tells me that in a strange way she is pleased that fame came later in life for her, because she knows people “who have achieved success very early on in their career and their heads are turned”. But the years she spent trying and failing to get parts were gruelling. “I taught, I waitressed, I pulled pints, I went on the dole, I worked at music festivals,” she says. “And I was shit at every single one of them.”She remembers being particularly “shit” at the waitressing. “Sure, I didn’t know anything about food. I was pouring the wine the way my parents would drink wine, which would be wine right up to the top of the glass, and I didn’t know about al dente,” she says. “I thought, who is this Al Dente?”There was a point in the 2010s when she considered giving up acting completely. “I hadn’t worked in over a year and I had just got a litany of nos,” she remembers. “And now it’s getting harder and harder for not-rich people to be an actor.” McSweeney had received grants from the EU and a scholarship to study drama at the Central School of Speech and Drama – and that kind of funding literally doesn’t exist any more. “I get really panicky thinking about the other Siobháns who don’t get what they’re meant to do,” she says, and her face is unusually serious for a moment – but then she looks at me and her eyes begin to twinkle. “I mean it should be better, it should be a bit more useful than being a clown – but, you know, it’s what I’m meant to do.”Part of the struggle when she was being rejected at auditions was the lack of decent roles available for women. In previous interviews, McSweeney has said that casting directors explicitly told her that even though she was the funniest person in the audition room, they were going to give the part to a “prettier, younger, less funny” woman. “I graduated into a world where I really hoped somebody had a girlfriend because there was no way on earth a programme was going to centre on a woman,” she says to me now. But she wouldn’t even be in the running for the girlfriend part because “they wanted somebody who was more ‘girlfriend material’, ie, more acceptable – so, bland and pretty”.McSweeney says she would never be considered for the main character, “always the satellite”. She rolls her eyes. “And now I’m the mother.”McSweeney tells me that sheis deliberately taking on more presenting work because properly meaty, complex acting roles for women on TV are still so rare. As well as The Traitors Ireland, McSweeney hostsThe Great Pottery Throw Down.She landed the job after an appearance on a Great British Bake Off festive special in which she had a meltdown over making a trifle and ended up sitting on a bench with Sandi Toksvig, drinking champagne (“They went, that’s who we want”).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWith presenter Sandi Toksvig in the 2020 Great Festive Bake Off (above) and on the set of The Great Pottery Throw Down in 2023 (below). Photographs: Mark Bourdillon/Love ProductionsView image in fullscreenMcSweeney is also an acclaimed theatre actor. She played opposite her Derry Girls co-star Nicola Coughlan last year inThe Playboy of the Western Worldat the National Theatre, andsays that being onstage is what she has always enjoyed the most (she remembers being a child and “seeing red curtains on the telly and having a funny feeling in my belly”). But presenting is “work I find interesting – and it also pays more than the theatre”, she says, with characteristic honesty.Presenting jobs pay better than TV shows do, too – even the most successful ones. McSweeneyhas said publicly“I think I got 40 quid” in residuals when Derry Girlssold to Netflix. The programme has beenviewed for a total of 17.3m hourson the platform. Can that figure possibly be true? McSweeney nods enthusiastically. “When Netflix bought it we got fuck all!”When she was 27, McSweeney lost her mother, who never saw her daughter succeed as an actor. In herBafta acceptance speech, which has been viewed 467,000 times on YouTube, McSweeney told a story about how, as her mother lay dying, she pleaded with her to retrain as a teacher. “If she could see me now, winning a Bafta for playing a teacher,” she said, wearing a red vinyl dress and laughing, lifting her bare arm above her head to punch the air with her award: “Joke’s on you, Mam!”Would her mother feel pride, if she could see her daughter now? Or relief? “Er, relief,” says McSweeney, quick as a flash. Then she pauses for a second. “And I think she would like … I have a lot of opinions and she would like the way I speak about certain opinions.” In the same Bafta speech, McSweeney thanked the people of Derry, calling out the “ignorance and stupidity” of their political leadership, and she is a vocal critic of both English and Irish policy. Last year she was among those who campaigned successfully for the thousands of UK-based survivors of the work camps for “fallen women” that were in operation until the 90s in Ireland – known as the Magdalene laundries –to be given compensationwithout losing their rights to benefits.Would her mother have been proud of her feminism? “I think she would have been as close to proud as I would allow her to be,” says McSweeney, almost shyly. “And my dad, too … He was a natural feminist rather than a learned one – couldn’t think of anything I couldn’t do because of my gender, that would make no sense to him.”View image in fullscreenMcSweeney accepts the female performance in a comedy programme award for Derry Girls at the 2023 Bafta Television Awards.Photograph: Stuart Wilson/Bafta/Getty Images for BaftaHer father died in 2018. McSweeney moved back into the family home to live with him during his final illness. She drew on those experiences to makeSpudin 2024, a beautiful, surprisingly funny short film about a middle-aged woman caring for her dying father (McSweeney summarises the plot, with fabulous bluntness, as being about “an unfuckable woman who is rural and who cleans her daddy in a bath”).In one particularly tender scene, the father and the daughter, who is played by McSweeney herself, sit eating rice pudding together in front of the telly. Was that drawn from life? Was food a comfort for them both during that time? “The really sad thing about illness is that it often takes your appetite away,” she says. “I found it with my mum, too: her appetite went towards the end.” She tells me a story about sneaking a carbonara into the hospital to give to her mother, and the sadness of her not being able to eat it. “She was so beautiful and everybody’s mam is beautiful, but she ended up with a flat belly – and I was, like, what use is a flat belly? I want a lovely big belly.”Right at the end of Spud, McSweeney’s character finds out her father has died, and the camera closes in on her face. There is pain there but there is also something else: she is smiling slightly. It’s a great moment because it is so unexpected – and so honest. You can see in the daughter’s expression that, on some level, her father’s death has come as a relief. “I remember when my dad died, I was sort of manic for about six months because I suddenly was free, and I was grieving, but I was also free,” McSweeney says. In the immediate aftermath of her father’s death, McSweeney was bursting with ideas for new projects. “With no parents, you don’t feel like you’re letting the entire family down if you say or do something.”Comfort Eating with Grace Dent is backRead moreBetween 2018 and 2021, McSweeney went through a period that she has described – in a moment of understatement worthy of Sister Michael herself – as containing lots of “life stuff”. Her aunt, who had been a kind of surrogate mother to her, died the year after she lost her father. In 2019, her London flat burned down because of a faulty plug adaptor. Then, in 2021, in the middle of filming a Kathy Burke-directed crime drama,Holding, she broke her leg so badly that at one point the doctors thought they would have to amputate it.How did she cope? “We place romantic and biological relationships at the heart of our sort of experience,” says McSweeney, but it was her friends who got her through it. She tells me that when she was struggling the most, she became furious with one of her friends and accused him of talking about her behind her back with the rest of the group. “I was, like, ‘Are you all talking about me?’” She puts her hands on her hips here and mimes outrage, and then she switches characters so she can play her friend’s role: “And he was, like, ‘Yeah! We’remeantto do that! We care about you! We’re making sure you’re OK, we’re asking each other, how do you think she’s doing?’”McSweeney talks about this being a moment of realisation. She saw that friendship has an elasticity and a resilience that no romantic relationship can ever really have. “You have a fight with your boyfriend and that could destroy the relationship, right?” she says. “You have a fight with your friend, you go into your respective corners, you sulk. You call other friends. You bitch about each other. Then you go back, you have a coffee, you get drunk!”McSweeney’s friends are annoyed with her at the moment, because she is getting her kitchen redone in her new flat, and she is refusing to install a dishwasher – as a way of preventing them from popping in for meals. “I don’t want you coming over and eating my food,” she says. She has described herself as a “sociable misanthrope” in previous interviews. As much as she loves her friends, she is not that fond of cooking and cleaning for them. I tell her I like going to other people’s homes and letting them cook for me, and then leaving without doing any washing up at all. “I bet you do!” she says. “It’s horrible for the other person – get out of my house!”So who does she cook for? “Myself!” she says, looking me right in the eye – and for the first time there is a kind of challenge in her voice. She doesn’t like to talk about any romantic partners.She lives alone in a flat she recently bought in London. What does she cook for herself? “It’s so boring, but I’ve been working so hard for the last five years that all my food is comfort food and I try to make it as healthy as possible,” she says. She makes a lot of bone broth and a lot of ramen. “Also, I like white bread toasted till it’s nearly black, with Kerrygold butter” – but the butter has to be sliced extremely thickly, she specifies. It has to be “sliced like cheese”.We’re nearly out of time – and Dair y Milk. McSweeney has been hospitably breaking off slabs of chocolate and handing them to me every few minutes for the last half hour, so I can keep making Guinness-crisp soup in my mouth. I’ve got time for just one final question, so I ask McSweeney what she is looking forward to. “I’ve got my first day off for 26 days tomorrow,” she says, “but I’ve got nothing in the fridge.” She plans to go to a bakery round the corner and buy some freshly made soda bread. Ironically, after all that teenage rebellion, she likes it now. Would her mother be pleased to look down on her doing that? “Yes,” she says. “And I’m going to buy it with the money I earned being a clown.”The new series of Comfort Eating, hosted by Siobhán McSweeney, launches on 11 November.Explore more on these topicsSiobhán McSweeneyFoodThe Great Pottery Throw DownThe TraitorsThe Great British Bake OffDerry GirlsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Our third date was at Buckingham Palace’: Marlon James and Nicholas Boggs on life as a literary power couple | Books | The Guardian
description: Shortlisted for the Booker and Baillie Gifford prizes respectively, the novelist and biographer talk about working and living together – and giving a voice to Black queer history
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Shortlisted for the Booker and Baillie Gifford prizes respectively, the novelist and biographer talk about working and living together – and giving a voice to Black queer history
Content: Marlon James, left, and Nicholas Boggs.Photograph: Maria Spann/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMarlon James, left, and Nicholas Boggs.Photograph: Maria Spann/The GuardianBooksInterview‘Our third date was at Buckingham Palace’: Marlon James and Nicholas Boggs on life as a literary power coupleEmma LoffhagenShortlisted for the Booker and Baillie Gifford prizes respectively, the novelist and biographer talk about working and living together – and giving a voice to Black queer historySat 24 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 14.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe literary power couple is a historically seductive concept. Two writers sharing a life, their private and creative worlds entwined, each becoming witness to and critic of the other’s work. Think Simone de Beauvoir and Jean-Paul Sartre, Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne. Or, less auspiciously, Sylvia Plath and Ted Hughes.Now, into this illustrious company steps a new pair: the novelist Marlon James and the biographer Nicholas Boggs, whose books have each been shortlisted for one of Britain’s most prestigious literary awards – James for the Booker prize and Boggs for theBaillie Gifford prize for nonfiction. Between them, they have produced two formidable books, each the culmination of years of work, and each concerned with the lives of Black queer men whose stories have often been overlooked.“I’m not sure what to do with it,” James says, when I ask how they feel about the inevitable impending “literary power couple” label. “I have all these romantic notions that we were like Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne or something – I don’t know. What do you think?” He turns to Boggs, who laughs. “It’s all very new,” he says. “We’re still getting used to it.”It is a warm October morning in Williamsburg, the fashionable writerly enclave in Brooklyn, and I am sitting across from the pair at their apartment. They are relaxing on a chaise longue, looking comfortable enough to have been there all morning. Their exchanges have the easy rhythm of a long relationship, full of small corrections and private jokes.James, the 55-year-old Jamaican-born novelist whose 2015 bookA Brief History of Seven Killingswon the Booker prize, is back on the shortlist this year withThe Disappearers, a sprawling, dark reckoning with the brutality of Aids-era gay life and homophobia in Jamaica. Boggs, his 53-year-old partner of nearly nine years, has been shortlisted for the Baillie Gifford prize for his first book,Baldwin: A Love Story, a biography of James Baldwin that draws on two decades of research into the writer’s intimate life and creative relationships.“The Baillie Gifford’s a prize I know well,” James says. “So when Nick was on the shortlist, I knew what a big deal it was.” Boggs remembers James’s reaction when the nonfiction shortlist was announced on 1 October. “His eyes got very wide. I don’t think I’ve seen his eyes get quite that wide before.”James had the first taste of the excitement, when the Booker shortlist was announced in September. “You got shortlisted first, so the pressure was on!” Boggs jokes. “No matter how many times you do this, it’s always a great surprise,” James adds.View image in fullscreenBoggs and James at home in Brooklyn, New York.Photograph: Maria Spann/The GuardianThe pair have been together since 2018 and have lived in this apartment for a little under a year. Its walls form something of a shrine to their work and interests, crowded with art by African American and queer artists, from intimate, often erotic photography to paintings. At one point they rummage beneath the bed to retrieve an original 1938 painting by Beauford Delaney, the Harlem renaissance artist who became one of Baldwin’s mentors, and features heavily in Boggs’s book. A monumental horse sculpture dominates the room – or, as Boggs points out with a laugh, “it’s really just the horse’s ass, isn’t it!” Bought by James after his 2015 Booker win and christened “Booker” by Boggs, it stands alongside a similarly imposing gorilla.Their romance began not in a rarefied literary salon, but through the very ordinary business of a dating app. “I was on the apps and was like, well, I’m only dating in my neighbourhood,” Boggs says. “He was three blocks away, so it was perfect.”double quotation markMarlon has an incredible work ethic – we’re not screaming from the other room or complaining at dinnerBy then, they were both in their 40s. Boggs, who had never been out with a writer before – “it was mostly bartenders”, he jokes – knew of James’s work, but hadn’t read any of his books.
