James, for his part, didn’t know Boggs was a writer prior to their first meeting.“It was a very chaste first date,” James says, with a twinkle in his eye. “We were gentlemen.” The relationship developed “healthily slowly” over a summer spent apart while Boggs was teaching in London, until they reunited when James invited Boggs to a Booker anniversary event in the capital. He was keen to set the bar high.“Our third date was at Buckingham Palace,” James says, with a faux shrug. “I try to keep it classy, you know, gotta impress him. We actually made out in the queen’s bathroom.”Their relationship may have brought them into the same orbit, but the worlds they each came from – and the experiences that inform their writing – are markedly different.Growing up in Washington DC, where his father was a civil rights attorney, Boggs read Baldwin from a young age. While studying the writer at college, he came across a reference in a 1994 biography to an out-of-print children’s book by Baldwin, illustrated by a French artist, Yoran Cazac. Boggs had suspicions that there was a love affair behind the collaboration, tried to track down Cazac, but was told he was most likely dead. A few weeks later, the phone rang.“It was Yoran saying, ‘I’m alive, I’m in Paris, come on over, I have many stories to tell you about Jimmy,’” Boggs recalls. “That was 23 years ago, and it began a realisation that there were these untold stories in Baldwin’s life that needed to be unearthed.”For James, rampant homophobia shaped his upbringing and his storytelling. Growing up gay and closeted in 1980s Kingston, in the classroom he was “the school homo”; at church, he tried to become straight. He only began to build a more comfortable queer identity after moving to Minneapolis to teach in 2007, away from the scrutiny of family and friends in Jamaica. Unlike Boggs, his queer literary education came late. He picked up Baldwin’s Giovanni’s Room for the first time when he was 50. “The first thing I thought was I could never have read this at 20,” he says. “I was so in the closet.”Across his fiction, James has repeatedly excavated Jamaica’s histories of violence and political upheaval, from his debut 2005 novel John Crow’s Devil (famously rejected 78 times by publishers), to the gang warfare and state corruption of A Brief History of Seven Killings, which made him the first Jamaican to win theBooker prize. The Disappearers, his sixth novel, grew out of a rumoured homophobic attack in a middle-class area of Kingston in the late 1980s.“I first heard about it when I was 21,” he says. “I knew it happened, I just couldn’t prove it. It haunted me: the idea that that could happen – and in a posh neighbourhood – was one of the things that certainly pushed me firmly into the closet.”He was unable to establish exactly what had happened until he began researching the novel, interviewing almost 20 people in Jamaica who helped him piece together the incident over several years. “I wanted to fill in the blanks,” he says. “I wanted to give those guys back some sort of agency and power.”In different ways, both men are trying to recover Black queer histories that have been marginalised or lost. “We both respond to gaps,” Boggs says.For James, one such gap became the starting point for The Disappearers. He wanted to build his novel around the production of a play, but couldn’t find one that would fit. The solution came, serendipitously, from Boggs: while researching his biography, he discovered Baldwin directed a 1969 production of John Herbert’s Fortune and Men’s Eyes in Turkey. He suggested James consider it for his novel.“At first you were like, ‘no’,” Boggs recalls. “And I was like, ‘just read these 60 pages’. And I was right.”It is no exaggeration to say that the play serves as the novel’s structural and emotional scaffolding, and is central to Boggs’s chapters on Baldwin’s life in Turkey, too. “I like to say I plundered his book with his permission,” James says, smiling. “It’s one way in which our books wouldn’t be possible or wouldn’t have ended up the way they did were we not together.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenOn a table in the couple’s living room there sits a 25 September edition of the New York Times. It contains a review now infamous in the literary world, in which the notoriously harsh critic Dwight Garner devoted an almostnovella-length appraisalto The Disappearers, hailing it as “a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century”, placing it alongside the work of Salman Rushdie, Toni Morrison and William Faulkner.“I still don’t quite believe it,” James says. The morning the piece came out, an author friend had emailed to alert him to what he described as a “stonking review” from Garner. “I didn’t know what stonking meant, I thought it was something bad!” he laughs. “So I’m like, ‘God, no. I’m not going to read this.’” But he clicked the link anyway, and saw the word “masterpiece”.“I went to the newsstand to go find it, because I still didn’t believe it,” he says. “I was like, ‘if I leave this bed, I’m going to wake up.’”He is wary of the idea that acclaim should ever become an expectation, or success a fait accompli. “There’s a part of me that still thinks I’m this underground, scrapping writer who got lucky,” he says. “For me, it’s still a genuine surprise. It still catches me off guard. I don’t know if I want to get to that point where I start to expect good reviews. I don’t know if I want that level of entitlement.” He laughs. “I know some writers who are like that – I’m not going to name any names,” he adds, with a mischievous look.Joan Didion once described her collaboration with John Gregory Dunne as a process of creative osmosis: “One of us writes the first draft, and the other functions as really kind of a super-editor and writes the second draft. In the end, you can’t really tell who has done what.”View image in fullscreenJames receives the Man Booker prize for fiction in 2015.Photograph: Neil Hall/ReutersThere is no such blurring of authorship in the James-Boggs household. The pair keep their manuscripts to themselves until the work is finished, even as they discuss the ideas and research behind it.“People are always surprised to hear that,” Boggs says. “Marlon didn’t read my book until after it was finished, I finished his on the publication date.”Their working habits are almost opposite, too. Boggs describes himself as a binge writer, while James writes every day and keeps regular hours. James needs music – “lots of free jazz” – while Boggs requires “perfect peace and quiet”. They work on opposite sides of the house, and Boggs also has a separate office a few blocks away. But living with James has helped Boggs reconsider his idea of what writing should feel like.“Marlon has an incredible work ethic, and it was really a reminder that this is a job,” he says. “That was really helpful. It’s not screaming from the other room in frustration, or complaining about it at dinner every night.”They insist there is no competition between them. “I think I really worried about that when we first met,” Boggs says. “But we write so differently, even stylistically. And because of the time that we’re living in, getting these stories told is so much more important than any individual anyway.”Just this month, new research from PEN America found that the US saw almost 12,000 book bans in public schools during the 2025-2026 school year, the highest number in a single year. For James and Boggs, whose work is concerned with recovering the lives and histories that have been overlooked or suppressed, the stakes are difficult to ignore.James refuses to censor himself in anticipation of a backlash, but he is not oblivious to the risks. “I do sometimes get this fear that the oppressors are coming, because they always burn the books first,” he says. “The forces stacked against me are immense. But then, when have the forces against us not been immense?”I ask if they have thought about leaving the US altogether. “Yes, 100%,” James says, without skipping a beat. He is uncompromising in his diagnosis of the country’s downward slide. “For me, it’s weird seeing America become the type of country America has spent the past 60 years creating everywhere else. I think we’re becoming a banana republic, which, coming from the Caribbean, I know a lot about.”He is not, however, a pessimist. “I have to have a pretty big sense of optimism to think that my big-ass books are going to sell,” he says. “Throughout all of this, I’ve never lost faith in the reader. Writing has always been an art form that had to struggle against oppression, that speaks truth to power. If you decide to be a writer, part of it is to say that you’re going to take this on.”For all their independence on the page, Boggs and James are now embarking on a creative collaboration. Baldwin: A Love Story has been optioned for film by Anonymous Content. Higher Ground (Barack and Michelle Obama’s production company) will be co-producing. Boggs knew immediately with whom he wanted to write the screenplay: James, who has experience writing for the screen, including the television series Get Millie Black. Anonymous Content hired them to write the screenplay together.So far, the process has been seamless. “I think even we are surprised how smooth it’s going,” Boggs says, laughing. “But we’re just so interested in each other’s work and interested in how one another thinks.”I ask how it feels to be adding to the queer literary canon, in their shared and solo endeavours. They look at each other for a moment before Boggs responds. “Just to be alive is wonderful,” he says. “Something that Marlon and I both share is that when you grow up in the shadow of Aids, you don’t necessarily think that you have a future.”“We lost so many great artists, gay artists,” Boggs adds. “So there’s a certain kind of responsibility to telling those stories. There are so many that still need to be told.”Explore more on these topicsBooksMarlon JamesFictionBooker prizeBaillie Gifford prize for nonfictionBiography booksAwards and prizesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Stone Roses showed me the power of being an introvert | Culture | The Guardian
description: At boarding school in the early 90s, quietness was seen as weakness. But then I saw the band’s guitarist John Squire making a vast noise while hiding behind a fringe – and learned the strength of understatement
Author: Henry Yates
Headline: At boarding school in the early 90s, quietness was seen as weakness. But then I saw the band’s guitarist John Squire making a vast noise while hiding behind a fringe – and learned the strength of understatement
Content: ‘I assumed Squire must be an extrovert axe hero: foot on the monitor, diamante codpiece, the works.’Illustration: Martin O’NeillView image in fullscreen‘I assumed Squire must be an extrovert axe hero: foot on the monitor, diamante codpiece, the works.’Illustration: Martin O’NeillMy cultural awakeningCultureThe Stone Roses showed me the power of being an introvertAt boarding school in the early 90s, quietness was seen as weakness. But then I saw the band’s guitarist John Squire making a vast noise while hiding behind a fringe – and learned the strength of understatementHenry YatesSat 24 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn September 1991, I had just been thrown into the meat-grinder of a Midlands boarding school. In this bear pit, there were predators and there was prey. You were either the swaggering rugby alpha, whipping a wet towel at pale bodies in the eight-boy dormitory; or the homesick ghost, keeping your guard up, endlessly braced for your toilet cubicle to be kicked open or your washbag chucked off the fire escape.My mind had always been loud, racing with opinions, stories, jokes. But by the time I adequately considered a thought, the conversation had raced on without me. Suddenly, under 24/7 social scrutiny in a world where bullhorn confidence is king, I felt dismissed.Up to that point, music hadn’t helped. Every rock star I had ever seen – Elton John, Freddie Mercury, Mick Jagger – was a showboating peacock, all hips, handclaps and absurd glasses, seeming to whisper in my ear: “This isn’t for you, bookworm.” But that September, I stumbled across the Stone Roses’ self-titled 1989 debut album. I must have seen John Squire’s genius before I heard it, on his paint-splashed, lemon-drizzled sleeve art.Hearing his cascading, iridescent guitar solos, I assumed Squire must be an extrovert axe hero: foot on the monitor, diamante codpiece, the works. But there he was on the CD inlay: pipecleaner-skinny, dressed in Manchester streetwear and inscrutable beneath a bird’s-nest fringe (until the mid-90s, I genuinely wasn’t sure if Squire had eyes), slinging a Gretsch Country Gentleman guitar but not treating it like a penis extension.Years before YouTube, it wasn’t easy to find out more. But when I dug up back issues of NME, I went from fan to disciple. A sometime model-maker who once worked on The Wind in the Willows – but also a child of 70s punk – Squire was enigmatic and otherworldly, softly spoken yet intense as a laser-cutter. Asked by one interviewer what the Roses were all about, his answer was the perfect collision of sky-scraping ambition and bone-dry Britishness: “Love and hate. War and peace. Morecambe and Wise …”In those formative weeks, for the first time, I realised that “quiet” could also mean charismatic, insolent, snarky, simmering with latent attitude and temperamentally suited for a life in the arts. Through Squire, I discovered painting (Jackson Pollock’s “drip and splash” influence was all over his sleeves and guitars), modern history (the Paris riots of May 68 referenced on Bye Bye Badman), fashion and even religion (you only had to read his lyric to 1994’s Love Spreads, a take on the Passion, with Jesus imagined as a Black woman, to sense the iconoclast claws below the still waters).Hearing the Roses at school, meanwhile, was my ticket into a secret society of indie kids that I hadn’t known existed, all swapping albums, making mixtapes, easy in each other’s company, building each other’s confidence. I picked up the guitar that same year, too, went on to write about it for the music press – and now play so loud in my own band that I can drown out a thousand braying show-offs.Squire doesn’t do many interviews, and when I drove to his Cheshire farmhouse for Guitarist Magazine, I was worried he wouldn’t actually speak. But perhaps he recognised a kindred spirit. Over an hour’s encounter in his studio, the musician who had meant so much to me proved thoughtful, witty and profound, signed the schoolboy-era guitar I’d flecked Pollock-style with paint, and even gave me a parting hug.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJohn Squire didn’t change me; he stopped me fighting myself. Under his influence, I stopped trying to turn up the volume, accepted being an introvert and held him in mind whenever anyone equated quietness with dullness. Fast-forward 35 years – to a time when influencers squeal and preen, flogging every last grain of themselves to the attention economy – and the Roses guitarist seems a few degrees cooler for existing on his own terms, leaving something to the imagination, and treating Jonathan Ross withchilly disdain. Perhaps we could all stand to be a little more Squire?Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: A Course Called Ireland: Bill Murray clearly hated making his new golfing show – but it’s extremely fun to binge | Bill Murray | The Guardian
description: In his rogue new travelogue, the Hollywood star tees off, has drunken pub singalongs – but mostly just proves how tired he is of fame
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: In his rogue new travelogue, the Hollywood star tees off, has drunken pub singalongs – but mostly just proves how tired he is of fame
Content: Driven … Bill Murray and Joanne McNally in A Course Called Ireland.Photograph: BBC/Stellify MediaView image in fullscreenDriven … Bill Murray and Joanne McNally in A Course Called Ireland.Photograph: BBC/Stellify MediaThe watcherBill MurrayA Course Called Ireland: Bill Murray clearly hated making his new golfing show – but it’s extremely fun to bingeIn his rogue new travelogue, the Hollywood star tees off, has drunken pub singalongs – but mostly just proves how tired he is of fameRhik SamadderSat 24 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m suspicious of travelogues, which often feature celebrities in contrived situations, serving up a sentimental postcard of a place that is tantamount to a lie. I also hate how famous people are inexorably drawn to golf: a boring game historically predicated on a rancid mix of social exclusivity and extensive land ownership. So it was perverse of me to watch a show in which author Tom Coyne drives around Ireland playing various courses with his friend, actorBill Murray. It’s the perfect intersection of none of my interests.I was, however, hooked by a strange promise in A Course Called Ireland’s introductory sequence. “This is not a show about golf,” it says. “It’s not even a show about Bill Murray.” This was immediately followed by a scene in which an Irish woman standing by the roadside misidentified the actor as Bill Cosby. OK, I thought. What are they teeing up here?There’s a hole in at least one of those promises. A Course Called Ireland (Sunday 25 October, 9.30pm, BBC Two) is intended to be a jocular road trip, in which the two friends meet colourful characters and reflect on their own Irish heritage, between spectacular rounds on the rugged links. It’s based on a journey Coyne documented in his book of the same name, in which he played every course in the country. Which again, sounds like a marriage in crisis to me – but the book is very popular.What we get is a fascinating, existential snapshot of fame. A camera crew trailing a Hollywood legend around a series of Irish villages is, unavoidably, the story. Murray can’t stop for a wee without being mobbed. The director wants as much Murray on screen as possible. The 76-year-old Ghostbuster wants to give the spotlight to anyone else who’ll take it. The wheels quickly start to come off. He rips up the itinerary, digs in his heels, grouches. He cringes at the artifice of making TV, such as pretending to meet people for the first time. He’s been famous for 50 years – and it shows.He also embodies the paradox of the reluctant celebrity, which is that most of them can’t stop doing things that perpetuate their myth. They hate the fame, they need the fame. The oddball actor is known for giving regular people “a Bill Murray story”, crashing graduation ceremonies or stepping behind the bar to pull pints. We see that here, as he hoists a groomsman on his shoulders, or gently pushes an ice-cream in a woman’s face. As he jokes, “If I wasn’t famous, I’d probably have a few more cuts and bruises to the face.”In one sequence, Murray refuses to attend a pub as scripted, and disappears to a nearby evening of folk music instead. Later, once filming has been aborted, he returns to the pub to lead the room in a drunken singalong. It’s exactly what the producers would have wanted; for Murray, such larks only have meaning if they aren’t being manufactured for the cameras. There is something heroic in his stubbornness. (Of course, someone films the whole thing on their mobile phone.)The show bends many of the format rules, by necessity or design. The BTS feeling of a crew working around a recalcitrant star is juicy. Each episode also boasts a voiceover from a supporting character – the proprietor of a tweed shop, a junior runner, Ireland’s former minister of the arts. The best is Margaret, an elderly woman outside a sweet shop who tells Murray he was the best thing in “Gorseboosters”. “Bill is 98% Irish if you look at his DNA, which I haven’t, but it says so here in the script,” she lilts. These unexpected and charming turns ground a show that otherwise feels like Lost in La Mancha set in Ballybunion.If the show fails by its own marker, it succeeds at being funny, peculiar and melancholy: a much higher bar. It’s as unconventional and highly watchable as its impish star, the one it pretends not to be hopelessly in thrall to. What’s more, I finally understand why celebrities love golf so much. They want to be as far away from other people as possible.Explore more on these topicsBill MurrayThe watcherTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dónal Lunny, ‘colossus of Irish music’, dies aged 79 | Folk music | The Guardian
description: Founding member of Planxty, Lunny went on to play for bands such as Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Founding member of Planxty, Lunny went on to play for bands such as Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin
Content: Dónal Lunny performing on stage at the Manchester Apollo in April 1999.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDónal Lunny performing on stage at the Manchester Apollo in April 1999.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianFolk musicDónal Lunny, ‘colossus of Irish music’, dies aged 79Founding member of Planxty, Lunny went on to play for bands such as Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and CoolfinPress AssociationSat 24 Oct 2026 04.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 05.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Irish traditional musician Dónal Lunny has died at the age of 79 from cancer.Lunny rose to prominence in the trio Rakes of Kildare alongside his brother Frank and Christy Moore. He went on to play in bands such asPlanxty,Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin among others and toured the world.A post on his Facebook page confirmed that Lunny died in St James’s hospital in Dublin on Friday morning.“We are heartbroken to confirm that our beloved Dónal passed away peacefully this morning in Dublin following a short stay in St James’s hospital,” the post said. “Thank you for helping us to remember and celebrate his immense contribution to music, to culture and to so many people’s lives all over the world.”View image in fullscreenCatherine Connolly said Lunny was ‘central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music’.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAThe Irish president, Catherine Connolly, expressed her “deepest condolences to the family, friends and many musical collaborators of Dónal Lunny”.In a statement, she said: “Dónal was one of Ireland’s greatest musical figures, a wonderfully talented musician and producer who was central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music.“Dónal will be particularly remembered for his long partnerships with fellow musicians such as Christy Moore and Andy Irvine and for the innovative music he has left behind both as a musician in groups including Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts and also as a renowned producer.“This rich musical legacy, including his central role in the introduction of the bouzouki into Irish music, was appropriately recognised by his fellow artists in Dónal’s membership of Aosdána, as well as the well-deserved recognition which he received in being awarded a lifetime achievement award at the 2025 RTÉ Radio 1 Irish folk awards.“Beyond his music, Dónal will be remembered for his warmth and the strong connection which he had with audiences all over Ireland and beyond. He will be deeply missed.”The post ended in Irish, saying his likes will not be seen again: “Ní bheidh a leithéid arís ann.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Irish folk group Planxty in London in January 1973. From left: Andy Irvine, Liam O’Flynn, Dónal Lunny and Christy Moore.Photograph: Michael Putland/GettyLunny was born in Tullamore, County Offaly, and was a multi-instrumentalist but was best known for his mastery of the bouzouki. He was a talented melody writer and considered central to the revival of traditional music as he produced 17 albums under his record label Mulligan Records.The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he was “deeply saddened” to hear of Lunny’s death. “A colossus of Irish music, as a performer, songwriter and producer,” he wrote in a post on social media.“Uniquely gifted, Dónal carried traditional and folk music to new audiences through Planxty and his many other endeavours.”Sinn Féin’s president, Mary Lou McDonald, also paid tribute online, saying: “Deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Dónal Lunny. A giant of Irish traditional music, Dónal helped shape the sound of Irish music for generations, bringing our rich musical heritage to audiences at home and around the world. His contribution to Irish music and culture will never be forgotten.“Ar dheis Dé go raibh a anam[May his soul rest in peace].”Explore more on these topicsFolk musicIrelandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Channel 4’s new social media drama has 90-second episodes – and it’s as enjoyable as watching adverts | Drama | The Guardian
description: Vertical dramas are a global phenomenon made in bite-sized addictive chunks to watch on phones. But Channel 4 has made a slow-release syrupy tale in five parts – without tension or actual drama
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Vertical dramas are a global phenomenon made in bite-sized addictive chunks to watch on phones. But Channel 4 has made a slow-release syrupy tale in five parts – without tension or actual drama
Content: Party people … the cast of the Guest List, Channel 4’s short-form phone drama.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenParty people … the cast of the Guest List, Channel 4’s short-form phone drama.Photograph: Channel 4DramaChannel 4’s new social media drama has 90-second episodes – and it’s as enjoyable as watching advertsVertical dramas are a global phenomenon made in bite-sized addictive chunks to watch on phones. But Channel 4 has made a slow-release syrupy tale in five parts – without tension or actual dramaHannah J DaviesSat 24 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVertical dramas – that is, short-form content made specifically for phones – are big business in 2026. They are particularly popular in countries such as China and India, and the global market is expected to be worth $26bn by 2030. It makes sense: much has been made of the double-screening epidemic, and of people scrolling so much thatNetflix has to remind them what is going on on their TV screensevery few seconds. Why not just cut out the middleman and ditch the telly bit altogether?Enter Channel 4, which has released its first vertical drama on social media in the UK. It’s described as “a bold, character-led series” that explores “the friendship, ambition and lives of a diverse group of intelligent young women”. The Guest List is made in partnership with the skincare brand Sol de Janeiro, and episodes are around 90 seconds to two minutes in length. The microdramas that have gripped Asia are camp and cliffhanger-heavy – one producer described them as“soap operas on cocaine”. The Guest List is less cocaine, more Coke Zero: sweet, syrupy, probably not bad for you but not especially good either. Anodyne. Sort of like watching the adverts before a YouTube video, instead of pressing the skip button at your earliest convenience.Part of the issue might be that many of these bite-size dramas release all their episodes at once, and viewers could watch 100 instalments in a day (if that sounds a lot, consider that a TikTok or Instagram user could devour many hundreds of shortform reels in 24 hours). Channel 4, however, is airing just one episode per week. If the idea is to get viewers addicted, surely 90 seconds every seven days will not cut it. Besides, I’m three episodes in and I barely know who is who. Will it be a month before I find out? There are also a mere five episodes in total; while this is the broadcaster’s first foray into the format, it does feel rather slight.That is not to say it isn’t fun. Episode one follows Amaka (Jadesola Odunjo) who – according to the publicity bumf – is “a PR guru who is bold, energetic and impossible to ignore – just like [the Sol de Janeiro perfume] Intense Mist Cheirosa 62”. It opens with her inviting friends to an exclusive boat party on the Thames ... only to have her phone snatched by a thief. She commands a passing rickshaw driver “Follow that bike!”, as she mourns the loss of “every client, every influencer, my press contact … my bank card”. (Could our reliance on our phones perhaps be bad?! Very meta). With barely 30 seconds to go and Amaka now arguing with the rickshaw driver who has realised he won’t get paid, I am hooked. Nothing else really happens, truth be told, but itcouldhave. There is youth. There is possibility. There is excellent eyeshadow. There is a woman telling Amaka that the Thames is now a 45-minute walk away.Next week’s episode finds finance intern Bella (Felicity Ali) on a work call, being patronised by her boss. She messages her mates: she won’t have time to go home and get changed before the boat party. A text pings from one of them: “ambition is your dress code”. Yes, girlboss! She fashions a dress out of a blazer, and uses her tie as a belt. (Carrie Bradshaw, eat your heart out.) Meanwhile, the episode due for release on 4 November is perhaps the most relatable for me – Mika (Mia Ito Smith) racing to collect her parcel from the corner shop then squatting in an aisle so her neighbour doesn’t see her in her sweatpants.I’m quite intrigued to find out whether the girls make it to that party, but the thought of waiting weeks to find out is the antithesis of what vertical dramas are all about. Releasing the episodes so far apart – refusing to hijack our eyeballs, glue us to our phones and make us cancel all social plans for the foreseeable future – just isn’t the microdrama way. UntilChannel 4is willing to give us the entire Guest List cinematic universe, this feels more like a gen Z Boots ad than the future of British television.The Guest List is released on 24 October on TikTok, Meta and YouTube.Explore more on these topicsDramaTelevisionChannel 4Television industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a starry celebration of the great Amy Winehouse | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Corinne Bailey Rae and Jorja Smith are among the performers at a Back to Black tribute show. Plus, Cynthia Erivo completes SNL UK’s excellent second run. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Corinne Bailey Rae and Jorja Smith are among the performers at a Back to Black tribute show. Plus, Cynthia Erivo completes SNL UK’s excellent second run. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Corinne Bailey Rae performs at Back to Black at 20.Photograph: Samir Hussein – Universal Music Recordings/Samir Hussein – Universal Music Recordings / The Amy Winehouse EstateView image in fullscreenCorinne Bailey Rae performs at Back to Black at 20.Photograph: Samir Hussein – Universal Music Recordings/Samir Hussein – Universal Music Recordings / The Amy Winehouse EstateTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a starry celebration of the great Amy WinehouseCorinne Bailey Rae and Jorja Smith are among the performers at a Back to Black tribute show. Plus, Cynthia Erivo completes SNL UK’s excellent second run. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Graeme Virtue,Jack Seale,Priya ElanandEllen E JonesSat 24 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmy Winehouse: Back to Black at 209.35pm, BBC TwoA fitting tribute to the late star’s breakout album 20 years after its release, this special concert was held at the Roundhouse in north London earlier this week. It’s led by a team close to Winehouse’s music, including the album’s producers Mark Ronson and Salaam Remi, and features the Amy Winehouse Band playing all the hits including Valerie and Rehab. Special guests include Corinne Bailey Rae, Flo, Jessie Reyez and Jorja Smith.Hollie RichardsonStrictly Come Dancing6.30pm, BBC OneWe’ve already had a few themed weeks in this year’s competition, but now it’s back to basics. Lacey and Vito will be doing the tango to a Blondie banger; Cach and Maddie will take on a cha cha to Måneskin; and it’s time to jive with Lawrence and Jowita.HRSecrets of the Viking Ship With Bettany Hughes8pm, Channel 4In 2008, the remains of a boatload of Vikings were discovered on an Estonian island. With typically infectious enthusiasm, historian Hughes embarks on a Euro-hopping trip to explain how this bonanza of physical objects and genetic material has cast new light on the Old Norse era.Graeme VirtueDark Winds9pm, U&AlibiThe hunt for a missing girl intensifies as the 1970s Navajo police respond to a spectacular shootout in a roadside diner. The cops begin a tracking operation, unaware that the two sides in the fight are, respectively, lethal and desperate. It’s the usual atmospheric mix of infinite dusty vistas and witnesses who all seem to hold a dark secret.Jack SealeMarble Hall Murders9.20pm, BBC One“A $200m deal with Netflix or the death of a sick, elderly woman 20 years ago. Which matters more?” asks Jonathan (Rupert Penry-Jones) in the penultimate episode. After last week’s shocking death, tensions in the Crace family are running high, while our heroine Susan (Lesley Manville) has found herself being investigated for the murder.Priya ElanSaturday Night Live UK10pm, Sky OneFans of her memeable lines from Chewing Gum will be cheering on Cynthia Erivo’s return to comedy as guest host in the final episode of this run. Obviously, we’d all like sketches based on the Wicked press tour too, thanks. Indie boys Blossoms provide the music.PEFilm choiceThe Seventh Seal (Ingmar Bergman, 1957), 9.30pm, BBC FourThe scene where the knight (Max von Sydow) plays chess with Death (Bengt Ekerot) is among the most recognisable in the history of cinema, and endlessly parodied by the less cultured likes of Bill & Ted’s Bogus Journey and The Muppets. But that shouldn’t eclipse the rest of Ingmar Bergman’s 1957 classic, worth seeing in full for its allegorical depiction of plague-ravaged medieval Europe, the austere black and white cinematography of Gunnar Fischer, and a climatic rendering of the Danse Macabre, performed before slowly dissolving dark clouds.Ellen E JonesCat Person (Susanna Fogel, 2023), 11.40pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenIs it love – or a horror show? … Emilia Jones and Nicholas Braun in Cat Person.Photograph: APIs Cat Person a romantic comedy? Or is it a psychological horror? The erratic tone shifts of this 2023 film, adapted from Kristen Roupenian’s viral short story of the same name, are entirely in keeping with its subject matter: what it means to be a single, straight woman and, in the internet parlance, “date your only natural predator”. Emilia Jones stars as Margot, a 20-year-old college student who begins an ambivalent relationship with Robert (Nicholas Braun, AKA Greg from Succession), a harmless if slightly pompous nice-guy lunk. Or is he?EEJLive sportMen’s Rugby League World Cup: England v France, 7.15am, Premier Sports 1Australia v England in the women’s competition follows at 9.45am.Premier League Football: Aston Villa v Man City, 11am, TNT Sports 1Chelsea v Tottenham is at 5pm on Sky Sports Main Event.Women’s Super League: Tottenham v Arsenal, 12.30pm, BBC OneMan United v Man City is on Sun at 5.30pm on Sky One.Gymnastics: World Championships, 1pm, BBC TwoThe apparatus finals in Rotterdam.Prem Rugby Union: Leicester v Northampton, 3pm, TNT Sports 1Bristol v Exeter follows at 5.15pm. title: Jackson Boxer’s vegetarian recipe for brown butter pumpkin soup | Food | The Guardian
description: This easy roast pumpkin soup is rich, nutty, Halloween heaven
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This easy roast pumpkin soup is rich, nutty, Halloween heaven
Content: Jackson Boxer’s brown butter pumpkin soup.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenJackson Boxer’s brown butter pumpkin soup.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.FoodJackson Boxer’s vegetarian recipe for brown butter pumpkin soupThe base of this easy roast pumpkin soup is rich, nutty, Halloween heaven –  you can go wild with the garnishesJackson BoxerSat 24 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlot of my early life in professional kitchens was spent making vegetable purees, which I find rather tiresome, not least because they can often lapse into baby food: creamy, bland and flattened by a cosseting blanket of dairy. With a judicious and considered approach, however, they can also be incredibly vivid, explosive and concentrated expressions of the very essence of the vegetable in question. I love this seasonal (not to mention Halloween-appropriate) soup for its simplicity of approach – essentially, you just roast a beautiful pumpkin with caramelised butter – and the remarkable complexity of its result.Brown butter pumpkin soupWhen browning butter, always bear in mind that it has a high water content, and that the initial seething cook is done to evaporate this – until all the water has cooked out, you won’t get the butter high enough above 100C for the milk solids and sugars to caramelise. That’s why browning butter happens two ways, like Hemingway’s bankruptcy – gradually, then suddenly. And pay close attention, or it will burn and you’ll have to start again.Prep5 minCook1 hrServes4250ml vegetable bouillon(homemade, ideally; seemy recipe last week)1 delica pumpkin(800g), cut in half, deseeded and peeled (I don’t bother peeling it, but cooked pumpkin skin is an acquired taste)250g butter10g flaky sea salt(about 2 tsp)Sherry vinegar, to tasteTo finishCreme fraicheChilli oilToasted pumpkin seedsGround black pepperA squeeze of lemonHeat the oven to 195C (175C fan)/385F/gas 5½. Pour the bouillon into a roasting tray large enough to hold both pumpkin halves, then put them cut side up in the tray.In a frying pan, simmer the butter on a high heat until it stops foaming, then turn down the heat and cook until it’s rich, brown and nutty. Immediately pour the scalding butter evenly into the pumpkin halves, then lay a sheet of greaseproof paper over the top of the pumpkins and tightly cover the whole tray in foil. Bake for 45 minutes, until the tip of a sharp knife meets no resistance and comes out clean.Cut the cooked pumpkin into chunks, put these and the bouillon from the tray in a food processor and blitz to a smooth puree. Add the salt and vinegar, then taste and adjust the seasoning. If the puree is too tight, add more vegetable broth just to loosen – it will depend on the water content of the pumpkin and how airtight the seal was on the foil tray.Transfer the mix to a large saucepan and reheat gently without boiling. Check and adjust for seasoning and acidity, then ladle into bowls – I serve this soup topped with creme fraiche, chilli oil, toasted pumpkin seeds, black pepper and a squeeze of lemon; other nice garnishes might include toasted croutons, fried sage leaves, chilli and garlic butter, and salsa verde, any and all of which would be very fine additions.Jackson Boxer is chef/owner ofBrunswick House,VesperandDove, all in London, and culinary director ofCowley Manornear Cheltenham andthe Henriettain LondonExplore more on these topicsFoodPumpkinHalloweenSoupVegetarian food and drinkVegetablesStarterrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Outrageously good’: the best (and worst) supermarket ready-made custard, tasted and rated | Dessert | The Guardian
description: Which supermarket pots are ambrosial heaven and which are a gummy disaster?
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Which supermarket pots are ambrosial heaven and which are a gummy disaster?
Content: Our tester found it hard to resist drinking some ‘by the pint’.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonView image in fullscreenOur tester found it hard to resist drinking some ‘by the pint’.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterDessertReview‘Outrageously good’: the best (and worst) supermarket ready-made custard, tasted and ratedWhich supermarket pots are ambrosial heaven and which are a gummy disaster?The best supermarket double creamTom HuntSat 24 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was only when I sat down to taste 10 custards that I realised this was a dangerous test to judge on my own. I tried a range of ready-made offerings, from cans to cartons to tubs of fresh custard from the supermarket chiller section, some of which I found hard not to drink by the pint.I analysed each custard for aroma, texture and taste, and awarded extra points for minimal processing and the use of free-range eggs; I deducted points for the inclusion of palm oil, modified maize starches and colourings, all of which are often used to replace the colour, fat and thickening ability of eggs. It was, however, the long-life cartons that most provoked nostalgic memories of bananas and custard as a child.My main take-home is that cans and cartons are great for when you need a quick dessert, but if you want the real thing – a proper crème anglaise made with hot, vanilla-infused cream and milk, egg yolks and sugar – go for the fresh stuff and check the label for additives.The best supermarket fresh custardBest overall:Waitrose No 1 Madagascan vanilla custardView image in fullscreen£2.52 for 500g at Waitrose (50p/100g)★★★★☆An outrageously good, medium-thick, pale cream-coloured custard made with West Country milk and cream. Seductively sweet (11.9% total sugar), and thickened with tapioca starch and free-range eggs.Best bargain:M&S Collection Madagascan vanilla luxury custardView image in fullscreen£3 for 500g at Ocado (60p/100g)★★★★☆A medium-thick, pale cream-coloured custard made with Jersey and Guernsey cows’ milk and British cream. Super-sweet (12.1%), and thickened with tapioca starch, cornflour and free-range eggs.And the rest …Ambrosia deluxe custardView image in fullscreen£2 for 750g at Asda (27p/100g)£3 for 750g at Morrisons (40p/100g)★★★☆☆Very thick, pale yellow and velvety-smooth, but a touch gloopy and lacking in substance. Egg-free, with buttermilk and vanilla extract, thickened with “sustainable” palm oil and modified starches. Contains colours (plain caramel and carotene) and pretty sweet (11.1%), too.Morrisons the Best Madagascan vanilla custardView image in fullscreen£2.95 for 500g at Morrisons (59p/100g)★★★☆☆A thick, pale custard with an even speckling of vanilla.
